prf-8 equivalence testing depends on adb-7 and cmp-6 but should also depend on cmp-1; prf-3 depends on prf-2 which is fine.
exp-5 depends only on exp-1, which is not a genuine dependency; likelihood tests need a modelling background and a prior test concept such as prf-1.
Misconception for adb stage about z vs t is stated as a rule rather than a wrong belief clearly, and exp-7 misconception is fine.

concepts.name: Tokens and context window
concepts.summary: Recall that models read and produce tokens rather than words and that the context window caps the combined input and output size.

concepts.name: Chat message roles
concepts.summary: Explain how system, user and assistant messages structure a conversation request and shape the model's behaviour.

concepts.name: Calling a completion API
concepts.summary: Understand the parts of an API request and response, including model name, messages, API key authentication and the returned text and usage.

concepts.name: Sampling parameters
concepts.summary: Explain how temperature, top-p and max output tokens change the randomness and length of generated output.

concepts.name: Basic prompt clarity
concepts.summary: Understand that specific instructions, context and a stated output format produce more reliable responses than vague requests.

concepts.name: Hallucination and model limits
concepts.summary: Recognise that models can produce confident but false output and lack knowledge of recent or private data.

concepts.name: Cost and latency drivers
concepts.summary: Recall that cost and response time grow with the number of input and output tokens and with model size.

misconceptions.text: The model looks up facts in a database, so its answers are always accurate.
Tokens are the same as words, so word count gives exact cost and limits.
The model remembers earlier API calls on its own without being sent the conversation again.

concepts.name: Few-shot prompting
concepts.summary: Apply worked input-output examples in a prompt to steer format, tone and task behaviour.

concepts.name: Prompt templates with variables
concepts.summary: Build reusable prompts that insert user data into fixed instructions in code.

concepts.name: JSON output parsing
concepts.summary: Request JSON output, parse it in Python and validate it against a schema such as a Pydantic model.

concepts.name: Streaming responses
concepts.summary: Consume partial output as it is generated to improve perceived latency in an application.

concepts.name: API error and rate-limit handling
concepts.summary: Handle timeouts, rate limits and server errors with retries, exponential backoff and clear failures.

concepts.name: Multi-turn conversation state
concepts.summary: Maintain and trim the message history sent on each call so conversations stay coherent within the context window.

concepts.name: Secret and key management
concepts.summary: Keep API keys out of source code and client-side code by using environment variables or a secrets store.

misconceptions.text: Asking for JSON in the prompt guarantees the output is always valid and matches the schema.
Retrying immediately and repeatedly is the right way to handle rate limit errors.
Few-shot examples teach the model permanently, so they only need to be sent once.

concepts.name: Embeddings and semantic similarity
concepts.summary: Use embedding vectors and a similarity measure to find text with related meaning.

concepts.name: Document chunking strategies
concepts.summary: Analyse how chunk size, overlap and boundaries affect retrieval quality and choose a splitting approach for a corpus.

concepts.name: Retrieval-augmented generation pipeline
concepts.summary: Assemble ingestion, indexing, retrieval and grounded generation, and trace failures to the right stage.

concepts.name: Vector store indexing and search
concepts.summary: Store embeddings with metadata and query for top-k neighbours with filters.

concepts.name: Tool calling and function schemas
concepts.summary: Define tool schemas, execute the calls the model requests and return results for the final answer.

concepts.name: Grounding and citation prompts
concepts.summary: Design prompts that restrict answers to retrieved context, cite sources and admit when information is missing.

concepts.name: Evaluation datasets and metrics
concepts.summary: Build a labelled test set and choose metrics such as exact match, retrieval recall and rubric scores to compare prompt changes.

concepts.name: Prompt injection risks
concepts.summary: Analyse how untrusted user or retrieved text can override instructions and apply basic mitigations.

misconceptions.text: Larger chunks always improve RAG because they give the model more context.
The model executes the functions itself when it makes a tool call.
Telling the model to use only the provided context completely eliminates hallucination.

concepts.name: Hybrid search and reranking
concepts.summary: Combine keyword and vector retrieval and rerank candidates, judging the precision and latency trade-offs.

concepts.name: Query rewriting and decomposition
concepts.summary: Transform conversational or complex questions into effective retrieval queries.

concepts.name: Component-level RAG evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate retrieval (recall, MRR) and generation (faithfulness, relevance) separately to locate defects.

concepts.name: LLM-as-judge evaluation
concepts.summary: Judge when model-based graders are valid by calibrating them against human labels and controlling for bias.

concepts.name: Agent loops and orchestration
concepts.summary: Design loops where the model plans and calls tools across steps, with step limits, state and error recovery.

concepts.name: Caching and cost optimisation
concepts.summary: Evaluate caching, model selection and prompt trimming to reduce cost and latency with acceptable quality.

concepts.name: Observability and tracing
concepts.summary: Instrument calls to capture prompts, outputs, tool steps, latency and cost so failures can be diagnosed.

concepts.name: Guardrails and output validation
concepts.summary: Assess and apply input and output checks, schema validation and fallbacks for safety and reliability.

misconceptions.text: Vector search alone is always enough, so keyword search adds nothing.
An LLM judge's scores are objective and need no validation against human judgement.
A good end-to-end answer score shows both retrieval and generation are working.

concepts.name: Architecture trade-off design
aliases: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning or long context best fits a requirement given cost, freshness and accuracy.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning and distillation decisions
concepts.summary: Judge when adapting or distilling a model beats prompting and plan the data and evaluation needed.

concepts.name: Continuous evaluation pipelines
concepts.summary: Create evaluation systems combining offline regression suites, production sampling and user feedback that gate releases.

concepts.name: Multi-agent system design
concepts.summary: Design systems of cooperating agents with defined roles, shared state, permissions and failure containment.

concepts.name: Security threat modelling for LLMs
concepts.summary: Evaluate risks such as indirect prompt injection, excessive tool permissions and data leakage and design layered defences.

concepts.name: Reliability under model change
concepts.summary: Assess the effect of model updates and provider outages and design pinning, fallbacks and migration tests.

concepts.name: Feedback-driven improvement loops
concepts.summary: Create processes that turn production failures and user signals into new test cases, prompt changes and training data.

misconceptions.text: Fine-tuning is the best way to add new knowledge to a model's answers.
More agents with more autonomy always yield better results on complex tasks.
Once prompts pass the evaluation suite, behaviour stays stable across model updates.

concepts.name: Vertices and edges
concepts.summary: Name the parts of a graph and describe a graph as a set of vertices with a set of edges joining pairs of them.

concepts.name: Degree of a vertex
concepts.summary: Compute the degree of each vertex and explain that it counts the edge ends meeting at that vertex.

concepts.name: Directed and undirected edges
concepts.summary: Distinguish edges that can be traversed both ways from arcs with a direction, and draw each kind.

concepts.name: Weighted graphs
concepts.summary: Explain that weights attach numeric costs or distances to edges and read them off a diagram.

concepts.name: Paths and cycles
concepts.summary: Define a path as a sequence of adjacent edges and a cycle as a closed path with no repeated vertices, and identify them in a drawing.

concepts.name: Connectedness
concepts.summary: Decide whether a small graph is connected and identify its connected components.

concepts.name: Handshaking lemma
concepts.summary: State that the sum of degrees equals twice the number of edges and explain why.

misconceptions.text: The way a graph is drawn, including edge lengths and crossings, is part of what the graph is.
A vertex's degree is the number of vertices in the graph.
Edges in a graph always have a direction.

concepts.name: Adjacency matrix representation
concepts.summary: Build the adjacency matrix of a graph and read degrees and edges from it.

concepts.name: Adjacency list representation
concepts.summary: Write an adjacency list for a graph and choose between list and matrix based on graph density.

concepts.name: Breadth-first search
concepts.summary: Trace BFS with a queue on a graph, giving the visiting order and the levels from the start vertex.

concepts.name: Depth-first search
concepts.summary: Trace DFS with a stack or recursion, giving the visiting order and the backtracking steps.

concepts.name: Trees and forests
concepts.summary: Recognise a tree as a connected acyclic graph and use the fact that a tree on n vertices has n-1 edges.

concepts.name: Euler circuits and trails
concepts.summary: Apply the degree conditions to decide whether a connected graph has an Euler circuit or trail and construct one.

concepts.name: Subgraphs and complete graphs
concepts.summary: Identify subgraphs and use the count n(n-1)/2 for the edges of a complete graph.

misconceptions.text: BFS and DFS visit vertices in the same order, so either one can be used for any purpose.
An adjacency matrix is always the better representation because lookup is constant time.
An Euler circuit visits every vertex exactly once.

concepts.name: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm
concepts.summary: Run Dijkstra with a priority queue on a graph with nonnegative weights and recover the shortest path tree.

concepts.name: Minimum spanning trees
concepts.summary: Compute a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal's or Prim's algorithm and justify each edge choice.

concepts.name: Hamilton cycles
concepts.summary: Contrast Hamilton cycles with Euler circuits, use sufficient conditions such as Dirac's theorem, and explain why no simple degree test exists.

concepts.name: Bipartite graphs
concepts.summary: Test bipartiteness through BFS two-colouring or the absence of odd cycles.

concepts.name: Graph coloring basics
concepts.summary: Colour a graph properly, apply greedy colouring, and bound the chromatic number using cliques and maximum degree.

concepts.name: Topological ordering of DAGs
concepts.summary: Order the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so all edges point forward, using DFS finishing times or in-degree removal.

concepts.name: Complexity of graph traversals
concepts.summary: Analyse the running time of BFS, DFS and Dijkstra in terms of vertices and edges under each representation.

misconceptions.text: Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly with negative edge weights as long as there is no negative cycle.
A minimum spanning tree gives the shortest path between every pair of vertices.
A graph with all degrees even is guaranteed to have a Hamilton cycle.

concepts.name: Correctness of greedy graph algorithms
concepts.summary: Evaluate proofs of Prim, Kruskal and Dijkstra using the cut property and invariants about settled vertices.

concepts.name: Planar graphs and Euler's formula
concepts.summary: Use V-E+F=2 to derive edge bounds and show that K5 and K3,3 are nonplanar.

concepts.name: Kuratowski and planarity testing
concepts.summary: Judge planarity by finding subdivisions or minors of K5 or K3,3 and relate it to the four colour theorem.

concepts.name: Maximum flow and Ford-Fulkerson
concepts.summary: Model a capacitated network, find a maximum flow with augmenting paths in a residual graph, and track flow conservation.

concepts.name: Max-flow min-cut theorem
concepts.summary: Evaluate a flow's optimality by exhibiting a cut of equal capacity and explain why the two values coincide.

concepts.name: Bipartite matching and Hall's theorem
concepts.summary: Find maximum matchings via augmenting paths or flow reduction and decide perfect matchings with Hall's condition.

concepts.name: Shortest paths with negative weights
concepts.summary: Choose among Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall and Dijkstra and detect negative cycles.

misconceptions.text: Greedily pushing flow along any path without ever undoing flow yields a maximum flow.
A graph is planar only if it contains no K5 as a subgraph, with no need to consider subdivisions.
A maximal matching, one that cannot be extended by adding an edge, is always a maximum matching.

concepts.name: Reductions to flow and matching
concepts.summary: Design reductions of problems such as project selection, edge-disjoint paths and assignment to max flow or matching.

concepts.name: Weighted matching and assignment
concepts.summary: Evaluate and select algorithms for minimum-cost perfect matching and min-cost flow, using dual potentials.

concepts.name: NP-hardness of graph problems
concepts.summary: Assess why Hamilton cycle, 3-colouring, clique and vertex cover are NP-complete and what that implies for algorithm choice.

concepts.name: Approximation and heuristics for graphs
concepts.summary: Design and justify approximation or heuristic algorithms, such as the MST-based metric TSP 2-approximation, with guarantees.

concepts.name: Strongly connected components
concepts.summary: Evaluate linear-time SCC algorithms and use the condensation DAG to structure analysis of directed graphs.

concepts.name: Treewidth and structural parameters
concepts.summary: Judge when bounded treewidth or other structure makes NP-hard graph problems tractable through dynamic programming.

concepts.name: Extremal and probabilistic graph arguments
concepts.summary: Construct proofs using extremal bounds, Ramsey-type arguments or the probabilistic method to show existence of graph structures.

misconceptions.text: Because Hamilton cycle is NP-complete, no algorithm can solve it on any realistic instance.
Approximation algorithms for NP-hard graph problems give optimal answers on small inputs.
Min-cost flow cannot be solved in polynomial time because it generalises shortest paths and flows.

concepts.name: Client-specified data selection
aliases: asking for exactly what you need
concepts.summary: Explain that a GraphQL client lists the fields it wants and the response mirrors that shape, avoiding fixed server-defined payloads.

concepts.name: Single endpoint model
concepts.summary: Describe how all operations go to one endpoint, with the operation in the request body rather than in the URL path and HTTP method.

concepts.name: Schema as contract
concepts.summary: Understand that the schema defines the types and operations available and acts as the contract between client and server.

concepts.name: Scalar and object types
concepts.summary: Recall the built-in scalars (Int, Float, String, Boolean, ID) and that object types group named fields.

concepts.name: Query field selection
concepts.summary: Read and write a simple query with nested selection sets and understand the JSON response it returns.

concepts.name: Three operation types
concepts.summary: Name query, mutation and subscription and state what each is for: reading, writing and receiving live updates.

misconceptions.text: GraphQL is a database or storage technology.
GraphQL needs a separate URL for each resource like REST.
A GraphQL query returns all fields of an object automatically.

concepts.name: Arguments and variables
concepts.summary: Pass arguments to fields and use typed variables with a separate variables payload instead of string-building queries.

concepts.name: Non-null and list modifiers
concepts.summary: Read type notation such as [String!]! and predict what nullability means for a response.

concepts.name: Mutations with input types
concepts.summary: Write mutations that take input object types and select the fields of the changed data in the response.

concepts.name: Aliases and fragments
concepts.summary: Use aliases to rename or repeat fields and fragments to reuse selection sets.

concepts.name: Schema definition language
concepts.summary: Write a small schema in SDL defining object types, Query and Mutation root types, enums and relationships.

concepts.name: Resolver basics
concepts.summary: Implement a resolver function per field that receives parent, arguments and context and returns data.

concepts.name: GraphQL error responses
concepts.summary: Interpret the response's data and errors keys, including that HTTP 200 can still carry errors.

misconceptions.text: Fields in a schema are nullable only if marked with an exclamation mark.
Any failed GraphQL operation returns a 4xx or 5xx HTTP status.
Variables are just string interpolation done by the client library.

concepts.name: Resolver chain execution
concepts.summary: Trace how the executor resolves fields level by level, passing each parent result to child resolvers, and analyse the cost.

concepts.name: N+1 problem and batching
concepts.summary: Diagnose N+1 queries caused by per-item resolvers and fix them with request-scoped batching and caching.

concepts.name: Interfaces and unions
concepts.summary: Model polymorphic data with interfaces and unions and query them using inline fragments and __typename.

concepts.name: Context and authorization
concepts.summary: Place authentication data in context and enforce authorization in resolvers or business logic layer rather than only at the edge.

concepts.name: Pagination patterns
concepts.summary: Compare offset and cursor-based pagination and design list fields using the connection pattern with edges and pageInfo.

concepts.name: Subscriptions over persistent connections
concepts.summary: Implement a subscription that streams events from a pub/sub source over a persistent transport such as WebSocket.

concepts.name: Client-side caching
concepts.summary: Analyse how clients normalise results by type and id and how this affects cache updates after mutations.

concepts.name: Error and null propagation
concepts.summary: Predict how an error in a non-null field bubbles up to the nearest nullable parent and design schemas accordingly.

misconceptions.text: GraphQL automatically prevents N+1 database queries.
Hiding a field from the UI is sufficient authorization.
Offset pagination is always fine for large, changing lists.

concepts.name: Schema design principles
concepts.summary: Evaluate schema designs against client needs, naming consistency and domain language rather than mirroring database tables.

concepts.name: Mutation payload design
concepts.summary: Judge designs for mutation inputs and payloads, including returning typed domain errors versus top-level errors.

concepts.name: Query cost and depth limiting
concepts.summary: Analyse abuse risks from deeply nested or expensive queries and apply depth, complexity and timeout limits.

concepts.name: Persisted queries and caching
concepts.summary: Analyse how persisted queries and CDN or response caching work given POST-based operations and personalised data.

concepts.name: Schema evolution and deprecation
concepts.summary: Evaluate changes as breaking or non-breaking and manage them with additive change and deprecation instead of versions.

concepts.name: Federation and schema composition
concepts.summary: Analyse how multiple services contribute to one graph through stitching or federation and the tradeoffs in ownership.

concepts.name: Observability and performance tracing
concepts.summary: Use per-field tracing and operation-level metrics to locate slow resolvers and track client usage.

concepts.name: Introspection and security hardening
concepts.summary: Evaluate exposure from introspection, batching and verbose errors and choose appropriate hardening for each environment.

misconceptions.text: A GraphQL schema should map one-to-one to database tables.
GraphQL needs API versions like v1 and v2 for any change.
Disabling introspection is enough to secure a GraphQL API.

concepts.name: Graph architecture governance
concepts.summary: Design an organisation-wide process for schema ownership, review, linting and change validation against real client traffic.

concepts.name: Federation architecture tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Evaluate when a federated gateway, a single server or a backend-for-frontend fits, weighing latency, ownership and failure modes.

concepts.name: Incremental delivery with defer and stream
concepts.summary: Assess incremental delivery of response parts and its effects on client rendering, caching and transport.

concepts.name: Custom directives and schema tooling
concepts.summary: Create directives, schema transforms and code generation pipelines that enforce conventions and type safety end to end.

concepts.name: Query planning and execution optimisation
concepts.summary: Evaluate strategies such as field lookahead, join pushdown and parallel fetching to cut backend load and latency.

concepts.name: Resilience and rate limiting design
concepts.summary: Design cost-based rate limiting, timeouts and fallbacks that degrade gracefully when downstream services fail.

concepts.name: Choosing GraphQL versus alternatives
concepts.summary: Judge when GraphQL, REST or RPC best suits a product given caching, tooling, team structure and client diversity.

misconceptions.text: Federation is always better than a single GraphQL server.
GraphQL is a replacement that makes REST obsolete in every case.
Request-count-based rate limiting is adequate for GraphQL.

concepts.name: Force as a vector
concepts.summary: Recognise force as a quantity with magnitude, direction and point of application, and state its units and line of action.

concepts.name: Newton's first and third laws
concepts.summary: Explain that a body at rest has zero net force and that contact forces occur in equal and opposite pairs.

concepts.name: Resolving forces into components
concepts.summary: Break a force into perpendicular x and y components and rebuild it from them using trigonometry.

concepts.name: Resultant of concurrent forces
concepts.summary: Explain how several forces acting at one point combine into a single equivalent force.

concepts.name: Moment of a force
concepts.summary: Describe the moment as force times perpendicular distance about a point and give its sense as clockwise or counterclockwise.

concepts.name: Rigid body and particle idealisation
concepts.summary: Recall that statics treats bodies as non-deforming and when a body can be modelled as a particle.

concepts.name: Common support types
concepts.summary: Name pin, roller and fixed supports and recall which reaction forces or moments each can provide.

misconceptions.text: A body at rest has no forces acting on it.
A moment depends only on the size of the force, not on where it acts.
The magnitude of a resultant is always the arithmetic sum of the force magnitudes.

concepts.name: Particle equilibrium equations
concepts.summary: Apply force sums in each direction to find unknown forces or angles for a particle in equilibrium.

concepts.name: Free-body diagram construction
concepts.summary: Isolate a body and draw all applied and reaction forces on it with chosen axes and dimensions.

concepts.name: Moment by vector cross product
concepts.summary: Compute the moment of a force about a point using perpendicular distance, components via Varignon, or the cross product.

concepts.name: Couples and couple moments
concepts.summary: Calculate the moment of a couple and apply that it is the same about every point.

concepts.name: Equilibrium of rigid bodies in 2D
concepts.summary: Use the three planar equilibrium equations to solve for support reactions of a single rigid body.

concepts.name: Distributed load replacement
concepts.summary: Replace a distributed load with an equivalent resultant acting at the centroid of the load diagram.

concepts.name: Two-force members
concepts.summary: Recognise that a member loaded at two points only carries force along the line joining them.

misconceptions.text: A free-body diagram should include the forces the body exerts on its surroundings.
The moment of a couple depends on the point about which it is taken.
A distributed load acts at the midpoint of the beam regardless of its shape.

concepts.name: Equivalent force-couple systems
concepts.summary: Reduce any force and couple system to a single resultant force and couple at a chosen point, or to a single force.

concepts.name: Three-dimensional equilibrium
concepts.summary: Use vector force and moment sums to solve for reactions of bodies in space, with correct 3D support reactions.

concepts.name: Static determinacy and constraints
concepts.summary: Compare unknowns to equations to classify a body as determinate, indeterminate or improperly constrained.

concepts.name: Truss idealisation and zero-force members
concepts.summary: Analyse truss assumptions (pinned joints, loads at joints) and identify zero-force members by joint inspection.

concepts.name: Method of joints
concepts.summary: Solve for tension or compression in each truss member by applying particle equilibrium joint by joint.

concepts.name: Method of sections
concepts.summary: Cut a truss through chosen members and use moment and force equilibrium of one part to find specific member forces.

concepts.name: Centroids by integration and composite areas
concepts.summary: Locate centroids and centers of gravity of lines, areas and composite bodies using first moments.

misconceptions.text: Every member of a truss must carry load, so zero-force members can be removed.
A member force assumed in the wrong direction means the analysis has failed.
The method of sections can cut through at most three members regardless of the geometry.

concepts.name: Frames and machines analysis
concepts.summary: Separate a frame into members, apply Newton's third law at pins, and solve for internal pin forces and reactions.

concepts.name: Coulomb dry friction
concepts.summary: Distinguish friction as an unknown force up to μsN from impending slip with F=μsN, and analyse sliding versus tipping.

concepts.name: Wedges, screws and belt friction
concepts.summary: Analyse wedges, screws and belts using friction angles and the relation T2=T1 e^(μβ).

concepts.name: Area moments of inertia
concepts.summary: Compute second moments of areas by integration and composite shapes using the parallel-axis theorem.

concepts.name: Product of inertia and principal axes
concepts.summary: Transform inertia values to rotated axes and find principal axes and principal moments.

concepts.name: Fluid pressure and distributed resultants
concepts.summary: Evaluate resultant forces from varying pressure on flat surfaces and use Pappus-Guldinus theorems to judge solution routes.

concepts.name: Solution strategy and checking
concepts.summary: Evaluate alternative equation choices, moment points and limiting cases to judge and verify a statics solution.

misconceptions.text: Friction force always equals μN, even when the body is not about to slip.
In a frame, pin forces on adjoining members need not be equal and opposite.
Moment of inertia of an area depends only on its area, not on its distribution about the axis.

concepts.name: Modelling real structures as idealisations
concepts.summary: Judge when rigid-body, pin-joint, point-load and frictional assumptions are valid and estimate the error when they are not.

concepts.name: Indeterminate structures by compatibility
concepts.summary: Evaluate how adding deformation compatibility to equilibrium resolves redundancies and where statics alone fails.

concepts.name: Virtual work and stability
concepts.summary: Judge equilibrium and its stability of mechanisms using virtual work and potential energy as alternatives to free-body analysis.

concepts.name: Cables and funicular shapes
concepts.summary: Evaluate the shape and tension of cables under distributed and concentrated loads and the link to arches.

concepts.name: Design of a load-resisting system
concepts.summary: Design a truss, frame or support arrangement that carries specified loads with justified member layout and constraints.

concepts.name: Optimising for efficiency and safety
concepts.summary: Create design variants and evaluate them for member forces, friction margins, tipping stability and sensitivity to load uncertainty.

concepts.name: Computational statics formulations
concepts.summary: Formulate equilibrium of a general truss or frame as a linear system and judge its solvability from rank and conditioning.

misconceptions.text: Equilibrium equations are enough to solve any structure that is in equilibrium.
A structure that satisfies equilibrium is automatically stable.
A cable under its own weight forms a parabola exactly.

concepts.name: Resources and URIs
concepts.summary: Explain that a REST API models things as resources, each identified by a URI such as /users/42.

concepts.name: Collections and single items
concepts.summary: Recognise the pattern of a plural collection URI (/orders) and an item URI (/orders/17) beneath it.

concepts.name: HTTP methods as actions
concepts.summary: Describe how GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE express reading, creating, replacing, updating and removing resources.

concepts.name: Status code classes
concepts.summary: Remember that 2xx means success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error, and recall common codes like 200, 201, 404 and 500.

concepts.name: JSON representations
concepts.summary: Understand that a resource is exchanged as a representation, typically JSON, separate from the server's internal storage.

concepts.name: Statelessness
concepts.summary: Explain that each request carries all information needed to process it, so the server keeps no client session between calls.

misconceptions.text: REST is the same thing as HTTP or JSON, so any API that uses them is RESTful.
URIs should contain verbs like /getUser or /deleteOrder to say what they do.
A response is successful whenever the server replies, so 200 is fine for everything.

concepts.name: Resource naming conventions
concepts.summary: Apply consistent naming: plural lowercase nouns, hyphenated words, no verbs, and no file extensions.

concepts.name: Nested resources and relationships
concepts.summary: Model relationships with paths like /customers/5/orders and judge when to keep nesting shallow.

concepts.name: Safe and idempotent methods
concepts.summary: Distinguish safe methods from idempotent ones and say which of GET, PUT, DELETE and POST has which property.

concepts.name: Choosing correct status codes
concepts.summary: Pick codes such as 201 with Location, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404 and 409 to match what actually happened.

concepts.name: Query parameters for filtering
concepts.summary: Use query parameters to filter, sort and select fields on a collection rather than creating new endpoints.

concepts.name: Basic pagination
concepts.summary: Return large collections in pages using limit/offset or page parameters along with total or next-page information.

concepts.name: Consistent error response body
concepts.summary: Return errors in a uniform JSON structure with a code, message and details alongside the proper status code.

misconceptions.text: POST and PUT are interchangeable for creating resources.
Deeper URI nesting always gives a clearer API, so /a/1/b/2/c/3/d/4 is good design.
Using 200 with an error message in the body is acceptable, so the status code need not reflect failure.

concepts.name: PUT versus PATCH semantics
concepts.summary: Analyse when full replacement (PUT) or partial update (PATCH, merge patch or JSON Patch) fits an update and its effect on idempotency.

concepts.name: Cursor-based pagination
concepts.summary: Compare offset and cursor pagination in terms of consistency under inserts, performance and navigation, and design cursor responses.

concepts.name: API versioning strategies
concepts.summary: Contrast URI, header and media-type versioning and decide which changes are breaking versus backward compatible.

concepts.name: Problem Details error format
concepts.summary: Structure errors using the standard problem details fields (type, title, status, detail, instance) with field-level validation errors.

concepts.name: Authentication and authorization design
concepts.summary: Design API access with bearer tokens or API keys, and separate 401 authentication failures from 403 permission failures.

concepts.name: Idempotency keys for POST
concepts.summary: Analyse how retries cause duplicate creations and use an idempotency key so POST can be retried safely.

concepts.name: HTTP caching with validators
concepts.summary: Use Cache-Control, ETag and If-None-Match/If-Match to enable caching and prevent lost updates.

concepts.name: Modelling non-CRUD actions
concepts.summary: Analyse options such as sub-resources or state fields for operations like cancel or publish that do not map neatly to CRUD.

misconceptions.text: PATCH is just another name for PUT and behaves identically.
Versioning is only needed when you remove a field; adding fields or changing meaning never breaks clients.
401 and 403 mean the same thing and either can be used for any access failure.

concepts.name: Hypermedia and HATEOAS trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate the Richardson maturity model and when hypermedia links justify their cost for discoverability and decoupling.

concepts.name: Evolution without breaking clients
concepts.summary: Judge change strategies such as additive changes, tolerant readers, Sunset and Deprecation headers, and migration timelines.

concepts.name: Rate limiting and quotas
concepts.summary: Analyse rate limiting schemes and communicate limits through 429, Retry-After and rate limit headers.

concepts.name: Long-running operations
concepts.summary: Design asynchronous operations using 202, a status resource and polling or callbacks rather than blocking requests.

concepts.name: Concurrency control
concepts.summary: Apply optimistic concurrency with ETags and 412 or 409 responses to analyse and prevent conflicting writes.

concepts.name: Bulk and batch operations
concepts.summary: Evaluate designs for bulk create or update, including partial-success reporting such as 207 versus all-or-nothing.

concepts.name: Contract-first with OpenAPI
concepts.summary: Evaluate describing an API in an OpenAPI document to drive documentation, validation, mocks and contract testing.

concepts.name: Webhooks and event notification
concepts.summary: Analyse webhook design including signed payloads, retries, ordering and delivery guarantees.

misconceptions.text: An API is truly RESTful as soon as it uses resource URIs and HTTP methods, even without hypermedia.
Bulk endpoints should always be atomic, since partial success is confusing and wrong.
A generated OpenAPI document is documentation enough and needs no design review or contract testing.

concepts.name: API style selection
concepts.summary: Evaluate when REST, GraphQL, gRPC or event-driven interfaces best fit given clients, performance, coupling and team constraints.

concepts.name: API governance and style guides
concepts.summary: Create organisation-wide design guidelines and automated linting that keep many teams' APIs consistent.

concepts.name: Designing for the client experience
concepts.summary: Create APIs whose naming, defaults, errors, SDKs and documentation minimise time to first successful call.

concepts.name: Resource granularity and aggregation
concepts.summary: Evaluate coarse versus fine-grained resources, embedding and expansion, and aggregation layers to balance round trips and coupling.

concepts.name: Long-term API lifecycle management
concepts.summary: Create lifecycle plans covering design review, versioning policy, deprecation, telemetry-driven change and retirement.

concepts.name: Security threat modelling for APIs
concepts.summary: Evaluate an API design against threats such as broken object-level authorisation, mass assignment and excessive data exposure.

concepts.name: Consistency and scale trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate how eventual consistency, caching layers and replication shape the guarantees an API can honestly promise.

misconceptions.text: REST is always the best choice, and GraphQL or gRPC are merely fashionable replacements.
Strict consistency rules matter less than flexibility, so each team should design its API freely.
Authentication on every endpoint is enough, with no need for per-object authorisation checks.

concepts.name: Hooks as function component features
concepts.summary: Recall that hooks are special functions starting with 'use' that let function components hold state and use React features without classes.

concepts.name: Rules of Hooks
concepts.summary: Explain that hooks must be called only at the top level of components or custom hooks, never inside conditions, loops or nested functions.

concepts.name: useState state variable and setter
concepts.summary: Understand that useState returns the current value and a setter function, and that calling the setter triggers a re-render.

concepts.name: State persists between renders
concepts.summary: Explain that state is kept by React across renders while ordinary local variables are reset on every call.

concepts.name: Initial state value
concepts.summary: Recall that the argument to useState is used only on the first render to set the initial value.

concepts.name: Controlled inputs with state
concepts.summary: Understand how an input's value and onChange handler are tied to a state variable.

misconceptions.text: Changing a state variable directly, such as count = count + 1, updates the screen.
Hooks can be called anywhere in a component, including inside if statements or loops.
Hooks only work in class components or are just a replacement syntax for this.state.

concepts.name: Functional state updates
concepts.summary: Apply the form setState(prev => next) when the new state depends on the previous state.

concepts.name: Immutable updates of objects and arrays
concepts.summary: Update object and array state by creating new copies with spread or array methods rather than mutating in place.

concepts.name: useEffect for side effects
concepts.summary: Use useEffect to run side effects such as fetching data or updating the document title after render.

concepts.name: Dependency array behaviour
concepts.summary: Choose no array, an empty array or a list of values to control when an effect re-runs.

concepts.name: Effect cleanup functions
concepts.summary: Return a cleanup function from an effect to remove subscriptions, timers or listeners.

concepts.name: Lazy state initialisation
concepts.summary: Pass a function to useState so an expensive initial value is computed only on the first render.

concepts.name: useRef for mutable values and DOM nodes
concepts.summary: Use useRef to hold a value that persists without causing re-renders or to access a DOM element.

misconceptions.text: Calling setState updates the variable immediately, so the next line sees the new value.
Pushing onto a state array and then calling the setter with the same array will trigger a re-render.
useEffect with an empty dependency array runs on every render.

concepts.name: Stale closures in hooks
concepts.summary: Analyse how event handlers and effects capture the values from the render in which they were created, and fix stale values.

concepts.name: Exhaustive dependencies
concepts.summary: Determine the correct dependency list for an effect and restructure code instead of suppressing the lint rule.

concepts.name: Data fetching in effects
concepts.summary: Implement fetching in useEffect with loading and error state and guard against race conditions using cleanup or abort signals.

concepts.name: useReducer state machines
concepts.summary: Use a reducer and dispatched actions to manage state with several related transitions.

concepts.name: useContext for shared values
concepts.summary: Provide a value with a context provider and read it in descendants with useContext, avoiding prop drilling.

concepts.name: Writing custom hooks
concepts.summary: Extract reusable stateful logic into functions beginning with 'use' that compose built-in hooks.

concepts.name: Effects versus event handlers
concepts.summary: Distinguish logic that belongs in event handlers or render calculation from logic that truly needs an effect to synchronise with an external system.

concepts.name: Derived state versus stored state
concepts.summary: Decide when a value should be computed during render from existing state or props rather than stored in separate state.

misconceptions.text: Omitting a dependency from the array is fine because the effect will always see the latest values anyway.
Syncing props into state with an effect is the normal way to compute derived values.
Two components using the same custom hook share the same state.

concepts.name: Memoization with useMemo and useCallback
concepts.summary: Analyse when caching a computed value or function identity preserves referential equality and actually avoids work.

concepts.name: React.memo and referential stability
concepts.summary: Trace how unstable object and function props defeat React.memo and decide which stabilisations are needed.

concepts.name: Evaluating optimisation cost
concepts.summary: Judge by measurement with the profiler whether memoization is worth its complexity or if restructuring components is better.

concepts.name: Context performance and splitting
concepts.summary: Evaluate how context value changes re-render all consumers and choose splitting, memoised values or state colocation in response.

concepts.name: Imperative handles with refs
concepts.summary: Use ref forwarding and useImperativeHandle to expose a limited imperative API from a child component.

concepts.name: Layout effects and timing
concepts.summary: Analyse the render, commit, layout effect and passive effect order to choose useLayoutEffect for DOM measurement before paint.

concepts.name: External stores with useSyncExternalStore
concepts.summary: Subscribe to non-React state sources safely so that concurrent rendering does not show inconsistent values.

concepts.name: Strict Mode double invocation
concepts.summary: Interpret why Strict Mode re-runs renders and effects in development and use it to expose impure renders and missing cleanup.

misconceptions.text: Wrapping every function in useCallback and every value in useMemo makes an app faster.
useMemo guarantees the value will never be recomputed.
useCallback prevents a child from re-rendering by itself, even if the child is not memoised.

concepts.name: Hooks implementation model
concepts.summary: Evaluate code against the model that React stores hook state per component instance in call order, explaining why the rules of hooks exist.

concepts.name: Concurrent rendering and hook safety
concepts.summary: Assess how interruptible renders, transitions and deferred values constrain purity of render and effects.

concepts.name: Transitions and deferred values
concepts.summary: Judge when to mark updates as non-urgent with useTransition or useDeferredValue to keep interfaces responsive.

concepts.name: Custom hook API design
concepts.summary: Design custom hooks with stable return identities, clear contracts, composability and minimal dependency on call-site details.

concepts.name: Event-like effect patterns
concepts.summary: Create solutions that read the latest values inside effects without re-synchronising, using event-effect or latest-ref patterns.

concepts.name: Choosing state architecture
concepts.summary: Evaluate hooks-only state, reducers with context, server-state libraries and external stores for a given app's needs.

concepts.name: Testing and debugging hooks
concepts.summary: Evaluate strategies to test custom hooks and diagnose render loops, stale values and leaked effects using the profiler and devtools.

misconceptions.text: Hooks are magic and track state by variable name or by the component's source location.
useTransition makes the slow work itself run faster.
Effects can be made safe by simply omitting dependencies when a value should be read without re-running.

concepts.name: Pure functions
concepts.summary: Explain that a pure function always returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself.

concepts.name: Side effects
concepts.summary: Recognise actions such as mutating variables, printing, or writing files as side effects that make code less predictable.

concepts.name: Immutable data
concepts.summary: Understand that values are not modified in place and that updates produce new values instead.

concepts.name: Functions as values
concepts.summary: Understand that functions can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, and returned like any other value.

concepts.name: Expressions versus statements
concepts.summary: Distinguish expressions that produce values from statements that perform actions, and see why functional style favours expressions.

concepts.name: Anonymous functions
concepts.summary: Recognise the syntax of an unnamed function written inline and know when it is used.

misconceptions.text: A function that prints output is still pure as long as it returns the right value.
Immutable data means a variable name can never be used again.
Functional programming simply means using functions, which every language already does.

concepts.name: Map, filter and reduce
concepts.summary: Apply map, filter and reduce to transform, select and aggregate collections without explicit loops.

concepts.name: Higher-order functions
concepts.summary: Write and use functions that accept or return other functions to parameterise behaviour.

concepts.name: Closures
concepts.summary: Use a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was defined, for example to build configurable functions.

concepts.name: Function composition
concepts.summary: Combine small functions so the output of one feeds the input of the next to build larger behaviour.

concepts.name: Recursion over data
concepts.summary: Replace loops with recursive functions that have a base case and a recursive case on lists or trees.

concepts.name: Copy-on-update techniques
concepts.summary: Update lists, maps and records by creating modified copies using spread, concat or similar operations.

misconceptions.text: Map and filter modify the original collection in place.
Reduce is only for summing numbers.
A closure copies the values of the captured variables at creation time.

concepts.name: Currying and partial application
concepts.summary: Transform multi-argument functions into chains of single-argument functions and fix some arguments to derive specialised functions.

concepts.name: Point-free pipelines
concepts.summary: Analyse and build data-transformation pipelines, judging when omitting explicit arguments helps or hurts readability.

concepts.name: Tail recursion and stack use
concepts.summary: Analyse when recursion grows the call stack and rewrite it with an accumulator in tail position.

concepts.name: Persistent data structures
concepts.summary: Explain how immutable collections share structure between versions to make updates efficient.

concepts.name: Explicit error handling types
concepts.summary: Represent absence and failure as values such as Option or Result rather than exceptions or nulls.

concepts.name: Isolating side effects
concepts.summary: Analyse a program and separate its pure logic from the I/O at its edges to improve testability.

concepts.name: Lazy evaluation and iterators
concepts.summary: Use deferred computation to process large or infinite sequences and know when evaluation actually occurs.

misconceptions.text: Currying and partial application are the same thing.
Immutable collections must be fully copied on every update, so they are always slow.
Point-free style is always more readable than naming arguments.

concepts.name: Functors and mappable containers
concepts.summary: Analyse types that support mapping a function over their contents while preserving structure, and check the functor laws.

concepts.name: Monads for sequencing
concepts.summary: Use flatMap or bind to chain computations that may fail or carry context, and explain how they flatten nested containers.

concepts.name: Applicative validation
concepts.summary: Combine independent effectful values, for example accumulating all validation errors rather than stopping at the first.

concepts.name: Referential transparency and equational reasoning
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether an expression can be replaced by its value and use this to justify refactors and optimisations.

concepts.name: Algebraic data types
concepts.summary: Model domains with sum and product types so illegal states are unrepresentable, and consume them with pattern matching.

concepts.name: Effect modelling with IO
concepts.summary: Evaluate approaches that represent side effects as values that are described first and run at the program boundary.

concepts.name: Property-based testing
concepts.summary: Judge and write properties that should hold for all inputs, using generated data to test pure functions.

misconceptions.text: A monad is just a container or a way to perform side effects.
Property-based tests replace all example-based tests.
Pure functional code cannot perform I/O at all.

concepts.name: Paradigm trade-off evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate where functional techniques help or hurt in a given system considering performance, team skill, and domain.

concepts.name: Free monads and interpreters
concepts.summary: Design programs as data or abstract algebras that separate description from multiple interpreters.

concepts.name: Monad transformers and effect stacks
concepts.summary: Evaluate ways of combining several effects, such as state, errors and reader, against alternatives like effect handlers.

concepts.name: Optics for immutable updates
concepts.summary: Design composable accessors that read and update deeply nested immutable structures.

concepts.name: Type-level domain design
concepts.summary: Create type designs that encode invariants so the compiler rejects invalid programs.

concepts.name: Functional architecture patterns
concepts.summary: Design systems whose state is a fold over events or streams, with side effects pushed to the boundary.

concepts.name: Performance and memory analysis
concepts.summary: Evaluate allocation, laziness-induced space leaks and fusion in functional code and decide on optimisations.

misconceptions.text: Functional code is always slower than imperative code because of immutability.
Stacking monad transformers is always the best way to combine effects.
A stronger type system removes the need for runtime validation and testing.

issues: nov-2 Side effects and cmp-6 Isolating side effects overlap; nov-2 is a necessary novice concept, but cmp-6 is better framed as a distinct architectural skill, so the name and summary need to separate them.

Novice prerequisite [nov-4, nov-6] is backwards: anonymous functions depend on the idea of functions as values, so the order should be nov-4 before nov-6 only if the arrow means prereq->dependent; the format is [prereq, dependent], so it is correct, but nov-6 is a pure syntax recall with no further dependency issue. However [nov-2, nov-1] is correct (prereq nov-2). [nov-1, nov-3] is not a genuine dependency: immutability does not depend on purity.
Missing dependencies: adb-3 closures should depend on nov-6 or nov-4; adb-5 recursion has no prerequisite; cmp-2 pipelines depend on adb-4 (present).
Novice misconception 3 is vague and about the definition of the paradigm rather than a real belief; 'Immutable data means a variable name can never be used again' is fine.

prf-4 referential transparency is a foundational idea that depends on purity; it is placed at proficient, which is late, but acceptable with C5. prf-7 depends on prf-4, which is weak: property-based testing depends on pure functions and cmp-6 rather than equational reasoning.
cmp-5 Explicit error handling types is C3 but appears before prf-2 as a dependency; fine. prf-3 applicative validation should also depend on cmp-5.
exp-7 depends on cmp-7 and cmp-4, fine. exp-2 Free monads is listed with tagless final alias which is a different technique; acceptable but the alias is misleading.
Misconception 'Pure functional code cannot perform I/O at all' is mapped to prf-4, which is a poor fit.

concepts.name: Pure functions
concepts.summary: Explain that a pure function always returns the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside itself.

concepts.name: Side effects
concepts.summary: Recognise actions such as mutating variables, printing, or writing files as side effects that make code less predictable.

concepts.name: Immutable data
concepts.summary: Understand that values are not modified in place and that updates produce new values instead.

concepts.name: Functions as values
concepts.summary: Understand that functions can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, and returned like any other value.

concepts.name: Expressions versus statements
concepts.summary: Distinguish expressions that produce values from statements that perform actions, and see why functional style favours expressions.

concepts.name: Anonymous functions
concepts.summary: Recognise the syntax of an unnamed function written inline and know when it is used.

misconceptions.text: A function that prints output is still pure as long as it returns the right value.
Immutable data means a variable name can never be used again.
Functional programming simply means using functions, which every language already does.

concepts.name: Map, filter and reduce
concepts.summary: Apply map, filter and reduce to transform, select and aggregate collections without explicit loops.

concepts.name: Higher-order functions
concepts.summary: Write and use functions that accept or return other functions to parameterise behaviour.

concepts.name: Closures
concepts.summary: Use a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was defined, for example to build configurable functions.

concepts.name: Function composition
concepts.summary: Combine small functions so the output of one feeds the input of the next to build larger behaviour.

concepts.name: Recursion over data
concepts.summary: Replace loops with recursive functions that have a base case and a recursive case on lists or trees.

concepts.name: Copy-on-update techniques
concepts.summary: Update lists, maps and records by creating modified copies using spread, concat or similar operations.

misconceptions.text: Map and filter modify the original collection in place.
Reduce is only for summing numbers.
A closure copies the values of the captured variables at creation time.

concepts.name: Currying and partial application
concepts.summary: Transform multi-argument functions into chains of single-argument functions and fix some arguments to derive specialised functions.

concepts.name: Point-free pipelines
concepts.summary: Analyse and build data-transformation pipelines, judging when omitting explicit arguments helps or hurts readability.

concepts.name: Tail recursion and stack use
concepts.summary: Analyse when recursion grows the call stack and rewrite it with an accumulator in tail position.

concepts.name: Persistent data structures
concepts.summary: Explain how immutable collections share structure between versions to make updates efficient.

concepts.name: Explicit error handling types
concepts.summary: Represent absence and failure as values such as Option or Result rather than exceptions or nulls.

concepts.name: Functional core, imperative shell
concepts.summary: Analyse a program and restructure it so pure decision logic sits in a core and I/O sits in a thin outer layer, improving testability.

concepts.name: Lazy evaluation and iterators
concepts.summary: Use deferred computation to process large or infinite sequences and know when evaluation actually occurs.

misconceptions.text: Currying and partial application are the same thing.
Immutable collections must be fully copied on every update, so they are always slow.
Point-free style is always more readable than naming arguments.

concepts.name: Functors and mappable containers
concepts.summary: Analyse types that support mapping a function over their contents while preserving structure, and check the functor laws.

concepts.name: Monads for sequencing
concepts.summary: Use flatMap or bind to chain computations that may fail or carry context, and explain how they flatten nested containers.

concepts.name: Applicative validation
concepts.summary: Combine independent effectful values, for example accumulating all validation errors rather than stopping at the first.

concepts.name: Referential transparency and equational reasoning
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether an expression can be replaced by its value and use this to justify refactors and optimisations.

concepts.name: Algebraic data types
concepts.summary: Model domains with sum and product types so illegal states are unrepresentable, and consume them with pattern matching.

concepts.name: Effect modelling with IO
concepts.summary: Evaluate approaches that represent side effects as values that are described first and run at the program boundary.

concepts.name: Property-based testing
concepts.summary: Judge and write properties that should hold for all inputs, using generated data to test pure functions.

misconceptions.text: A monad is just a container or a way to perform side effects.
Property-based tests replace all example-based tests.
Pure functional code cannot perform I/O at all.

concepts.name: Paradigm trade-off evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate where functional techniques help or hurt in a given system considering performance, team skill, and domain.

concepts.name: Free monads and interpreters
concepts.summary: Design programs as data or abstract algebras that separate description from multiple interpreters.

concepts.name: Monad transformers and effect stacks
concepts.summary: Evaluate ways of combining several effects, such as state, errors and reader, against alternatives like effect handlers.

concepts.name: Optics for immutable updates
concepts.summary: Design composable accessors that read and update deeply nested immutable structures.

concepts.name: Type-level domain design
concepts.summary: Create type designs that encode invariants so the compiler rejects invalid programs.

concepts.name: Functional architecture patterns
concepts.summary: Design systems whose state is a fold over events or streams, with side effects pushed to the boundary.

concepts.name: Performance and memory analysis
concepts.summary: Evaluate allocation, laziness-induced space leaks and fusion in functional code and decide on optimisations.

misconceptions.text: Functional code is always slower than imperative code because of immutability.
Stacking monad transformers is always the best way to combine effects.
A stronger type system removes the need for runtime validation and testing.

concepts.name: Purpose of feedback
concepts.summary: Explain that feedback exists to help someone continue or improve specific behaviours and results, not to judge or punish the person.

concepts.name: Positive versus constructive feedback
concepts.summary: Recognise the difference between feedback that reinforces what worked and feedback that redirects what should change.

concepts.name: Behaviour versus personality
concepts.summary: Distinguish observable behaviour from assumptions about character and explain why feedback should address only the former.

concepts.name: Specific and timely feedback
concepts.summary: Describe why feedback should cite concrete examples and be given soon after the event.

concepts.name: Listening to feedback openly
concepts.summary: Understand that receiving feedback starts with listening, clarifying and thanking rather than arguing or explaining away.

concepts.name: Private versus public setting
concepts.summary: Remember that corrective feedback is normally given privately while praise can often be shared publicly.

misconceptions.text: Feedback means criticism of what someone did wrong.
Telling someone they are careless or lazy counts as clear feedback.
Receiving feedback means I must explain why I acted as I did.

concepts.name: Situation-Behaviour-Impact model
concepts.summary: Structure a feedback message by naming the situation, the observed behaviour and its impact on others or results.

concepts.name: Separating facts from interpretations
concepts.summary: Rewrite judgemental statements into neutral, observable descriptions before delivering them.

concepts.name: Preparing a feedback conversation
concepts.summary: Gather examples, clarify the desired outcome and choose time and place before holding a conversation.

concepts.name: Asking clarifying questions
concepts.summary: Use open questions to check understanding of feedback received and to invite the other person's view.

concepts.name: Managing defensive reactions
concepts.summary: Notice common defensive responses in yourself and others and respond calmly without escalating.

concepts.name: Turning feedback into actions
concepts.summary: Convert feedback received or given into one or two concrete next steps with a follow-up point.

misconceptions.text: The feedback sandwich of praise, criticism, praise is always the best way to deliver a hard message.
If my intention was good, the impact on the other person does not matter.
Defensiveness from the other person means the feedback was wrong or badly given.

concepts.name: Adapting feedback to the person
concepts.summary: Adjust tone, directness and framing to the individual's experience, motivation and preferences while keeping the message intact.

concepts.name: Feedback versus coaching
concepts.summary: Analyse when to give direct feedback and when to use coaching questions so the person finds their own solution.

concepts.name: Forward-looking feedback
concepts.summary: Analyse how to pair a description of past behaviour with clear expectations and requests for future behaviour.

concepts.name: Building a feedback rhythm
concepts.summary: Embed frequent informal feedback and one-to-ones so formal reviews contain no surprises.

concepts.name: Handling emotional reactions
concepts.summary: Diagnose what drives a strong emotional reaction and decide whether to pause, acknowledge or continue the conversation.

concepts.name: Seeking feedback actively
concepts.summary: Ask specific, well-targeted questions of peers, reports and managers to gather useful input on your own work.

concepts.name: Filtering feedback for value
concepts.summary: Separate useful signal from bias, vague comments and unreliable sources when interpreting feedback you receive.

misconceptions.text: Being kind means softening feedback until the problem is no longer clear.
Annual reviews are enough, since regular feedback just adds noise.
All feedback I receive should be acted on, regardless of who gave it.

concepts.name: Diagnosing root causes of performance
concepts.summary: Determine whether a performance gap stems from skill, motivation, clarity, resources or context before choosing the feedback approach.

concepts.name: Feedback in psychological safety
concepts.summary: Evaluate how team norms, leader reactions and power differences affect whether people give and accept honest feedback.

concepts.name: Difficult and high-stakes conversations
concepts.summary: Plan and judge the approach for conversations involving repeated issues, strong disagreement or serious consequences.

concepts.name: Upward and peer feedback
concepts.summary: Choose and justify how to give feedback to managers and peers where there is no formal authority.

concepts.name: Cross-cultural feedback differences
concepts.summary: Analyse how cultural norms about directness, hierarchy and face change how feedback is given and interpreted.

concepts.name: Bias in feedback
concepts.summary: Identify patterns such as recency, halo and gendered language that distort feedback and correct for them.

concepts.name: Assessing feedback effectiveness
concepts.summary: Judge whether a feedback conversation changed behaviour and trust, and refine the approach accordingly.

misconceptions.text: Poor performance is always a motivation problem that feedback alone can fix.
Direct feedback works the same way in every culture and team.
Objective-sounding feedback is free from bias.

concepts.name: Designing organisational feedback systems
concepts.summary: Design review cycles, peer input and upward channels that fit an organisation's goals, size and culture.

concepts.name: Evaluating 360-degree feedback
concepts.summary: Critically assess the validity, risks and appropriate uses of multi-rater feedback instruments and their results.

concepts.name: Developing feedback capability in others
concepts.summary: Create programmes, practice and coaching that build feedback skill and norms across managers and teams.

concepts.name: Repairing trust after harmful feedback
concepts.summary: Evaluate damage from poorly delivered feedback and choose repair actions that restore the relationship.

concepts.name: Linking feedback to performance decisions
concepts.summary: Judge how developmental feedback should relate to ratings, pay and promotion without undermining candour.

concepts.name: Modelling a learning culture
concepts.summary: Create visible leadership habits of seeking, receiving and acting on feedback that shape norms across the organisation.

misconceptions.text: A formal feedback programme or tool alone creates a feedback culture.
Combining development feedback with ratings and pay makes it more honest.
Once trust is damaged by feedback, nothing can restore it.

concepts.name: Systematic judgment error
concepts.summary: Explain that a cognitive bias is a predictable, directional deviation from accurate or rational judgment, not just a random mistake.

concepts.name: Mental shortcuts (heuristics)
concepts.summary: Describe heuristics as fast, low-effort rules that usually work well but sometimes produce biased conclusions.

concepts.name: Confirmation bias
concepts.summary: Recognise and define the tendency to seek, notice and favour information that fits existing beliefs.

concepts.name: Anchoring effect
concepts.summary: Explain that an initial number or piece of information unduly pulls later estimates toward it.

concepts.name: Availability heuristic
concepts.summary: Explain that people judge how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

concepts.name: Bias as universal and unconscious
concepts.summary: State that everyone has biases, usually operating without awareness, so feeling objective is not proof of being objective.

misconceptions.text: Cognitive biases only affect unintelligent or uneducated people.
Heuristics are always wrong and should never be used.
If I know about a bias, I am automatically immune to it.

concepts.name: Spotting biases in everyday cases
concepts.summary: Identify which bias (confirmation, anchoring, availability) is at work in a short realistic scenario such as shopping, news or hiring.

concepts.name: Hindsight bias
concepts.summary: Explain that after learning an outcome people overestimate how predictable it was.

concepts.name: Overconfidence effect
concepts.summary: Describe how people's confidence in their judgments tends to exceed their actual accuracy.

concepts.name: Self-serving bias
concepts.summary: Apply the idea that people credit successes to themselves and blame failures on circumstances when analysing examples.

concepts.name: Framing effect
concepts.summary: Show how presenting the same information as gains or losses changes choices, using paired examples.

concepts.name: Simple debiasing habits
concepts.summary: Use basic strategies such as considering the opposite, pausing before deciding and seeking disconfirming evidence.

misconceptions.text: Hindsight makes past events look obvious because they really were obvious.
Confidence is a reliable signal that a judgment is correct.
Two descriptions with the same facts will lead to the same decision.

concepts.name: Dual-process account of judgment
concepts.summary: Analyse how fast intuitive and slow deliberate processing interact and where biases arise from the former going unchecked.

concepts.name: Representativeness and base rates
concepts.summary: Analyse how judging by similarity to a prototype leads people to ignore base rates, as in the Linda and taxi problems.

concepts.name: Conjunction fallacy
concepts.summary: Recognise and explain why a conjunction of events cannot be more probable than either event alone.

concepts.name: Loss aversion and sunk costs
concepts.summary: Analyse how losses weigh more than equal gains and how this drives sunk-cost and status-quo decisions.

concepts.name: Fundamental attribution error
concepts.summary: Analyse how observers overweight personality and underweight situation when explaining others' behaviour.

concepts.name: Bias blind spot
concepts.summary: Explain why people see bias in others more readily than in themselves and why introspection fails to detect it.

concepts.name: Structured debiasing techniques
concepts.summary: Select and apply methods such as pre-mortems, checklists, the outside view and independent estimates to counter particular biases.

misconceptions.text: Fast intuitive thinking is always biased and slow deliberate thinking is always correct.
A vivid description that fits a category makes that category more probable regardless of how rare it is.
Past investment is a valid reason to continue a project with poor prospects.

concepts.name: Heuristics and biases vs ecological rationality
concepts.summary: Evaluate the debate over whether heuristics are flaws or adaptive tools suited to particular environments.

concepts.name: Evaluating bias experiments
concepts.summary: Assess the design, effect sizes, replication status and ecological validity of classic bias studies such as anchoring and priming.

concepts.name: Bias in professional decisions
concepts.summary: Analyse how biases such as anchoring, premature closure and overconfidence shape decisions in fields like medicine, law and investing.

concepts.name: Group and organisational bias
concepts.summary: Analyse how group processes can amplify or dampen individual biases, as in groupthink and shared-information effects.

concepts.name: Motivated reasoning vs cognitive bias
concepts.summary: Distinguish biases arising from limited processing from those driven by goals, emotion or identity, and predict which remedies suit each.

concepts.name: Assessing debiasing effectiveness
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence on which debiasing interventions work, how well they transfer, and when changing the environment beats training.

concepts.name: Choice architecture and nudges
concepts.summary: Evaluate how defaults and framing can exploit or counter biases, including ethical limits.

misconceptions.text: Every famous bias effect is large, universal and has replicated unchanged.
Training people about biases reliably improves their decisions in new situations.
Groups always cancel out individual biases through diversity of opinion.

concepts.name: Normative standards for rationality
concepts.summary: Judge which normative benchmarks (Bayesian, expected utility, bounded rationality) legitimately define an error in a given task.

concepts.name: Noise versus bias decomposition
concepts.summary: Evaluate judgment errors by separating systematic bias from random noise and choose remedies for each.

concepts.name: Bias-aware decision process design
concepts.summary: Design organisational decision procedures, such as independent assessments and structured criteria, that reduce bias and noise.

concepts.name: Theory integration of bias mechanisms
concepts.summary: Construct explanations that unify many biases through mechanisms like attribute substitution, limited memory and resource-rational trade-offs.

concepts.name: Designing bias studies
concepts.summary: Create rigorous studies that test a bias claim with proper controls, sufficient power and preregistration.

concepts.name: Algorithmic and AI bias interplay
concepts.summary: Evaluate how human cognitive biases enter data and models and how automation bias alters reliance on algorithmic output.

concepts.name: Individual and cultural variation
concepts.summary: Critique claims of universality by weighing evidence on individual differences, expertise and cross-cultural variation.

misconceptions.text: All deviations from textbook probability theory count as irrational errors regardless of the task.
Reducing bias is enough to make human judgments consistent and accurate.
Algorithms remove human bias because they are not subject to cognition.

concepts.name: Algorithm as step-by-step procedure
concepts.summary: State that an algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that transforms input into output and solves a defined problem.

concepts.name: Linear search
concepts.summary: Explain how checking each element in turn finds a target and why it may need to inspect every element.

concepts.name: Binary search on sorted data
concepts.summary: Explain how repeatedly halving a sorted range locates a target and why sortedness is required.

concepts.name: Counting steps as input grows
concepts.summary: Describe how the number of basic operations grows with input size rather than measuring seconds on one machine.

concepts.name: Simple sorting by comparison
concepts.summary: Explain how a simple sort such as selection or insertion sort orders a list by comparing and moving elements.

concepts.name: Recursion as self-reference
concepts.summary: Explain that a recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance until a base case stops it.

misconceptions.text: Binary search works on any list as long as you pick the middle element.
A faster-running program on my computer always means a better algorithm.
A recursive function does not need a base case because it stops when the work is done.

concepts.name: Big O notation for growth rates
concepts.summary: Express the running time of simple loops and code as O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) or O(n²) by dropping constants and lower-order terms.

concepts.name: Tracing recursive calls
concepts.summary: Trace recursive calls and returns, including the call stack, for functions like factorial and Fibonacci.

concepts.name: Mergesort
concepts.summary: Apply the split, recursively sort and merge steps to sort a list in O(n log n) time.

concepts.name: Quicksort and partitioning
concepts.summary: Apply pivot selection and partitioning to sort a list recursively and recognise its typical and worst-case behaviour.

concepts.name: Iterative binary search implementation
concepts.summary: Implement binary search correctly with proper bounds and midpoint updates, avoiding off-by-one errors.

concepts.name: Breadth-first and depth-first traversal
concepts.summary: Apply BFS with a queue and DFS with a stack or recursion to visit all nodes of a graph or tree, tracking visited nodes.

misconceptions.text: Big O gives the exact running time, so an O(n) algorithm is always faster than an O(n²) one.
Quicksort is always O(n log n).
Graph traversal does not need a visited set because graphs have no repeated nodes.

concepts.name: Recurrence relations and Master theorem
concepts.summary: Write the recurrence for a divide-and-conquer algorithm and solve it to derive its running time.

concepts.name: Best, worst and average case
concepts.summary: Analyse how input shape changes running time and distinguish worst-case from average or expected behaviour.

concepts.name: Divide and conquer design
concepts.summary: Decompose a problem into independent subproblems, solve them recursively and combine results, as in closest pair or maximum subarray.

concepts.name: Greedy choice strategy
concepts.summary: Build a solution by repeatedly taking the locally best choice, as in interval scheduling or Huffman coding.

concepts.name: Dynamic programming with overlapping subproblems
concepts.summary: Solve problems like Fibonacci, knapsack and longest common subsequence by defining states and reusing stored subresults via memoization or tabulation.

concepts.name: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm
concepts.summary: Compute shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative weights using a priority queue and edge relaxation.

concepts.name: Graph representation and traversal cost
concepts.summary: Compare adjacency lists and matrices and derive the O(V+E) cost of BFS and DFS.

misconceptions.text: Dynamic programming is just recursion with a different name and gives no speedup.
A greedy choice that looks best locally always yields the optimal solution.
Dijkstra's algorithm works correctly with negative edge weights.

concepts.name: Proving greedy correctness
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a greedy strategy is optimal using exchange arguments or greedy-stays-ahead proofs and find counterexamples when it is not.

concepts.name: Optimal substructure and DP formulation
concepts.summary: Identify optimal substructure, define state and transitions, and choose an evaluation order including space optimization.

concepts.name: Amortized analysis
concepts.summary: Analyse the average cost per operation over a sequence, as with dynamic array doubling.

concepts.name: Shortest paths with negative weights
concepts.summary: Choose among Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, DAG relaxation and Floyd-Warshall based on weights, cycles and query type.

concepts.name: Sorting lower bound
concepts.summary: Explain the decision-tree argument that comparison sorts need Ω(n log n) and when linear-time non-comparison sorts apply.

concepts.name: Randomized quicksort analysis
concepts.summary: Evaluate how random pivot choice yields expected O(n log n) and compare pivot strategies.

concepts.name: Graph algorithm selection
concepts.summary: Select and justify algorithms such as topological sort, Kruskal, Prim, or BFS versus Dijkstra for a given graph problem.

misconceptions.text: Amortized cost is the same as average-case cost over random inputs.
Any sorting algorithm can beat O(n log n) with clever comparisons.
If a problem has optimal substructure, greedy will solve it.

concepts.name: NP-completeness and reductions
concepts.summary: Evaluate problem hardness by reducing known NP-complete problems to it and decide when exact algorithms are infeasible.

concepts.name: Approximation algorithms
concepts.summary: Judge approximation algorithms by their provable ratio, as for vertex cover or metric TSP.
