concepts.name: Designing novel algorithms from structure
concepts.summary: Create new algorithms by modelling a problem as a graph, DP or divide-and-conquer structure and proving correctness and complexity.

concepts.name: Cache and real-world performance
concepts.summary: Evaluate how constants, cache locality and hybrid designs like introsort or Timsort make asymptotically equal algorithms differ in practice.

concepts.name: Advanced analysis techniques
concepts.summary: Apply and critique advanced tools such as potential functions, probabilistic analysis and smoothed analysis to bound running time.

concepts.name: Network flow and matching
concepts.summary: Create reductions of problems like assignment and cuts to maximum flow and analyse the resulting algorithms.

concepts.name: Randomized and parallel algorithm design
concepts.summary: Design randomized or parallel algorithms, specifying error probability or work and span tradeoffs.

misconceptions.text: NP-complete means a problem cannot be solved, so it is pointless to try.
Asymptotically faster algorithms always win in practice.
Randomized algorithms are unreliable because they may return wrong answers.

concepts.name: Elements of design
concepts.summary: Recognise and name the basic elements: line, shape, color, texture, space and form.

concepts.name: Principles of design
concepts.summary: Name the core principles such as balance, contrast, repetition, alignment, proximity and emphasis.

concepts.name: Alignment and proximity
concepts.summary: Explain how aligning items and grouping related items close together creates order and shows relationships.

concepts.name: Visual hierarchy
concepts.summary: Understand that size, weight and contrast guide the viewer to read some items before others.

concepts.name: Typeface categories
concepts.summary: Distinguish serif, sans serif, script and display typefaces and describe their general character.

concepts.name: Color wheel and hue
concepts.summary: Understand hue, primary, secondary and complementary colors and how they relate on the color wheel.

concepts.name: White space
concepts.summary: Explain that empty space gives content room to breathe and improves clarity.

misconceptions.text: Empty space is wasted and should be filled with content or decoration.
Using more fonts, colors and effects makes a design more interesting and professional.
Design is just about making things look pretty rather than communicating clearly.

concepts.name: Grid-based layout
concepts.summary: Build a layout using columns, margins and gutters so elements align consistently.

concepts.name: Type size and weight contrast
concepts.summary: Create a clear typographic hierarchy for headings, subheads and body text using size, weight and style.

concepts.name: Line length and leading
concepts.summary: Set comfortable line spacing and line length so body text is easy to read.

concepts.name: Font pairing
concepts.summary: Combine two typefaces with enough contrast and a shared feel, limiting the number used.

concepts.name: Color schemes
concepts.summary: Build palettes using monochromatic, analogous, complementary and neutral-plus-accent schemes.

concepts.name: Text and background contrast
concepts.summary: Choose text and background combinations with enough value contrast to be legible.

concepts.name: Balance types
concepts.summary: Distinguish symmetrical and asymmetrical balance and apply each to arrange visual weight.

concepts.name: Repetition and consistency
concepts.summary: Reuse styles, spacing and colors to unify a multi-element design such as a slide deck.

misconceptions.text: Any two colors that look good individually will work well together in a design.
Centering all text and elements is the safest way to get a balanced layout.
Bright, saturated colors on a colored background are always readable if they are different hues.

concepts.name: Gestalt grouping principles
concepts.summary: Analyse how similarity, closure, continuity and figure-ground shape how viewers perceive and group elements.

concepts.name: Reading patterns and flow
concepts.summary: Analyse how viewers' eyes move through a layout and arrange content to lead them along an intended path.

concepts.name: Focal point creation
concepts.summary: Establish a single clear focal point using scale, isolation, color or contrast.

concepts.name: Color meaning and context
concepts.summary: Analyse how color associations vary by audience and culture and fit palette choices to message and purpose.

concepts.name: Value and saturation control
concepts.summary: Adjust value and saturation to build depth, emphasis and a cohesive palette.

concepts.name: Composition frameworks
concepts.summary: Use rule of thirds, diagonals and similar frameworks to position elements in a composition.

concepts.name: Kerning, tracking and spacing
concepts.summary: Diagnose and correct spacing between letters, words and lines for display and body text.

concepts.name: Accessible color and type
concepts.summary: Evaluate designs for contrast ratios, color-blind safety and minimum text sizes.

misconceptions.text: Following the rule of thirds or golden ratio guarantees a good composition.
Each color has a universal meaning that works the same for every audience.
Making everything bold or large ensures that the important message gets noticed.

concepts.name: Design critique method
concepts.summary: Evaluate a design against its goals and audience, giving reasoned feedback rather than personal taste.

concepts.name: Brief-driven design decisions
concepts.summary: Derive layout, type and color choices from the objective, audience and context in a brief.

concepts.name: Rule-breaking with intent
concepts.summary: Judge when breaking alignment, balance or hierarchy conventions strengthens a message and when it harms it.

concepts.name: Systematic type scales
concepts.summary: Analyse and build type scales with consistent ratios that hold across sizes and formats.

concepts.name: Adapting across formats
concepts.summary: Adapt one design to varied sizes and media such as poster, social post and slide while preserving hierarchy.

concepts.name: Imagery and text integration
concepts.summary: Analyse how images, cropping, overlays and text interact to support or undermine legibility and message.

concepts.name: Cognitive load in visuals
concepts.summary: Evaluate how density, number of elements and competing cues affect comprehension, and simplify accordingly.

misconceptions.text: Design critique is about whether the critic personally likes the design.
Once the rules are learned, a good designer follows them strictly in every situation.
A layout that works at poster size can simply be scaled down for social media or slides.

concepts.name: Design systems thinking
concepts.summary: Create a coherent system of type, color, spacing and layout rules that scales across many pieces and designers.

concepts.name: Concept-driven visual language
concepts.summary: Originate a distinctive visual concept and language that expresses a message beyond conventional solutions.

concepts.name: Evaluating design effectiveness
concepts.summary: Judge a design's success using evidence such as user testing and outcome metrics, not just aesthetics.

concepts.name: Historical and cultural context
concepts.summary: Evaluate how movements such as Modernism, Swiss style and Bauhaus and cultural norms shape and justify choices.

concepts.name: Ethical and inclusive design
concepts.summary: Assess designs for misleading emphasis, exclusion and stereotyping, and adapt them for diverse audiences.

concepts.name: Synthesising constraints and trade-offs
concepts.summary: Resolve competing demands of brand, budget, medium, accessibility and message into a justified design solution.

concepts.name: Mentoring and critique leadership
concepts.summary: Develop critique frameworks and guidance that raise the quality of others' work and align teams on direction.

misconceptions.text: A design system is only a style guide that removes creativity.
Award-winning or visually striking designs are necessarily the most effective ones.
Good design is universal and independent of cultural and historical context.

concepts.name: Devanagari vowels and matras
concepts.summary: Recognise the independent vowels and explain how each attaches to a consonant as a matra sign.

concepts.name: Consonant grid and sounds
concepts.summary: Recall the consonants in their articulation groups and pronounce them, including aspirated and retroflex contrasts.

concepts.name: Inherent a and reading
concepts.summary: Understand that each consonant carries an inherent a and that this is sometimes dropped, so words are read as syllables.

concepts.name: Basic greetings and courtesies
concepts.summary: Remember and use common greetings, thanks and farewells appropriate to the situation.

concepts.name: Numbers one to hundred
concepts.summary: Recall the Hindi number words up to 100, which are largely irregular, and the Devanagari numerals.

concepts.name: Pronouns and hona present
concepts.summary: Understand the personal pronouns and form simple present sentences of identity and state with hona.

concepts.name: Anusvara chandrabindu and nukta
concepts.summary: Understand how nasalisation marks and the nukta dot change the sound of a letter.

misconceptions.text: Devanagari is an alphabet where each letter is a pure consonant or vowel, just like English.
Matras are separate letters written after the consonant in sound order.
Every consonant is always pronounced with its a sound, including at the end of words.

concepts.name: Conjunct consonant formation
concepts.summary: Read and write common conjuncts by combining half forms and stacked letters, including kshа, tra and gya.

concepts.name: Noun gender and number
concepts.summary: Identify masculine and feminine nouns by endings and form their plural and oblique forms.

concepts.name: Adjective agreement
concepts.summary: Make -a ending adjectives agree with the gender and number of the noun they describe.

concepts.name: Possessive postposition ka ki ke
concepts.summary: Choose ka, ki or ke according to the gender and number of the possessed noun.

concepts.name: Postpositions ko se mein par
concepts.summary: Use ko, se, mein and par after nouns to express location, direction, means and recipients.

concepts.name: Three-way honorific levels
concepts.summary: Select tu, tum or aap with the matching verb form according to relationship and setting.

concepts.name: Present habitual with karna
concepts.summary: Form habitual present sentences with karna and other verbs, agreeing with the subject's gender and number.

misconceptions.text: Postpositions come before the noun like English prepositions.
Ka, ki and ke agree with the possessor, like his and her in English.
Gender can be guessed from meaning, so all words for males are masculine and everything else follows English logic.

concepts.name: Ergative ne construction
concepts.summary: Analyse why transitive perfective verbs agree with the object rather than the subject when the subject takes ne.

concepts.name: Past and future tenses
concepts.summary: Form the simple past, past habitual and future tenses with correct agreement.

concepts.name: Oblique case before postpositions
concepts.summary: Apply oblique endings to nouns, adjectives and pronouns before postpositions, such as ladke ko and mujhe.

concepts.name: Progressive and perfect aspects
concepts.summary: Distinguish ongoing actions with rahna from completed ones and use present and past perfect forms.

concepts.name: Compound verbs
concepts.summary: Analyse how verbs such as dena, lena and jana add completion or direction to a main verb.

concepts.name: Dative experiencer constructions
concepts.summary: Explain how feelings, need and possession are expressed with the experiencer in ko or ke paas.

concepts.name: Subordinate clauses with ki and jo
concepts.summary: Build complex sentences using ki, jo-woh and jab-tab, and analyse their word order.

misconceptions.text: With ne, the verb agrees with the subject as in other tenses.
Ne is used with the subject in every past tense sentence.
Mujhe chahiye is a direct translation of I want, so the speaker is the grammatical subject.

concepts.name: Subjunctive and conditional moods
concepts.summary: Distinguish real, hypothetical and counterfactual conditions and select the proper verb forms.

concepts.name: Passive and impersonal forms
concepts.summary: Analyse passive sentences with jana and capability or inability forms such as likha nahin jata.

concepts.name: Register and Hindi-Urdu variation
concepts.summary: Evaluate Sanskrit-derived versus Persian-Arabic vocabulary and judge the register that fits a context.

concepts.name: Colloquial speech and Bollywood idiom
concepts.summary: Interpret informal contractions, slang, code-mixing and dialogue conventions in films and songs.

concepts.name: Causative and derived verbs
concepts.summary: Analyse how verb stems form transitive and causative pairs like banna, banana, banwana.

concepts.name: Discourse particles and emphasis
concepts.summary: Evaluate the effect of particles hi, bhi, to and word order on emphasis and tone.

concepts.name: Idioms and proverbs
concepts.summary: Interpret common muhavare and proverbs and choose them appropriately in speech.

misconceptions.text: Hindi and Urdu differ only in script, so register differences do not matter.
Filmi Hindi is a reliable model for everyday polite speech.
Particles like hi and bhi are filler that does not change meaning.

concepts.name: Stylistic choice across genres
concepts.summary: Evaluate how diction, syntax and register differ across news, poetry, film and conversation and justify choices.

concepts.name: Literary and poetic forms
concepts.summary: Assess meter, imagery and traditional forms such as doha and ghazal in Hindi literature.

concepts.name: Translation and cultural adaptation
concepts.summary: Produce translations that preserve tone, honorific level and cultural reference rather than literal wording.

concepts.name: Dialect and language contact
concepts.summary: Evaluate how Awadhi, Braj, Bhojpuri and English shape standard Hindi, and judge code-switching norms.

concepts.name: Original writing and speech
concepts.summary: Compose original essays, dialogues or scripts with register control, idiom and natural rhythm.

concepts.name: Orthographic and normative issues
concepts.summary: Judge disputes over spelling, nukta use, anusvara versus nasal consonant and loanword adoption using normative sources.

misconceptions.text: Standard Hindi is a single uniform language and dialects are just incorrect speech.
A good translation maps each Hindi word to one English word.
Using English words in Hindi always signals poor command of the language.

concepts.name: Hiragana character set
concepts.summary: Recall the 46 basic hiragana, their sounds, and their stroke order, including dakuten and handakuten variants.

concepts.name: Katakana character set
concepts.summary: Recall the katakana characters and recognise their use for loanwords, foreign names and emphasis.

concepts.name: Mora-based pronunciation rhythm
concepts.summary: Understand that Japanese is timed in morae and distinguish long vowels, geminate consonants and contracted sounds like kya.

concepts.name: Basic sentence order
concepts.summary: Explain that the verb or predicate comes at the end of the sentence and that subjects and objects are often omitted.

concepts.name: Copula desu sentences
concepts.summary: Understand how to state and identify things with X wa Y desu and form simple questions with ka.

concepts.name: Core topic and object particles
concepts.summary: Understand the basic roles of wa for topic, wo for object and no for possession.

concepts.name: Greetings and set phrases
concepts.summary: Remember everyday expressions such as konnichiwa, arigatou gozaimasu and sumimasen and when they are used.

concepts.name: Numbers and basic kanji
concepts.summary: Recall numbers up to 10,000 and a first set of simple kanji such as the digits, day, month and person.

misconceptions.text: Japanese is written with a single script where every character is a word.
The particle wa is read and written as ha in every word.
Long vowels and short vowels are interchangeable because they sound almost the same.

concepts.name: Polite verb conjugation
concepts.summary: Conjugate verbs into present, past and negative masu forms and use them in polite sentences.

concepts.name: Verb groups and dictionary form
concepts.summary: Classify verbs as ichidan, godan or irregular and derive the dictionary form from the masu stem.

concepts.name: Location and direction particles
concepts.summary: Choose ni, de, he and to correctly for time, place of existence, place of action, destination and companions.

concepts.name: Existence verbs aru and iru
concepts.summary: Use aru for inanimate and iru for animate existence with correct particles to describe locations.

concepts.name: I-adjectives and na-adjectives
concepts.summary: Conjugate both adjective types in present, past and negative and connect them to nouns.

concepts.name: Te-form basics
concepts.summary: Form the te-form for each verb group and use it for requests, sequencing and the progressive teiru.

concepts.name: Basic counters
concepts.summary: Use common counters such as tsu, nin, mai and hon with numbers and the correct sound changes.

concepts.name: Kanji readings introduction
concepts.summary: Distinguish on'yomi from kun'yomi readings and read common N5 kanji in simple compounds.

misconceptions.text: Wa and ga are interchangeable and mean the same thing.
Every verb ending in -eru or -iru is an ichidan verb.
Counters can be replaced by the plain number and a noun as in English.

concepts.name: Wa versus ga contrast
concepts.summary: Analyse when wa marks a known or contrasted topic and ga marks new information or the focus of the sentence.

concepts.name: Plain form and casual speech
concepts.summary: Use plain forms of verbs and adjectives in casual speech and in embedded clauses.

concepts.name: Nai-form and ta-form patterns
concepts.summary: Apply the nai and ta forms in patterns such as nakereba naranai and tara conditionals.

concepts.name: Conditional forms comparison
concepts.summary: Distinguish to, ba, tara and nara conditionals by nuance, and choose the appropriate one.

concepts.name: Relative clauses
concepts.summary: Analyse and build clauses that modify nouns using plain forms, with ga replacing wa inside the clause.

concepts.name: Potential and passive forms
concepts.summary: Form and use potential, passive and causative forms of each verb group, noting object particle changes.

concepts.name: Giving and receiving verbs
concepts.summary: Analyse the direction of benefit expressed by ageru, kureru and morau and their te-form uses.

concepts.name: Kanji compound reading strategies
concepts.summary: Infer readings of kanji compounds from on'yomi and kun'yomi patterns and recognise common exceptions.

misconceptions.text: Ga marks the subject and wa marks the subject too, so the choice is only a matter of style.
Tara, ba, to and nara conditionals can always be swapped without a change in meaning.
The passive form is used only when the subject is harmed, as in English passive voice.

concepts.name: Keigo system structure
concepts.summary: Analyse the three keigo categories of respectful, humble and polite speech and who each raises or lowers.

concepts.name: Honorific and humble verb forms
concepts.summary: Choose between special verbs like irassharu and mairu and productive patterns like o-V ni naru and o-V suru for a given context.

concepts.name: Uchi-soto social perspective
concepts.summary: Evaluate how in-group and out-group relations decide the keigo level, including speaking about one's own family to outsiders.

concepts.name: Formal written grammar patterns
concepts.summary: Analyse N3 to N2 patterns such as wake, hazu, ni tsuite and ni yotte and distinguish their nuance.

concepts.name: Modality and evidential expressions
concepts.summary: Evaluate the evidential strength of souda, rashii, you da and mitai to select the most accurate expression.

concepts.name: Kanji vocabulary at N2 level
concepts.summary: Analyse the structure of abstract compounds and use radicals and components to deduce meaning of unfamiliar kanji.

concepts.name: Causative-passive and nuance verbs
concepts.summary: Analyse the causative-passive and aspectual auxiliaries like te shimau and te oku for implied attitude.

misconceptions.text: Keigo means adding more polite words, so using the honorific form for oneself is the most respectful choice.
Masu form alone is enough for every formal or business situation.
Souda, rashii, you da and mitai are all synonyms for it seems.

concepts.name: Register and style shifting
concepts.summary: Evaluate and manage shifts between plain, polite, honorific and written registers to fit the relationship, medium and intent.

concepts.name: Literary and classical grammar remnants
concepts.summary: Evaluate how forms like nari, beki and zu survive in modern writing, proverbs and formal documents.

concepts.name: Pragmatics of indirectness
concepts.summary: Evaluate how hedging, omission and sentence-final particles convey stance and avoid direct refusal.

concepts.name: Authentic text analysis
concepts.summary: Evaluate dense news, essays and literature by resolving implied subjects, nominalisations and long modification chains.

concepts.name: Idiomatic and mimetic expression
concepts.summary: Create natural expression using onomatopoeia, idioms and four-character compounds appropriate to context.

concepts.name: Composing formal and business writing
concepts.summary: Compose emails, reports and persuasive essays with correct keigo, conventional openings and cohesive structure.

concepts.name: Dialect and variation awareness
concepts.summary: Evaluate regional dialects, gendered and generational speech and decide when to understand versus produce them.

misconceptions.text: Mastering JLPT N1 vocabulary and patterns means a learner can write and speak naturally in every context.
Textbook Japanese is the standard form that every native speaker uses in daily conversation.
Ambiguity and omission in Japanese are signs of vague thinking and should be replaced with explicit subjects in all writing.

concepts.name: Shell and prompt
concepts.summary: Recognise the shell as a text interface that reads commands and shows output, and read the parts of a prompt.

concepts.name: Filesystem directory tree
concepts.summary: Explain that files live in a single tree rooted at / with directories nested inside, including the home directory.

concepts.name: Absolute and relative paths
concepts.summary: Distinguish paths starting at / from paths relative to the current directory, and use . and .. correctly.

concepts.name: Navigation commands
concepts.summary: Use pwd, ls and cd to find where you are, list contents and move between directories.

concepts.name: Command structure
concepts.summary: Describe a command as a program name followed by options and arguments, such as ls -l /etc.

concepts.name: Getting help
concepts.summary: Look up a command's usage with man and --help and find key facts in the output.

misconceptions.text: Linux commands and file names are not case sensitive, so File.txt and file.txt are the same file.
The cd command changes directory only for the single command that follows it.
A leading slash on a path is optional and makes no difference to where it points.

concepts.name: File and directory manipulation
concepts.summary: Create, copy, move, rename and delete files and directories with mkdir, touch, cp, mv and rm.

concepts.name: Viewing file contents
concepts.summary: Choose cat, less, head or tail to read all or part of a text file.

concepts.name: Wildcards and globbing
concepts.summary: Use *, ? and [ ] patterns so the shell expands them to matching file names.

concepts.name: Permission bits
concepts.summary: Read the read, write and execute bits for owner, group and others in ls -l output.

concepts.name: Changing permissions
concepts.summary: Use chmod with symbolic and octal modes to grant or remove access on files.

concepts.name: Redirection basics
concepts.summary: Send command output to files with > and >>, and read input from files with <.

concepts.name: Pipes
concepts.summary: Connect the output of one command to the input of another using |.

concepts.name: Searching text with grep
concepts.summary: Find lines matching a pattern in files or piped input using grep and common flags.

misconceptions.text: rm moves files to a trash folder from which they can be restored.
Using > to redirect output appends to the file rather than overwriting it.
Wildcards such as * are interpreted by each command, not by the shell.

concepts.name: Standard streams and file descriptors
concepts.summary: Redirect stdout and stderr separately or together using 2>, 2>&1 and /dev/null.

concepts.name: Text-processing filters
concepts.summary: Combine sort, uniq, cut, tr and wc in pipelines to summarise and reshape text data.

concepts.name: Shell variables and environment
concepts.summary: Set shell variables, export them to child processes, and explain how PATH resolves commands.

concepts.name: Quoting and expansion
concepts.summary: Predict how single quotes, double quotes, variable expansion and $(...) change what a command receives.

concepts.name: Script structure and execution
concepts.summary: Write a script with a shebang line, make it executable, and run it with arguments $1, $2 and $@.

concepts.name: Conditionals and loops
concepts.summary: Use if, test expressions, for and while to branch and repeat in scripts.

concepts.name: Exit status
concepts.summary: Interpret exit codes and chain commands with && and || based on success or failure.

concepts.name: Process management
concepts.summary: List processes, run jobs in the background, and stop them with kill and signals.

misconceptions.text: Single and double quotes behave identically in the shell.
Redirecting with > also captures error messages.
A variable set in a shell is automatically visible to every program it starts.

concepts.name: Regular expressions in tools
concepts.summary: Compose basic and extended regular expressions and judge which match a given text.

concepts.name: Stream editing with sed and awk
concepts.summary: Transform text with sed substitutions and awk field-based programs, choosing the right tool.

concepts.name: Robust find and xargs usage
concepts.summary: Select files by name, type, size or time with find and act on them safely, including names with spaces.

concepts.name: Defensive scripting options
concepts.summary: Evaluate how set -e, -u and pipefail change failure handling and decide when to use them.

concepts.name: Functions and argument handling
concepts.summary: Structure scripts with functions, local variables and option parsing for reusable tools.

concepts.name: Special permissions and ownership
concepts.summary: Analyse setuid, setgid, sticky bit, umask and chown effects on shared file access.

concepts.name: Scheduling and automation
concepts.summary: Schedule recurring tasks with cron, accounting for its minimal environment and logging.

misconceptions.text: Shell globs and regular expressions use the same syntax, so * means the same in both.
Piping find output into xargs is always safe regardless of file names.
set -e makes a script stop on every possible error in every context.

concepts.name: Script security hardening
concepts.summary: Assess scripts for injection, unsafe temp files, unquoted expansion and privilege risks, and fix them.

concepts.name: Advanced shell features
concepts.summary: Judge when to use process substitution, here documents, arrays and traps for cleanup.

concepts.name: Pipeline performance design
concepts.summary: Evaluate pipeline designs for speed and memory, avoiding needless processes and large intermediate files.

concepts.name: Portable shell scripting
concepts.summary: Distinguish POSIX sh from Bash-specific features and decide what portability a script requires.

concepts.name: Command-line tool design
concepts.summary: Design composable tools with clear interfaces, stdin and stdout use, exit codes and usage text.

concepts.name: Automation framework creation
concepts.summary: Create tested, logged and idempotent automation that combines scripts, scheduling and error reporting.

concepts.name: Diagnosing with system tools
concepts.summary: Diagnose misbehaving processes and scripts using tools such as strace, lsof, top and journal logs.

misconceptions.text: A script that works in Bash will work in any shell that runs it.
Quoting variables is only a style choice and never affects security.
Shell pipelines are always the best choice for any data processing task regardless of scale.

concepts.name: Image versus container
concepts.summary: Explain that an image is a read-only packaged template and a container is a running (or stopped) instance created from it.

concepts.name: Pulling and listing images
concepts.summary: Recall how to fetch an image from a registry by name and tag and list local images.

concepts.name: Running a container
concepts.summary: Understand that docker run creates and starts a container from an image and runs its default command.

concepts.name: Container lifecycle commands
concepts.summary: Remember the commands to list, stop, start and remove containers and distinguish running from stopped ones.

concepts.name: Image tags
concepts.summary: Understand that a tag labels a version of an image in the form repository:tag and that omitting it defaults to latest.

concepts.name: Dockerfile as build recipe
concepts.summary: Understand that a Dockerfile is a text file of instructions from which docker build produces an image.

misconceptions.text: A container is a full virtual machine with its own kernel.
Stopping a container deletes it.
The latest tag always points to the newest version of an image.

concepts.name: Core Dockerfile instructions
concepts.summary: Write a Dockerfile using FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN and EXPOSE to package a simple application.

concepts.name: CMD versus ENTRYPOINT
concepts.summary: Apply CMD for overridable default commands and ENTRYPOINT for the fixed executable, and predict how arguments to docker run combine with them.

concepts.name: Building and tagging images
concepts.summary: Run docker build with a tag and build context to produce a named image.

concepts.name: Port mapping
concepts.summary: Use -p host:container to make a containerized service reachable from the host.

concepts.name: Environment variables and run options
concepts.summary: Use flags to run detached, name containers, remove on exit and pass environment variables.

concepts.name: Bind mounts and volumes
concepts.summary: Persist or share data by mounting a host directory or a named volume into a container.

concepts.name: Logs and exec inspection
concepts.summary: Use docker logs and docker exec to see output and run commands inside a running container.

misconceptions.text: Data written inside a container persists after the container is removed.
EXPOSE in a Dockerfile publishes the port to the host.
CMD and ENTRYPOINT are interchangeable and behave the same.

concepts.name: Layers and build cache
concepts.summary: Analyse how each instruction creates a layer and how cache invalidation propagates to later layers, then order instructions to maximise reuse.

concepts.name: Multi-stage builds
concepts.summary: Separate build and runtime stages so only needed artifacts are copied into a small final image.

concepts.name: Bridge networks and name resolution
concepts.summary: Explain how containers on a user-defined bridge network reach each other by name and how this differs from the default bridge.

concepts.name: Compose service definitions
concepts.summary: Describe multi-container applications in a compose file with image or build, ports, environment, volumes and depends_on.

concepts.name: Compose lifecycle commands
concepts.summary: Start, stop, rebuild and tear down a compose project, including removing volumes deliberately.

concepts.name: Dockerignore and context size
concepts.summary: Exclude unneeded files from the build context to speed builds and avoid leaking files into images.

concepts.name: Publishing to Docker Hub
concepts.summary: Log in, tag an image with a repository name and push it to Docker Hub so others can pull it.

concepts.name: Debugging failing containers
concepts.summary: Diagnose crashes using logs, exit codes, inspect output and interactive shells.

misconceptions.text: depends_on guarantees the dependency service is ready to accept connections.
Deleting a file in a later RUN layer shrinks the image.
Containers must use localhost to reach other containers on the same network.

concepts.name: Image size and layer optimisation
concepts.summary: Evaluate base image choices and layer strategies to trade off size, build speed and debuggability.

concepts.name: Secrets and configuration handling
concepts.summary: Judge where configuration belongs among ARG, ENV, env files and secrets, and avoid baking credentials into layers.

concepts.name: Non-root and least privilege
concepts.summary: Assess and reduce risk by running as a non-root user, dropping capabilities and using read-only filesystems.

concepts.name: Health checks and restart policies
concepts.summary: Analyse how health checks and restart policies affect availability and startup ordering in compose.

concepts.name: Compose environments and overrides
concepts.summary: Structure compose files with overrides, profiles and variable substitution for dev and production differences.

concepts.name: Signal handling and PID 1
concepts.summary: Explain why exec-form commands and init handling matter for receiving SIGTERM and shutting down cleanly.

concepts.name: Tagging and versioning strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate tagging schemes and digest pinning for reproducibility and safe rollbacks.

misconceptions.text: Secrets passed with ARG or deleted in a later layer are safe from image inspection.
Processes in containers run as an unprivileged user by default.
Shell-form CMD handles SIGTERM just as well as exec form.

concepts.name: Reproducible and cacheable CI builds
concepts.summary: Design build pipelines with cache mounts, remote cache and pinned inputs for fast, deterministic images.

concepts.name: Supply chain integrity
concepts.summary: Evaluate provenance, scanning, signing and base image trust policies for images entering production.

concepts.name: Multi-architecture images
concepts.summary: Create images that run on several CPU architectures using multi-platform builds and manifests.

concepts.name: Isolation internals
concepts.summary: Evaluate the guarantees and limits of container isolation based on namespaces, cgroups and shared kernel, and set resource limits accordingly.

concepts.name: Storage and network driver trade-offs
concepts.summary: Judge when to use volumes, tmpfs, host or macvlan networking and understand copy-on-write storage costs.

concepts.name: Container platform design standards
concepts.summary: Create team standards and templated Dockerfiles and compose setups that balance security, size and developer experience.

concepts.name: Moving beyond single-host Docker
concepts.summary: Evaluate when compose on one host stops being sufficient and what must change to move to an orchestrator.

misconceptions.text: Containers provide the same isolation strength as virtual machines.
Scanning an image once at build time keeps it secure over its lifetime.
An image built on one CPU architecture runs unchanged on any other.

concepts.name: HTML elements and attributes
concepts.summary: Recognise that HTML marks up content with opening and closing tags, nested elements and attributes such as href, src and alt.

concepts.name: Document skeleton structure
concepts.summary: Explain the roles of the doctype, html, head and body and what belongs in each.

concepts.name: Text content elements
concepts.summary: Choose headings, paragraphs, lists, links and images to mark up basic content correctly.

concepts.name: CSS rule syntax
concepts.summary: Read and explain a rule made of a selector and declarations of property and value pairs.

concepts.name: Linking CSS to HTML
concepts.summary: Name the three ways to apply CSS and recognise the link element for external stylesheets.

concepts.name: Basic selectors
concepts.summary: Understand how element, class and id selectors pick which elements a rule applies to.

concepts.name: Common text and color properties
concepts.summary: Recall properties that change color, font, size and background of elements.

misconceptions.text: HTML is used to control the visual design of a page, such as colors and layout.
Headings should be chosen by how big they look rather than by their meaning.
Content in the head element is displayed on the page.

concepts.name: Semantic page elements
concepts.summary: Apply header, nav, main, section, article, aside and footer to give a page meaningful structure.

concepts.name: Box model
concepts.summary: Use content, padding, border and margin to size and space elements and predict their rendered size.

concepts.name: Block and inline display
concepts.summary: Explain how block, inline and inline-block elements flow and which properties apply to each.

concepts.name: Forms and inputs
concepts.summary: Build a form with labelled inputs, buttons and appropriate input types.

concepts.name: Cascade and specificity
concepts.summary: Predict which declaration wins using source order, specificity and inheritance.

concepts.name: Combinators and pseudo-classes
concepts.summary: Write selectors using descendant and child combinators and states like :hover and :focus.

concepts.name: CSS units and values
concepts.summary: Distinguish absolute and relative units and choose among them for sizes and colors.

concepts.name: Accessible images and links
concepts.summary: Write useful alt text and descriptive link text for images and links.

misconceptions.text: The width property sets the total visible width of an element including padding and border.
An id selector and class selector have the same weight, so the last rule always wins.
Semantic elements like section and nav look different by default, so they are only for styling.

concepts.name: Flexbox layout
concepts.summary: Lay out items in a row or column using flex direction, alignment, wrapping and gap.

concepts.name: Flex item sizing
concepts.summary: Analyse how grow, shrink and basis distribute free space among flex items.

concepts.name: CSS Grid layout
concepts.summary: Define two-dimensional layouts with grid tracks, fr units, gaps and item placement.

concepts.name: Positioning and stacking
concepts.summary: Analyse how position values, containing blocks and stacking order place elements.

concepts.name: Media queries
concepts.summary: Adapt styles to viewport conditions with media queries and the viewport meta tag.

concepts.name: Mobile-first responsive approach
concepts.summary: Structure CSS from a small-screen base with fluid widths and flexible images, adding enhancements at larger sizes.

concepts.name: Margin collapsing and normal flow
concepts.summary: Diagnose spacing problems caused by margin collapse and normal flow behavior.

concepts.name: Choosing flex or grid
concepts.summary: Compare flexbox and grid and select the right one for a given layout problem.

misconceptions.text: Flexbox and grid are interchangeable and grid is simply a newer replacement for flexbox.
Position absolute places an element relative to the page regardless of its ancestors.
Responsive design means building a separate mobile site with media queries only.

concepts.name: Custom properties and theming
concepts.summary: Use custom properties with inheritance to build maintainable themes and design tokens.

concepts.name: Fluid sizing functions
concepts.summary: Use clamp, min, max and viewport units to create fluid type and spacing with fewer breakpoints.

concepts.name: Advanced grid patterns
concepts.summary: Build intrinsically responsive grids with auto-fit, minmax and named areas.

concepts.name: CSS architecture and naming
concepts.summary: Evaluate methods for organising CSS so specificity stays low and styles remain scalable.

concepts.name: Accessible markup and ARIA
concepts.summary: Evaluate pages for keyboard access, contrast, landmarks and appropriate use of ARIA.

concepts.name: Transitions and animations
concepts.summary: Apply transitions and keyframe animations of cheap properties while respecting reduced motion preferences.

concepts.name: Responsive images and media
concepts.summary: Serve appropriate image sources with srcset, sizes and picture, avoiding layout shift.

concepts.name: Container and modern selectors
concepts.summary: Judge when container queries and selectors like :has or :where give better component-level styling than viewport queries.

misconceptions.text: ARIA attributes should be added everywhere to make a page accessible.
Animating any property is equally cheap for browser performance.
Using more specific selectors and !important is the right way to manage overrides in large stylesheets.

concepts.name: Rendering pipeline and performance
concepts.summary: Evaluate how CSS and HTML choices affect parsing, layout, paint and compositing and so page speed.

concepts.name: Design system architecture
concepts.summary: Design a scalable CSS system of tokens, layers and component patterns shared across projects.

concepts.name: Intrinsic and algorithmic layout
concepts.summary: Create layouts that adapt from content and available space through min-content, max-content and flexible primitives.

concepts.name: Internationalisation and logical properties
concepts.summary: Evaluate and build layouts that work across writing directions using logical properties.

concepts.name: Cross-browser and progressive enhancement
concepts.summary: Judge support trade-offs and design fallbacks using feature queries and progressive enhancement.

concepts.name: Accessibility auditing strategy
concepts.summary: Plan and evaluate audits combining automated checks, keyboard and screen reader testing against standards.

concepts.name: Advanced CSS engineering patterns
concepts.summary: Create robust cascade strategies using layers, scoping and low-specificity conventions for large codebases.

misconceptions.text: Minified or fewer CSS rules alone determine page performance, regardless of render-blocking and layout cost.
Passing an automated accessibility checker means a page is accessible.
Physical properties like left and margin-left are sufficient for any international site.

concepts.name: Artificial neuron and weights
concepts.summary: Explain that a neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias and passes it through a nonlinearity.

concepts.name: Layers and network depth
concepts.summary: Describe how stacking input, hidden and output layers lets a network build progressively more abstract features.

concepts.name: Activation functions
concepts.summary: Explain why nonlinear activations such as ReLU, sigmoid and tanh are needed and how their output ranges differ.

concepts.name: Loss function
concepts.summary: Understand that a loss measures prediction error and that training aims to minimise it, e.g. cross-entropy or mean squared error.

concepts.name: Forward pass
concepts.summary: Recall that a forward pass computes layer by layer from input to prediction.

concepts.name: Training by gradient descent
concepts.summary: Understand that weights are repeatedly nudged opposite the gradient of the loss, scaled by a learning rate.

concepts.name: Backpropagation idea
concepts.summary: Describe backpropagation as applying the chain rule backward to get the gradient of the loss for every weight.

misconceptions.text: A neural network with more layers is always more accurate.
Stacking layers without activation functions still gives a more powerful model than a single layer.
Backpropagation is the algorithm that updates the weights.

concepts.name: Mini-batch SGD and epochs
concepts.summary: Train a model with mini-batches, setting batch size and number of epochs and reading the resulting loss curves.

concepts.name: Tensors and autograd
concepts.summary: Use a framework such as PyTorch to build tensors, compute gradients automatically and apply optimiser steps.

concepts.name: Training loop structure
concepts.summary: Write a loop with forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimiser step and gradient reset, plus separate evaluation mode.

concepts.name: Overfitting and validation curves
concepts.summary: Diagnose overfitting from diverging training and validation loss and apply early stopping.

concepts.name: Convolution and pooling layers
concepts.summary: Apply convolutional filters, stride, padding and pooling to image tensors and compute output shapes.

concepts.name: Softmax and cross-entropy
concepts.summary: Turn logits into class probabilities with softmax and train classifiers with cross-entropy loss.

concepts.name: Weight initialisation
concepts.summary: Understand why random, scaled initial weights are needed to break symmetry and keep signals stable.

concepts.name: Using GPUs for training
concepts.summary: Move models and data to a GPU and understand why parallel matrix operations speed training.

misconceptions.text: Training loss going down means the model is getting better in general.
Initialising all weights to zero is a safe default.
Softmax outputs are calibrated probabilities that can be trusted as certainty.

concepts.name: Vanishing and exploding gradients
concepts.summary: Analyse how repeated multiplication through depth shrinks or inflates gradients and choose remedies such as ReLU, init and clipping.

concepts.name: Batch normalisation
concepts.summary: Apply normalisation layers, and handle their different behaviour in training versus evaluation mode.

concepts.name: Dropout and weight decay
concepts.summary: Apply dropout and weight decay to reduce overfitting and tune their strength.

concepts.name: Adaptive optimisers and schedules
concepts.summary: Compare SGD with momentum and Adam, and use learning rate schedules and warmup.

concepts.name: CNN architecture patterns
concepts.summary: Analyse how depth, receptive field and skip connections shape CNN design and trainability.

concepts.name: Transfer learning and fine-tuning
concepts.summary: Reuse a pretrained network by freezing layers or fine-tuning for a new dataset.

concepts.name: Recurrent networks and LSTMs
concepts.summary: Analyse how recurrence and gated memory cells process sequences and mitigate gradient problems.

concepts.name: Data augmentation and pipelines
concepts.summary: Build input pipelines with batching, shuffling and augmentation to improve generalisation.

misconceptions.text: Dropout and batch normalisation behave the same during training and inference.
Adam always outperforms SGD and needs no learning rate tuning.
LSTMs completely eliminate vanishing gradients and long-range dependency problems.

concepts.name: Self-attention mechanism
concepts.summary: Analyse how queries, keys and values yield context-weighted representations and why scaling and softmax matter.

concepts.name: Transformer block design
concepts.summary: Dissect transformer blocks including multi-head attention, feed-forward layers, residuals, normalisation and positional information.

concepts.name: Encoder, decoder and masking
concepts.summary: Distinguish encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder models and the role of causal and padding masks.

concepts.name: Pretraining and fine-tuning paradigms
concepts.summary: Evaluate masked and autoregressive pretraining objectives and adaptation methods such as fine-tuning and parameter-efficient tuning.

concepts.name: Tokenisation and embeddings
concepts.summary: Analyse how subword tokenisation and learned embeddings represent text for neural models.

concepts.name: Training diagnostics and debugging
concepts.summary: Judge causes of training failure from loss, gradient norms and activations, and verify with sanity checks.

concepts.name: Mixed precision and multi-GPU training
concepts.summary: Analyse memory and throughput tradeoffs of mixed precision, gradient accumulation and data-parallel training.

concepts.name: Model evaluation and ablation
concepts.summary: Evaluate architectural choices with controlled ablations, appropriate metrics and multiple seeds.

misconceptions.text: Self-attention inherently understands word order without positional information.
Transformers are strictly better than CNNs and RNNs on any task and data size.
Attention weights are a faithful explanation of why a model made its prediction.

concepts.name: Scaling laws and compute tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Evaluate how loss scales with parameters, data and compute and decide allocations for a given budget.

concepts.name: Efficient attention and long context
concepts.summary: Judge approaches to reduce quadratic attention cost and memory, including caching and sparse or linear variants.

concepts.name: Generative model families
concepts.summary: Compare autoregressive, latent-variable, adversarial and diffusion generative models by objective, quality and stability.

concepts.name: Novel architecture design
concepts.summary: Design architectures whose inductive biases match a problem's structure, such as equivariance or modality fusion.

concepts.name: Large-scale distributed training
concepts.summary: Design a training setup combining data, tensor and pipeline parallelism and sharding for models that exceed one device.

concepts.name: Generalisation and optimisation theory
concepts.summary: Evaluate explanations for why overparameterised networks generalise, including flat minima and double descent.

concepts.name: Robustness and distribution shift
concepts.summary: Assess model vulnerability to adversarial and shifted inputs and choose mitigations and evaluation protocols.

concepts.name: Alignment and preference tuning
concepts.summary: Create pipelines that adapt pretrained models to human preferences and critique their failure modes.

misconceptions.text: Scaling up model size alone will reliably fix reasoning and robustness failures.
Classical bias-variance reasoning implies overparameterised networks must overfit.
Adversarial robustness comes for free with higher clean accuracy.

concepts.name: Macronutrient types and roles
concepts.summary: Name carbohydrates, proteins and fats and state the main job of each in the body.

concepts.name: Calories as energy units
concepts.summary: Explain that calories measure the energy food provides and that bodies need a steady supply to function.

concepts.name: Vitamins and minerals
concepts.summary: Recognise that vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for body processes and come from varied foods.

concepts.name: Water and hydration
concepts.summary: Explain why the body needs water and recognise signs of poor hydration such as thirst and dark urine.

concepts.name: Food groups
concepts.summary: List the main food groups and give examples of foods in each.

concepts.name: Dietary fibre
concepts.summary: Describe what fibre is, which foods contain it and why it supports digestion.

misconceptions.text: All fats are bad for you and should be avoided completely.
Calories are something harmful in food rather than a measure of energy.
Only thirst tells you that you need water, and only plain water counts toward hydration.

concepts.name: Reading nutrition labels
concepts.summary: Find serving size, calories and nutrient amounts on a label and compute totals for the portion actually eaten.

concepts.name: Energy balance equation
concepts.summary: Explain how intake versus expenditure leads to weight gain, loss or maintenance.

concepts.name: Types of carbohydrate
concepts.summary: Distinguish sugars, starches and fibre and choose foods accordingly in everyday meals.

concepts.name: Fat types and sources
concepts.summary: Classify foods by main fat type and prefer unsaturated sources over saturated and trans fats.

concepts.name: Protein sources and quality
concepts.summary: Describe essential amino acids and identify animal and plant protein sources.

concepts.name: Key vitamins and minerals
concepts.summary: Match important nutrients such as iron, calcium, vitamin C and vitamin D to foods and functions.

concepts.name: Balanced plate building
concepts.summary: Assemble a meal with appropriate proportions of vegetables, protein, starch and fat.

misconceptions.text: A product labelled low fat is automatically healthy or low in calories.
The nutrition panel values describe the whole package rather than one serving.
All carbohydrates are equally unhealthy and should be cut out.

concepts.name: Estimating energy needs
concepts.summary: Estimate basal metabolic rate and total daily energy expenditure from body size, age and activity level.

concepts.name: Setting macronutrient targets
concepts.summary: Set protein, carbohydrate and fat ranges suited to a person's goal and activity.

concepts.name: Glycaemic response and carbohydrate quality
concepts.summary: Analyse how food composition, fibre and processing affect blood glucose response.

concepts.name: Meal planning for goals
concepts.summary: Build a multi-day meal plan that meets energy and nutrient targets within budget and preferences.

concepts.name: Dietary pattern comparison
concepts.summary: Compare dietary patterns by foods emphasised, nutrient strengths and likely gaps.

concepts.name: Nutrient gaps and deficiencies
concepts.summary: Identify nutrients at risk in particular diets or life stages and the foods that address them.

concepts.name: Hydration and electrolytes
concepts.summary: Apply fluid and electrolyte guidance to exercise, heat and illness situations.

misconceptions.text: Calorie needs calculated from a formula are exact and never need adjusting.
Low glycaemic index foods are always healthy and high glycaemic index foods always unhealthy.
A vegetarian or vegan diet is inherently deficient or inherently complete without planning.

concepts.name: Appraising nutrition evidence
concepts.summary: Judge nutrition studies by design, confounding, outcomes measured and funding.

concepts.name: Evaluating popular diet claims
concepts.summary: Assess diets such as low-carb, keto and intermittent fasting for mechanism, evidence and sustainability.

concepts.name: Adaptive thermogenesis and weight regulation
concepts.summary: Analyse how metabolism, appetite hormones and activity adapt to weight change and shape plateaus.

concepts.name: Nutrient timing and sports fuelling
concepts.summary: Evaluate fuelling, protein and recovery strategies for different training demands.

concepts.name: Supplement efficacy and safety
concepts.summary: Weigh evidence, dose, interactions and regulation to decide when a supplement is justified.

concepts.name: Ultra-processed food and satiety
concepts.summary: Analyse how processing, energy density and palatability influence intake and health outcomes.

concepts.name: Nutrition for health conditions
concepts.summary: Evaluate dietary adjustments for conditions such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol.

misconceptions.text: Any weight loss plateau means the person is miscounting or lacking willpower, not that physiology adapted.
Supplements are harmless because they are natural and can fill any dietary gap.
A single observational study showing an association proves a food causes or prevents disease.

concepts.name: Synthesising conflicting nutrition evidence
concepts.summary: Reconcile discordant trials, cohorts and meta-analyses into calibrated, hedged conclusions.

concepts.name: Individualised nutrition design
concepts.summary: Design a complete plan integrating physiology, medical history, preferences, culture and constraints.

concepts.name: Behaviour change in dietary practice
concepts.summary: Create strategies that sustain dietary change using adherence, environment and motivation principles.

concepts.name: Critiquing dietary guidelines
concepts.summary: Evaluate how guidelines are built, their evidence limits, and industry or policy influences.

concepts.name: Nutrigenomics and microbiome limits
concepts.summary: Judge the current strength and practical value of genetic and microbiome based dietary advice.

concepts.name: Food systems and sustainability tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Develop dietary recommendations that balance nutrient adequacy, environmental impact, cost and access.

misconceptions.text: Personalised nutrition based on DNA or microbiome tests reliably predicts the best diet for an individual.
Official dietary guidelines are purely objective summaries of settled science.
The diet that performs best in trials on average is the best choice for every client.

issues: nov-3 'Vitamins and minerals' and adb-6 'Key vitamins and minerals' are near-duplicates; the novice concept is generic and the advanced one overlaps it.
nov-3 prerequisite from nov-5 is fine, but nov-4 hydration and nov-6 fibre have no links; adb-3 should build on nov-6 fibre.
adb-5 is Bloom C2 and adb-2 is C2, which is allowed, but adb-5 lacks a dependency on food groups for sources.
cmp-6 depends on cmp-5 which is weak; nutrient gaps rely mainly on adb-6. cmp-7 should depend on nov-4 hydration, which is missing.
prf-6 is prerequisite-linked to adb-1 only; it should build on cmp-3 or cmp-5 and relates to energy balance (adb-2).
prf-3 misconception is stated oddly as an absolute but acceptable; exp-2 prerequisites omit prf-1/exp-1 evidence base, which is an obvious dependency.
