concepts.name: Decision, options and criteria
concepts.summary: Identify the decision to be made, the available options and the criteria that matter for judging them.

concepts.name: Risk versus uncertainty
concepts.summary: Explain that outcomes of a choice are not certain and distinguish known probabilities from unknown ones.

concepts.name: Pros and cons listing
concepts.summary: Use a simple pros and cons list to compare options and explain its limits when items differ in importance.

concepts.name: Reversible versus irreversible choices
concepts.summary: Tell apart decisions that can be undone cheaply from those that cannot and explain why this affects how much care to take.

concepts.name: Opportunity cost
aliases: cost of the next best alternative
concepts.summary: Explain that choosing one option means giving up the value of the best alternative forgone.

concepts.name: Outcome versus decision quality
concepts.summary: Recognise that a good decision can have a bad outcome through luck and vice versa.

concepts.name: Common bias names
concepts.summary: Recall and describe in plain words anchoring, sunk cost and overconfidence as ways judgment goes wrong.

misconceptions.text: A good decision is one that turns out well.
Choosing to do nothing has no cost.
A pros and cons list with more pros than cons means that option should win.

concepts.name: Estimating probabilities
concepts.summary: Assign rough numeric probabilities to outcomes using base rates and available evidence.

concepts.name: Expected value calculation
concepts.summary: Compute the expected value of an option by multiplying each outcome's payoff by its probability and summing.

concepts.name: Drawing a decision tree
concepts.summary: Lay out decision nodes, chance nodes and payoffs in a tree for a simple choice.

concepts.name: Weighted decision matrix
concepts.summary: Score options against weighted criteria and total the results to compare them.

concepts.name: Basic cost-benefit comparison
concepts.summary: List and put money values on costs and benefits of an option and compare net benefit.

concepts.name: Sunk cost recognition
concepts.summary: Spot past unrecoverable costs in a situation and exclude them from the forward-looking choice.

concepts.name: Anchoring in estimates
concepts.summary: Notice how a first number shapes later estimates and apply simple countermeasures such as forming an estimate before seeing others.

misconceptions.text: The option with the highest expected value is always the right choice.
Weights and scores in a decision matrix are objective facts rather than judgments.
Money already spent should count in deciding whether to continue.

concepts.name: Utility and risk attitude
concepts.summary: Analyse why expected utility can differ from expected value and how diminishing marginal utility explains risk aversion.

concepts.name: Multi-stage decision trees
concepts.summary: Solve trees with sequential decisions by folding back from the final payoffs to the first choice.

concepts.name: Sensitivity analysis
concepts.summary: Vary probabilities, weights and payoffs to find which inputs change the preferred option.

concepts.name: Regret and minimax analysis
concepts.summary: Build a regret table and compare it with maximin and maximax when probabilities are unknown.

concepts.name: Discounting and time value
concepts.summary: Adjust costs and benefits occurring at different times to present value in cost-benefit analysis.

concepts.name: Pre-mortem technique
concepts.summary: Run a pre-mortem by assuming the plan failed and listing the likely causes to find weaknesses before committing.

concepts.name: Calibration and overconfidence
concepts.summary: Analyse the gap between stated confidence and actual accuracy and use interval estimates and track records to correct it.

concepts.name: Value of information
concepts.summary: Judge whether gathering more information is worth its cost by estimating how much it could change the decision.

misconceptions.text: Risk aversion is irrational because it departs from maximising expected value.
A sensitivity analysis is only needed if you doubt your best estimates.
Feeling very sure about an estimate means it is likely to be accurate.

concepts.name: Framing and prospect theory
concepts.summary: Analyse how gain versus loss framing, reference points and loss aversion shift choices away from expected utility.

concepts.name: Decision under deep uncertainty
concepts.summary: Choose between approaches such as robustness, scenario planning and option preservation when probabilities cannot be credibly assigned.

concepts.name: Real options and reversibility
concepts.summary: Evaluate the value of keeping options open, staging commitments and delaying irreversible choices.

concepts.name: Bayesian updating of beliefs
concepts.summary: Revise probability estimates in a decision model as new evidence arrives, respecting base rates.

concepts.name: Multi-criteria trade-offs
concepts.summary: Critique and select methods for combining conflicting criteria, including rank reversal and weight-elicitation problems.

concepts.name: Group decision pitfalls
concepts.summary: Analyse how groupthink, authority and shared-information bias degrade group decisions and how structured methods counter them.

concepts.name: Decision process evaluation
concepts.summary: Assess decision quality separately from outcomes using records of reasoning, assumptions and forecasts.

misconceptions.text: Biases can be removed by simply knowing about them.
When probabilities are unknown, any numeric estimate is as good as none and analysis is pointless.
Delaying a decision to keep options open is always the safer choice.

concepts.name: Choosing decision methods
concepts.summary: Judge which technique fits a given decision's stakes, uncertainty, time and data, including when to use heuristics instead of formal analysis.

concepts.name: Heuristics and ecological rationality
concepts.summary: Evaluate when simple rules outperform complex models and when they systematically mislead.

concepts.name: Designing decision architecture
concepts.summary: Design organisational procedures, defaults, checklists and review gates that reduce bias and noise in recurring decisions.

concepts.name: Noise and judgment variability
concepts.summary: Distinguish noise from bias in repeated judgments and apply practices such as independent assessment and structured scoring to reduce it.

concepts.name: Modelling strategic interaction
concepts.summary: Assess decisions where others respond to your choice by incorporating their incentives and likely reactions.

concepts.name: Tail risk and ruin avoidance
concepts.summary: Evaluate choices where rare catastrophic losses make expected-value reasoning misleading and impose survival constraints.

concepts.name: Building a decision framework
concepts.summary: Create a tailored end-to-end framework combining framing, modelling, pre-mortem, review and learning loops for a domain.

misconceptions.text: More elaborate quantitative models always yield better decisions than simple rules.
Inconsistency between different people's judgments is just diversity of views, not a flaw.
Maximising expected value is safe for any repeated gamble regardless of possible ruin.

concepts.name: Native versus cross-platform apps
concepts.summary: Explain how native, cross-platform and web-based apps differ and what trade-offs each brings for a simple app.

concepts.name: App project structure
concepts.summary: Identify the main parts of a mobile project: source code, resources, manifest or configuration, and build files.

concepts.name: Screens and UI components
concepts.summary: Describe how a screen is composed from components such as text, buttons, images and input fields.

concepts.name: Emulators and device testing
concepts.summary: Recall how to run and view an app on an emulator, simulator or physical phone.

concepts.name: App lifecycle states
concepts.summary: Explain that an app moves between running, background and terminated states and why this matters on phones.

concepts.name: Touch input and events
concepts.summary: Understand how taps and gestures on components trigger event handlers in code.

concepts.name: Platform ecosystems and SDKs
concepts.summary: Name the main platforms, their languages and IDEs, and the role of the SDK.

misconceptions.text: A mobile app runs continuously like a desktop program once it has been opened.
An app written for Android will run unchanged on iOS.
Testing in an emulator is enough to know the app works on real phones.

concepts.name: Layout containers and constraints
concepts.summary: Arrange components with rows, columns and constraints so a screen looks right at different sizes.

concepts.name: Screen navigation stack
concepts.summary: Move between screens, pass data to them and handle the back action using a navigation stack.

concepts.name: Component state and re-rendering
concepts.summary: Hold changing values in state and update the screen when that state changes.

concepts.name: Lists and adapters
concepts.summary: Display scrollable collections efficiently by binding data items to reusable row views.

concepts.name: Lifecycle callbacks
concepts.summary: Place setup and cleanup code in the correct lifecycle callbacks of a screen or app.

concepts.name: Simple local persistence
concepts.summary: Save and reload small settings or values using the platform's key-value storage.

concepts.name: Fetching remote data
concepts.summary: Call a REST endpoint asynchronously, parse the JSON and show the result on screen.

misconceptions.text: Changing a variable that holds screen data automatically updates what the user sees.
Network calls can be made on the main UI thread without noticeable effect.
Data kept in memory survives the app being closed or the screen being rotated.

concepts.name: Architecture patterns for apps
concepts.summary: Separate UI, presentation logic and data access, and analyse how a pattern such as MVVM organises responsibilities.

concepts.name: Runtime permissions
concepts.summary: Request and handle permissions for camera, location or notifications, including denial and rationale flows.

concepts.name: Device sensors and hardware APIs
concepts.summary: Use device features such as location or camera through platform APIs while managing battery and privacy cost.

concepts.name: Structured local databases
concepts.summary: Model, store and query structured data locally with a database layer and schema migrations.

concepts.name: Concurrency and async work
concepts.summary: Run network and disk work off the main thread and diagnose problems such as race conditions and UI freezes.

concepts.name: Repository and offline caching
concepts.summary: Combine remote and local sources behind a repository so the app works with poor or no connectivity.

concepts.name: Handling errors and loading states
concepts.summary: Represent loading, success, empty and failure states and show appropriate feedback to the user.

concepts.name: Push and local notifications
concepts.summary: Implement notifications and understand how a push message reaches a device through the platform service.

misconceptions.text: Putting all logic in the screen class is fine because the app is small.
If the user denies a permission, the app can ask again as often as it likes and the feature still must work.
Offline support just means catching the network error and showing a message.

concepts.name: Performance profiling and optimisation
concepts.summary: Use profilers to find slow rendering, memory leaks and excess work, and fix their causes.

concepts.name: Authentication and secure storage
concepts.summary: Evaluate sign-in flows and choose secure storage for tokens and sensitive data on the device.

concepts.name: Automated testing strategy
concepts.summary: Decide what to cover with unit, integration and UI tests and judge the cost and reliability of each.

concepts.name: Build variants and CI/CD
concepts.summary: Configure environments, signing and automated builds so releases are repeatable.

concepts.name: Adaptive and accessible design
concepts.summary: Judge how well a design supports tablets, screen readers, dynamic text size and multiple languages.

concepts.name: Store release and review compliance
concepts.summary: Prepare listings, privacy declarations and staged rollouts, and analyse common causes of review rejection.

concepts.name: Crash reporting and analytics
concepts.summary: Instrument an app to analyse crashes and user behaviour while respecting privacy.

concepts.name: Dependency injection and modularity
concepts.summary: Assess how injecting dependencies and splitting modules improves testability and build times.

misconceptions.text: Storing tokens in ordinary preferences is safe because other apps cannot read app storage.
Performance tuning should be done up front on every screen rather than guided by profiling.
Accessibility and localisation can be added at the end without redesign.

concepts.name: Cross-platform strategy design
concepts.summary: Evaluate native, shared-logic and fully cross-platform approaches against product, team and performance constraints.

concepts.name: Scalable app architecture design
concepts.summary: Design an app architecture that lets many teams ship features independently with clear boundaries.

concepts.name: Offline sync and conflict resolution
concepts.summary: Create a synchronisation design that handles conflicts, retries and partial failure between device and server.

concepts.name: Release engineering and feature flags
concepts.summary: Create a release process using flags, staged rollouts and rollback to reduce risk of shipping.

concepts.name: Mobile security threat modelling
concepts.summary: Assess threats such as tampering, insecure transport and data leakage, and judge which defences are worth their cost.

concepts.name: Platform evolution and migration
concepts.summary: Judge when and how to adopt new OS APIs and migrate legacy code without breaking users.

concepts.name: Energy and resource budgeting
concepts.summary: Evaluate background work, networking and sensor use against battery, data and OS restrictions across a device range.

misconceptions.text: A cross-platform framework always lowers cost compared with native development.
Last-write-wins is an adequate sync strategy for any data.
Obfuscation and certificate pinning make an app's secrets safe on the device.

concepts.name: Continuous integration idea
concepts.summary: Explain that CI means merging changes often and automatically building and testing each one to catch problems early.

concepts.name: Delivery versus deployment
concepts.summary: Distinguish continuous delivery, where releases are ready to ship on demand, from continuous deployment, where every passing change goes live automatically.

concepts.name: Pipeline stages and jobs
concepts.summary: Describe a pipeline as an ordered series of stages made of jobs, such as build, test and deploy, each passing or failing.

concepts.name: Pipeline triggers
concepts.summary: Recall the events that start a pipeline, such as a push, a pull request, a tag or a schedule.

concepts.name: Build artifacts
concepts.summary: Explain that an artifact is the packaged output of a build, such as a binary or container image, that later stages test and deploy.

concepts.name: Pipeline as code
concepts.summary: Understand that the pipeline is defined in a versioned file kept in the repository alongside the code.

concepts.name: Runners and agents
concepts.summary: Recall that pipeline jobs execute on runners, which are separate machines or containers, not on the developer's laptop.

misconceptions.text: A green pipeline means the software has no bugs.
Continuous delivery and continuous deployment are the same thing.
CI is just a tool you install rather than a practice of merging and verifying changes frequently.

concepts.name: Writing a basic pipeline file
concepts.summary: Write a working pipeline definition with triggers, jobs and steps that checks out code, builds it and runs the tests.

concepts.name: Automated test gating
concepts.summary: Configure the pipeline so failing tests or lint checks stop later stages and block merging.

concepts.name: Storing and passing artifacts
concepts.summary: Publish build outputs and pass them between jobs so the same artifact tested is the one deployed.

concepts.name: Dependency caching
concepts.summary: Cache downloaded dependencies with keys based on lockfiles to speed up runs without stale results.

concepts.name: Pipeline environment variables
concepts.summary: Use variables to configure jobs and keep environment-specific values out of the pipeline logic.

concepts.name: Basic secrets handling
concepts.summary: Store credentials in the CI system's secret store, inject them at runtime and keep them out of the repository and logs.

concepts.name: Reading pipeline logs
concepts.summary: Locate the failing step in a run's logs and reproduce the failure locally to fix it.

misconceptions.text: It is safe to commit secrets to the repository if the repository is private.
Caching always makes builds faster and never causes incorrect results.
Masking a secret in logs makes it impossible to leak.

concepts.name: Multi-environment promotion
concepts.summary: Design a pipeline that promotes one built artifact through environments, with per-environment configuration and approvals.

concepts.name: Deployment strategies
concepts.summary: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments in terms of downtime, risk and resource cost, and pick one for a case.

concepts.name: Rollback mechanisms
concepts.summary: Implement rollback by redeploying a previous artifact and decide when rolling forward is better.

concepts.name: Build once, deploy many
concepts.summary: Analyse why rebuilding per environment breaks traceability and how immutable, versioned artifacts avoid this.

concepts.name: Pipeline parallelism and matrices
concepts.summary: Run independent jobs in parallel and use matrices to test across versions or platforms while managing total run time.

concepts.name: Test pyramid in pipelines
concepts.summary: Analyse where unit, integration and end-to-end tests belong in the pipeline to balance speed and confidence.

concepts.name: Flaky test handling
concepts.summary: Diagnose intermittent failures and decide to fix, quarantine or retry them without eroding trust in the pipeline.

concepts.name: Containerised build and deploy
concepts.summary: Build a container image in the pipeline, tag it by version or commit and push it to a registry for deployment.

misconceptions.text: Rebuilding the code for each environment is fine because it is the same source.
Rollback is always just redeploying the old version, even when database schema changes are involved.
Automatically retrying flaky tests until they pass solves the flakiness.

concepts.name: Pipeline security hardening
concepts.summary: Evaluate pipeline risks such as untrusted pull request code, over-privileged tokens and compromised dependencies, and apply least privilege.

concepts.name: Short-lived credentials
concepts.summary: Analyse why short-lived, identity-based credentials are safer than long-lived stored keys and how pipelines obtain them.

concepts.name: Progressive delivery with feature flags
concepts.summary: Evaluate using feature flags and staged exposure to separate deployment from release and limit blast radius.

concepts.name: Automated release verification
concepts.summary: Judge which health checks and metrics should gate a release and trigger automatic rollback.

concepts.name: Database migration in pipelines
concepts.summary: Analyse how to apply schema changes safely using backward-compatible expand and contract steps.

concepts.name: Pipeline performance optimisation
concepts.summary: Analyse the critical path of a pipeline and cut feedback time through caching, test selection and parallelism.

concepts.name: Artifact provenance and signing
concepts.summary: Evaluate how signing, provenance records and dependency scanning establish trust in what is deployed.

concepts.name: Reusable pipeline templates
concepts.summary: Analyse how to share and version pipeline logic across repositories without hindering team autonomy.

misconceptions.text: Running pipelines only on trusted branches removes the need to worry about pipeline security.
Deploying a feature to production and releasing it to users must be the same event.
A database migration can be rolled back as simply as application code.

concepts.name: Delivery performance metrics
concepts.summary: Evaluate a delivery process using deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and recovery time, and avoid gaming them.

concepts.name: Pipeline architecture design
concepts.summary: Design pipeline architecture for many services and teams, covering monorepo change detection, dependency ordering and shared infrastructure.

concepts.name: GitOps and declarative delivery
concepts.summary: Evaluate pull-based, reconciled deployment from a Git source of truth against push-based pipelines.

concepts.name: Governance and compliance automation
concepts.summary: Create controls such as policy checks, approvals and audit evidence that satisfy compliance without slowing delivery.

concepts.name: Resilient release engineering
concepts.summary: Design release processes that bound blast radius, support multi-region rollout and improve from incident learnings.

concepts.name: CI/CD platform trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate hosted versus self-hosted runners, tooling and cost against security, scale and maintenance needs.

concepts.name: Pipeline reliability engineering
concepts.summary: Evaluate and improve pipeline reliability and observability by treating the delivery system as a product with its own objectives.

misconceptions.text: Maximising deployment frequency alone shows a healthy delivery process.
GitOps is just a CI/CD pipeline with a different name and removes the need for any pipeline.
Strict manual approvals for every release are the best way to guarantee compliance and safety.

concepts.name: Main asset classes
concepts.summary: Name and describe stocks, bonds and cash equivalents and how each makes money for an owner.

concepts.name: Risk and return trade-off
concepts.summary: Explain why higher expected returns generally come with greater uncertainty and possible losses.

concepts.name: Investment funds
concepts.summary: Explain that a fund pools many investors' money to hold a basket of assets, and distinguish index funds from actively managed funds.

concepts.name: Compound growth
concepts.summary: Understand how returns earn further returns over time and why starting early matters.

concepts.name: Saving versus investing
concepts.summary: Distinguish keeping money safe for near-term needs from investing it for long-term goals, and explain inflation's role.

concepts.name: Investment time horizon
concepts.summary: Define time horizon as the time until money is needed and recall that it shapes which investments suit a goal.

misconceptions.text: Investing is the same as gambling or picking winning stocks.
Money in a savings account is risk-free in every sense, so it is the best place for long-term money.
You need a large sum of money to start investing.

concepts.name: Diversification
concepts.summary: Apply the idea of spreading money across many assets so one failure does not sink the portfolio.

concepts.name: Fund fees and expense ratios
concepts.summary: Calculate how annual fees reduce returns over decades and compare the cost of funds.

concepts.name: Asset allocation
concepts.summary: Choose a split between stocks, bonds and cash that fits a goal and time horizon.

concepts.name: Investment accounts and tax wrappers
concepts.summary: Explain the purpose of general brokerage and tax-advantaged accounts and choose an appropriate one for a goal.

concepts.name: Market volatility and drawdowns
concepts.summary: Understand that prices fluctuate, that declines are normal, and that markets have historically recovered over long periods.

concepts.name: Regular contributions and dollar-cost averaging
concepts.summary: Set up automatic recurring investments and explain how they spread out purchase prices.

concepts.name: Bond basics: yield and maturity
concepts.summary: Describe coupons, maturity and credit quality, and why bond prices fall when interest rates rise.

misconceptions.text: Owning many different funds always means a portfolio is well diversified.
A fee of 1 percent a year is trivial and does not matter much.
Bonds are completely safe and cannot lose value.

concepts.name: Portfolio construction from goals
concepts.summary: Design a simple diversified portfolio of low-cost funds matched to specific goals, horizons and risk tolerance.

concepts.name: Risk tolerance versus risk capacity
aliases: willingness vs ability to take risk
concepts.summary: Distinguish emotional comfort with losses from financial ability to absorb them, and use both to set allocation.

concepts.name: Rebalancing strategies
concepts.summary: Restore target weights using calendar or threshold rules and new contributions, accounting for costs and taxes.

concepts.name: Return decomposition and real returns
concepts.summary: Break returns into price change and income, and adjust for inflation and fees to judge actual growth.

concepts.name: Tax-efficient asset location
concepts.summary: Analyse which holdings suit taxable versus tax-advantaged accounts to reduce tax drag.

concepts.name: Correlation and diversification benefit
concepts.summary: Analyse how assets that do not move together reduce portfolio volatility, and when correlations rise.

concepts.name: Behavioural biases in investing
concepts.summary: Identify loss aversion, herding, overconfidence and recency bias in one's own decisions and set rules to counter them.

misconceptions.text: Risk tolerance is only how you feel about losses, so your financial situation does not matter.
Rebalancing is meant to boost returns rather than control risk.
Last year's best-performing fund is the best choice going forward.

concepts.name: Evaluating active versus passive
concepts.summary: Judge the evidence on active manager performance after fees and decide when active strategies might be justified.

concepts.name: Factor and style exposures
concepts.summary: Analyse a portfolio's tilts toward factors such as value, size or quality and what they imply for risk and returns.

concepts.name: Sequence-of-returns risk and withdrawals
concepts.summary: Evaluate withdrawal strategies and how the order of returns affects portfolio longevity in retirement.

concepts.name: Risk-adjusted performance measures
concepts.summary: Use Sharpe ratio, standard deviation and maximum drawdown to compare investments and portfolios critically.

concepts.name: Valuation and expected returns
concepts.summary: Evaluate how starting valuations and risk premiums inform realistic long-run return assumptions.

concepts.name: Glide paths and lifecycle allocation
concepts.summary: Assess how allocation should shift over a lifetime given human capital, goals and target-date fund designs.

concepts.name: Bond duration and credit risk
concepts.summary: Analyse how duration, credit quality and inflation affect bond fund behaviour and its role in a portfolio.

misconceptions.text: A higher Sharpe ratio or past return proves a manager has skill rather than luck.
Factor premiums are guaranteed to pay off over any reasonable period.
A safe withdrawal rate based on average returns will work regardless of when you retire.

concepts.name: Critiquing portfolio theory assumptions
concepts.summary: Evaluate the assumptions and limits of mean-variance optimisation and efficient markets, including fat tails and regime change.

concepts.name: Designing an investment policy
concepts.summary: Create a complete policy covering allocation, rebalancing, tax, withdrawal and behavioural rules tailored to a client's circumstances.

concepts.name: Total-wealth and liability-driven planning
concepts.summary: Construct portfolios that integrate human capital, housing, pensions and future liabilities with matching assets.

concepts.name: Assessing alternatives and complex products
concepts.summary: Judge the costs, risks, liquidity and complexity of products such as leveraged funds, private assets and crypto before including any.

concepts.name: Stress testing and tail risk
concepts.summary: Evaluate a portfolio's resilience using historical scenarios and simulations and recognise their model limits.

concepts.name: Advice quality and conflicts of interest
concepts.summary: Evaluate advice, products and marketing for incentives, hidden costs and evidence quality.

concepts.name: Adapting strategy to regime shifts
concepts.summary: Develop principled responses to shifts in inflation, rates or market structure without abandoning a disciplined plan.

misconceptions.text: Sophisticated optimisation or complex products reliably beat a simple diversified portfolio.
Monte Carlo or backtest results give accurate probabilities of future outcomes.
Changing strategy to match each macro forecast is a sign of expertise rather than risk.

concepts.name: Levels of body organization
concepts.summary: Name the levels from cells to tissues, organs, organ systems and the whole organism, and give an example of each.

concepts.name: Major organ systems and roles
concepts.summary: Describe in one sentence the main job of each major organ system, such as circulatory, respiratory, digestive, skeletal and nervous.

concepts.name: Skeleton and joints
concepts.summary: Identify major bones and joint types and explain that the skeleton supports, protects and allows movement.

concepts.name: Muscle types and movement
concepts.summary: Distinguish skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle and explain how muscles pull on bones to move the body.

concepts.name: Heart and blood circuit
concepts.summary: Explain that the heart pumps blood through arteries, capillaries and veins to deliver oxygen and nutrients and carry away wastes.

concepts.name: Breathing and gas exchange
concepts.summary: Trace air from nose to alveoli and explain that oxygen enters the blood while carbon dioxide leaves.

concepts.name: Digestive tract path
concepts.summary: List the organs food passes through from mouth to anus and state what each mainly does.

concepts.name: Homeostasis as stable internal conditions
concepts.summary: Explain that the body keeps conditions such as temperature and blood sugar within a narrow range.

misconceptions.text: Air we breathe goes into the stomach or directly into the blood as whole breaths.
Veins always carry deoxygenated blood and arteries always carry oxygenated blood.
Muscles can push bones as well as pull them.

concepts.name: Heart chambers and valves
concepts.summary: Describe the four chambers, the valves and the pulmonary and systemic circuits and follow blood through them.

concepts.name: Blood components and functions
concepts.summary: Relate red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma to oxygen transport, defence and clotting.

concepts.name: Ventilation mechanics
concepts.summary: Apply the roles of the diaphragm, intercostal muscles and pressure changes to explain inhalation and exhalation.

concepts.name: Digestion and absorption sites
concepts.summary: Match enzymes and organs (salivary glands, stomach, pancreas, liver, small intestine) to the nutrients they break down and where absorption occurs.

concepts.name: Nephron filtration and urine formation
concepts.summary: Outline how kidneys filter blood, reabsorb useful substances and excrete urea and excess water as urine.

concepts.name: Skin layers and functions
concepts.summary: Name epidermis, dermis and hypodermis and link them to protection, sensation and temperature control.

concepts.name: Nervous and endocrine signalling
concepts.summary: Contrast fast electrical nerve signals with slower hormonal signals carried in blood, using examples.

concepts.name: Simple negative feedback loops
concepts.summary: Apply the sensor, control centre and effector pattern to examples such as body temperature.

misconceptions.text: Most digestion and nutrient absorption happens in the stomach.
The right side of the heart carries blood to the body and the left side to the lungs.
Lungs inflate themselves by actively pulling in air with their own muscle.

concepts.name: Cardiac cycle and conduction
concepts.summary: Explain systole, diastole, valve action and the SA node to AV node to Purkinje conduction sequence and link them to an ECG.

concepts.name: Blood pressure regulation
concepts.summary: Analyse how cardiac output, vessel resistance and baroreceptor reflexes determine blood pressure.

concepts.name: Gas transport and oxygen dissociation
concepts.summary: Analyse how hemoglobin loads and unloads oxygen and how CO2 is carried, including effects of pH and temperature.

concepts.name: Muscle contraction mechanism
concepts.summary: Explain sliding filaments, calcium and ATP use, and the neuromuscular junction in contraction.

concepts.name: Hormone axes and glands
concepts.summary: Analyse hypothalamus-pituitary-target gland axes and the actions of insulin, glucagon, thyroid hormones and cortisol.

concepts.name: Nephron transport and fluid balance
concepts.summary: Analyse filtration, reabsorption and secretion along the nephron and how ADH and aldosterone adjust urine.

concepts.name: Innate and adaptive immunity
concepts.summary: Compare nonspecific defences with B and T cell responses, antibodies and immune memory, and the role of lymph nodes.

concepts.name: Reproductive systems and cycles
concepts.summary: Describe male and female reproductive anatomy and apply hormonal control of gametogenesis, ovulation and the menstrual cycle.

misconceptions.text: Hormones act on every cell, so target specificity does not matter.
Antibiotics strengthen the immune system and work against viruses.
Muscle contraction shortens the filaments themselves.

concepts.name: Integrated cardiovascular-renal control
concepts.summary: Analyse how the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, ADH and the heart together defend blood pressure and volume.

concepts.name: Acid-base balance mechanisms
concepts.summary: Analyse how buffers, respiration and the kidneys together hold blood pH near 7.4 and interpret respiratory versus metabolic disturbances.

concepts.name: Exercise and stress responses
concepts.summary: Analyse how sympathetic activation and hormones redistribute blood flow, ventilation and metabolism during exercise and stress.

concepts.name: Glucose and energy homeostasis
concepts.summary: Evaluate how insulin, glucagon and the liver regulate blood glucose and judge what goes wrong in type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

concepts.name: Positive feedback and feedforward control
concepts.summary: Distinguish positive feedback in childbirth and clotting from negative feedback and explain anticipatory control.

concepts.name: Pathophysiology from organ dysfunction
concepts.summary: Evaluate how failure in one organ, such as heart failure or kidney disease, cascades to other systems.

concepts.name: Immune dysregulation and tolerance
concepts.summary: Evaluate how loss of self-tolerance or overreaction produces autoimmunity, allergy and immunodeficiency.

concepts.name: Interpreting physiological measurements
concepts.summary: Interpret ECG, spirometry, blood gases and urinalysis to infer the state of organ systems.

misconceptions.text: Homeostasis means variables are held constant rather than regulated around a set point with fluctuations.
Type 2 diabetes is simply a lack of insulin, same as type 1.
Positive feedback is always harmful to the body.

concepts.name: Systems-level modelling of regulation
concepts.summary: Build models of multi-organ regulation including gain, delay and oscillation and predict responses to perturbation.

concepts.name: Evaluating physiological evidence
concepts.summary: Judge the quality of human and animal physiology studies, including limits of extrapolating across species and populations.

concepts.name: Variation across age and sex
concepts.summary: Evaluate how development, ageing, pregnancy and sex differences alter normal ranges and regulatory set points.

concepts.name: Adaptation and acclimatization
concepts.summary: Evaluate short and long-term adaptations to altitude, heat, training and disuse and distinguish their mechanisms.

concepts.name: Multi-system differential reasoning
concepts.summary: Weigh competing physiological explanations for a complex presentation across several organ systems and justify the most likely.

concepts.name: Designing physiological interventions
concepts.summary: Design interventions or experiments that target a feedback loop and anticipate compensatory responses and side effects.

concepts.name: Teaching integrated physiology
concepts.summary: Create coherent explanations and teaching models that connect structure, mechanism and regulation across systems.

misconceptions.text: Normal reference ranges apply identically to all people regardless of age, sex or conditions.
Animal model results transfer directly to humans.
Correcting one abnormal variable with a treatment has no knock-on effects because feedback loops are independent.

concepts.name: Cargo project workflow
concepts.summary: Create, build, run and check a Rust project with Cargo and explain what Cargo.toml and the src directory hold.

concepts.name: Immutable bindings and mutability
concepts.summary: Explain that variables are immutable by default and use mut to allow reassignment.

concepts.name: Scalar and compound types
concepts.summary: Recall integer, float, bool and char types plus tuples and fixed-size arrays, and how Rust infers types.

concepts.name: Functions and expressions
concepts.summary: Write functions with typed parameters and return values and explain that the last expression without a semicolon is returned.

concepts.name: Control flow constructs
concepts.summary: Use if as an expression and choose between loop, while and for over ranges.

concepts.name: Ownership and move semantics
concepts.summary: State the rules that each value has one owner, ownership moves on assignment, and the value is dropped when the owner goes out of scope.

concepts.name: String and &str
concepts.summary: Distinguish the owned, growable String from the borrowed string slice &str.

misconceptions.text: Assigning a String to another variable copies it so both remain usable.
A semicolon at the end of the last line of a function makes no difference to what it returns.
Variables in Rust are mutable like in most languages and mut is only a hint.

concepts.name: Shared and mutable references
concepts.summary: Borrow values with & and &mut and apply the rule of many readers or one writer.

concepts.name: Structs and impl blocks
concepts.summary: Define structs and implement methods and associated functions taking self, &self or &mut self.

concepts.name: Enums and pattern matching
concepts.summary: Model variants with data in enums and handle them exhaustively with match and if let.

concepts.name: Option and Result basics
concepts.summary: Represent absence and failure with Option and Result and unpack them with match, unwrap_or and the ? operator.

concepts.name: Vec and HashMap collections
concepts.summary: Store, iterate and update data in Vec and HashMap while respecting ownership of the elements.

concepts.name: Slices
concepts.summary: Borrow a contiguous part of a collection or string as a slice without copying.

concepts.name: Modules and visibility
concepts.summary: Organise code into modules, control visibility with pub and bring items into scope with use.

concepts.name: Copy versus Clone
concepts.summary: Explain which types are copied implicitly and when an explicit clone is needed.

misconceptions.text: A reference works like a C pointer, so any number of mutable references to the same value may exist at once.
Calling unwrap is the normal way to handle an Option or Result.
Cloning a value is free, so it is the right fix for every borrow checker error.

concepts.name: Lifetime annotations
concepts.summary: Annotate functions and structs with lifetime parameters to relate the validity of references and apply elision rules.

concepts.name: Traits and implementations
concepts.summary: Define traits with required and default methods and implement them for your own types.

concepts.name: Generics with trait bounds
concepts.summary: Write generic functions and types constrained by trait bounds and analyse how they compile to specialised code.

concepts.name: Custom error types
concepts.summary: Design error enums implementing Display and Error with From conversions so the ? operator propagates them.

concepts.name: Iterators and closures
concepts.summary: Compose map, filter and collect pipelines and analyse how closures capture their environment.

concepts.name: Smart pointers Box and Rc
concepts.summary: Choose Box for heap allocation and recursive types and Rc for shared ownership within a single thread.

concepts.name: Unit and integration tests
concepts.summary: Write unit tests in modules and integration tests in the tests directory and run them with cargo test.

concepts.name: Cargo dependencies and features
concepts.summary: Add crates, manage Cargo.lock and workspaces and toggle optional features.

misconceptions.text: Lifetime annotations extend how long a value lives.
Generics in Rust are resolved at runtime like virtual dispatch, so they cost performance.
Iterator adapters like map do work immediately and allocate a new collection at each step.

concepts.name: Interior mutability patterns
concepts.summary: Analyse when Cell and RefCell move borrow checking to runtime and combine them with Rc safely.

concepts.name: Threads and message passing
concepts.summary: Spawn threads, move data into them and coordinate with channels.

concepts.name: Shared state with Arc and Mutex
concepts.summary: Share mutable state across threads with Arc and Mutex and reason about contention and deadlock.

concepts.name: Send and Sync marker traits
concepts.summary: Explain how Send and Sync encode thread-safety at compile time and determine which types satisfy them.

concepts.name: Trait objects and dynamic dispatch
concepts.summary: Evaluate trait objects against generics in terms of flexibility, performance and object-safety limits.

concepts.name: Async and await model
concepts.summary: Explain how futures are polled by a runtime and decide when async fits I/O-bound services.

concepts.name: Advanced trait features
concepts.summary: Use associated types, default generic parameters, supertraits and the orphan rule to design coherent APIs.

concepts.name: Profiling and release optimisation
concepts.summary: Measure performance with release builds and benchmarks and judge which optimisations are justified.

misconceptions.text: Rust's type system prevents all concurrency bugs, including deadlocks and logic races.
RefCell bypasses the borrow rules so they no longer apply.
Async code runs on multiple threads automatically and is always faster than threads.

concepts.name: Unsafe Rust and invariants
concepts.summary: Judge when unsafe is justified and state the invariants a safe wrapper must uphold to avoid undefined behaviour.

concepts.name: Foreign function interface
concepts.summary: Evaluate and build safe bindings to C libraries handling layout, ownership and error boundaries.

concepts.name: Declarative and procedural macros
concepts.summary: Create macros that remove boilerplate while keeping errors clear and hygiene intact.

concepts.name: Library API design
concepts.summary: Design public crate APIs with ergonomic types, stable semver guarantees and sensible error and trait choices.

concepts.name: Pin and self-referential futures
concepts.summary: Evaluate why pinning is needed for async state machines and apply it correctly in custom futures.

concepts.name: Memory model and atomics
concepts.summary: Choose atomic memory orderings and judge whether lock-free designs are worth their complexity.

concepts.name: Verifying unsafe code
concepts.summary: Assess the soundness of unsafe code with Miri, fuzzing and property tests.

concepts.name: Embedded and no_std design
concepts.summary: Architect libraries that work without the standard library, relying on core and optional alloc.

misconceptions.text: Unsafe code turns off the borrow checker and all of Rust's safety rules inside the block.
If code with unsafe compiles and passes tests, it is sound.
Relaxed atomic ordering is always safe and fastest, so it can be used everywhere.

concepts.name: Sample space and outcomes
concepts.summary: List all possible outcomes of a simple experiment such as a coin toss, die roll or card draw.

concepts.name: Events as outcome subsets
concepts.summary: Describe an event as a subset of the sample space and identify which outcomes belong to it.

concepts.name: Classical probability formula
concepts.summary: Compute probability as favourable outcomes divided by total equally likely outcomes and explain why.

concepts.name: Probability scale and complement
concepts.summary: Interpret probabilities between 0 and 1 and use P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

concepts.name: Relative frequency interpretation
concepts.summary: Explain probability as the long-run proportion of times an event occurs in repeated trials.

concepts.name: Standard dice, coins and cards
concepts.summary: Recall the structure of a fair coin, six-sided die and 52-card deck (suits, ranks, face cards).

misconceptions.text: After several heads in a row, tails is more likely on the next toss.
Any two outcomes of an experiment are equally likely, so the probability of a sum of 7 with two dice equals that of a sum of 2.
A probability of 1/2 means the event will happen exactly once in every two trials.

concepts.name: Addition rule for events
concepts.summary: Apply P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), including the mutually exclusive case.

concepts.name: Multiplication rule for independent events
concepts.summary: Compute the probability of joint events by multiplying when events are independent, and check independence.

concepts.name: Tree diagrams
concepts.summary: Build and read tree diagrams to find probabilities of sequences of events, with or without replacement.

concepts.name: Counting principle and factorials
concepts.summary: Count outcomes of multi-step procedures by multiplying choices and use factorial notation.

concepts.name: Permutations versus combinations
concepts.summary: Choose between and calculate nPr and nCr according to whether order matters.

concepts.name: Two-way tables and Venn diagrams
concepts.summary: Organise overlapping events in Venn diagrams and two-way tables to read off probabilities.

concepts.name: Conditional probability definition
concepts.summary: Calculate P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) from tables and trees and interpret it as a restricted sample space.

misconceptions.text: Mutually exclusive events are the same as independent events.
Combinations and permutations of the same selection give the same count, so order never matters.
P(A|B) is the same as P(B|A).

concepts.name: Bayes' theorem
concepts.summary: Use Bayes' theorem with the law of total probability to reverse conditional probabilities, as in diagnostic test problems.

concepts.name: Law of total probability
concepts.summary: Split an event over a partition of the sample space and sum weighted conditional probabilities.

concepts.name: Conditional independence checks
concepts.summary: Test whether events are independent by comparing joint and product probabilities, and distinguish this from pairwise versus mutual independence.

concepts.name: Random variables and distributions
concepts.summary: Define a discrete random variable and build and validate its probability distribution table.

concepts.name: Expected value and variance
concepts.summary: Compute E(X), Var(X) and standard deviation from a distribution and interpret them.

concepts.name: Binomial distribution
concepts.summary: Recognise binomial settings and compute probabilities, mean np and variance np(1-p).

concepts.name: Counting with repetition and restrictions
concepts.summary: Analyse counting problems with repeated items, restrictions or complements to choose a valid method.

misconceptions.text: A positive result on a 99% accurate test means a 99% chance of having the condition, regardless of how rare it is.
The expected value must be a value the random variable can actually take.
Any experiment with two outcomes is binomial, even if trials are dependent or the probability changes.

concepts.name: Poisson distribution
concepts.summary: Model counts of events in a fixed interval with rate lambda, and decide when Poisson fits better than binomial.

concepts.name: Normal distribution and z-scores
concepts.summary: Standardise values and use the normal curve and its 68-95-99.7 behaviour to find probabilities and quantiles.

concepts.name: Continuous random variables and density
concepts.summary: Interpret probability as area under a density, and relate density to the cumulative distribution function.

concepts.name: Approximating binomial distributions
concepts.summary: Judge when normal or Poisson approximations to the binomial are valid and apply continuity correction.

concepts.name: Linearity of expectation
concepts.summary: Use indicator variables and linearity of expectation, even for dependent variables, to solve counting-expectation problems.

concepts.name: Variance of sums and covariance
concepts.summary: Analyse how variance of a sum depends on independence and covariance, and how scaling transforms mean and variance.

concepts.name: Law of large numbers
concepts.summary: Explain how sample averages converge to the expected value and what this does and does not guarantee.

misconceptions.text: The law of large numbers means deviations from expected results must be 'corrected' by opposite results.
For a continuous variable, P(X = x) is the height of the density curve at x.
The variance of a sum is always the sum of the variances.

concepts.name: Central limit theorem reasoning
concepts.summary: Evaluate when the CLT justifies normal approximations for sums and means and assess its limits with heavy tails or small samples.

concepts.name: Modelling choice among distributions

concepts.name: Bayesian updating with priors
concepts.summary: Evaluate how prior choice and sequential evidence shape posterior beliefs, including base-rate neglect.

concepts.name: Probability paradoxes and fallacies

issues: Advanced_beginner misconception about P(A|B) vs P(B|A) is thin: it is stated as a bare equation rather than a wrong belief a learner holds.

Conditional probability (adb-7) is a gateway to Bayes but cmp-1 lacks a direct dependency on adb-7; fine via cmp-2, but cmp-3 'Conditional independence checks' is misnamed since it covers plain independence testing and duplicates adb-2's 'check independence'.
cmp-1 (Bayes) and cmp-2 (total probability) overlap: Bayes summary repeats total probability.

cmp-5 expected value and variance is C3 while prerequisites list lacks cmp-4 to cmp-6 logic; binomial depends on expectation which is not a genuine dependency (binomial probabilities do not need E(X)).
Law of large numbers at proficient depends on variance of sums unnecessarily; also the LLN needs only expectation and independence; Chebyshev proof route is optional.
prf-7 and exp-1 and exp-5 overlap somewhat; exp-5 listing Markov/Chebyshev is fine but prf-6 dependency is okay.
Misconception 'Any two outcomes equally likely' is weakly phrased; also nov-5 misconception 3 links are fine.
Expert misconception 3 maps to exp-3 and exp-4 properly, but exp-3 lacks a direct misconception about priors; acceptable.

concepts.name: Relative frequency interpretation

concepts.name: Testing independence of events

concepts.name: Monitoring versus observability
concepts.summary: Explain that monitoring watches for known failure conditions while observability lets you ask new questions about system behaviour from its outputs.

concepts.name: Three telemetry signals
concepts.summary: Name metrics, logs and traces and state what kind of information each one provides.

concepts.name: Metrics and time series
concepts.summary: Describe a metric as a numeric measurement sampled over time, such as CPU use, request count or error rate.

concepts.name: Log entries and levels
concepts.summary: Read a log line, identify its timestamp, severity level and message, and explain what each level is for.

concepts.name: Health checks and uptime
concepts.summary: Explain how a simple health check or ping reports whether a service is up and what it cannot tell you.

concepts.name: Dashboards and alerts purpose
concepts.summary: Distinguish a dashboard for human exploration from an alert that notifies someone when action is needed.

concepts.name: Host resource metrics
concepts.summary: Interpret basic CPU, memory, disk and network usage figures for a machine and recognise saturation.

misconceptions.text: Observability is just another word for monitoring dashboards.
If the health check passes, users must be having a good experience.
High CPU usage always means something is broken.

concepts.name: Metric types
concepts.summary: Choose between counter, gauge and histogram for a given measurement and use each correctly.

concepts.name: Metric labels and cardinality
concepts.summary: Add labels to metrics to slice data by dimension while avoiding labels with unbounded values.

concepts.name: Structured logging
concepts.summary: Emit logs as structured key-value fields so they can be filtered and searched by machine.

concepts.name: Basic instrumentation with a library
concepts.summary: Add counters, gauges and timers to application code and expose them for collection.

concepts.name: Scrape versus push collection
concepts.summary: Explain how a collector pulls metrics from endpoints versus applications pushing data, and when each fits.

concepts.name: Rates and percentiles
concepts.summary: Compute and read request rates and latency percentiles rather than relying on raw counter values or averages.

concepts.name: Threshold alert rules
concepts.summary: Write a simple alert rule with a threshold and duration that fires on a clear symptom.

concepts.name: Log search and filtering
concepts.summary: Find relevant entries in centralised logs using time ranges, fields and text filters.

misconceptions.text: Average latency is enough to describe how fast a service is for users.
Adding more labels to a metric is free and always makes it more useful.
A counter's raw value is meaningful on its own, rather than its rate of change.

concepts.name: Distributed tracing spans
concepts.summary: Instrument a request path so that spans with parent-child relationships form a trace across services.

concepts.name: Context propagation and correlation IDs
concepts.summary: Pass trace or request identifiers across service boundaries and into logs to link signals for one request.

concepts.name: Golden signals and RED/USE
concepts.summary: Select latency, traffic, errors and saturation, or RED and USE, to structure what to measure for a service or resource.

concepts.name: Service level indicators and objectives
concepts.summary: Define an SLI from user-facing behaviour and set an SLO target, analysing what it implies for reliability.

concepts.name: Dashboard design
concepts.summary: Analyse and organise dashboards so that panels answer specific questions and reveal problems quickly.

concepts.name: Actionable alerting
concepts.summary: Distinguish alerts that need human action from noise, and favour symptom-based alerts over cause-based ones.

concepts.name: Incident triage with telemetry
concepts.summary: Move from an alert to a narrowed cause by correlating metrics, logs and traces systematically.

concepts.name: Log aggregation pipelines
concepts.summary: Set up agents and pipelines that collect, parse, enrich and store logs from many hosts.

misconceptions.text: Alert on every metric that could indicate a problem so nothing is missed.
An SLO of 100% is the right goal for a reliable service.
Traces replace the need for logs and metrics.

concepts.name: Error budgets and burn rate alerts
concepts.summary: Evaluate alerting based on error budget consumption speed and choose windows that balance speed and precision.

concepts.name: Cardinality and cost management
concepts.summary: Assess the storage and query cost of telemetry and decide what to drop, aggregate or keep.

concepts.name: Sampling strategies for traces
concepts.summary: Compare head and tail sampling and judge which retains the traces needed for diagnosis at acceptable cost.

concepts.name: Vendor-neutral instrumentation standards
concepts.summary: Analyse how a common instrumentation API and collector decouple application code from backends.

concepts.name: High-cardinality event analysis
concepts.summary: Use wide, context-rich events to slice by arbitrary dimensions and find unknown-unknown causes.

concepts.name: Alert quality evaluation
concepts.summary: Review alerts by precision, recall, detection time and actionability, and retire or redesign poor ones.

concepts.name: Blameless postmortem analysis
concepts.summary: Evaluate incidents to find contributing factors and turn the findings into observability improvements.

concepts.name: Monitoring dependencies and synthetic checks
concepts.summary: Combine black-box probes with internal metrics to detect failures in dependencies and user journeys.

misconceptions.text: Collecting and keeping all telemetry at full fidelity is always the safest approach.
Random head sampling reliably keeps the slow or erroring traces you need.
Postmortems should identify the single person or root cause that failed.

concepts.name: Observability strategy design
concepts.summary: Design an organisation-wide telemetry architecture that balances coverage, cost, latency and ownership.

concepts.name: Scalable telemetry backend architecture
concepts.summary: Evaluate sharding, federation, downsampling and retention designs for metrics, log and trace backends.

concepts.name: Anomaly detection and automated diagnosis
concepts.summary: Judge when statistical or learned detection beats static thresholds and how to limit false positives.

concepts.name: SLO programme and reliability governance
concepts.summary: Create SLO practices and error budget policies that guide product and engineering trade-offs across teams.

concepts.name: Observability of complex failure modes
concepts.summary: Evaluate instrumentation needed to expose cascading failures, retry storms, queueing effects and partial outages.

concepts.name: Observability-driven development
concepts.summary: Create development, release and testing practices that build observability in and use it to verify changes safely.

concepts.name: Telemetry pipeline reliability and security
concepts.summary: Evaluate how to keep telemetry pipelines reliable, independent of the systems they watch, and free of sensitive data.

misconceptions.text: Machine-learning anomaly detection removes the need for well-designed SLO alerts.
Buying a single observability platform solves the observability problem.
The monitoring stack can safely share the same failure domain as the production system.

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.summary: Explain that a class defines a template of data and behaviour and that objects are individual instances created from it.

concepts.name: Attributes and methods
concepts.summary: Identify attributes as the data an object holds and methods as the operations it can perform.

concepts.name: Constructors and initialisation
concepts.summary: Describe how a constructor sets an object's initial state when it is created.

concepts.name: Object state and identity
concepts.summary: Understand that each object has its own state and that two objects with equal data are still distinct objects.

concepts.name: Calling methods on objects
concepts.summary: Explain that using an object means invoking its methods, which read or change its state.

concepts.name: Self reference
concepts.summary: Understand that this or self refers to the current object inside its methods.

misconceptions.text: A class and an object are the same thing.
Two objects with the same attribute values are the same object.
Changing an attribute in one object changes it in every object of that class.

concepts.name: Encapsulation and access control
concepts.summary: Apply private fields and public methods so that an object's state is changed only through a controlled interface.

concepts.name: Getters, setters and validation
concepts.summary: Write accessors and mutators that enforce rules on state instead of exposing raw fields.

concepts.name: Inheritance and subclassing
concepts.summary: Create a subclass that reuses and extends a superclass's attributes and methods.

concepts.name: Method overriding
concepts.summary: Override an inherited method in a subclass and call the superclass version when needed.

concepts.name: Basic polymorphism
concepts.summary: Use a superclass-typed reference to call methods whose behaviour depends on the actual object type.

concepts.name: Class-level members
concepts.summary: Distinguish data and methods that belong to the class from those that belong to each instance.

concepts.name: Composition between objects
concepts.summary: Build objects that hold references to other objects and delegate work to them.

misconceptions.text: Making fields private is only about hiding them and does not protect the object's consistency.
Inheritance is the best way to reuse any code.
Overriding a method and overloading a method are the same thing.

concepts.name: Abstract classes and interfaces
concepts.summary: Define abstract types that specify behaviour without implementation and implement them in concrete classes.

concepts.name: Dynamic dispatch
concepts.summary: Analyse how the method executed is chosen at runtime from the object's actual class.

concepts.name: Composition over inheritance
concepts.summary: Compare inheritance and composition for a design and choose based on coupling and flexibility.

concepts.name: Liskov substitution principle
concepts.summary: Analyse whether a subclass can stand in for its superclass without breaking the expectations of callers.

concepts.name: Responsibility-driven class design
concepts.summary: Decompose a problem into classes with focused responsibilities and high cohesion.

concepts.name: Coupling and dependencies
concepts.summary: Analyse how dependencies between classes affect changeability and reduce them through abstractions.

concepts.name: Object relationships in UML
concepts.summary: Model classes and their associations, aggregations and inheritance in class diagrams.

concepts.name: Equality, copying and immutability
concepts.summary: Distinguish identity from value equality, shallow from deep copies, and know when to make objects immutable.

misconceptions.text: An interface is just an abstract class with no code, so the two are interchangeable.
If a subclass compiles and overrides all methods, it is a valid substitute for its parent.
Deep inheritance hierarchies show good object-oriented design.

concepts.name: SOLID principles in tension
concepts.summary: Evaluate a design against the SOLID principles and judge where applying one conflicts with another or with simplicity.

concepts.name: Creational design patterns
concepts.summary: Analyse when factory, builder or singleton patterns solve object-creation problems and what costs they bring.

concepts.name: Behavioural design patterns
concepts.summary: Select and apply strategy, observer or template method to vary behaviour without altering clients.

concepts.name: Structural design patterns
concepts.summary: Use adapter, decorator or facade to compose and integrate objects while keeping interfaces stable.

concepts.name: Dependency injection and inversion
concepts.summary: Evaluate designs that depend on abstractions supplied from outside to improve testability and flexibility.

concepts.name: Refactoring toward better design
concepts.summary: Diagnose design smells such as god classes and feature envy and judge refactorings that fix them.

concepts.name: Designing for testability
concepts.summary: Structure classes so collaborators can be replaced by test doubles and behaviour verified in isolation.

misconceptions.text: Design patterns should be applied wherever possible because they make any design better.
A singleton is a harmless way to share global access to an object.
Following every SOLID principle maximally always yields the best design.

concepts.name: Fit of object-oriented paradigm
concepts.summary: Judge when an object-oriented approach suits a problem compared with functional, procedural or data-oriented styles.

concepts.name: Domain-driven object modelling
concepts.summary: Create a rich domain model with entities, value objects and aggregates that express business rules and invariants.

concepts.name: Designing extensible frameworks
concepts.summary: Design class hierarchies and interfaces for libraries that third parties can extend without breaking them.

concepts.name: Evolving hierarchies and compatibility
concepts.summary: Evaluate how changes to base classes and public interfaces ripple to subclasses and clients, and plan safe evolution.

concepts.name: Object design under concurrency
concepts.summary: Evaluate object designs for shared mutable state hazards and choose immutability, confinement or synchronisation.

concepts.name: Architectural use of objects
concepts.summary: Create system architectures that place object boundaries and dependencies to isolate domain logic from infrastructure.

concepts.name: Anemic versus rich models
concepts.summary: Critique designs that separate data from behaviour and justify where each style is appropriate.

misconceptions.text: Object-oriented design is always the right choice for large systems.
Modelling every real-world noun as a class produces a good domain model.
Wrapping fields in getters and setters makes an object safe to share between threads.

concepts.name: Celestial Objects and Their Types
concepts.summary: Name and distinguish stars, planets, moons, asteroids, comets and galaxies.

concepts.name: Earth's Rotation and Day
concepts.summary: Explain that Earth's spin on its axis causes day and night and the apparent daily motion of the sky.

concepts.name: Earth's Orbit and Seasons
concepts.summary: Explain that seasons result from Earth's axial tilt as it orbits the Sun, not from distance.

concepts.name: Phases of the Moon
concepts.summary: Describe the monthly cycle of lunar phases as changing views of the Moon's sunlit half.

concepts.name: Planets of the Solar System
concepts.summary: Recall the eight planets in order from the Sun and group them as rocky or giant.

concepts.name: Stars as Distant Suns
concepts.summary: Understand that stars are self-luminous balls of gas like the Sun, appearing faint because of great distance.

concepts.name: Constellations and Navigation
concepts.summary: Recognise that constellations are apparent patterns and use a few, such as the Big Dipper, to find Polaris.

misconceptions.text: Seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer and farther in winter.
The phases of the Moon are caused by Earth's shadow falling on it.
Stars in a constellation are all close together in space.

concepts.name: Eclipses of Sun and Moon
concepts.summary: Use the alignment of Sun, Earth and Moon and the tilted lunar orbit to explain when each eclipse type occurs.

concepts.name: Tides and the Moon
concepts.summary: Explain how the Moon's gravity produces two tidal bulges and spring and neap tides.

concepts.name: Kepler's Laws of Motion
concepts.summary: Apply the ideas that orbits are ellipses, that planets speed up nearer the Sun, and that farther planets take longer to orbit.

concepts.name: Gravity Governing Orbits
concepts.summary: Use gravity's dependence on mass and distance to explain why bodies orbit and how orbital speed varies.

concepts.name: Light-Years and Cosmic Distances
concepts.summary: Convert and compare distances in astronomical units and light-years, and see that looking far means looking back in time.

concepts.name: Stellar Brightness and Colour
concepts.summary: Relate a star's colour to its temperature and distinguish apparent brightness from true luminosity.

concepts.name: Telescope Types and Light Gathering
concepts.summary: Explain that telescopes mainly gather light, and compare refracting and reflecting designs.

misconceptions.text: Astronauts float on the space station because there is no gravity there.
A telescope's main job is to magnify, so higher magnification is always better.
A brighter-looking star must be physically more luminous than a dimmer one.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic Spectrum in Astronomy
concepts.summary: Match wavelength bands to the objects and processes they reveal and why some need space telescopes.

concepts.name: Stellar Spectra and Composition
concepts.summary: Interpret absorption and emission lines to infer a star's composition and temperature.

concepts.name: Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram
concepts.summary: Analyse where stars fall by luminosity and temperature and what the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs represent.

concepts.name: Doppler Shift and Radial Velocity
concepts.summary: Use shifts in spectral lines to determine motion toward or away from us.

concepts.name: Stellar Parallax Distances
concepts.summary: Calculate distances to nearby stars from their apparent shift as Earth orbits, in parsecs.

concepts.name: Stellar Life Cycle by Mass
concepts.summary: Compare the evolution of low-mass and high-mass stars from nebula to white dwarf, neutron star or black hole.

concepts.name: Nuclear Fusion in Stars
concepts.summary: Explain how hydrogen fusion powers stars and how hydrostatic balance sets their stability.

concepts.name: Exoplanet Detection Methods
concepts.summary: Analyse how transit and radial-velocity methods find planets and what biases each carries.

misconceptions.text: Stars on the HR diagram move along the main sequence as they age like a path through life.
Stars burn fuel by chemical combustion like a fire.
Redshift means an object is red or that it is hot.

concepts.name: Mass-Luminosity and Stellar Lifetimes
concepts.summary: Evaluate why massive stars are far more luminous yet live much shorter lives than low-mass stars.

concepts.name: Cosmic Distance Ladder
concepts.summary: Evaluate how parallax, Cepheids and Type Ia supernovae chain together and where uncertainties accumulate.

concepts.name: Galaxy Types and Structure
concepts.summary: Analyse differences between spiral, elliptical and irregular galaxies and the Milky Way's components.

concepts.name: Dark Matter Evidence
concepts.summary: Assess evidence from rotation curves, lensing and cluster dynamics for unseen mass and alternative explanations.

concepts.name: Hubble's Law and Expansion
concepts.summary: Interpret the redshift-distance relation as space expanding and estimate the age scale from the Hubble constant.

concepts.name: Big Bang Evidence
concepts.summary: Evaluate how the CMB, light-element abundances and expansion jointly support the Big Bang model.

concepts.name: Compact Objects and Black Holes
concepts.summary: Analyse the properties of white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes, including event horizons and how they are detected.

concepts.name: Planetary System Formation
concepts.summary: Analyse how accretion in a protoplanetary disk explains planet types, orbits and observed exoplanet systems.

misconceptions.text: The Big Bang was an explosion at a point in space into empty space.
Black holes act like cosmic vacuum cleaners that suck in everything nearby.
Distant galaxies are moving away because they are flying through space from a central point.

concepts.name: Hubble Tension Assessment
concepts.summary: Critique why local distance-ladder and CMB-based values of the Hubble constant disagree and what resolutions are proposed.

concepts.name: Dark Energy and Cosmic Fate
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence for accelerating expansion and compare scenarios for the universe's long-term future.

concepts.name: Inflation and Structure Origin
concepts.summary: Evaluate how inflation addresses the horizon and flatness problems and seeds structure seen in CMB fluctuations.

concepts.name: Gravitational Wave Astronomy
concepts.summary: Judge what gravitational-wave signals from mergers reveal that light cannot, including multi-messenger cases.

concepts.name: Galaxy and Black Hole Coevolution
concepts.summary: Evaluate how mergers, feedback and supermassive black holes shape galaxy growth in a dark-matter framework.

concepts.name: Designing Observational Programs
concepts.summary: Design an observation plan choosing instruments, wavelengths, sampling and controls to test a specific astrophysical question.

concepts.name: Biosignature and Habitability Assessment
concepts.summary: Construct a case for a planet's habitability from atmospheric, orbital and stellar data while weighing false positives.

misconceptions.text: Dark energy and dark matter are the same unseen thing acting in different ways.
Inflation is simply the Big Bang's expansion and is fully confirmed as a theory.
Detecting a single gas such as oxygen in an exoplanet atmosphere proves life exists there.

concepts.name: Objective function and decision variables
concepts.summary: Identify the quantity to be maximized or minimized and the variables one is free to choose.

concepts.name: Constraints and feasible set
concepts.summary: Explain how equality and inequality constraints restrict choices and define the set of feasible points.

concepts.name: Minimization versus maximization
concepts.summary: Understand that maximizing f is equivalent to minimizing -f and that both share the same optimal points.

concepts.name: Local and global optima
concepts.summary: Distinguish a point that is best in its neighbourhood from one that is best over the entire feasible set.

concepts.name: Translating word problems into models
concepts.summary: Turn a verbal problem such as maximizing area with fixed perimeter into variables, an objective and constraints.

concepts.name: Optimal value versus optimal point
concepts.summary: Distinguish the best objective value from the input at which it is attained.

misconceptions.text: The optimal value of the objective and the point where it is attained are the same thing.
Maximization and minimization are completely different problems needing unrelated methods.
A local minimum is always the lowest value the function can take.

concepts.name: First-order optimality condition
concepts.summary: Find candidate unconstrained optima by solving that the gradient equals zero.

concepts.name: Second-order test with Hessian
concepts.summary: Classify stationary points as minima, maxima or saddles using the definiteness of the Hessian.

concepts.name: Optimization on closed intervals
concepts.summary: Find extrema of a function on a bounded domain by comparing interior critical points with boundary values.

concepts.name: Constraint substitution
concepts.summary: Solve simple equality-constrained problems by eliminating a variable using the constraint.

concepts.name: Graphical solution of two-variable LP
concepts.summary: Sketch a polygonal feasible region and find the best vertex of a linear objective.

concepts.name: Gradient descent iteration
concepts.summary: Carry out update steps moving against the gradient with a chosen step size.

concepts.name: Existence of optima
concepts.summary: Recognize that continuous functions on closed bounded sets attain optima while others may not.

misconceptions.text: Every point where the gradient is zero is a minimum.
Optima of a function on an interval always occur at critical points in the interior.
A positive step size always guarantees gradient descent decreases the objective.

concepts.name: Lagrange multipliers for equality constraints
concepts.summary: Set up and solve the Lagrangian stationarity system to find constrained extrema.

concepts.name: Geometric meaning of multipliers
concepts.summary: Explain that gradients of objective and constraint are parallel at optimum and the multiplier measures sensitivity of the optimal value.

concepts.name: KKT conditions
concepts.summary: Apply stationarity, primal and dual feasibility and complementary slackness to inequality-constrained problems.

concepts.name: Convex sets and functions
concepts.summary: Test convexity via definition, Hessian semidefiniteness or composition rules and analyse its consequences.

concepts.name: Standard form linear programs
concepts.summary: Convert LPs to standard form using slack, surplus and split variables.

concepts.name: Simplex method
concepts.summary: Move between basic feasible solutions via pivots until optimality.

concepts.name: Step size and convergence in gradient methods
concepts.summary: Analyse how step size, conditioning and line search affect convergence of gradient descent.

concepts.name: Newton's method for optimization
concepts.summary: Use Hessian-based steps and compare their cost and speed with gradient descent.

misconceptions.text: Lagrange multiplier conditions alone identify the global optimum, not just candidates.
In KKT conditions every inequality constraint must be active at the optimum.
The simplex method moves through the interior of the feasible region.

concepts.name: Convex optimization problem structure
concepts.summary: Recognize convex problems and exploit that local optima are global and KKT conditions are sufficient.

concepts.name: Lagrangian duality
concepts.summary: Construct the dual function and problem and relate dual bounds to the primal optimum.

concepts.name: Strong duality and constraint qualifications
concepts.summary: Judge when strong duality and KKT necessity hold, and when they fail.

concepts.name: LP duality and sensitivity
concepts.summary: Derive LP duals and interpret dual variables and complementary slackness for sensitivity analysis.

concepts.name: Convergence rate analysis
concepts.summary: Compare algorithms by convergence rates and the effect of conditioning of smooth strongly convex objectives.

concepts.name: Quasi-Newton and conjugate gradient
concepts.summary: Explain how these methods approximate curvature cheaply and when to choose them.

concepts.name: Penalty and barrier methods
concepts.summary: Convert constrained problems into sequences of unconstrained ones and understand interior-point ideas.

concepts.name: Stochastic gradient methods
concepts.summary: Evaluate trade-offs of noisy gradient estimates, step schedules and batch size on large-scale problems.

misconceptions.text: Strong duality holds for every optimization problem so the dual gap is always zero.
Newton-type methods are always better than gradient methods regardless of problem size.
Stochastic gradient descent converges with a constant step size to the exact minimizer.

concepts.name: Choosing a problem class and reformulating
concepts.summary: Design reformulations or relaxations that turn hard problems into tractable LP, QP, conic or convex forms.

concepts.name: Conic and semidefinite programming
concepts.summary: Evaluate when second-order cone and semidefinite models capture a problem and how duality extends to cones.
