concepts.name: Nonconvex landscape analysis
concepts.summary: Assess how saddles, local minima and initialization affect algorithm guarantees in nonconvex problems.

concepts.name: Integer and combinatorial optimization
concepts.summary: Judge relaxation bounds, branching and cut strategies for discrete decision problems and their complexity.

concepts.name: Proximal and splitting methods
concepts.summary: Design algorithms for nonsmooth composite objectives using proximal operators and operator splitting.

concepts.name: Complexity lower bounds and acceleration
concepts.summary: Evaluate optimal first-order rates and when accelerated methods achieve them.

concepts.name: Robust and stochastic optimization
concepts.summary: Formulate models that handle uncertain data and justify the chosen uncertainty model and its tractable counterpart.

concepts.name: Algorithm and solver selection
concepts.summary: Choose and diagnose methods and solvers based on structure, scale, scaling and accuracy requirements.

misconceptions.text: Any nonconvex problem is intractable and gradient methods on it are useless.
Rounding the solution of an LP relaxation yields an optimal integer solution.
Robust optimization simply optimizes the average case over scenarios.

concepts.name: Purpose of user research
concepts.summary: Explain that user research uncovers real behaviors, needs and context so teams decide on evidence rather than assumptions.

concepts.name: Behavior versus opinion
concepts.summary: Distinguish what people do from what they say they do or would do, and why observed behavior is stronger evidence.

concepts.name: Qualitative versus quantitative data
concepts.summary: Describe how qualitative methods explain why and quantitative methods measure how many or how much.

concepts.name: Research participants and users
concepts.summary: Recall that participants should resemble the people who will actually use the product, not colleagues or friends.

concepts.name: Common research method types
concepts.summary: Name the main methods such as interviews, usability tests, surveys, diary studies and card sorting and what each is for.

concepts.name: Research questions and goals
concepts.summary: Explain that a study starts from a clear question about what the team needs to learn.

concepts.name: Informed consent and privacy
concepts.summary: Recall that participants must understand the study, agree voluntarily and have their data protected.

misconceptions.text: Asking users what they want is enough to know what to build.
Five friends or coworkers are as good as real target users for research.
Qualitative research is unreliable because it is not numbers.

concepts.name: Writing neutral interview questions
concepts.summary: Write open, non-leading questions about past behavior instead of hypotheticals or yes/no prompts.

concepts.name: Discussion guide structure
concepts.summary: Build a guide with introduction, warm-up, core topics, probes and wrap-up that fits the session time.

concepts.name: Screeners and recruiting criteria
concepts.summary: Turn target-user traits into screener questions that qualify participants without revealing the right answers.

concepts.name: Moderated usability test session
concepts.summary: Run a task-based session using think-aloud, neutral prompts and observation without helping or defending the design.

concepts.name: Usability task scenarios
concepts.summary: Write realistic goal-based tasks that avoid naming interface labels or hinting at the path.

concepts.name: Note-taking and observation capture
concepts.summary: Record observations, quotes and timestamps separately from interpretations during sessions.

concepts.name: Sample size for qualitative studies
concepts.summary: Understand why small iterative rounds of about five per segment reveal most major usability problems.

misconceptions.text: Good interview questions ask people whether they would use a feature.
A moderator should help participants when they get stuck so the session continues smoothly.
Screeners should state the desired profile so participants can self-identify.

concepts.name: Method selection by question
concepts.summary: Analyse a research question and constraints to pick a method that fits, such as attitudinal versus behavioral and generative versus evaluative.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.summary: Observe and interview people in their own environment while they do real work, using the master-apprentice approach.

concepts.name: Diary studies
concepts.summary: Design prompts, duration and reminders so participants log experiences over time with manageable effort.

concepts.name: Survey design and bias
concepts.summary: Design surveys with clear scales, balanced options and ordering, and identify sampling and response bias.

concepts.name: Unmoderated remote testing
concepts.summary: Set up self-guided tasks with clear instructions and success measures, and judge their tradeoffs against moderated sessions.

concepts.name: Card sorting and tree testing
concepts.summary: Run open and closed card sorts and tree tests to learn users' mental models of categories and findability.

concepts.name: Affinity mapping synthesis
concepts.summary: Cluster observations bottom-up into themes and separate evidence from interpretation to produce insights.

concepts.name: Severity rating of findings
concepts.summary: Rate issues by frequency, impact and persistence to prioritise what the team should fix.

misconceptions.text: Surveys can explain why users behave as they do.
Affinity mapping means grouping notes by predefined categories.
Unmoderated tests are simply a cheaper replacement for moderated tests.

concepts.name: Evidence-based personas
concepts.summary: Build and critique personas grounded in observed behavior patterns and quotes rather than demographics or stereotypes.

concepts.name: Journey mapping from observed data
concepts.summary: Construct journey maps showing stages, actions, thoughts, emotions and pain points traced back to research evidence.

concepts.name: Triangulating multiple methods
concepts.summary: Combine qualitative and quantitative sources, judging where they agree or conflict, to strengthen conclusions.

concepts.name: Recruiting hard-to-reach segments
concepts.summary: Plan sourcing, incentives and screening for specialist or vulnerable groups while managing sampling bias.

concepts.name: Interview and moderation bias analysis
concepts.summary: Analyse recordings for leading, confirmation and social desirability effects and correct the approach.

concepts.name: Insight framing and recommendations
concepts.summary: Turn findings into evidence-backed insights and recommendations tailored to stakeholder decisions.

concepts.name: Research ethics and data governance
concepts.summary: Evaluate consent, anonymisation, retention and vulnerable-participant risks in a study design.

misconceptions.text: A persona needs a name, photo and demographics to be useful.
When survey data and interview findings disagree, one of them must be wrong.
A journey map is a workshop artifact that can be drawn from team assumptions.

concepts.name: Research program strategy
concepts.summary: Design a portfolio of studies aligned to product strategy, balancing generative and evaluative work over time.

concepts.name: Evaluating evidence quality
concepts.summary: Judge the validity, reliability and limits of studies, including those run by others, and decide how much weight to give them.

concepts.name: Research democratisation governance
concepts.summary: Create guidelines, training and review so non-researchers can run research without eroding quality or ethics.

concepts.name: Research repository and insight systems
concepts.summary: Design tagging and storage that make findings traceable, reusable and findable across projects.

concepts.name: Adapting methods to constraints
concepts.summary: Invent or tailor methods for tight timelines, remote contexts or novel products while defending the tradeoffs.

concepts.name: Influencing decisions with research
concepts.summary: Evaluate how findings affect decisions and shape communication and stakeholder involvement to increase impact.

concepts.name: Cross-cultural and inclusive research
concepts.summary: Assess and adapt study design for cultural, accessibility and language differences so findings generalise appropriately.

misconceptions.text: Scaling research means letting anyone run studies with a template.
Strong findings automatically lead to action by stakeholders.
A rigorous method is one fixed protocol applied identically everywhere.

concepts.name: Electric charge and conservation
concepts.summary: Recall that charge comes in positive and negative kinds, is quantized in units of e, and is conserved in every process.

concepts.name: Conductors versus insulators
concepts.summary: Explain how charges move freely in conductors but not insulators and how objects become charged by friction, contact and induction.

concepts.name: Coulomb's law for point charges
concepts.summary: State and interpret the force between two point charges as proportional to the charges and inversely proportional to distance squared, attractive or repulsive by sign.

concepts.name: Electric field as force per charge
concepts.summary: Understand the electric field as the force per unit test charge and its direction as that of the force on a positive charge.

concepts.name: Electric field lines
concepts.summary: Read field line pictures to infer direction and relative strength of the field near charges and dipoles.

concepts.name: Magnets and magnetic poles
concepts.summary: Recall that magnets have two poles that attract or repel, that poles cannot be isolated, and that field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.

concepts.name: Currents create magnetic fields
concepts.summary: Explain that moving charges produce magnetic fields and describe the circular field around a straight wire using the right-hand rule.

misconceptions.text: Charge is created or destroyed when objects are rubbed together.
Electric field lines are the actual paths that charges follow.
Cutting a magnet in half yields separate north and south poles.

concepts.name: Superposition of electric forces
concepts.summary: Compute the net force or field from several point charges by adding vector components.

concepts.name: Electric potential energy and potential
concepts.summary: Calculate potential energy of charge pairs and potential of point charges as scalar quantities, and relate potential difference to work per charge.

concepts.name: Equipotentials and field relationship
concepts.summary: Sketch equipotentials and use the fact that the field points toward decreasing potential with magnitude equal to the potential gradient.

concepts.name: Capacitor and capacitance
concepts.summary: Calculate capacitance, charge, voltage and stored energy for a parallel-plate capacitor and for simple series and parallel combinations.

concepts.name: Magnetic force on moving charges
concepts.summary: Find the magnitude and direction of the force on a charge moving in a uniform magnetic field, including circular motion.

concepts.name: Magnetic force on current-carrying wires
concepts.summary: Compute the force on a straight wire in a uniform field and between two parallel currents.

concepts.name: Field of simple current geometries
concepts.summary: Use standard results for the field of a long straight wire, loop centre and ideal solenoid.

misconceptions.text: A point where the electric field is zero must also have zero potential.
A magnetic field does work on a moving charge and speeds it up.
A capacitor stores net charge, so total charge on it is Q.

concepts.name: Gauss's law applications
concepts.summary: Choose Gaussian surfaces to derive fields of spherical, cylindrical and planar charge distributions.

concepts.name: Fields from continuous distributions
concepts.summary: Integrate Coulomb's law over lines, rings and disks to obtain fields and potentials.

concepts.name: Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium
concepts.summary: Analyse why the field inside a conductor is zero, charge resides on the surface, and cavities are shielded.

concepts.name: Dielectrics in capacitors
concepts.summary: Analyse how a dielectric reduces the field, raises capacitance by factor κ, and changes energy under fixed charge or fixed voltage.

concepts.name: Biot-Savart law
concepts.summary: Integrate current elements to find magnetic fields of wire segments and loops.

concepts.name: Ampère's law applications
concepts.summary: Use symmetric Amperian loops to find fields of wires, solenoids and toroids.

concepts.name: Faraday's and Lenz's laws
concepts.summary: Calculate EMF from changing flux and determine induced current direction by opposing the change.

concepts.name: Motional EMF
concepts.summary: Analyse EMF in conductors moving through fields and relate it to flux change and magnetic force on charges.

misconceptions.text: Gauss's law only holds for symmetric charge distributions.
Induced EMF depends on the magnitude of the magnetic flux rather than its rate of change.
Ampère's law gives the field at the loop from only the current enclosed, ignoring other currents.

concepts.name: Differential forms of field laws
concepts.summary: Translate Gauss's, Faraday's and Ampère's laws between integral and differential form using divergence and curl.

concepts.name: Laplace and Poisson equations
concepts.summary: Set up electrostatic problems as potential equations with boundary conditions and appeal to uniqueness.

concepts.name: Method of images
concepts.summary: Evaluate when image charges replace induced surface charge and use them to solve conductor problems.

concepts.name: Displacement current
concepts.summary: Analyse why Ampère's law fails for a charging capacitor and how the changing electric flux term restores consistency.

concepts.name: Maxwell's equations as a system
concepts.summary: Interpret the four equations together, show they imply charge conservation, and identify the sources of each field.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic wave solutions
concepts.summary: Derive the vacuum wave equation and judge the transverse, speed-of-light plane-wave solutions it permits.

concepts.name: Inductance and magnetic energy
concepts.summary: Analyse self and mutual inductance and the energy stored in a magnetic field.

concepts.name: Fields in matter
concepts.summary: Distinguish free from bound charge and current, and use D and H with polarization and magnetization.

misconceptions.text: Displacement current is a flow of real charge across the capacitor gap.
The image charge physically exists behind the conducting plane and the field there is also given by the image solution.
Faraday's law only applies to loops of wire, not to empty space.

concepts.name: Potentials and gauge freedom
concepts.summary: Evaluate gauge choices for the scalar and vector potentials and show that physical fields are gauge invariant.

concepts.name: Poynting theorem and energy flow
concepts.summary: Use energy and momentum conservation in fields to assess power transport in circuits, waves and radiation pressure.

concepts.name: Radiation from accelerating charges
concepts.summary: Judge how retarded potentials lead to radiation fields and dipole radiation from accelerated charges.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic boundary conditions
concepts.summary: Apply interface conditions on E, D, B and H to derive reflection and transmission at material boundaries.

concepts.name: Relativistic unification of fields
concepts.summary: Construct the transformation of E and B between frames and the field tensor formulation showing magnetism as a relativistic effect.

concepts.name: Multipole expansion
concepts.summary: Construct multipole expansions of potentials to model localized sources and assess the dominant far-field term.

concepts.name: Modelling waves in media
concepts.summary: Design models of wave propagation in dispersive media, conductors and waveguides from Maxwell's equations with material response.

misconceptions.text: Potentials are only mathematical tools with no physical significance, since only fields matter.
Magnetic force is a separate fundamental interaction unrelated to relativity and electric force.
A charge moving at constant velocity radiates electromagnetic waves.

concepts.name: Atomic structure and subatomic particles
concepts.summary: Recall that atoms consist of a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons, and state each particle's charge and relative mass.

concepts.name: Atomic number and mass number
concepts.summary: Explain how atomic number defines an element and how mass number and neutron count give isotopes.

concepts.name: Periodic table organization
concepts.summary: Describe how elements are arranged in periods and groups and locate metals, nonmetals, and metalloids.

concepts.name: Elements, compounds, and mixtures
concepts.summary: Distinguish elements, compounds, and homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures by composition.

concepts.name: Physical versus chemical change
concepts.summary: Classify changes as physical or chemical and identify evidence that a new substance has formed.

concepts.name: Chemical formulas and symbols
concepts.summary: Read chemical symbols and formulas to state which elements and how many atoms are present.

concepts.name: States of matter and particle model
concepts.summary: Describe solids, liquids, and gases in terms of particle arrangement and motion and name the phase changes.

misconceptions.text: Atoms of the same element always have the same number of neutrons.
Dissolving or changing state creates a new substance, so it is a chemical change.
A compound is just a mixture of elements that can be separated by physical means.

concepts.name: Electron configuration and valence electrons
concepts.summary: Write electron configurations for light elements and determine valence electrons from group position.

concepts.name: Ionic and covalent bonding
concepts.summary: Explain bond formation by electron transfer versus sharing and predict which type forms between given elements.

concepts.name: Naming compounds and writing formulas
concepts.summary: Apply naming rules to ionic and simple molecular compounds and derive formulas from ion charges.

concepts.name: Balancing chemical equations
concepts.summary: Balance equations by adjusting coefficients so each element's atoms are conserved.

concepts.name: Molar mass and the mole
concepts.summary: Convert between mass, moles, and number of particles using molar mass and Avogadro's number.

concepts.name: Periodic trends
concepts.summary: Use group and period position to predict trends in atomic radius, ionization energy, and electronegativity.

concepts.name: Reaction types
concepts.summary: Classify reactions as synthesis, decomposition, single or double replacement, or combustion and predict simple products.

misconceptions.text: Changing subscripts in a formula is an acceptable way to balance an equation.
A mole is a fixed mass of 6.022×10^23 grams of any substance.
Ionic compounds exist as discrete molecules like covalent ones.

concepts.name: Limiting reagent and percent yield
concepts.summary: Identify the limiting reactant from given quantities and calculate theoretical and percent yield.

concepts.name: Mole-ratio stoichiometry
concepts.summary: Use balanced-equation coefficients to convert between masses, moles, volumes, and particle counts of reactants and products.

concepts.name: Lewis structures and VSEPR geometry
concepts.summary: Draw Lewis structures and use electron-domain repulsion to predict shape and bond angles.

concepts.name: Molecular polarity and intermolecular forces
concepts.summary: Analyse bond polarity and geometry to determine molecular polarity and the dominant intermolecular forces.

concepts.name: Gas laws and ideal gas equation
concepts.summary: Apply Boyle's, Charles's, and the ideal gas law to relate pressure, volume, temperature, and moles.

concepts.name: Solution concentration and dilution
concepts.summary: Calculate molarity and use dilution relationships to prepare and analyse solutions.

concepts.name: Enthalpy and calorimetry
concepts.summary: Calculate heat transfer with q = mcΔT and interpret exothermic and endothermic enthalpy changes.

concepts.name: Acid-base definitions and pH
concepts.summary: Apply Arrhenius and Brønsted-Lowry definitions and calculate pH and pOH of strong acids and bases.

misconceptions.text: The limiting reagent is the reactant present in the smallest mass.
Molecules with polar bonds are always polar molecules.
Temperature in gas law calculations can be used in Celsius.

concepts.name: Chemical equilibrium and Le Chatelier
concepts.summary: Write equilibrium expressions, use K and Q to predict direction, and analyse how stresses shift equilibrium.

concepts.name: Weak acid-base equilibria and buffers
concepts.summary: Calculate pH for weak acids and bases using Ka and Kb and explain how buffers resist pH change.

concepts.name: Titration curves and indicators
concepts.summary: Interpret titration curves to locate equivalence points and choose suitable indicators.

concepts.name: Reaction kinetics and rate laws
concepts.summary: Determine rate laws from experimental data and relate rate to concentration, temperature, and activation energy.

concepts.name: Thermodynamics and spontaneity
concepts.summary: Evaluate spontaneity using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS and relate ΔG to the equilibrium constant.

concepts.name: Hess's law and thermochemical cycles
concepts.summary: Combine reaction enthalpies and formation data to find unknown enthalpy changes.

concepts.name: Solubility equilibria
concepts.summary: Use Ksp to evaluate solubility, precipitation, and the common-ion effect.

concepts.name: Redox reactions and electrochemistry
concepts.summary: Balance redox equations and analyse cell potentials in galvanic cells.

misconceptions.text: At equilibrium, reactions have stopped and concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
Exothermic reactions are always spontaneous, and a catalyst changes the equilibrium position.
A larger Ksp always means a more soluble salt regardless of formula stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Quantum model and orbital theory
concepts.summary: Evaluate how orbitals, hybridization, and molecular orbital theory explain bonding, magnetism, and exceptions to simple models.

concepts.name: Mechanistic analysis of kinetics
concepts.summary: Judge proposed mechanisms against rate laws using rate-determining steps and intermediates.

concepts.name: Statistical basis of entropy
concepts.summary: Explain entropy and free energy through microstates and energy dispersal, and evaluate their predictions across systems.

concepts.name: Nonideal solutions and colligative properties
concepts.summary: Evaluate deviations from ideal behaviour in solutions and gases and use colligative properties to determine molar mass.

concepts.name: Nernst equation and cell thermodynamics
concepts.summary: Connect cell potential, ΔG, and K, and predict potentials under nonstandard conditions.

concepts.name: Experimental design and error analysis
concepts.summary: Design quantitative experiments, propagate uncertainties, and critique methods and conclusions.

concepts.name: Multi-equilibria system modelling
concepts.summary: Construct models of systems with coupled acid-base, solubility, and complexation equilibria and justify approximations.

misconceptions.text: Lewis structures and VSEPR accurately describe all bonding, including delocalized and paramagnetic species.
Entropy simply means disorder, so any increase in apparent messiness means spontaneity.
Ideal-solution and dilute-approximation equations hold accurately at any concentration.

concepts.name: Moral versus non-moral questions
concepts.summary: Distinguish questions of right, wrong and value from questions of fact, taste or law.

concepts.name: Descriptive versus normative claims
concepts.summary: Explain the difference between describing how people behave and claiming how they should behave.

concepts.name: Moral reasons and justification
concepts.summary: Understand that a moral position needs supporting reasons rather than mere assertion or feeling.

concepts.name: Consequentialist idea
concepts.summary: Explain that consequentialism judges actions by the goodness of their outcomes.

concepts.name: Deontological idea
concepts.summary: Explain that deontology judges actions by their conformity to duties, rules or rights.

concepts.name: Virtue ethics idea
concepts.summary: Explain that virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do and focuses on traits.

concepts.name: Moral dilemma
concepts.summary: Recognise a situation where moral considerations conflict and no option satisfies them all.

misconceptions.text: Ethics is just a matter of personal feelings, so no moral view can be better supported than another.
Whatever is legal is morally right, and whatever is illegal is wrong.
Because people disagree about what is right, there is no point reasoning about ethics.

concepts.name: Utilitarian calculation
concepts.summary: Apply the utilitarian principle to a simple case by identifying affected parties and comparing total benefits and harms.

concepts.name: Categorical imperative tests
concepts.summary: Apply Kant's universalisability and treat-people-as-ends tests to a proposed action.

concepts.name: Rights and duties
concepts.summary: Explain how rights and corresponding duties constrain what may be done to people.

concepts.name: Virtues and the mean
concepts.summary: Identify a virtue as a mean between excess and deficiency and apply it to a situation.

concepts.name: Stakeholder identification
concepts.summary: List who is affected by a decision and how, including those without a voice.

concepts.name: Moral relativism versus universalism
concepts.summary: Contrast the view that morality depends on culture with the view that some standards apply to everyone.

concepts.name: Intention versus outcome
concepts.summary: Distinguish what an agent intended from what resulted and show how each framework weighs them.

misconceptions.text: Utilitarianism means doing whatever benefits the majority, regardless of cost to individuals.
Kantian ethics simply means following whatever rules exist, including laws and customs.
The virtuous mean is always moderation or the midpoint between two extremes in a numerical sense.

concepts.name: Act versus rule consequentialism
concepts.summary: Analyse how evaluating individual acts differs from evaluating rules by their general consequences.

concepts.name: Conflicting duties resolution
concepts.summary: Analyse cases where duties clash and explain how to weigh them as prima facie obligations.

concepts.name: Doing versus allowing harm
concepts.summary: Analyse whether causing harm differs morally from allowing it, including intended versus foreseen effects.

concepts.name: Framework comparison on cases
concepts.summary: Analyse a dilemma through consequentialist, deontological and virtue lenses and identify where they agree and diverge.

concepts.name: Trolley problem variants
concepts.summary: Use thought experiments to isolate which morally relevant features drive intuitions.

concepts.name: Moral argument reconstruction
concepts.summary: Break a moral argument into premises, factual and normative, and conclusion to find where it is weak.

concepts.name: Objections to each framework
concepts.summary: Identify the standard objections to each major framework, such as demandingness, rigidity and action-guidance.

misconceptions.text: Rule consequentialism is just deontology under another name.
Killing and letting die are morally identical whenever the outcome is the same.
If a framework produces a counterintuitive verdict in one case, it is refuted.

concepts.name: Reflective equilibrium
concepts.summary: Evaluate and adjust principles and case judgements against each other to reach a coherent position.

concepts.name: Moral uncertainty
concepts.summary: Evaluate how to act when unsure which ethical theory is correct.

concepts.name: Contractualism and social contract
concepts.summary: Analyse justification by principles no one could reasonably reject and the veil of ignorance.

concepts.name: Care ethics and relational views
concepts.summary: Analyse how care ethics emphasises relationships, dependence and context against impartial theories.

concepts.name: Metaethical positions
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing accounts of the status and meaning of moral claims.

concepts.name: Applied ethics case judgement
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing arguments in applied domains and judge which position is best supported.

concepts.name: Justice and fairness theories
concepts.summary: Analyse egalitarian, utilitarian, libertarian and desert-based accounts of fair distribution.

misconceptions.text: Metaethical anti-realism entails that anything goes in first-order ethics.
Reflective equilibrium just means keeping your initial intuitions.
Moral uncertainty means one should suspend judgement and not act.

concepts.name: Constructing original arguments
concepts.summary: Create a defended moral position that anticipates and answers the strongest objections.

concepts.name: Hybrid and pluralist theories
concepts.summary: Design or defend an account combining insights from several frameworks with a principled way to resolve conflicts.

concepts.name: Debunking and evolutionary arguments
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether empirical findings about the origins of moral intuitions undermine their evidential weight.

concepts.name: Population and future ethics
concepts.summary: Evaluate arguments about obligations to future and merely possible people, including the repugnant conclusion.

concepts.name: Moral status and expanding circle
concepts.summary: Evaluate criteria for moral standing and judge their application to animals, ecosystems and artificial systems.

concepts.name: Ethical guidance for institutions
concepts.summary: Create decision procedures or policies that embed ethical reasoning under disagreement and uncertainty.

concepts.name: Evaluating philosophical methodology
concepts.summary: Evaluate the reliability of intuitions, thought experiments and consensus as methods in ethics.

misconceptions.text: A sufficiently refined single theory will eventually resolve all moral conflicts without residual tension.
Showing that moral intuitions evolved automatically proves they are false.
Moral status requires being human, so extending concern further is a category error.

concepts.name: Tables, rows and columns
concepts.summary: Recognise that relational data is stored in tables of rows (records) and typed columns (fields) and describe what each represents.

concepts.name: Primary and foreign keys
concepts.summary: Explain how a primary key uniquely identifies a row and how a foreign key references another table to link related data.

concepts.name: SELECT and FROM
concepts.summary: Read and explain a query that retrieves chosen columns from a table, including the meaning of SELECT *.

concepts.name: Filtering with WHERE
concepts.summary: Understand that WHERE keeps only rows satisfying a condition built from comparison operators.

concepts.name: Sorting with ORDER BY
concepts.summary: Explain how ORDER BY sorts result rows ascending or descending by one or more columns.

concepts.name: Common data types
concepts.summary: Recall the main column data types (integer, decimal, text, date/time, boolean) and what kind of value each stores.

misconceptions.text: A SQL table has a guaranteed row order, so rows come back in the order they were inserted without ORDER BY.
SELECT changes or removes the data in the table it reads from.
A foreign key column must contain unique values just like a primary key.

concepts.name: Compound conditions with AND/OR
concepts.summary: Combine conditions using AND, OR, NOT and parentheses so the intended rows are selected.

concepts.name: Pattern, range and set predicates
concepts.summary: Use LIKE, BETWEEN and IN to filter on text patterns, ranges and lists of values.

concepts.name: NULL handling
concepts.summary: Test for missing values with IS NULL and understand that comparisons with NULL are neither true nor false.

concepts.name: Aggregate functions
concepts.summary: Compute COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX over a set of rows to answer summary questions.

concepts.name: Grouping with GROUP BY
concepts.summary: Produce one summary row per group by combining GROUP BY with aggregate functions.

concepts.name: Inner joins on keys
concepts.summary: Combine rows from two tables by matching a foreign key to a primary key using JOIN ... ON.

concepts.name: Inserting, updating and deleting rows
concepts.summary: Add, change and remove records using INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, with a WHERE clause to limit the affected rows.

concepts.name: Aliases and DISTINCT
concepts.summary: Rename columns and tables with aliases and remove duplicate result rows with DISTINCT.

misconceptions.text: WHERE column = NULL finds rows with missing values.
UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause only affects one row.
Any selected column can appear alongside aggregates in a GROUP BY query without being grouped.

concepts.name: Outer joins and unmatched rows
concepts.summary: Use LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins to keep unmatched rows and identify them via NULLs.

concepts.name: Filtering groups with HAVING
concepts.summary: Filter aggregated groups with HAVING and distinguish it from row-level filtering with WHERE.

concepts.name: Logical order of query evaluation
concepts.summary: Analyse why clauses are evaluated in the order FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY and predict what aliases and filters are visible where.

concepts.name: Subqueries in WHERE and FROM
concepts.summary: Write scalar, list and table subqueries and decide when a nested query answers a question better than a join.

concepts.name: Correlated subqueries and EXISTS
concepts.summary: Use correlated subqueries and EXISTS to test for related rows, and compare them with joins.

concepts.name: Set operations
concepts.summary: Combine compatible result sets with UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT and EXCEPT.

concepts.name: Self joins and multi-table joins
concepts.summary: Model hierarchies and comparisons within one table and chain several joins, including many-to-many link tables.

concepts.name: Expressions and CASE
concepts.summary: Use CASE, COALESCE and string, numeric and date functions to derive values inside queries.

misconceptions.text: HAVING and WHERE are interchangeable, so any condition can go in either.
A column alias defined in SELECT can be used in the WHERE clause of the same query.
Filtering on the right-hand table in the WHERE clause of a LEFT JOIN still preserves unmatched left rows.

concepts.name: Window functions
concepts.summary: Compute rankings, running totals and per-partition values with OVER, PARTITION BY and ORDER BY without collapsing rows.

concepts.name: Common table expressions
concepts.summary: Structure complex queries into named, readable steps with CTEs and judge when they beat nested subqueries.

concepts.name: Recursive queries
concepts.summary: Traverse hierarchical or graph-like data using recursive CTEs with an anchor and a recursive member.

concepts.name: Indexes and query performance
concepts.summary: Evaluate how indexes speed reads, slow writes and are used or ignored depending on the predicates.

concepts.name: Reading execution plans
concepts.summary: Interpret execution plans to find scans, join strategies and costly steps, then judge rewrites.

concepts.name: Transactions and ACID
concepts.summary: Group statements into transactions and analyse how atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability protect data.

concepts.name: Constraints and normalisation
concepts.summary: Judge schema designs using normal forms and enforce integrity with primary, foreign, unique, check and not-null constraints.

concepts.name: Rewriting queries for correctness
concepts.summary: Detect and fix wrong results caused by join fan-out, duplicate counting and NULL semantics, and evaluate equivalent formulations.

misconceptions.text: Window functions and GROUP BY do the same thing and both collapse rows.
Adding more indexes always makes the database faster.
A CTE always materialises results and is therefore always faster than a subquery.

concepts.name: Isolation levels and concurrency anomalies
concepts.summary: Evaluate which isolation level prevents which anomalies and its trade-offs for throughput and correctness in a given workload.

concepts.name: Locking and deadlock design
concepts.summary: Assess locking behaviour and design access patterns that avoid contention and deadlocks.

concepts.name: Optimiser behaviour and statistics
concepts.summary: Judge how statistics and cardinality estimates drive plan choice and diagnose bad plans from misestimates.

concepts.name: Schema and index design for workloads
concepts.summary: Design schemas, composite, covering and partial indexes, and partitioning tailored to a specific read/write workload.

concepts.name: Denormalisation and analytical modelling
concepts.summary: Create dimensional or denormalised models for analytics and justify the departure from normal forms.

concepts.name: Safe large-scale data changes
concepts.summary: Plan batched, idempotent and reversible bulk modifications and schema migrations that limit locking and risk.

concepts.name: SQL injection defence and access control
concepts.summary: Evaluate code and permission setups for injection risk and apply parameterised statements and least-privilege roles.

concepts.name: Dialect portability and trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate which SQL features are standard versus engine-specific and choose approaches balancing portability and capability.

misconceptions.text: The SERIALIZABLE isolation level should always be used because it is simply the safest and costs nothing.
Escaping quotes by hand is as reliable as using parameterised queries.
The optimiser always finds the best plan, so query shape and statistics never matter.

concepts.name: Repository and working tree
concepts.summary: Recall that a repository stores a project's full history and that the working tree holds the current editable files.

concepts.name: Commits as snapshots
concepts.summary: Explain that a commit records a snapshot of the project with a message, author and link to its parent.

concepts.name: Staging area workflow
concepts.summary: Describe how changes move from the working tree to the staging area to a commit using add and commit.

concepts.name: Inspecting status and history
concepts.summary: Use status, log and diff to see what has changed and what has been recorded.

concepts.name: Local versus remote repositories
concepts.summary: Distinguish a local repository from a remote one and explain that cloning copies the full history.

concepts.name: Writing commit messages
concepts.summary: Understand why a commit message should briefly say what changed and why.

misconceptions.text: Git and GitHub are the same thing.
Git add saves the file to the repository as a commit.
A commit stores only the lines that changed rather than a snapshot of the project.

concepts.name: Branch creation and switching
concepts.summary: Create branches and switch between them to work on changes in isolation.

concepts.name: Push, fetch and pull
concepts.summary: Sync commits with a remote and tell fetch apart from pull.

concepts.name: Merging branches
concepts.summary: Merge one branch into another and recognise fast-forward versus merge-commit outcomes.

concepts.name: Resolving simple merge conflicts
concepts.summary: Read conflict markers, choose the correct content and complete the merge.

concepts.name: Ignoring files with gitignore
concepts.summary: Keep build output, dependencies and secrets out of version control using ignore patterns.

concepts.name: Undoing uncommitted changes
concepts.summary: Discard working-tree edits or unstage files without touching commits.

concepts.name: Amending the last commit
concepts.summary: Fix the most recent local commit's message or content before sharing it.

misconceptions.text: Git pull only downloads changes and never alters my working branch.
A merge conflict means something has broken and the repository is damaged.
Adding a file to gitignore removes it from the repository if it is already tracked.

concepts.name: Commit graph and references
concepts.summary: Analyse history as a graph of commits where branches, tags and HEAD are movable pointers.

concepts.name: Rebasing versus merging
concepts.summary: Compare how rebase and merge integrate work and the history each produces.

concepts.name: Interactive rebase cleanup
concepts.summary: Reorder, squash and reword local commits to produce a clean, reviewable history.

concepts.name: Reset, revert and restore
concepts.summary: Choose among reset modes and revert based on whether history is shared and what must be preserved.

concepts.name: Recovery with reflog
concepts.summary: Find and restore lost commits after a bad reset, rebase or deleted branch.

concepts.name: Pull request workflow
concepts.summary: Use short-lived feature branches, pull requests and review to integrate changes into a shared branch.

concepts.name: Stashing and cherry-picking
concepts.summary: Shelve unfinished work and apply individual commits to another branch.

concepts.name: Tracking branches and upstreams
concepts.summary: Explain how remote-tracking branches relate to local ones and diagnose ahead/behind/diverged states.

misconceptions.text: Branches are separate copies of the code rather than pointers to commits.
Git reset --hard is always safe because Git keeps everything.
Rebase is always better than merge because it gives a cleaner history.

concepts.name: Branching strategy selection
concepts.summary: Evaluate trunk-based, Gitflow and similar strategies against team size, release cadence and risk.

concepts.name: Rewriting shared history safely
concepts.summary: Judge when rewriting published history is acceptable and use force-with-lease and team coordination to limit damage.

concepts.name: Bisecting regressions
concepts.summary: Locate the commit that introduced a bug using binary search, ideally automated with a test script.

concepts.name: Complex conflict resolution
concepts.summary: Analyse conflicts using the merge base and both sides, and reuse resolutions across repeated rebases.

concepts.name: Worktrees and submodules
concepts.summary: Choose among worktrees, submodules and subtrees for parallel checkouts and nested dependencies.

concepts.name: Hooks and automated checks
concepts.summary: Assess where local hooks, server-side rules and CI should enforce quality and message conventions.

concepts.name: Signed commits and provenance
concepts.summary: Explain how commit signing verifies authorship and judge when to require it.

concepts.name: Removing sensitive data from history
concepts.summary: Evaluate remediation of committed secrets, including rotation and history rewriting.

misconceptions.text: Deleting a leaked secret in a new commit removes the exposure.
One branching model such as Gitflow suits every team.
Client-side hooks guarantee that rules are enforced for everyone.

concepts.name: Git object model internals
concepts.summary: Evaluate behaviour and performance through the model of content-addressed blobs, trees, commits and tags.

concepts.name: Packfiles and repository maintenance
concepts.summary: Diagnose repository size and speed issues using packing, garbage collection and maintenance tasks.

concepts.name: Scaling large repositories
concepts.summary: Design workflows for very large repositories using partial clones, sparse checkout and shallow history.

concepts.name: Custom merge strategies and drivers
concepts.summary: Create attribute-based merge, diff and filter rules for special file types.

concepts.name: Repository migration and history surgery
concepts.summary: Plan migrations, splits and merges of repositories while preserving meaningful history and references.

concepts.name: Team Git policy design
concepts.summary: Design branch protection, review, signing and release tagging policies that fit an organisation's risk profile.

concepts.name: Plumbing commands and scripting
concepts.summary: Use low-level commands to script reliable tooling and inspect or repair repository state.

misconceptions.text: Git stores history as a chain of diffs between versions.
Shallow or partial clones are just smaller full clones with no workflow trade-offs.
Rewriting history with filter tools leaves old commits unreachable everywhere immediately.

concepts.name: Compiler versus interpreter distinction
concepts.summary: Explain how a compiler translates a whole program to another form before running while an interpreter executes the program directly, and that many implementations mix both.

concepts.name: Phases of translation pipeline
concepts.summary: Describe the sequence from source text through lexing, parsing, analysis and code generation to output, and what each phase consumes and produces.

concepts.name: Tokens and lexemes
concepts.summary: Recall that a lexer groups characters into tokens such as identifiers, keywords, literals and operators, discarding whitespace and comments.

concepts.name: Grammar as language specification
concepts.summary: Understand that a grammar with terminals, nonterminals and productions defines which token sequences are valid programs.

concepts.name: Syntax tree structure
concepts.summary: Understand that program structure is represented as a tree where operators and constructs are nodes and operands are children.

concepts.name: Syntax versus semantics errors
concepts.summary: Distinguish errors in program form (syntax) from errors in meaning (such as undeclared variables or type mismatches) and runtime errors.

concepts.name: Machine code, bytecode, and targets
concepts.summary: Name the kinds of output a compiler can produce, including native machine code, bytecode and another high-level language.

misconceptions.text: A language is either compiled or interpreted, as an inherent property of the language itself.
A compiler only checks syntax and does not look at the meaning of the program.
The lexer understands program structure such as nested expressions.

concepts.name: Writing a hand-coded lexer
concepts.summary: Implement a scanner that reads characters and emits tokens with type, text and position, using longest-match for operators and keywords.

concepts.name: Regular expressions for tokens
concepts.summary: Describe token classes with regular expressions and relate them to finite automata that recognise them.

concepts.name: Recursive descent parsing
concepts.summary: Write a parser with one function per grammar rule that consumes tokens and builds an abstract syntax tree.

concepts.name: Operator precedence and associativity
concepts.summary: Encode precedence and associativity in the grammar or with precedence climbing so expressions parse into the correct tree.

concepts.name: Abstract syntax tree design
concepts.summary: Define node types for expressions and statements that keep meaning and drop punctuation and grouping tokens.

concepts.name: Tree-walking evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate an AST by recursively visiting nodes to compute values and carry out statements.

concepts.name: Environments and variable scope
concepts.summary: Store variable bindings in nested environments so lookups and assignments respect block scope.

concepts.name: Syntax error reporting
concepts.summary: Report errors with line and column and recover enough to continue and report further errors.

misconceptions.text: Precedence is handled by the evaluator, so the parser can build any tree shape for an expression.
A recursive descent parser can handle any grammar, including left-recursive rules, without changes.
The AST should keep every token from the source, including parentheses and semicolons.

concepts.name: Grammar ambiguity and LL/LR
concepts.summary: Analyse a grammar for ambiguity, left recursion and lookahead conflicts, and decide whether LL(k) or LR parsing suits it.

concepts.name: Bottom-up shift-reduce parsing
concepts.summary: Trace a shift-reduce parse using a stack and tables, and interpret shift/reduce conflicts reported by a parser generator.

concepts.name: Symbol tables and name resolution
concepts.summary: Build symbol tables during a pass over the AST to resolve each name to its declaration and detect undeclared or duplicate names.

concepts.name: Static type checking
concepts.summary: Apply typing rules to expressions and statements to detect mismatches and annotate the tree with types.

concepts.name: Intermediate representations
concepts.summary: Lower an AST into a linear IR such as three-address code with temporaries and labelled jumps.

concepts.name: Control flow graphs
concepts.summary: Partition IR into basic blocks and connect them into a graph that shows all possible execution paths.

concepts.name: Stack-based bytecode virtual machine
concepts.summary: Compile an AST to stack bytecode and run it in a dispatch loop, and compare this with tree walking.

concepts.name: Runtime call stack and frames
concepts.summary: Analyse how activation records hold arguments, locals and return addresses to implement function calls and recursion.

misconceptions.text: Any grammar that accepts the right programs is fine for a parser, since ambiguity only affects performance.
Static type checking can be skipped for dynamic languages because they have no notion of types.
A bytecode VM is always faster than a tree-walking interpreter regardless of design.

concepts.name: Data-flow analysis
concepts.summary: Formulate forward and backward data-flow problems over the CFG and solve them iteratively to a fixed point.

concepts.name: Static single assignment form
concepts.summary: Analyse how SSA gives each variable one definition, using phi nodes at merges, to simplify optimisations.

concepts.name: Local and global optimisations
concepts.summary: Judge when optimisations such as constant propagation, dead code elimination and inlining are safe and worthwhile.

concepts.name: Register allocation
concepts.summary: Analyse how live ranges, interference and spilling determine register assignment, and compare graph colouring with linear scan.

concepts.name: Instruction selection and calling conventions
concepts.summary: Map IR operations to target instructions and conform to the ABI for argument passing, stack layout and saved registers.

concepts.name: Type inference and polymorphism
concepts.summary: Evaluate unification-based inference and generic implementation strategies such as monomorphisation versus boxing.

concepts.name: Closures and first-class functions
concepts.summary: Analyse how captured variables are stored so functions outlive their defining scope, including heap-allocated environments.

concepts.name: Garbage collection strategies
concepts.summary: Compare mark-sweep, copying, generational and reference-counting collectors by cost, pauses and handling of cycles.

misconceptions.text: An optimisation that speeds up one benchmark is always valid and beneficial for all programs.
Reference counting reclaims all unreachable memory, including cyclic structures.
Closures copy the values of captured variables at creation time, so later changes are never visible.

concepts.name: JIT compilation and tiering
concepts.summary: Evaluate profile-guided JIT designs, including speculation, deoptimisation and tier trade-offs between warm-up and peak speed.

concepts.name: Optimisation correctness and undefined behaviour
concepts.summary: Assess how language semantics, undefined behaviour and memory models constrain valid transformations.

concepts.name: Interprocedural and alias analysis
concepts.summary: Evaluate precision versus cost of analyses like points-to and escape analysis and their effect on optimisation.

concepts.name: Language design and implementation trade-offs
concepts.summary: Design language features such as exceptions, coroutines or pattern matching with a plan for their efficient implementation.

concepts.name: Compiler infrastructure and retargetability
concepts.summary: Design a compiler architecture with layered IRs and reusable passes that supports multiple front ends and back ends.

concepts.name: Verifying compilers and testing
concepts.summary: Evaluate approaches such as differential testing, fuzzing and formal verification for finding miscompilation.

concepts.name: Advanced parsing and incremental tooling
concepts.summary: Create parsers and front ends that support ambiguity, robust error recovery and incremental reparsing for editors.

misconceptions.text: A JIT compiler always outperforms ahead-of-time compilation because it has runtime information.
Compilers treat undefined behaviour as a platform-specific result that behaves predictably at runtime.
If a compiler passes its test suite, it is free of miscompilation bugs.

concepts.name: German sound-letter correspondences
concepts.summary: Understand how umlauts, ß, ch (ich/ach), sch, z, w, v and ei/ie map to sounds and read words aloud accurately.

concepts.name: Noun gender and articles
concepts.summary: Remember that every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, learn nouns with their articles, and recall the plural article die.

concepts.name: Noun capitalisation and plurals
concepts.summary: Understand that all nouns are capitalised and recognise the main plural patterns (-e, -n, -er, umlaut, -s).

concepts.name: Present tense of sein and haben
concepts.summary: Recall the irregular present forms of sein and haben for all persons.

concepts.name: Regular present-tense conjugation
concepts.summary: Understand how stem plus -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en marks person and number, including du/Sie formality.

concepts.name: Basic main-clause word order
concepts.summary: Understand that the conjugated verb sits in second position in simple statements and begins yes/no questions.

concepts.name: Nominative and accusative basics
concepts.summary: Understand that the subject is nominative and the direct object is accusative, with the masculine article changing from der to den.

misconceptions.text: German nouns only need a capital letter at the start of a sentence or when they are names.
The gender of a noun can be predicted from its meaning, so a girl must be feminine.
The ch in ich and in Buch is the same sound.

concepts.name: Dative case and its triggers
concepts.summary: Apply dative articles for indirect objects and after prepositions such as mit, nach, bei, von, zu, aus, seit and verbs like helfen.

concepts.name: Two-way prepositions
concepts.summary: Choose accusative for movement toward a place and dative for location with in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben and zwischen.

concepts.name: Modal verbs with infinitive
concepts.summary: Use können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen and mögen with the infinitive at the end of the clause.

concepts.name: Separable and inseparable verbs
concepts.summary: Apply the split of the prefix to the clause end in main clauses, as in anrufen, and recognise inseparable prefixes like be-, ver- and er-.

concepts.name: Perfekt formation
concepts.summary: Form the Perfekt with haben or sein plus the past participle, choosing the auxiliary and building ge- participles for regular, irregular and separable verbs.

concepts.name: Negation with nicht and kein
concepts.summary: Apply kein to negate nouns with indefinite or no article and nicht for verbs, adjectives and definite phrases, placing it correctly.

concepts.name: Possessive articles and personal pronouns
concepts.summary: Understand and use possessive articles and personal pronouns across nominative, accusative and dative.

concepts.name: Subordinating conjunctions and verb-final
concepts.summary: Apply verb-final word order in clauses introduced by weil, dass, wenn and ob.

misconceptions.text: Nicht ein and kein are interchangeable, so Ich habe nicht Geld is correct.
All verbs form the Perfekt with haben.
After weil the verb stays in second position as in a normal statement.

concepts.name: Adjective endings
concepts.summary: Select the correct adjective ending by combining case, gender, number and whether the article is definite, indefinite or absent.

concepts.name: Genitive case usage
concepts.summary: Use the genitive for possession and with prepositions like wegen, trotz, während and statt, and contrast it with von plus dative.

concepts.name: Präteritum versus Perfekt
concepts.summary: Analyse when Präteritum is preferred in writing and with sein, haben and modals, and when Perfekt suits spoken or conversational past reference.

concepts.name: Relative clauses and pronouns
concepts.summary: Build relative clauses where the pronoun takes gender and number from its antecedent and case from its role, with the verb final.

concepts.name: Reflexive verbs and pronouns
concepts.summary: Use reflexive verbs with accusative or dative reflexive pronouns and distinguish them from non-reflexive uses.

concepts.name: Infinitive clauses with zu
concepts.summary: Form infinitive clauses with zu, um...zu and ohne...zu, including the placement of zu with separable verbs.

concepts.name: Inversion and word order variation
concepts.summary: Analyse how fronting elements triggers verb-second inversion and how time, manner, place and pronoun order arrange middle-field elements.

concepts.name: Compound noun analysis
concepts.summary: Decompose compound nouns, determine gender from the last element and interpret linking elements like -s- and -n-.

misconceptions.text: Adjective endings are arbitrary and must simply be memorised word by word.
A relative pronoun takes its case from the noun it refers back to.
Präteritum and Perfekt are fully interchangeable in any context.

concepts.name: Konjunktiv II for hypotheticals
concepts.summary: Analyse and form Konjunktiv II and the würde-construction to express wishes, unreal conditions and polite requests.

concepts.name: Konjunktiv I and reported speech
concepts.summary: Analyse how Konjunktiv I reports speech neutrally and when Konjunktiv II substitutes for forms identical to the indicative.

concepts.name: Passive voice and alternatives
concepts.summary: Analyse Vorgangs- and Zustandspassiv, agent phrases, passive with modals and substitutes like man, sich lassen and sein+zu.

concepts.name: Verb-preposition and case government
concepts.summary: Analyse verbs, adjectives and nouns bound to particular prepositions and cases, including da- and wo- compounds.

concepts.name: Extended participial attributes
concepts.summary: Analyse nominal phrases that pack a participle and its complements before a noun, as typical in formal written German.

concepts.name: Modal particles and pragmatics
concepts.summary: Evaluate how particles like doch, ja, mal, eben and halt colour tone, and judge register differences between du and Sie, spoken and written.

concepts.name: Textual cohesion with connectors
concepts.summary: Evaluate the choice among adverbial and coordinating connectors such as deshalb, trotzdem, außerdem and obwohl for logical and word-order fit.

misconceptions.text: Konjunktiv II is only a polite form and cannot express unreal conditions.
Indirect speech simply requires Konjunktiv I in every case.
German passive always requires werden and cannot express a resulting state.

concepts.name: Register and style evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a text's vocabulary, syntax and nominal style suit contexts such as bureaucratic, academic, journalistic or colloquial German.

concepts.name: Regional variation and standard norms
concepts.summary: Evaluate differences among German, Austrian and Swiss standard varieties and dialect influence, judging acceptability against norms.

concepts.name: Information structure and theme-rheme
concepts.summary: Evaluate how fronting, passive, and middle-field ordering shape emphasis and discourse flow beyond grammatical correctness.

concepts.name: Crafting nuanced argumentative prose
concepts.summary: Create coherent, well-structured argumentative or essayistic texts that combine subjunctives, nominalisation and connectors with precision.

concepts.name: Translation and equivalence judgments
concepts.summary: Create translations that preserve meaning and tone, resolving German-specific features like compounds, particles and long sentences.

concepts.name: Language change and contested usage
concepts.summary: Evaluate evolving usage such as the weil verb-second, dative replacing genitive and gender-inclusive forms against prescriptive and descriptive views.

concepts.name: Word formation and neologism
concepts.summary: Create new, idiomatic words using derivation, compounding and prefix-verb patterns, and justify their acceptability.

misconceptions.text: There is one correct standard German, and regional forms from Austria or Switzerland are simply errors.
Long, nominalised sentences are always better German style.
A correct translation maps each German word to a single English equivalent.

concepts.name: Cloud computing definition
concepts.summary: Recall that cloud computing delivers shared computing resources over a network on demand, rented rather than owned.

concepts.name: Essential cloud characteristics
concepts.summary: Explain on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

concepts.name: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS models
concepts.summary: Distinguish infrastructure, platform and software as a service by what the provider supplies and what the customer manages.

concepts.name: Deployment models
concepts.summary: Describe public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud deployments and who owns and uses each.

concepts.name: Pay-as-you-go pricing
concepts.summary: Explain that customers pay for metered usage instead of buying hardware upfront, shifting capital expense to operating expense.

concepts.name: Data centres and servers
concepts.summary: Recall that cloud services run on providers' physical servers, storage and networks housed in large data centres.

misconceptions.text: The cloud is a mysterious place with no physical hardware behind it.
Cloud computing is just storing files online.
Cloud is always cheaper than running your own servers.

concepts.name: Virtualization and hypervisors
concepts.summary: Explain how a hypervisor shares one physical host among isolated virtual machines, and tell type 1 from type 2.

concepts.name: Regions and availability zones
concepts.summary: Choose regions and zones for a simple workload, knowing a region contains multiple isolated zones.

concepts.name: Shared responsibility model
aliases: security of vs in the cloud
concepts.summary: Apply the split of security duties between provider and customer for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

concepts.name: Elasticity versus scalability
concepts.summary: Distinguish scalability as capacity to grow from elasticity as automatic matching of capacity to demand, and apply vertical and horizontal scaling.

concepts.name: Matching service model to need
concepts.summary: Pick IaaS, PaaS or SaaS for a simple scenario based on required control and management effort.

concepts.name: Resource pooling and multi-tenancy
concepts.summary: Explain how many customers share pooled hardware while logically isolated from each other.

misconceptions.text: The provider is responsible for securing everything you put in the cloud.
Elasticity and scalability mean the same thing.
A virtual machine is a separate physical computer.

concepts.name: High availability across zones
concepts.summary: Design a workload that survives a zone failure by distributing redundant components across availability zones.

concepts.name: Cloud cost analysis
concepts.summary: Compare cloud and on-premises total cost of ownership, including usage patterns, data transfer and idle resources.

concepts.name: Pricing options trade-offs
concepts.summary: Analyse when on-demand, reserved or committed, and interruptible spot capacity fit different workloads.

concepts.name: Hybrid and multi-cloud rationale
concepts.summary: Analyse the drivers and costs of hybrid and multi-cloud, such as compliance, latency, resilience and added complexity.

concepts.name: Auto scaling policies
concepts.summary: Configure scaling rules and load balancing that add or remove instances based on metrics.

concepts.name: Data residency and compliance
concepts.summary: Analyse how regulations and data location constrain region choice and service use.

concepts.name: Responsibility boundaries by service
concepts.summary: Analyse who owns patching, identity, data and configuration for a given service and find gaps.

misconceptions.text: Running in the cloud automatically makes an application highly available.
Multi-cloud always improves resilience and lowers cost.
Autoscaling removes the need for capacity planning or cost monitoring.

concepts.name: Workload placement evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate which workloads belong in public, private, hybrid or on-premises environments against technical and business criteria.

concepts.name: Migration strategy selection
concepts.summary: Judge between rehost, replatform, refactor, replace and retire for an application, weighing effort against benefit.

concepts.name: Resilience and disaster recovery
concepts.summary: Analyse recovery objectives and compare backup, pilot light, warm standby and active-active strategies across regions.

concepts.name: Vendor lock-in assessment
concepts.summary: Evaluate lock-in risk from proprietary services against portability costs and the benefits of managed services.

concepts.name: Cloud financial governance
concepts.summary: Assess cost controls such as tagging, budgets, showback and rightsizing for their effect on spending accountability.

concepts.name: Performance and latency trade-offs
concepts.summary: Analyse how region distance, data gravity and egress charges shape architecture and performance.

concepts.name: Provider and service evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate providers and services by SLAs, compliance attestations, support and service fit.

misconceptions.text: Lifting and shifting an application to the cloud delivers cloud benefits unchanged.
A provider's SLA guarantees your application will never go down.
Avoiding lock-in is always worth the cost of using only generic services.

concepts.name: Cloud strategy design
concepts.summary: Create an organisation-wide cloud strategy aligning deployment models, service models, governance and business goals.

concepts.name: Multi-region resilient architecture
concepts.summary: Design architectures spanning regions that meet stated availability, latency, consistency and cost targets.

concepts.name: Landing zone and governance framework
concepts.summary: Create a multi-account governance framework with guardrails, identity boundaries and standard controls.

concepts.name: Cloud risk and compliance critique
concepts.summary: Evaluate risks such as provider concentration, misconfiguration and jurisdictional exposure, and justify mitigations.

concepts.name: Economic modelling of cloud
concepts.summary: Critique and build business cases and unit-cost models that test when cloud, repatriation or hybrid is justified.

concepts.name: Sustainability in cloud design
concepts.summary: Evaluate energy efficiency and carbon impact of placement, utilisation and architecture choices.

concepts.name: Cloud portfolio evolution
concepts.summary: Create a roadmap and exit strategy that adapt the cloud portfolio as services, costs and regulations change.

misconceptions.text: A single cloud strategy with one standard architecture fits every workload in an organisation.
Moving to the cloud transfers accountability for compliance and risk to the provider.
Cloud is inherently greener, so sustainability needs no design attention.

concepts.name: Red-green-refactor cycle
concepts.summary: Explain the three steps of writing a failing test, making it pass, then cleaning up, and why they occur in that order.

concepts.name: Test-first principle
concepts.summary: Understand that the test is written before the production code it exercises and why that ordering matters.

concepts.name: Failing test as specification
concepts.summary: Describe how a failing test states one small piece of required behaviour before it exists.

concepts.name: Smallest step to pass
concepts.summary: Recognise that in the green step you write only enough code to make the current failing test pass.

concepts.name: Refactoring under green tests
concepts.summary: Remember that refactoring changes structure without changing behaviour and is done only while all tests pass.

concepts.name: Fast feedback from test runs
concepts.summary: Understand why running the tests after each small change quickly shows whether the last change broke something.

misconceptions.text: TDD means writing all the tests for a feature up front and then writing all the code.
A test that fails at the start means something has gone wrong.
Refactoring means adding new features to make the code better.

concepts.name: Writing a single failing unit test
concepts.summary: Write one focused unit test that fails for the right reason, using arrange-act-assert structure.

concepts.name: Fake it and obvious implementation
aliases: fake it till you make it
concepts.summary: Pass a test with a hard-coded value or direct implementation and choose between them based on confidence.

concepts.name: Triangulation by added examples
concepts.summary: Add a second test case with different data to force a hard-coded result to become a general implementation.

concepts.name: Choosing the next test
concepts.summary: Keep a list of behaviours to test and pick the next simple case that moves the design forward.

concepts.name: Removing duplication in refactoring
concepts.summary: Spot duplication in code and tests during the refactor step and remove it while keeping the tests green.

concepts.name: Test naming and readability
concepts.summary: Name tests after the behaviour they check so a failure message explains what broke.

concepts.name: Verifying the test fails first
concepts.summary: Run a new test before implementing to confirm it fails for the expected reason and does not pass vacuously.

misconceptions.text: Hard-coding a return value to pass a test is cheating and should be avoided.
If a new test passes immediately, that is a good sign and no check is needed.
Refactoring only applies to production code, not to the tests.

concepts.name: Test doubles for isolation
concepts.summary: Use stubs, fakes and mocks to isolate the unit under test from slow or nondeterministic collaborators.

concepts.name: Tests driving design
concepts.summary: Analyse how difficulty in writing a test reveals coupling or poor responsibilities and change the design in response.

concepts.name: Dependency injection for testability
concepts.summary: Introduce seams so collaborators can be supplied from outside and replaced in tests.

concepts.name: Behaviour versus implementation testing
concepts.summary: Distinguish tests that assert observable behaviour from those coupled to internals and rewrite the latter.

concepts.name: Testing legacy code safely
concepts.summary: Analyse untested code and add characterization tests before changing it.

concepts.name: Edge cases and error paths
concepts.summary: Drive boundary values, invalid input and failure handling through tests added one at a time.

concepts.name: Test suite speed and independence
concepts.summary: Diagnose tests that depend on shared state, order or slow resources and restructure them to be fast and independent.

misconceptions.text: Every collaborator should be mocked so each class is tested in complete isolation.
High code coverage from TDD proves the tests are good.
TDD can only be used on new code, not on existing code.

concepts.name: Outside-in and inside-out TDD
concepts.summary: Evaluate the classicist and mockist styles and choose between them for a given design context.

concepts.name: Acceptance-test-driven outer loop
concepts.summary: Analyse how a failing acceptance test drives inner unit-level TDD cycles toward a feature.

concepts.name: Test suite maintainability audit
concepts.summary: Evaluate a suite for smells such as fragility, obscure tests and duplication, and judge which to fix first.

concepts.name: Test pyramid balance
concepts.summary: Judge the mix of unit, integration and end-to-end tests so TDD remains fast and confidence is adequate.

concepts.name: Evolutionary design with TDD
concepts.summary: Analyse how small refactorings under tests let architecture emerge and when upfront design is still needed.

concepts.name: TDD in hard domains
concepts.summary: Evaluate strategies for applying TDD to user interfaces, databases, concurrency and external services.

concepts.name: Mutation testing as feedback
concepts.summary: Use mutation analysis to find tests that run code without truly verifying it.

misconceptions.text: There is one correct style of TDD and the other style is a mistake.
TDD replaces the need for acceptance and integration testing.
Following TDD guarantees a good architecture without any deliberate design thinking.

concepts.name: Adapting TDD to context
concepts.summary: Judge when strict TDD, relaxed test-after or spikes are most economical given risk, uncertainty and codebase.

concepts.name: Spike and discard practice
concepts.summary: Evaluate when to explore with throwaway code and then reimplement it test-first.

concepts.name: Designing team TDD adoption
concepts.summary: Create a plan for introducing TDD to a team, including katas, pairing, mob sessions and shared conventions.

concepts.name: Evidence on TDD outcomes
concepts.summary: Critically appraise empirical studies of TDD's effect on quality, productivity and design and their limitations.

concepts.name: Test architecture for large systems
concepts.summary: Design a test architecture with contract tests, test data strategies and build pipeline stages that keeps TDD feedback fast at scale.

concepts.name: Property-based test-driven design
concepts.summary: Combine example-driven cycles with property-based tests to specify general behaviour and discover edge cases.

concepts.name: Evolving legacy systems with TDD
concepts.summary: Create incremental strategies that bring large untested systems under test while delivering change.

misconceptions.text: Experts apply strict test-first to every line of code without exception.
Studies have conclusively proven that TDD always improves quality and productivity.
Mandating TDD with a coverage target is enough to get a team to adopt it well.

concepts.name: Organic versus paid results
concepts.summary: Distinguish unpaid organic listings from ads on a search results page and recognise that SEO targets the organic ones.

concepts.name: Crawl, index, rank pipeline
concepts.summary: Explain that a search engine discovers pages by crawling, stores them in an index, and then ranks indexed pages for each query.

concepts.name: Keywords and search queries
concepts.summary: Recognise that people type queries into search engines and that pages are matched to those words and their meaning.

concepts.name: Search intent types
concepts.summary: Explain the informational, navigational, commercial and transactional intents behind queries and why a page must match the intent.

concepts.name: Title tag and meta description
concepts.summary: Describe how the title tag and meta description appear in results and what role each plays in attracting clicks.

concepts.name: Headings and page content
concepts.summary: Understand how headings structure a page's content for readers and search engines.

concepts.name: Links as votes of trust
concepts.summary: Explain that links from other sites act as signals of a page's credibility and help crawlers discover pages.

misconceptions.text: SEO means tricking Google with hidden keywords to get to the top.
Once a page is published it is automatically in Google's results.
The meta description directly makes a page rank higher.

concepts.name: Basic keyword research workflow
concepts.summary: Use a keyword tool to find terms, compare search volume and difficulty, and shortlist keywords for a page.

concepts.name: Mapping keywords to intent
concepts.summary: Inspect the top results for a query to judge intent and choose the right page type for it.

concepts.name: Writing effective title tags
concepts.summary: Write unique titles with the primary keyword near the front, suitable length and a clear reason to click.

concepts.name: Writing meta descriptions
concepts.summary: Write unique, accurate descriptions that summarise the page and encourage clicks, knowing Google may rewrite them.

concepts.name: Heading hierarchy and URLs
concepts.summary: Apply a single descriptive H1, logical subheadings and short readable URLs to a page.

concepts.name: Internal linking with anchor text
concepts.summary: Add contextual links between related pages using descriptive anchor text so users and crawlers can navigate.

concepts.name: Robots.txt and XML sitemaps
concepts.summary: Explain what robots.txt and XML sitemaps do and set up simple versions for a small site.

concepts.name: Search Console basics
concepts.summary: Verify a site, submit a sitemap and read the performance report for queries, clicks, impressions and position.

misconceptions.text: Targeting the highest-volume keyword is always the best choice.
Robots.txt keeps a page out of Google's index reliably.
More keywords stuffed into the title and headings improves rankings.

concepts.name: Topic clusters and content gaps
concepts.summary: Analyse a keyword set to group queries into topics, spot gaps against competitors and plan pillar and supporting pages.

concepts.name: Indexing diagnostics
concepts.summary: Use Search Console to diagnose why pages are not indexed, such as noindex, crawled-not-indexed or blocked URLs.

concepts.name: Canonicalisation and duplicates
concepts.summary: Handle duplicate or parameterised URLs with canonical tags and redirects so signals consolidate on one URL.

concepts.name: Redirects and status codes
concepts.summary: Choose among 200, 301, 302, 404 and 410 responses and implement redirects during migrations or URL changes.

concepts.name: Core Web Vitals metrics
concepts.summary: Interpret LCP, INP and CLS using lab and field data and trace poor scores to causes like large images or layout shifts.

concepts.name: Structured data with schema
concepts.summary: Add JSON-LD markup for types like Article, Product or FAQ and validate it to qualify for rich results.

concepts.name: Backlink quality assessment
concepts.summary: Evaluate links by relevance, authority and editorial context rather than raw count.

concepts.name: Technical site audit
concepts.summary: Run a crawler and Search Console review to find and prioritise issues like broken links, thin pages and missing tags.

misconceptions.text: Schema markup is a direct ranking boost.
Duplicate content triggers a penalty that must be avoided at all costs.
A good Lighthouse score guarantees good Core Web Vitals for real users.

concepts.name: Crawl budget optimisation
concepts.summary: Analyse server logs and crawl stats to find wasted crawling on faceted, parameter or low-value URLs and fix it.

concepts.name: Rendering and JavaScript SEO
