issues: nov-1 (voltage, current and resistance) and adb-2 flagged as near-duplicates is a false alarm: adb-2 is dividers, so the names do not really overlap. Still, nov-1 bundles three quantities, which is acceptable at novice level.

prf-3 and exp-1 flagged as near-duplicates is partly real: both are 'circuit analysis in a transformed domain'. They differ (phasor steady-state vs Laplace), but exp-1 is a stretch at C5 and its summary 'evaluate when to transform' is vague, so rename it more specifically.

Missing prerequisite: adb-7 (passive sign convention) should come before adb-3/adb-4 and is placed correctly, but nov-6 -> adb-7 is weak; power sign interpretation is fine, though adb-7 would rather depend on nov-1.

Missing prerequisite: cmp-5 (maximum power transfer) needs nov-6 power, covered transitively, fine. cmp-6 depends on cmp-4 (Thevenin), which is a genuine dependency via equivalent resistance seen by C or L.
Missing prerequisite: adb-2 (dividers) lacks nov-3 link, covered transitively through adb-1.
exp-6 depends on exp-7 but exp-7 depends on prf-5 only; a parasitics concept at expert stage overlaps with the exp-6 summary on non-ideal components, so exp-6 duplicates part of exp-7.
Misconception on adb-3/adb-1 ('current shared out in a series circuit') is tagged to KCL, which is fine, but nov-2 would fit better; the novice misconception about current used up is already covered.
prf-7 second-order transient response depends on cmp-6 and prf-2, but also needs prf-5 (damping ties to resonance); minor.
exp-3 two-port models sit at C6 'construct', which is acceptable; exp-4 depends on prf-4 but also on phasors (prf-1), covered transitively.

concepts.name: Session management flaws

concepts.name: Security misconfiguration review

concepts.name: Broken access control analysis

concepts.name: Server-side request forgery

concepts.name: Authentication architecture evaluation

concepts.name: Business logic and race flaws

concepts.summary: Use possessive and atomic constructs to prevent needless backtracking and understand when they change results.

concepts.name: Unicode-aware matching
concepts.summary: Analyse how encodings, normalisation, and property classes like \p{L} affect what \w, case folding and the dot match.

concepts.name: Engine flavour differences
concepts.summary: Evaluate how dialects differ in supported syntax and semantics and judge portability of a pattern.

concepts.name: Regex versus parser choice
concepts.summary: Judge when regex is the right tool and when nested or context-sensitive formats such as HTML require a real parser.

concepts.name: Validation pattern design
concepts.summary: Evaluate validation patterns for false positives and negatives, such as emails and dates, and decide how strict to be.

misconceptions.text: Regex can reliably parse arbitrary nested HTML or balanced brackets.
All regex engines run in linear time regardless of pattern.
A single regex can fully validate an email address according to the specification.

concepts.name: Automata theory foundations
concepts.summary: Evaluate regex features against finite automata, explaining which constructs keep a language regular and which exceed it.

concepts.name: Linear-time engine trade-offs
concepts.summary: Judge when to choose non-backtracking engines for guaranteed performance and what features such engines give up.

concepts.name: ReDoS-resistant pattern design
concepts.summary: Design patterns and surrounding controls such as timeouts and input limits that keep untrusted-input matching safe.

concepts.name: Regex-based tokenizer design
concepts.summary: Create a tokenizer from ordered regex rules, handling longest-match and priority conflicts.

concepts.name: Maintainable regex architecture
concepts.summary: Create patterns that are composed, commented, tested and documented so teams can maintain them.

concepts.name: Large-scale text transformation strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate approaches to bulk searching and rewriting, weighing regex, structured parsing and tooling for correctness and speed.

concepts.name: Regex test strategy
concepts.summary: Create test suites with adversarial, boundary and fuzzed inputs that expose false matches and performance faults.

misconceptions.text: Modern regex with backreferences and lookarounds still describes only regular languages.
Switching to a linear-time engine lets you keep every feature, including backreferences.
Tests that pass on typical inputs show a pattern is safe.

concepts.name: Problem worth solving
concepts.summary: Recognise that a venture starts from a specific, painful problem faced by identifiable people rather than from a clever idea.

concepts.name: Target customer segment
concepts.summary: Explain who the customer is and why a narrow, well-defined group is a better starting point than everyone.

concepts.name: Customer discovery interviews
concepts.summary: Understand that interviews are used to learn about customers' real behaviour and problems, not to pitch or validate your idea.

concepts.name: Value proposition
concepts.summary: State in one sentence what benefit the product gives a specific customer and why it is better than the alternatives.

concepts.name: Minimum viable product
concepts.summary: Explain that an MVP is the smallest thing that tests a key assumption and generates learning, not a poor-quality full product.

concepts.name: Business model basics
concepts.summary: Name the ways a startup earns revenue, such as subscriptions, one-off sales, ads or commissions, and what costs it must cover.

concepts.name: Founder roles and commitment
concepts.summary: Describe why founding teams need complementary skills and shared commitment, and what co-founders are responsible for.

misconceptions.text: A great idea is the most important ingredient and should be kept secret until launch.
Customer interviews are for asking people whether they like your idea.
An MVP is a low-quality, stripped-down version of the finished product.

concepts.name: Past-behaviour interview technique
concepts.summary: Conduct interviews asking about specific past events and current workarounds, avoiding hypotheticals and compliments.

concepts.name: Lean canvas
concepts.summary: Fill in a lean canvas covering problem, segment, solution, channels, revenue, costs, key metrics and unfair advantage, and mark the riskiest assumptions.

concepts.name: Problem-solution fit
concepts.summary: Judge from interview evidence whether the problem is frequent and painful enough and whether your solution addresses it.

concepts.name: Riskiest assumption testing
concepts.summary: List the assumptions behind an idea and design a cheap experiment for the one that would break the business if wrong.

concepts.name: MVP types
concepts.summary: Choose and build a suitable MVP form such as a landing page, concierge service, Wizard of Oz or prototype to test a hypothesis.

concepts.name: Pricing and unit economics basics
concepts.summary: Set an initial price and compute simple per-customer revenue and cost to see if each sale makes money.

concepts.name: Founder equity split basics
concepts.summary: Explain how founders divide ownership, why vesting with a cliff protects the team, and what the cap table records.

misconceptions.text: If friends and family say they love the idea, the problem has been validated.
A lean canvas is a finished plan that should be completed once and then followed.
Splitting equity 50/50 immediately with no vesting is fair and simple, so nothing can go wrong.

concepts.name: Synthesising interview evidence
concepts.summary: Analyse many interviews to separate patterns from anecdotes and decide what the evidence supports.

concepts.name: Validation metrics and thresholds
concepts.summary: Set success criteria in advance for experiments and tell actionable metrics from vanity metrics.

concepts.name: Customer acquisition channels
concepts.summary: Test channels such as outbound sales, content and referrals and compare how well each reaches the target segment.

concepts.name: Landing first paying customers
concepts.summary: Win initial customers through direct outreach and manual sales, using preorders or paid pilots as proof of willingness to pay.

concepts.name: CAC, LTV and payback
concepts.summary: Calculate customer acquisition cost, lifetime value and payback period and analyse whether the model can be profitable.

concepts.name: Pivot or persevere decision
concepts.summary: Analyse evidence against hypotheses to decide whether to continue, adjust a part of the model or pivot.

concepts.name: Bootstrapping versus outside funding
concepts.summary: Compare bootstrapping, angels and venture capital by control, speed, expectations and fit with the business.

concepts.name: Vesting and equity agreements
concepts.summary: Apply vesting schedules, cliffs and role-based adjustments to structure a fair founder equity agreement.

misconceptions.text: Signups, page views and compliments show the startup has traction.
Every startup should raise venture capital, and raising money is a sign of success.
A pivot means the startup has failed and starts again from nothing.

concepts.name: Product-market fit assessment
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether retention, organic demand and customer pull show real product-market fit rather than early enthusiasm.

concepts.name: Pitch deck narrative design
concepts.summary: Judge and shape a pitch deck so that problem, solution, market, traction, team and ask form a credible story for investors.

concepts.name: Market sizing critique
concepts.summary: Analyse top-down and bottom-up market estimates and spot unrealistic claims about market size.

concepts.name: Funding terms evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate valuation, dilution, SAFEs, liquidation preferences and board control to decide whether an offer is acceptable.

concepts.name: Dilution and cap table modelling
concepts.summary: Model how successive rounds, option pools and convertibles dilute founders and affect their incentives.

concepts.name: Scalable sales and channel repeatability
concepts.summary: Judge whether acquisition is repeatable beyond founder-led sales and decide when to invest in scaling it.

concepts.name: Strategic pivot types
concepts.summary: Distinguish customer, problem, channel and business-model pivots and choose the one suggested by the data.

misconceptions.text: A high valuation is always the best term in a funding offer.
A huge total addressable market proves the opportunity is attractive.
Revenue growth from founder-led sales means the company is ready to scale.

concepts.name: Opportunity selection strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing opportunities against founder strengths, market timing, defensibility and risk appetite to commit to one.

concepts.name: Designing a funding strategy
concepts.summary: Create a funding plan sequencing bootstrapping, grants, angels and venture rounds to match milestones and keep control.

concepts.name: Defensibility and moat creation
concepts.summary: Design sources of durable advantage such as network effects, data, brand or switching costs into the business.

concepts.name: Founder conflict and governance
concepts.summary: Evaluate governance structures and resolve founder conflicts, departures and control disputes in a way that protects the company.

concepts.name: Business model innovation
concepts.summary: Create or redesign a business model, pricing and distribution to unlock a market that existing models fail to serve.

concepts.name: Portfolio of experiments system
concepts.summary: Build a company-wide system of prioritised experiments and metrics that keeps learning fast as the company grows.

concepts.name: Exit and long-term outcomes
concepts.summary: Evaluate exit paths, including acquisition, IPO or staying independent, and how they align with investor and founder goals.

misconceptions.text: Strong execution alone makes a company defensible, so a moat is unnecessary.
Founder disputes can be settled informally later without hurting the company.
Every venture-backed company should aim for an IPO as the only successful exit.

concepts.name: Pitch and note names
concepts.summary: Name the seven natural notes A to G, know that pitch is how high or low a sound is, and recognise that the pattern repeats at each octave.

concepts.name: Staff, clefs and ledger lines
concepts.summary: Explain how the five-line staff and the treble and bass clefs assign pitches to lines and spaces, and how ledger lines extend the range.

concepts.name: Beat and pulse
concepts.summary: Understand the beat as the steady underlying pulse of music and tempo as its speed.

concepts.name: Note and rest values
concepts.summary: Identify whole, half, quarter and eighth notes and their matching rests, and explain how each relates in length to the others.

concepts.name: Time signatures and bars
concepts.summary: Explain what the top and bottom numbers of a simple time signature mean and how bar lines group beats into measures.

concepts.name: Sharps, flats and naturals
concepts.summary: Describe how accidentals raise or lower a pitch by a semitone and how they relate to black keys on a keyboard.

concepts.name: Semitones and whole tones
concepts.summary: Understand the semitone as the smallest step on the keyboard and the whole tone as two semitones.

concepts.name: Dynamics and basic markings
concepts.summary: Recall common dynamic markings such as p, mf and f and basic tempo terms such as allegro and andante.

misconceptions.text: Every white key is a natural note and every black key is a separate letter name unrelated to the white keys.
A faster tempo means the notes have shorter written values.
There is always a semitone between any two adjacent letter names, such as B and C or C and D.

concepts.name: Major scale construction
concepts.summary: Build a major scale on any starting note using the whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half step pattern.

concepts.name: Key signatures and the circle of fifths
concepts.summary: Identify and write the key signatures of major keys and use the circle of fifths to find how many sharps or flats a key has.

concepts.name: Scale degrees and solfège
concepts.summary: Number and name the degrees of a scale, including tonic, dominant and leading note, and relate them to solfège syllables.

concepts.name: Interval size and quality
concepts.summary: Name an interval by number and quality (major, minor, perfect) above a given note, using the major scale as reference.

concepts.name: Triads
concepts.summary: Build major and minor triads from a root by stacking thirds and distinguish them by the quality of the third.

concepts.name: Natural minor scale
concepts.summary: Construct the natural minor scale and find the relative minor of any major key.

concepts.name: Compound meter and dotted rhythms
concepts.summary: Apply dots and ties to notes and count compound time such as 6/8 in groups of three subdivisions.

concepts.name: Reading simple melodies
concepts.summary: Read a short melody in a major or minor key, naming pitches and clapping or counting its rhythm accurately.

misconceptions.text: A key signature tells you whether a piece is major or minor.
An interval's size is found by counting semitones only, so a major third and a diminished fourth are the same thing.
Minor triads sound sad and major triads sound happy because of the root note, not the third.

concepts.name: Diatonic triads and Roman numerals
concepts.summary: Build the seven triads of a major or minor key and label them with Roman numerals showing their quality and function.

concepts.name: Harmonic and melodic minor
concepts.summary: Construct harmonic and melodic minor scales and explain why the leading note is raised to create a dominant chord.

concepts.name: Chord inversions and figured bass
concepts.summary: Identify and write triads in root position and inversions and read the figures and slash chord symbols that indicate them.

concepts.name: Seventh chords
concepts.summary: Build and name the main seventh chord types, especially dominant seventh, major seventh and minor seventh.

concepts.name: Harmonic function and cadences
concepts.summary: Analyse chords as tonic, predominant or dominant function and identify authentic, plagal, half and deceptive cadences.

concepts.name: Common chord progressions
concepts.summary: Analyse typical progressions such as I-IV-V-I, ii-V-I and I-vi-IV-V and explain why they feel stable or move forward.

concepts.name: Modes
concepts.summary: Construct the diatonic modes from a common scale and describe the characteristic note that distinguishes each.

concepts.name: Phrase and form structure
concepts.summary: Analyse a piece into phrases and sections such as verse, chorus, binary and ternary and describe how repetition and contrast shape it.

misconceptions.text: Minor keys use only the natural minor scale, so the V chord is always minor.
An inverted chord is a different chord with a different root.
Modes are just the major scale played starting on a different note with no difference in sound or tonal centre.

concepts.name: Secondary dominants
concepts.summary: Identify and explain chords borrowed from another key's dominant that tonicise a diatonic chord, such as V7/V.

concepts.name: Modal interchange
concepts.summary: Analyse chords borrowed from the parallel major or minor, such as iv in a major key, and judge their expressive effect.

concepts.name: Modulation techniques
concepts.summary: Analyse how a piece moves to a new key using pivot chords, common tones or direct changes and tell modulation from tonicisation.

concepts.name: Voice leading principles
concepts.summary: Evaluate chord connections by smoothness, avoiding parallel fifths and octaves and resolving tendency tones.

concepts.name: Extended and altered chords
concepts.summary: Analyse chords with added ninths, elevenths, thirteenths and alterations and explain their function within a progression.

concepts.name: Non-chord tones
concepts.summary: Distinguish passing tones, neighbour tones, suspensions and appoggiaturas and explain how they create tension against the harmony.

concepts.name: Complex and irregular rhythm
concepts.summary: Analyse syncopation, hemiola, polyrhythm and asymmetric meters such as 5/4 and 7/8 and how they affect feel.

concepts.name: Harmonic analysis of real repertoire
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing analyses of a real piece and justify a harmonic reading using evidence from the score.

misconceptions.text: Any chord with an accidental means the music has modulated to a new key.
Voice-leading rules such as banning parallel fifths are absolute laws of all music.
Non-chord tones are mistakes or notes that do not belong in the music.

concepts.name: Chromatic harmony and mediants
concepts.summary: Evaluate the use of Neapolitan, augmented sixth and chromatic mediant chords and judge how they extend tonal language.

concepts.name: Reharmonisation
concepts.summary: Create new harmonisations of a melody using substitutions and justify how each alters its character.

concepts.name: Counterpoint and texture design
concepts.summary: Compose independent melodic lines that work together and choose textures such as homophony or polyphony to suit an expressive aim.

concepts.name: Symmetrical and extended tonality
concepts.summary: Evaluate whole tone, octatonic and pentatonic systems and non-tonal approaches, judging when they replace functional harmony.

concepts.name: Arranging and orchestration
concepts.summary: Create arrangements that assign material to instruments by range, timbre and balance for a chosen ensemble.

concepts.name: Original composition in a style
concepts.summary: Compose a complete piece in a chosen idiom, integrating melody, harmony, rhythm and form with deliberate choices.

concepts.name: Critical evaluation of theory systems
concepts.summary: Evaluate the strengths and limits of analytical systems such as Roman numerals, functional theory and Schenkerian analysis for different repertoires.

misconceptions.text: Music theory is a set of rules a composer must obey to write good music.
Atonal or non-functional music has no structure or organisation.
Reharmonisation just means swapping in more complex chords, whatever the melody.

concepts.name: Genes and alleles
concepts.summary: Recall that a gene is a unit of heredity at a locus and that alleles are alternative versions of it.

concepts.name: Genotype versus phenotype
concepts.summary: Explain that genotype is the allele combination an individual carries while phenotype is the resulting observable trait.

concepts.name: Dominant and recessive alleles
concepts.summary: Explain how a dominant allele masks a recessive one in heterozygotes.

concepts.name: Homozygous and heterozygous
concepts.summary: Recall the terms for carrying two identical or two different alleles at a locus.

concepts.name: Chromosomes and diploid inheritance
concepts.summary: Understand that each parent gives one chromosome of each pair so offspring carry two alleles per gene.

concepts.name: Gametes and allele segregation
concepts.summary: Understand that the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation so each gamete carries one.

concepts.name: Mendel's pea experiments
concepts.summary: Recall how Mendel crossed pea lines and observed the 3:1 ratio in the F2 generation.

misconceptions.text: Dominant alleles are always more common or stronger than recessive alleles.
Offspring inherit all their traits from only one parent, or a blend of the parents' traits.
Genotype and phenotype mean the same thing.

concepts.name: Punnett square monohybrid crosses
concepts.summary: Construct Punnett squares to predict genotype and phenotype ratios for one-gene crosses.

concepts.name: Test cross
concepts.summary: Use a cross with a homozygous recessive individual to determine an unknown genotype.

concepts.name: Dihybrid crosses and independent assortment
concepts.summary: Predict two-gene outcomes, including the 9:3:3:1 ratio, assuming genes assort independently.

concepts.name: Probability rules in genetics
concepts.summary: Apply multiplication and addition rules to calculate probabilities of genetic outcomes.

concepts.name: Incomplete dominance and codominance
concepts.summary: Distinguish patterns where heterozygotes show an intermediate or both phenotypes.

concepts.name: Sex determination and sex-linked traits
concepts.summary: Predict inheritance of X-linked traits in males and females.

concepts.name: Multiple alleles and blood groups
concepts.summary: Work out ABO blood group inheritance using three alleles with dominance and codominance.

misconceptions.text: A Punnett square result means exactly that ratio will appear in every family or small sample.
If parents have had three children of one phenotype, the next child is more likely to be different.
Incomplete dominance shows that alleles blend permanently and cannot separate in later generations.

concepts.name: Pedigree analysis
concepts.summary: Analyse pedigrees to infer the mode of inheritance and the likely genotypes of individuals.

concepts.name: Gene linkage and recombination
concepts.summary: Explain how linked genes deviate from independent assortment and how crossing over produces recombinants.

concepts.name: Genetic mapping from recombination frequency
concepts.summary: Calculate recombination frequencies from cross data to order genes and estimate map distances.

concepts.name: Chi-square test for ratios
concepts.summary: Use a chi-square test to judge whether observed offspring counts fit expected ratios.

concepts.name: Epistasis and gene interaction
concepts.summary: Interpret modified dihybrid ratios such as 9:3:4 or 12:3:1 as interactions between genes.

concepts.name: Penetrance and expressivity
concepts.summary: Distinguish incomplete penetrance from variable expressivity when genotype does not predict phenotype cleanly.

concepts.name: Chromosomal mutations and nondisjunction
concepts.summary: Analyse how nondisjunction, deletions, duplications, inversions and translocations alter inheritance.

concepts.name: Point mutation types and effects
concepts.summary: Classify substitutions and indels and predict their effect on the protein.

misconceptions.text: Linked genes can never be separated and always are inherited together.
A non-significant chi-square result proves the hypothesized ratio is correct.
Epistasis is the same as dominance between alleles of one gene.

concepts.name: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
concepts.summary: Derive and apply expected genotype frequencies and the assumptions required for equilibrium.

concepts.name: Evolutionary forces on allele frequencies
concepts.summary: Analyse how selection, genetic drift, gene flow and mutation shift allele frequencies.

concepts.name: Inbreeding and heterozygosity loss
concepts.summary: Explain how non-random mating changes genotype frequencies and exposes recessive disease.

concepts.name: Quantitative traits and heritability
concepts.summary: Evaluate what heritability estimates do and do not say about genetic influence on a trait.

concepts.name: Epigenetic and imprinting effects
concepts.summary: Analyse inheritance patterns that depend on parent of origin or chromatin state rather than DNA sequence.

concepts.name: Mitochondrial inheritance
concepts.summary: Interpret pedigrees showing maternal transmission and heteroplasmy.

concepts.name: Genetic risk calculation with Bayes
concepts.summary: Evaluate carrier or disease risk by combining prior pedigree probability with conditional evidence.

misconceptions.text: Dominant alleles increase in frequency over generations simply because they are dominant.
High heritability means a trait is fixed by genes and cannot be changed by environment.
Hardy-Weinberg proportions describe real populations that are evolving.

concepts.name: Genome-wide association study design
concepts.summary: Evaluate the design, confounding by population structure, multiple testing and interpretation of association studies.

concepts.name: Linkage disequilibrium and haplotypes
concepts.summary: Assess how nonrandom allele association arises and how it supports mapping and inference.

concepts.name: Coalescent and population structure inference
concepts.summary: Judge inferences about ancestry, divergence and demographic history from genetic variation.

concepts.name: Detecting natural selection signatures
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence for selection against drift using sequence and frequency patterns.

concepts.name: Complex trait genetic architecture
concepts.summary: Critique models of polygenic architecture, gene-environment interaction and the limits of polygenic prediction.

concepts.name: Designing genetic studies
concepts.summary: Design a cross, family study or sampling strategy with suitable power and controls to answer a genetic question.

concepts.name: Ethics of genetic information
concepts.summary: Evaluate the ethical and interpretive issues of genetic testing, screening and data use.

misconceptions.text: A significant GWAS hit identifies the causal variant.
Polygenic scores predict individuals equally well across all ancestries.
Any allele-frequency pattern showing a shift implies natural selection.

concepts.name: Network nodes and links
concepts.summary: Recall that a network is made of hosts, intermediate devices and links, and name common examples such as LAN, WAN and the internet.

concepts.name: Protocols as shared rules
concepts.summary: Explain that a protocol is an agreed set of message formats and rules that lets different machines communicate.

concepts.name: Layered model idea
concepts.summary: Describe why networking is split into layers and name the layers of the TCP/IP and OSI models in order.

concepts.name: Packets and encapsulation
concepts.summary: Explain that data is broken into packets, each wrapped in headers added by successive layers.

concepts.name: IP and MAC addresses
concepts.summary: Distinguish an IP address (logical, network-level) from a MAC address (hardware, link-level) and recognise their formats.

concepts.name: Client-server communication
concepts.summary: Describe how a client sends a request to a server that listens and replies, such as a browser fetching a web page.

concepts.name: Common network devices
concepts.summary: Name the role of a switch, router, modem and wireless access point in a home or office network.

misconceptions.text: The internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing.
A router and a switch do the same job and the terms are interchangeable.
Data travels between computers as one continuous stream rather than as separate packets.

concepts.name: IPv4 address structure
concepts.summary: Read an IPv4 address in dotted decimal and split it into network and host parts using a subnet mask.

concepts.name: Private and public addresses
concepts.summary: Identify private address ranges and explain how NAT lets many private hosts share one public address.

concepts.name: TCP versus UDP
concepts.summary: Choose between TCP and UDP for a given application based on reliability, ordering and latency needs.

concepts.name: Ports and sockets
concepts.summary: Use port numbers to identify services and match well-known ports such as 80, 443 and 53 to their protocols.

concepts.name: DNS name resolution
concepts.summary: Trace how a hostname is translated into an IP address and recognise common record types A, AAAA, CNAME and MX.

concepts.name: DHCP address assignment
concepts.summary: Describe how a host obtains an address, gateway and DNS server automatically, and apply it to a simple LAN.

concepts.name: Basic connectivity tools
concepts.summary: Use ping, traceroute and interface configuration commands to check reachability and view addressing.

concepts.name: Default gateway role
concepts.summary: Explain that traffic to addresses outside the local network is sent to the default gateway.

misconceptions.text: UDP is simply a worse version of TCP and should never be used.
A port number identifies a computer rather than a service on it.
Private IP addresses can be reached directly from anywhere on the internet.

concepts.name: CIDR and subnet design
concepts.summary: Calculate network address, broadcast address and usable host range, and divide an address block into subnets that fit requirements.

concepts.name: IP routing decisions
concepts.summary: Determine the next hop for a packet by applying longest prefix match against a routing table.

concepts.name: ARP and local delivery
concepts.summary: Explain how ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a LAN and how frames are delivered within a subnet.

concepts.name: Switching and VLANs
concepts.summary: Analyse how switches learn MAC addresses and forward frames, and how VLANs segment broadcast domains.

concepts.name: TCP connection mechanics
concepts.summary: Analyse connection setup and teardown, sequence numbers, acknowledgements, windowing and retransmission.

concepts.name: DNS resolution hierarchy
concepts.summary: Analyse the roles of resolvers, root, TLD and authoritative servers and the effect of TTL caching.

concepts.name: Systematic connectivity troubleshooting
concepts.summary: Isolate a fault by working through layers, testing the link, address, gateway, DNS and service in turn.

concepts.name: Firewalls and access rules
concepts.summary: Write and interpret basic allow and deny rules based on addresses, protocols and ports.

misconceptions.text: A switch forwards traffic based on IP addresses.
A failed ping proves the destination host is down.
Splitting a network into VLANs automatically lets the VLANs communicate with each other.

concepts.name: Dynamic routing protocols
concepts.summary: Compare distance-vector and link-state protocols and analyse convergence and metric behaviour.

concepts.name: BGP and inter-domain routing
concepts.summary: Explain how autonomous systems exchange reachability through BGP and how policy shapes path choice.

concepts.name: TCP congestion control
concepts.summary: Analyse how slow start, congestion avoidance and loss response govern throughput and fairness.

concepts.name: Packet capture analysis
concepts.summary: Diagnose faults such as retransmissions, resets and DNS failures by reading captured packets.

concepts.name: Secure transport with TLS
concepts.summary: Evaluate how TLS provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication, including certificate chain validation.

concepts.name: IPv6 addressing and transition
concepts.summary: Analyse IPv6 address types, autoconfiguration and the trade-offs of dual stack and tunnelling.

concepts.name: Network performance metrics
concepts.summary: Evaluate throughput, latency, loss and jitter measurements to locate bottlenecks and judge fitness for applications.

concepts.name: Load balancing and NAT design
concepts.summary: Evaluate load balancing, NAT and redundancy designs against availability and complexity trade-offs.

misconceptions.text: More bandwidth always means lower latency and faster page loads.
BGP picks the shortest or fastest path automatically.
IPv6 is just IPv4 with longer addresses and works identically.

concepts.name: Scalable network architecture design
concepts.summary: Design a network topology that balances scale, resilience, cost and manageability for stated requirements.

concepts.name: Routing policy and traffic engineering
concepts.summary: Create routing policies that steer traffic to meet performance, cost and failover goals.

concepts.name: Protocol design trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate how protocols such as QUIC change head-of-line blocking, handshake cost and middlebox compatibility versus TCP.

concepts.name: Network security architecture
concepts.summary: Design layered defences covering segmentation, filtering, DDoS resilience and spoofing prevention.

concepts.name: Overlay and virtual networking
concepts.summary: Evaluate tunnelling, overlays and software-defined control for cloud and multi-site networks.

concepts.name: Failure diagnosis in complex networks
concepts.summary: Judge evidence from multiple layers and vantage points to find root causes of intermittent or partial failures.

concepts.name: Capacity planning and resilience
concepts.summary: Create capacity and failover plans using traffic models, failure domains and convergence requirements.

misconceptions.text: Adding redundant links and devices always improves availability.
A VPN or encrypted tunnel makes traffic fully secure and anonymous end to end.
A perimeter firewall alone is sufficient network security.

concepts.name: Inertial reference frames
concepts.summary: Explain that an inertial frame is one moving at constant velocity without acceleration, and that observers describe events relative to such a frame.

concepts.name: Principle of relativity
concepts.summary: State that the laws of physics take the same form in every inertial frame, so no experiment reveals absolute rest.

concepts.name: Constancy of light speed
concepts.summary: Recall that light in vacuum has the same speed c for all inertial observers regardless of source or observer motion.

concepts.name: Events and spacetime coordinates
concepts.summary: Describe an event as a point specified by position and time in a given frame.

concepts.name: Failure of Galilean addition
concepts.summary: Understand why simply adding velocities contradicts the constant light speed and so must be replaced at high speeds.

concepts.name: Relativity of simultaneity idea
concepts.summary: Explain qualitatively that two events simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another moving frame.

misconceptions.text: Light's speed adds to the speed of its source, like a ball thrown from a moving train.
Relativity means that everything is relative and there are no absolute quantities.
Special relativity is only about observers who are moving, and a stationary observer sees the true physics.

concepts.name: Time dilation formula
concepts.summary: Apply Δt = γΔt0 to compute elapsed time in a frame where a clock moves.

concepts.name: Lorentz factor
concepts.summary: Calculate γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²) and judge how it grows as v approaches c.

concepts.name: Proper time
concepts.summary: Identify the proper time as the interval measured by a single clock present at both events.

concepts.name: Length contraction formula
concepts.summary: Apply L = L0/γ to find the length along the motion measured in a frame where the object moves.

concepts.name: Proper length
concepts.summary: Identify proper length as the length measured in the object's rest frame.

concepts.name: Light clock derivation
concepts.summary: Use a light bouncing between mirrors and the Pythagorean theorem to derive time dilation.

concepts.name: Muon decay evidence
concepts.summary: Explain how muons reaching Earth's surface confirm time dilation and length contraction.

misconceptions.text: Time dilation is an illusion caused by signal delay as light travels to the observer.
Lengths contract in all directions, including perpendicular to the motion.
The moving clock is the one whose own observer notices it running slow.

concepts.name: Lorentz transformation equations
concepts.summary: Apply x' = γ(x−vt) and t' = γ(t−vx/c²) to convert event coordinates between frames.

concepts.name: Relativistic velocity addition
concepts.summary: Use u' = (u−v)/(1−uv/c²) to combine velocities and show no result exceeds c.

concepts.name: Quantitative simultaneity and ordering
concepts.summary: Analyse how the term vx/c² makes spatially separated events non-simultaneous and when time order can differ.

concepts.name: Spacetime interval invariance
concepts.summary: Compute Δs² = c²Δt² − Δx² and use its invariance to classify intervals as timelike, spacelike or lightlike.

concepts.name: Spacetime diagrams
concepts.summary: Read and draw worldlines, light cones and tilted axes of a moving frame.

concepts.name: Causality and light cones
concepts.summary: Analyse why only spacelike-separated events can change order, preserving cause before effect.

concepts.name: Relativistic Doppler effect
concepts.summary: Calculate frequency shifts for sources moving relative to an observer using the relativistic formula.

misconceptions.text: Lorentz transformations can be applied to any two numbers like durations without regard to which events are measured.
Velocity addition just gives u+v unless speeds are very close to c.
Time order of any two events can be reversed by a suitable observer.

concepts.name: Four-vectors
concepts.summary: Represent events, velocity and momentum as four-vectors whose Minkowski norms are invariant under boosts.

concepts.name: Relativistic momentum and energy
concepts.summary: Use p = γmv and E = γmc² and analyse why they replace Newtonian forms.

concepts.name: Energy-momentum relation
concepts.summary: Apply E² = (pc)² + (mc²)² to systems including massless particles.

concepts.name: Mass-energy equivalence
concepts.summary: Evaluate binding energies and reaction Q-values by relating mass changes to energy released.

concepts.name: Invariant mass of systems
concepts.summary: Compute and justify the invariant mass of a multi-particle system, which is not the sum of the rest masses.

concepts.name: Relativistic collisions and decays
concepts.summary: Solve collision, decay and threshold problems using four-momentum conservation, choosing the most convenient frame.

concepts.name: Apparent paradoxes resolution
concepts.summary: Evaluate twin and ladder-barn paradoxes by identifying frame asymmetry and simultaneity differences.

misconceptions.text: Mass increases with speed, so relativistic mass is the real mass of a moving object.
E = mc² applies only to nuclear reactions.
Total mass of a system always equals the sum of its parts' masses.

concepts.name: Lorentz group structure
concepts.summary: Evaluate how boosts and rotations form the Lorentz group, including rapidity addition and Thomas-Wigner rotation.

concepts.name: Covariant electromagnetism
concepts.summary: Judge how E and B mix under boosts and how the field tensor unifies Maxwell's equations as covariant.

concepts.name: Accelerated motion and Rindler frames
concepts.summary: Analyse worldlines under constant proper acceleration and the horizon seen by accelerated observers.

concepts.name: Lagrangian relativistic mechanics
concepts.summary: Construct a relativistic particle action and derive its equations of motion and conserved quantities.

concepts.name: Visual appearance of fast objects
concepts.summary: Evaluate how light-travel time and aberration make fast objects appear rotated rather than contracted.

concepts.name: Derivation from postulates
concepts.summary: Derive the Lorentz transformations from the postulates, homogeneity and isotropy, and design arguments for the invariant speed.

concepts.name: Limits of special relativity
concepts.summary: Assess where special relativity fails in gravitational and quantum regimes and when it applies locally.

misconceptions.text: A fast-moving object would be photographed as visibly length-contracted.
Special relativity cannot handle accelerating objects or observers.
Electric and magnetic fields are separate entities, and their mixing under boosts is only a coordinate trick.

concepts.name: Heritable variation in populations
concepts.summary: Explain that individuals in a population differ in traits and that some of this variation is inherited and so can be passed on.

concepts.name: Natural selection process
concepts.summary: Describe how variation, inheritance and differential survival and reproduction lead to changes in trait frequencies across generations.

concepts.name: Adaptation as a trait
concepts.summary: Recognise an adaptation as an inherited trait that increases survival or reproduction in a particular environment, with examples.

concepts.name: Evolutionary fitness
concepts.summary: State that fitness means relative reproductive success, not strength or health alone.

concepts.name: Common descent
concepts.summary: Explain that all living species trace back to shared ancestors through branching lineages.

concepts.name: Fossil record evidence
concepts.summary: Describe how fossils show past life forms and changes in lineages over geological time.

concepts.name: Species and speciation
concepts.summary: Define a species in simple terms and state that new species arise when populations diverge.

misconceptions.text: Individual organisms evolve during their lifetime by needing or trying to change.
Survival of the fittest means the strongest individual always wins.
Humans evolved from modern chimpanzees rather than sharing a common ancestor with them.

concepts.name: Mutation as variation source
concepts.summary: Explain that mutation produces new alleles randomly with respect to need, while selection acts on existing variation.

concepts.name: Allele frequency change
concepts.summary: Define evolution as change in allele frequencies in a population and calculate simple frequency shifts.

concepts.name: Types of selection
concepts.summary: Apply directional, stabilising and disruptive selection to trait distributions in examples.

concepts.name: Genetic drift
concepts.summary: Show how chance changes allele frequencies, especially in small populations, including bottleneck and founder effects.

concepts.name: Gene flow
concepts.summary: Explain how movement of alleles between populations reduces differences among them.

concepts.name: Homology and analogy
concepts.summary: Distinguish homologous structures from analogous ones and use them as evidence of ancestry versus convergence.

concepts.name: Reading simple phylogenetic trees
concepts.summary: Interpret nodes, branches and tips to identify relative relatedness and common ancestors.

concepts.name: Reproductive isolation barriers
concepts.summary: Describe prezygotic and postzygotic barriers that keep gene pools separate.

misconceptions.text: Mutations occur because an organism needs them to adapt.
Genetic drift only happens in tiny populations and has no effect elsewhere, or it is the same as selection.
In a phylogenetic tree, species at the tips are more advanced than those drawn nearer the left, and sister branches order implies ancestry.

concepts.name: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium
concepts.summary: Use p and q and the equation p²+2pq+q²=1 to compute genotype frequencies and state the assumptions of the null model.

concepts.name: Testing deviation from equilibrium
concepts.summary: Analyse data to infer which assumption violation (selection, drift, gene flow, mutation, nonrandom mating) explains a deviation.

concepts.name: Selection coefficients and relative fitness
concepts.summary: Calculate relative fitness and selection coefficients and predict allele frequency change per generation.

concepts.name: Modes of speciation
concepts.summary: Compare allopatric, peripatric, parapatric and sympatric speciation and the conditions favouring each.

concepts.name: Building trees from characters
concepts.summary: Construct cladograms from shared derived characters and distinguish synapomorphies from ancestral traits.

concepts.name: Monophyly and grouping
concepts.summary: Classify groups as monophyletic, paraphyletic or polyphyletic and justify which are valid clades.

concepts.name: Molecular evidence for relatedness
concepts.summary: Use DNA and protein sequence differences and molecular clock reasoning to estimate relatedness and divergence.

concepts.name: Sexual selection
concepts.summary: Analyse how mate choice and competition produce traits that may reduce survival yet raise reproductive success.

misconceptions.text: Hardy-Weinberg describes how real populations normally behave and shows they stay unchanged.
Grouping organisms by overall similarity gives valid evolutionary groups, so reptiles as a group excluding birds is a clade.
A molecular clock ticks at a constant rate across all genes and lineages.

concepts.name: Quantitative trait evolution
concepts.summary: Use heritability and the selection differential to predict response to selection and analyse its limits.

concepts.name: Kin selection and inclusive fitness
concepts.summary: Apply Hamilton's rule to evaluate when altruistic behaviour can evolve through relatedness.

concepts.name: Coevolution dynamics
concepts.summary: Analyse reciprocal selection in host-parasite, predator-prey and mutualistic systems.

concepts.name: Phylogenetic inference methods
concepts.summary: Evaluate parsimony, distance, likelihood and Bayesian methods and interpret support values and long-branch artefacts.

concepts.name: Comparative method and ancestral states
concepts.summary: Reconstruct ancestral traits and test trait correlations while accounting for shared ancestry.

concepts.name: Neutral theory and selection tests
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence for neutral versus selected change using substitution ratios and population genomic signatures.

concepts.name: Hybridisation and reinforcement
concepts.summary: Assess species concepts and the role of hybrid zones and reinforcement in completing or reversing speciation.

concepts.name: Constraints and evolutionary trade-offs
concepts.summary: Analyse how pleiotropy, developmental limits and life-history trade-offs shape the course of adaptation.

misconceptions.text: High heritability means a trait is genetically determined and cannot be changed by environment.
Altruism evolves for the good of the species rather than through effects on gene transmission.
Every observed trait is an adaptation shaped by selection and has an optimal design.

concepts.name: Critiquing adaptationist explanations
concepts.summary: Evaluate adaptive hypotheses against alternatives such as drift, exaptation and byproducts, and judge what evidence would discriminate them.

concepts.name: Levels and units of selection
concepts.summary: Assess gene, individual, group and clade-level selection arguments and the major evolutionary transitions.

concepts.name: Macroevolutionary pattern and process
concepts.summary: Judge how microevolution, stasis, extinction and radiation explain patterns in the fossil and phylogenetic record.

concepts.name: Evo-devo and innovation
concepts.summary: Evaluate how changes in regulatory genes and development generate novelty and homology.

concepts.name: Human origins reconstruction
concepts.summary: Weigh fossil, archaeological and ancient genomic evidence on hominin phylogeny, dispersal and admixture.

concepts.name: Designing evolutionary studies
concepts.summary: Design experiments, simulations or comparative analyses that test a specific evolutionary hypothesis with appropriate controls.

concepts.name: Horizontal transfer and reticulate evolution
concepts.summary: Evaluate how horizontal gene transfer, endosymbiosis and introgression challenge strictly tree-like descent.

concepts.name: Integrating evidence into models
concepts.summary: Synthesise population genetic, phylogenetic and ecological evidence into a coherent model of a lineage's evolution and critique rival theories.

misconceptions.text: Punctuated equilibrium contradicts gradual natural selection and Darwinian evolution.
Human evolution was a single linear progression from ape to modern human.
Horizontal gene transfer undermines common descent and makes phylogenetic trees meaningless.

concepts.name: Exposure as light reaching sensor
concepts.summary: Explain that exposure is the amount of light recorded by the sensor and that images can be under-, over- or correctly exposed.

concepts.name: Aperture and f-numbers
concepts.summary: Describe aperture as the lens opening whose f-number is inversely related to its size and controls how much light enters.

concepts.name: Shutter speed and motion
concepts.summary: Explain that shutter speed sets how long the sensor is exposed, freezing motion when fast and blurring it when slow.

concepts.name: ISO sensitivity and noise
concepts.summary: Understand that ISO amplifies the sensor signal, brightening images at the cost of increased noise.

concepts.name: Autofocus and focus point
concepts.summary: Recall how to half-press the shutter to focus and place the focus point on the intended subject.

concepts.name: Rule of thirds
concepts.summary: Understand how placing subjects along thirds lines or intersections creates balanced framing.

concepts.name: Camera exposure modes
aliases: auto, P, A, S, M modes
concepts.summary: Identify what automatic, aperture priority, shutter priority and manual modes let the camera or photographer control.

misconceptions.text: A bigger f-number means a bigger lens opening.
More megapixels or a more expensive camera automatically produces better photos.
Raising ISO is free and has no effect on image quality.

concepts.name: Exposure triangle trade-offs
concepts.summary: Adjust aperture, shutter speed and ISO together to keep exposure constant while choosing the desired effect.

concepts.name: Depth of field control
concepts.summary: Use aperture, focal length and subject distance to make backgrounds sharp or blurred.

concepts.name: Reading the histogram
concepts.summary: Use the histogram to judge exposure and spot clipped highlights or shadows.

concepts.name: Exposure compensation
concepts.summary: Apply plus or minus compensation to correct the camera's metered exposure in bright or dark scenes.

concepts.name: White balance and color temperature
concepts.summary: Set white balance to match light sources so colors look natural or intentionally warm or cool.

concepts.name: Leading lines and framing
concepts.summary: Use lines, foreground elements and frames to direct the viewer's eye to the subject.

concepts.name: Hand-holding shutter speed guidelines
concepts.summary: Choose shutter speeds that avoid camera shake based on focal length and use stabilization or tripods when needed.

concepts.name: Basic RAW editing adjustments
concepts.summary: Apply crop, exposure, contrast and white balance adjustments to a RAW or JPEG file.

misconceptions.text: A correct exposure is whatever the camera meter says, so compensation is never needed.
A histogram bunched to one side always means a bad exposure.
Blurred backgrounds depend only on aperture and not on distance or focal length.

concepts.name: Metering modes and scene evaluation
concepts.summary: Choose a metering mode by analysing scene contrast and subject placement to predict how the camera will expose.

concepts.name: Dynamic range and highlight protection
concepts.summary: Analyse a scene's contrast against sensor limits and decide how to expose or bracket to retain detail.

concepts.name: Focus modes and tracking
concepts.summary: Match single, continuous and tracking autofocus to static or moving subjects and choose the focus area.

concepts.name: Direction and quality of light
concepts.summary: Analyse how light direction, size and diffusion shape texture, shadows and mood.

concepts.name: Compositional balance and visual weight
concepts.summary: Analyse how subject placement, contrast, color and negative space distribute visual weight.

concepts.name: Focal length and perspective
concepts.summary: Explain how focal length and shooting distance change perspective, compression and background relationships.

concepts.name: Selective editing and color adjustment
concepts.summary: Use masks, tone curves and color controls to refine specific areas while keeping the result natural.

concepts.name: Non-destructive editing workflow
concepts.summary: Organize, cull, edit non-destructively and export files appropriately for web or print.

misconceptions.text: Shooting in the golden hour is the only time good light exists.
Wide-angle and telephoto lenses differ only in how much they zoom, not in perspective.
Any exposure error can be fully fixed in editing.

concepts.name: Artificial and flash lighting
concepts.summary: Balance flash with ambient light using power, sync speed, modifiers and position to shape a subject.

concepts.name: Low-light and long-exposure technique
concepts.summary: Plan exposures for low light or motion blur using tripods, ND filters and noise trade-offs.

concepts.name: Anticipation and timing
concepts.summary: Evaluate a situation to predict peak action and choose when and how to capture it.

concepts.name: Visual storytelling and series
concepts.summary: Judge how images combine in a sequence to convey narrative, theme and consistency.

concepts.name: Color grading and tonal intent
concepts.summary: Evaluate color palettes and tone to support mood and refine grades deliberately.

concepts.name: Genre-specific technique adaptation
concepts.summary: Adapt exposure, focus, lens and approach to the demands of different genres.

concepts.name: Critique and image selection
concepts.summary: Evaluate images against intent and craft to select the strongest frames and diagnose weaknesses.

misconceptions.text: Flash always looks harsh and is only for dark scenes.
Rapid burst shooting replaces the need for anticipation.
A strong portfolio simply collects the best individual photos regardless of coherence.

concepts.name: Developing a personal visual style
concepts.summary: Synthesize subject choice, light, composition and processing into a recognizable, intentional style.

concepts.name: Concept-driven project design
concepts.summary: Design a multi-image project from a concept, planning methods, constraints and presentation.

concepts.name: Deliberate rule-breaking
concepts.summary: Judge when departing from conventions of exposure, focus or composition strengthens meaning.

concepts.name: Advanced lighting design
concepts.summary: Create custom lighting setups, combining natural and artificial sources, to realize a specific vision.

concepts.name: Ethics and context in photography
concepts.summary: Evaluate ethical issues of consent, representation and manipulation in making and presenting images.

concepts.name: Output, print and presentation
concepts.summary: Evaluate and choose output media, color management and sequencing for prints, books and screens.

concepts.name: Mentoring and critical analysis
concepts.summary: Analyse the work of others against historical and contemporary context to give constructive critique.

misconceptions.text: Style comes from applying a signature preset or filter to every photo.
Breaking the rules is always a sign of creativity regardless of whether it serves the image.
Photographs are objective records, so editing and framing choices carry no ethical weight.

concepts.name: Pronunciation and spelling rules
concepts.summary: Recall the regular letter-to-sound mapping, including rolled r, c as 'ch', ng, ny, and stress that is light and near-even.

concepts.name: Greetings and polite formulas
concepts.summary: Understand and use time-of-day greetings (selamat pagi, siang, sore, malam) and courtesy words like terima kasih, maaf, tolong and silakan.

concepts.name: Personal pronouns and address
concepts.summary: Understand the difference between saya, aku, kamu, Anda and kinship or title address like Bapak and Ibu in choosing formality.

concepts.name: Basic SVO sentence order
concepts.summary: Build simple subject-verb-object sentences where verbs take no conjugation and no tense marking.

concepts.name: Copula-free equational sentences
concepts.summary: Understand that predicates like adjectives and nouns follow the subject without 'to be', with adalah only optional before nouns.

concepts.name: Question words and yes-no questions
concepts.summary: Form questions with apa, siapa, di mana, kapan, berapa and the particle apakah.

concepts.name: Numbers and basic negation
concepts.summary: Recall numbers 1 to 1000 and choose between tidak for verbs and adjectives and bukan for nouns.

misconceptions.text: Indonesian verbs change form to show past, present and future.
Tidak and bukan are interchangeable words for 'not'.
Anda is the normal word for 'you' in everyday conversation with anyone.

concepts.name: Time markers sudah, belum, akan
concepts.summary: Apply sudah, belum, sedang and akan to express completion, non-completion, ongoing action and future as optional aspect markers.

concepts.name: Classifiers buah, orang, ekor
concepts.summary: Apply the right classifier after a number, such as dua orang, tiga ekor, lima buah, when counting objects.

concepts.name: Noun-adjective order and possession
concepts.summary: Form phrases with the head noun first, such as rumah besar and buku saya, and use yang for modifiers.

concepts.name: Market and shopping dialogue
concepts.summary: Use phrases for prices, quantities and bargaining, such as berapa harganya, boleh kurang, and mahal.

concepts.name: Travel and directions phrases
concepts.summary: Ask for and follow directions and transport using lurus, kiri, kanan, dekat, jauh, and place prepositions di, ke, dari.

concepts.name: Base verbs and the prefix ber-
concepts.summary: Understand and form common intransitive ber- verbs for having, doing or using, such as bekerja, berjalan and bermain.

concepts.name: Reduplication for plurals
concepts.summary: Understand reduplication such as buku-buku and use it appropriately, noting it is unnecessary after a quantity word.

misconceptions.text: Sudah means 'past tense' and must be used for every past event.
Classifiers can be dropped or swapped freely, so buah works for people and animals.
Plurals always need reduplication, even after numbers like tiga.

concepts.name: Active prefix meN- and its variants
concepts.summary: Apply the meN- prefix with its sound changes (mem-, men-, meny-, meng-, menge-) and dropping of initial k, p, t, s.

concepts.name: Passive di- and object-fronted passive
concepts.summary: Form di- passives with an agent introduced by oleh, and the pronoun-verb passive like buku itu saya baca.

concepts.name: Prefix ter- meanings
concepts.summary: Distinguish ter- as accidental or already-completed state, ability, and superlative, as in terbuka and tercepat.

concepts.name: Nominalising circumfix pe-an and peN-
concepts.summary: Analyse nouns formed by pe-an, per-an, peN- and ke-an to tell process, doer and result apart.

concepts.name: Suffix -kan causative and benefactive
concepts.summary: Analyse how -kan makes a causative or benefactive verb, as in membersihkan and membelikan.

concepts.name: Suffix -i locative and repetitive
concepts.summary: Analyse how -i marks a location target or repeated action, as in menduduki and mendatangi.

concepts.name: Relative clauses with yang
concepts.summary: Build relative and nominalised clauses with yang and conjunctions such as karena, supaya and kalau.

misconceptions.text: Me- is a single fixed prefix with the same spelling on every root.
-kan and -i are interchangeable and give the same meaning on any verb.
Ter- always means 'most' like a superlative.

concepts.name: Choosing between -kan and -i
concepts.summary: Analyse minimal pairs such as menanami versus menanamkan and mengirimi versus mengirimkan to select the correct argument structure.

concepts.name: Register and formal versus colloquial
concepts.summary: Evaluate formal baku usage against colloquial forms such as nggak, gue, ngomong and drop of prefixes to fit the context.

concepts.name: Stacked affixation and word derivation
concepts.summary: Analyse complex derived words such as mempertanggungjawabkan, memperbaiki and keberlangsungan into root and layers.

concepts.name: Prefix memper- and its effect
concepts.summary: Analyse memper- forms like memperbesar and mempelajari for causation, intensification and added valency.

concepts.name: Discourse connectors and cohesion
concepts.summary: Evaluate the use of connectors such as meskipun, sehingga, padahal and oleh karena itu to structure paragraphs.

concepts.name: Loanwords and borrowed vocabulary
concepts.summary: Analyse borrowings from Dutch, Arabic, Sanskrit and English and their adapted spelling in formal writing.

concepts.name: Passive choice and topic focus
concepts.summary: Evaluate when to use active, di- or fronted-agent passive to manage topic, definiteness and politeness.

misconceptions.text: Colloquial Jakarta speech is simply wrong Indonesian and should never be used.
The passive is rare and merely a stylistic variant of the active.
Any root can take any affix combination to form a real word.

concepts.name: Writing in varied registers
concepts.summary: Create texts such as reports, speeches and informal messages that apply the register, affixation and cohesion fitting each genre.

concepts.name: Evaluating usage norms
concepts.summary: Evaluate usage against EYD or PUEBI and KBBI norms and judge when divergence is acceptable.

concepts.name: Regional language influence
concepts.summary: Evaluate how Javanese, Betawi and Malay varieties shape Indonesian grammar, vocabulary and speech practices.

concepts.name: Creating neologisms with affixes
concepts.summary: Create and justify new terms using productive affixes and compounding consistent with the language's morphology.

concepts.name: Translating between English and Indonesian
concepts.summary: Produce translations that handle missing tense, definiteness, classifiers and pronoun choice without calquing English.

concepts.name: Pragmatics and politeness strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate address terms, indirectness and face-saving strategies in negotiation, hierarchy and cross-cultural settings.

misconceptions.text: Good Indonesian translation follows English word order and tense one to one.
There is a single correct standard that all speakers follow in every context.
Formal pronoun Anda is always the safest and most polite choice.

concepts.name: French nasal vowels
concepts.summary: Recognise and pronounce the nasal vowels /ɑ̃/, /ɔ̃/ and /ɛ̃/ without sounding a final n or m, as in blanc, bon and vin.

concepts.name: Silent final letters
concepts.summary: Understand that most final consonants and the final e are not pronounced, as in petit, grand and parle, and apply this when reading aloud.

concepts.name: Accents and cedilla
concepts.summary: Remember the acute, grave, circumflex and cedilla marks and what sound each signals, such as é versus è and soft ç.

concepts.name: Uvular French r
concepts.summary: Understand and produce the French r at the back of the throat rather than a rolled or English r.

concepts.name: Definite and indefinite articles
concepts.summary: Choose le, la, l' or les and un, une or des according to the noun's gender and number.

concepts.name: Être and avoir present
concepts.summary: Recall and understand the present-tense forms of être and avoir and use them in simple statements about identity and possession.

concepts.name: Greetings and tu vs vous
concepts.summary: Understand when to use informal tu and formal or plural vous in basic greetings and introductions.

misconceptions.text: The final n or m in a nasal vowel is pronounced as a separate consonant.
Accents on French letters are optional decoration that do not change pronunciation or meaning.
The French r should be rolled with the tip of the tongue like in Spanish.

concepts.name: Liaison rules
concepts.summary: Apply obligatory liaison, as in les amis and vous avez, and avoid it in forbidden contexts such as after et.

concepts.name: Partitive articles
concepts.summary: Use du, de la, de l' for unspecified quantities of food and abstractions, and switch to de after negation.

concepts.name: Regular present tense verbs
concepts.summary: Conjugate regular -er, -ir and -re verbs in the present tense and use them in everyday sentences.

concepts.name: Adjective agreement and position
concepts.summary: Make adjectives agree in gender and number and place them correctly, including the common pre-noun adjectives.

concepts.name: Negation with ne pas
concepts.summary: Form negative sentences by wrapping ne around the verb with pas, using n' before vowels.

concepts.name: Passé composé formation
concepts.summary: Form the passé composé with avoir or être and a past participle to report completed actions.

concepts.name: Question formation
concepts.summary: Ask yes/no and information questions using intonation, est-ce que and question words.

misconceptions.text: Partitive articles stay du or de la after a negation.
All past participles are formed by simply adding é to the infinitive stem.
Adjectives always follow the noun as in Spanish.

concepts.name: Imparfait formation and use
concepts.summary: Form the imparfait from the nous stem and use it for habits, descriptions and ongoing states in the past.

concepts.name: Passé composé versus imparfait
concepts.summary: Analyse a narrative to decide whether each verb is a completed event (passé composé) or background/habitual (imparfait).

concepts.name: Auxiliary choice and agreement
concepts.summary: Distinguish verbs taking être, including reflexives, and apply participle agreement with the subject or a preceding direct object.

concepts.name: Object and adverbial pronouns
concepts.summary: Replace direct and indirect objects and places or quantities with le, lui, y and en in the correct position.

concepts.name: Register and politeness choice
concepts.summary: Analyse social context to choose tu or vous and adapt vocabulary and phrasing between familiar and formal registers.

concepts.name: Future and conditional forms
concepts.summary: Form and use the futur simple, futur proche and present conditional for plans, predictions and polite requests.

concepts.name: DELF A2-B1 task formats
concepts.summary: Apply strategies to the four DELF skills at A2 to B1, including listening, reading, structured writing and interview.

misconceptions.text: The imparfait is simply the French equivalent of one English past tense and can replace the passé composé whenever the action is old.
Every past participle agrees with the subject.
Vous is always the safe choice, so tu never needs to be learned or used with peers.

concepts.name: Subjunctive mood triggers
concepts.summary: Analyse which expressions of necessity, emotion, doubt and wish require the subjunctive and form it correctly.

concepts.name: Pluperfect and sequence of tenses
concepts.summary: Use the plus-que-parfait and conditional perfect to sequence events and build si-clauses across time frames.

concepts.name: Relative pronouns complex
concepts.summary: Select qui, que, dont, où and lequel forms according to the grammatical function in the relative clause.

concepts.name: Argumentative writing structure
concepts.summary: Evaluate and structure an argument with thesis, connectors, counterpoints and conclusion for DELF B2 writing.

concepts.name: Discourse connectors and nuance
concepts.summary: Judge which connectors such as cependant, néanmoins and en revanche best express the intended logical relation.

concepts.name: Passive and nominalisation
concepts.summary: Transform active constructions into passive or nominal forms to achieve a more formal, impersonal style.

concepts.name: DELF B2 exam strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate own performance against DELF B2 criteria and refine timing and strategy for each exam component.

misconceptions.text: The subjunctive is used whenever the main clause is in a certain tense or whenever que appears.
Si can be followed by the conditional in any si-clause.
Connectors like pourtant, donc and cependant are interchangeable in a written argument.

concepts.name: Literary tenses recognition
concepts.summary: Evaluate the stylistic effect of the passé simple and imperfect subjunctive when interpreting literary and formal texts.

concepts.name: Stylistic register manipulation
concepts.summary: Create texts that deliberately shift register, from argot and familier to soutenu, for rhetorical effect.

concepts.name: Synthesis writing for DALF C1
concepts.summary: Produce a coherent synthesis combining several source documents and a reasoned argumentative essay at C1 level.

concepts.name: Oral argumentation DALF C1-C2
concepts.summary: Construct and defend a structured oral presentation and respond to challenge with spontaneous, precise language.

concepts.name: Idiom and figurative language
concepts.summary: Judge the appropriateness of idioms, proverbs and figures of speech in context and across regional varieties.

concepts.name: Phonetic variation and prosody
concepts.summary: Evaluate regional and social pronunciation variation, including optional liaison and schwa deletion, and control prosody.

concepts.name: DALF C2 critical commentary
concepts.summary: Design and deliver a nuanced critical commentary on complex texts that meets DALF C2 expectations of precision and fluency.

misconceptions.text: Literary tenses like the passé simple should be used in everyday speech to sound advanced.
A DALF synthesis should include the writer's own opinion on the sources.
There is one correct standard pronunciation, and liaison is always pronounced in careful speech.

concepts.name: Client-server request-response model
concepts.summary: Explain that a client sends a request to a server, which returns exactly one response, and that HTTP is initiated by the client.

concepts.name: URL structure
concepts.summary: Recall the parts of a URL: scheme, host, port, path, query string and fragment.

concepts.name: Request methods GET and POST
concepts.summary: Describe that GET retrieves a resource while POST submits data for processing.

concepts.name: Status code classes
concepts.summary: Recall that 2xx means success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error, and know 200, 404 and 500.

concepts.name: Message anatomy
concepts.summary: Describe that a message has a start line, header fields and an optional body.

concepts.name: HTTP versus HTTPS
concepts.summary: Explain that HTTPS is HTTP carried over an encrypted connection that protects data from eavesdropping.

misconceptions.text: HTTP and the Internet or the web are the same thing.
A 404 status code means the server is down.
POST is secure because the data is not shown in the URL.

concepts.name: Common request headers
concepts.summary: Read and set headers such as Host, User-Agent, Accept and Authorization to shape a request.

concepts.name: Content-Type and body encoding
concepts.summary: Match Content-Type and Content-Length to bodies such as form data, JSON and HTML.

concepts.name: Method semantics PUT DELETE
concepts.summary: Choose among GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and HEAD for a given operation on a resource.

concepts.name: Redirects with Location
concepts.summary: Follow and produce 301, 302 and 307/308 redirects using the Location header.

concepts.name: Cookies basics
concepts.summary: Use Set-Cookie and Cookie to keep state such as a session across stateless requests.

concepts.name: Inspecting traffic with tools
concepts.summary: Use curl and browser developer tools to view and send requests and read responses.

concepts.name: Query strings and parameters
concepts.summary: Encode parameters in the query string with percent-encoding and read them on the server side.

misconceptions.text: Cookies are programs that can run on the user's computer.
PUT and POST are interchangeable.
Any redirect status code behaves the same way and preserves the method.

concepts.name: Safe and idempotent methods
concepts.summary: Analyse which methods are safe or idempotent and what that implies for retries and caches.

concepts.name: Cache validation with ETag
concepts.summary: Use ETag, Last-Modified and conditional headers to get 304 Not Modified responses.

concepts.name: Cache-Control directives
concepts.summary: Analyse how max-age, no-cache, no-store, public and private determine what may be cached and for how long.

concepts.name: Cookie attributes and sessions
concepts.summary: Analyse how Domain, Path, Expires, Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite affect scope and security of session cookies.

concepts.name: TLS handshake and certificates
concepts.summary: Trace how TLS negotiates keys and how certificates and authorities authenticate the server.

concepts.name: Connection management
concepts.summary: Explain persistent connections and their effect on latency compared with a new connection per request.

concepts.name: Content negotiation and compression
concepts.summary: Use Accept headers and Content-Encoding to select representation, language and compression.

concepts.name: Diagnosing 4xx and 5xx errors
concepts.summary: Distinguish 400, 401, 403, 404, 429, 502 and 503 and locate the likely fault from traces.

misconceptions.text: no-cache means the response is never stored.
HttpOnly cookies protect against all cross-site attacks.
Idempotent means the response is the same every time.

concepts.name: HTTP/2 multiplexing
concepts.summary: Analyse how HTTP/2 streams, binary framing and header compression remove HTTP/1.1 head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.

concepts.name: HTTP/3 over QUIC
concepts.summary: Compare HTTP/3 over QUIC and UDP with HTTP/2 over TCP regarding loss, handshake and connection migration.

concepts.name: CORS and same-origin policy
concepts.summary: Analyse how the same-origin policy and CORS headers and preflights govern cross-origin browser requests.

concepts.name: Caching strategy with CDNs
concepts.summary: Evaluate cache layers, Vary, and invalidation approaches such as fingerprinted URLs for a given site.

concepts.name: Authentication schemes
concepts.summary: Evaluate Basic, bearer token and cookie-based authentication for their security tradeoffs.

concepts.name: Web security headers
concepts.summary: Judge the protection provided by HSTS, CSP and related headers against threats such as downgrade and injection.

concepts.name: Proxies and intermediaries
concepts.summary: Analyse how proxies, load balancers and gateways alter requests, using Forwarded and X-Forwarded-For.

misconceptions.text: CORS protects the server from unauthorised requests.
HTTP/2 makes all head-of-line blocking disappear.
HTTPS alone makes a web application secure.

concepts.name: Designing resource APIs
concepts.summary: Design HTTP APIs with coherent resources, method semantics, status codes, pagination and error formats.

concepts.name: API evolution and compatibility
concepts.summary: Evaluate versioning, content negotiation and deprecation strategies for evolving APIs without breaking clients.

concepts.name: Performance optimisation strategy
concepts.summary: Design a delivery strategy combining protocol version, caching, compression, prioritisation and preloading from measured latency.

concepts.name: Request smuggling and desync
concepts.summary: Evaluate how inconsistent parsing of message framing between proxies and servers enables smuggling attacks and how to mitigate them.

concepts.name: Resilient retries and rate limiting
concepts.summary: Design retry, timeout, backoff, idempotency-key and rate-limit behaviour using 429 and Retry-After.

concepts.name: Streaming and real-time delivery
concepts.summary: Evaluate chunked transfer, server-sent events, long polling and WebSocket upgrade for real-time needs.

concepts.name: Protocol standards reasoning
concepts.summary: Judge implementation behaviour against HTTP specifications and resolve ambiguities in real-world interoperability.

misconceptions.text: A RESTful API must use only GET, POST, PUT and DELETE with strict CRUD mapping.
Retrying failed requests is always safe if the client backs off.
Request smuggling is only a flaw in server code, not in how components interact.

concepts.name: Learning objectives
concepts.summary: Explain that a learning objective states what a learner will be able to do after instruction and why it guides every other design decision.

concepts.name: Target audience
concepts.summary: Recall that instruction is designed for a specific group of learners whose prior knowledge, context and motivation shape what will work.

concepts.name: Content versus learning
concepts.summary: Understand that presenting information is not the same as ensuring learners can use it, and that design aims at the latter.

concepts.name: Instructional activities
concepts.summary: Describe how activities such as explanation, demonstration, practice and discussion give learners chances to engage with content.

concepts.name: Assessment purpose
concepts.summary: Understand that assessment gathers evidence of whether learners reached the objectives, rather than just assigning grades.

concepts.name: ADDIE phases
concepts.summary: Name the five ADDIE phases and state what each one is for in the design process.

misconceptions.text: Good instruction means covering all the content as thoroughly as possible.
Learning objectives describe what the instructor will teach.
Assessment happens only at the end to give a grade.

concepts.name: Writing measurable objectives
concepts.summary: Write objectives with an observable performance, conditions and criterion, using action verbs instead of vague ones like understand.

concepts.name: Bloom's taxonomy for objectives
concepts.summary: Classify objectives by cognitive level and pick verbs that match the intended depth of learning.

concepts.name: Basic needs analysis
concepts.summary: Use surveys, interviews and observation to identify the gap between current and desired performance and the audience's starting point.

concepts.name: Objective-assessment alignment
concepts.summary: Create assessment items that measure exactly the performance stated in an objective.

concepts.name: Content chunking and sequencing
concepts.summary: Break content into manageable units and order them logically, such as simple to complex or prerequisite first.

concepts.name: Feedback to learners
concepts.summary: Provide timely, specific feedback on practice that tells learners what to do to improve.
