concepts.name: Arabic letters and sounds
concepts.summary: Recognise and pronounce the 28 letters, including emphatic and guttural sounds like ع, ح, ق, ص and ط.

concepts.name: Right-to-left connected script
concepts.summary: Explain that Arabic is written right to left and that most letters join to the following letter, with six non-connecting letters.

concepts.name: Positional letter forms
concepts.summary: Recognise the isolated, initial, medial and final shapes of a letter and identify the same letter in each position.

concepts.name: Short vowels and harakat
concepts.summary: Read fatha, damma and kasra, plus sukun and shadda, and understand that they are usually omitted in ordinary texts.

concepts.name: Long vowels and madd letters
concepts.summary: Distinguish the long vowels ā, ū, ī written with ا, و, ي from the short vowels and from the consonant uses of و and ي.

concepts.name: Definite article al-
concepts.summary: Use ال to make nouns definite and know that Arabic has no indefinite article.

concepts.name: Sun and moon letters
concepts.summary: Predict when the lam of al- assimilates to the following letter, as in ash-shams, and when it does not, as in al-qamar.

concepts.name: Gender and basic greetings
concepts.summary: Recognise the feminine ending ة and use common greetings such as salām and marḥaban.

misconceptions.text: Arabic letters keep one shape wherever they appear in a word.
Short vowels are always written, so they can be read directly from every text.
ع, ح and ق are just variants of English sounds like a, h and k.

concepts.name: Nominal sentence structure
concepts.summary: Build verbless sentences such as al-bayt kabīr, with a definite subject and an indefinite predicate and no verb for 'is'.

concepts.name: Noun gender and agreement
concepts.summary: Make adjectives agree with nouns in gender, number and definiteness.

concepts.name: Sound plurals and dual
concepts.summary: Form the dual with -ān/-ayn and sound masculine and feminine plurals with -ūn/-īn and -āt.

concepts.name: Case endings and tanwin
concepts.summary: Recognise the three cases marked by -u, -a, -i and the indefinite tanwin endings.

concepts.name: Attached possessive pronouns
concepts.summary: Attach suffixes such as -ī, -ka, -hu, -hā to nouns to express possession.

concepts.name: Independent pronouns and demonstratives
concepts.summary: Use independent pronouns and this/that words with correct gender and number.

concepts.name: Prepositions and sentence use
concepts.summary: Use common prepositions and recall that they put the following noun in the genitive.

concepts.name: Three-letter root concept
concepts.summary: Identify the root of simple words and see how related words share a core of consonants and meaning.

misconceptions.text: Arabic needs a verb meaning 'is' in every sentence.
Adjectives agree with the noun only in gender.
Case endings are optional decoration that never affect grammar.

concepts.name: Idafa construct phrase
concepts.summary: Build noun-noun possessives in which the first noun loses al- and tanwin and the second noun is genitive.

concepts.name: Past tense conjugation
concepts.summary: Conjugate Form I verbs in the past tense with suffixes for person, gender and number.

concepts.name: Present tense and moods
concepts.summary: Conjugate the present with prefixes and suffixes and distinguish the indicative, subjunctive and jussive endings.

concepts.name: Verbal sentence word order
concepts.summary: Form verb-first sentences in which the verb agrees in gender but stays singular before a plural subject.

concepts.name: Broken plural patterns
concepts.summary: Identify common broken plural patterns, such as afʿāl and fuʿūl, and relate them to the singular's root.

concepts.name: Derivation from roots with patterns
concepts.summary: Analyse how patterns like kātib, maktūb and maktab derive agent, patient and place words from a root.

concepts.name: Negation and particles
concepts.summary: Choose the correct negator for tense and sentence type and apply its effect on the verb or predicate.

concepts.name: Numbers and counted nouns
concepts.summary: Use numbers 1–10 with counted nouns, including the reversed gender agreement of 3–10 and the plural noun.

misconceptions.text: The first noun in an idafa takes al- when the phrase is definite.
A verb before its subject must agree in number as well as gender.
Broken plurals follow no patterns and must be memorised word by word.

concepts.name: Derived verb forms II-X
concepts.summary: Analyse the patterns of Forms II–X and the typical meaning shifts such as causative, reciprocal or reflexive.

concepts.name: Weak and hamzated roots
concepts.summary: Predict how roots with و, ي or hamza change in conjugation, as in qāla and wajada.

concepts.name: Verbal nouns masdar
concepts.summary: Derive and use the verbal noun for each form and analyse its role in clauses and idafa.

concepts.name: Participles and their functions
concepts.summary: Form active and passive participles and analyse their use as nouns, adjectives and predicates.

concepts.name: Passive voice
concepts.summary: Form and interpret the passive through vowel changes and identify the agentless subject.

concepts.name: Relative clauses and subordination
concepts.summary: Join clauses with alladhī and 'anna/inna, and apply the resumptive pronoun rule for definite antecedents.

concepts.name: Inna and kāna sisters
concepts.summary: Evaluate how these particles alter the case of subject and predicate and choose them to express time or emphasis.

concepts.name: Diptotes and case nuance
concepts.summary: Recognise nouns that take no tanwin and only two case forms and explain why.

misconceptions.text: Derived verb forms are unrelated verbs that must be learned separately from the root.
Weak-root verbs are random exceptions rather than predictable sound changes.
Alladhī is used with every relative clause regardless of definiteness.

concepts.name: Diglossia and register choice
concepts.summary: Evaluate when Modern Standard Arabic is appropriate versus spoken dialect and adapt language to context.

concepts.name: Rhetorical style and parallelism
concepts.summary: Assess how rhythm, parallelism and rhetorical devices shape persuasive Arabic prose.

concepts.name: Full vocalisation of unvowelled text
concepts.summary: Infer correct vowels and case endings from root, pattern and syntax in a text with no harakat.

concepts.name: Complex syntax and clause chaining
concepts.summary: Compose and edit long sentences with circumstantial, conditional and subordinate clauses and correct agreement.

concepts.name: Semantic nuance of root derivatives
concepts.summary: Evaluate how different derivatives of one root shade meaning and select the most precise word.

concepts.name: Genre-appropriate writing
concepts.summary: Create original texts in news, academic or literary genres using the conventions, vocabulary and syntax each expects.

concepts.name: Translation and equivalence
concepts.summary: Produce translations that preserve meaning, tone and structure while handling untranslatable idiom and syntax differences.

misconceptions.text: Spoken dialects and Modern Standard Arabic are interchangeable in formal writing.
Good translation means rendering Arabic word by word in the same order.
Words from the same root always mean nearly the same thing.

concepts.name: Manual versus code-defined infrastructure
concepts.summary: Explain why defining resources in files is more repeatable and auditable than configuring them by hand in a console.

concepts.name: Declarative versus imperative styles
concepts.summary: Distinguish describing the desired end state from scripting the steps to reach it.

concepts.name: Resources and their attributes
concepts.summary: Recognise that a configuration is made of resources of a given type with named attributes, such as a virtual machine or a network.

concepts.name: Configuration files in version control
concepts.summary: Understand that infrastructure code is stored in Git so changes are tracked, reviewed and reversible.

concepts.name: Plan then apply workflow
concepts.summary: Describe the cycle of writing code, previewing the proposed changes and then applying them.

concepts.name: Reproducible environments
concepts.summary: Explain how the same code can create identical dev, test and production environments.

misconceptions.text: Infrastructure as code is just a shell script that runs commands in order.
Once infrastructure is written as code, nobody needs to understand the underlying cloud services.
Applying the code twice will create two copies of every resource.

concepts.name: Input variables and outputs
concepts.summary: Parameterise a configuration with variables and expose values such as addresses through outputs.

concepts.name: Idempotency
concepts.summary: Explain and observe that re-applying unchanged code leaves infrastructure unchanged.

concepts.name: State as record of reality
concepts.summary: Understand that the tool keeps state mapping code resources to real resources and uses it to compute changes.

concepts.name: Reading a change plan
concepts.summary: Interpret a plan to identify what will be created, updated or destroyed.

concepts.name: Resource dependencies
concepts.summary: Use references between resources so they are created in the correct order.

concepts.name: Secrets kept out of code
concepts.summary: Keep passwords and keys out of committed files by using environment variables or a secrets store.

concepts.name: Provider configuration and authentication
concepts.summary: Configure a provider and authenticate it to a cloud account with limited permissions.

misconceptions.text: Editing a resource in the cloud console is harmless because the code will simply pick up the change.
If the plan shows a change, it only modifies the resource in place.
Private repositories make it safe to commit secrets in configuration files.

concepts.name: Reusable modules
concepts.summary: Package related resources into modules with clear inputs and outputs and reuse them across configurations.

concepts.name: Remote state and locking
concepts.summary: Store state in a shared backend with locking so teams do not corrupt it by concurrent runs.

concepts.name: Environment separation
concepts.summary: Structure code and state to isolate dev, staging and production while sharing common modules.

concepts.name: Configuration drift
concepts.summary: Detect and analyse differences between declared and actual infrastructure and decide how to reconcile them.

concepts.name: Importing existing resources
concepts.summary: Bring manually created resources under code management without recreating them.

concepts.name: Pipeline-driven changes
concepts.summary: Run validation, plan and apply through a pipeline with pull request review.

concepts.name: Replacement versus in-place update
concepts.summary: Analyse which attribute changes force resource replacement and their impact on data and availability.

misconceptions.text: Copying the same configuration folder for each environment is as maintainable as using shared modules.
Storing state in the Git repository is the best way to share it with the team.
Drift only happens when someone is careless, so it does not need monitoring.

concepts.name: Automated infrastructure testing
concepts.summary: Combine static analysis, unit-style checks and ephemeral integration deployments to catch defects before production.

concepts.name: Policy as code
concepts.summary: Evaluate and encode security and cost rules that automatically block non-compliant changes.

concepts.name: State blast radius design
concepts.summary: Judge how to split state and stacks by lifecycle, ownership and risk to limit the impact of a bad change.

concepts.name: Module versioning and contracts
concepts.summary: Assess module interface stability and use versioning to roll out changes safely across consumers.

concepts.name: Safe refactoring of live infrastructure
concepts.summary: Restructure code and move resources in state without causing destruction or recreation.

concepts.name: Immutable versus mutable infrastructure
concepts.summary: Evaluate replacing resources against patching them in place, and how image building and configuration management fit in.

concepts.name: Zero-downtime rollout strategies
concepts.summary: Analyse lifecycle rules and deployment patterns that change infrastructure without interrupting service.

misconceptions.text: A successful plan guarantees the apply will succeed and behave correctly.
One large state for everything is simplest and therefore safest.
Renaming a resource in code is purely cosmetic.

concepts.name: Platform engineering with IaC
concepts.summary: Design paved-road modules and self-service workflows that let teams provision safely without central bottlenecks.

concepts.name: Multi-account governance architecture
concepts.summary: Create an account, permission and pipeline structure that scales across teams, regions and possibly providers.

concepts.name: Tool selection trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate declarative DSLs, general-purpose-language tools and cloud-native templates against organisational needs.

concepts.name: State security and recovery
concepts.summary: Evaluate protection, access control and recovery procedures for state that contains sensitive data.

concepts.name: Custom providers and extensions
concepts.summary: Build providers or extensions that manage resources from APIs not covered by existing tooling.

concepts.name: Continuous reconciliation and automated remediation
concepts.summary: Design systems that continuously compare and correct actual state against declared intent, with human override.

concepts.name: Migration of legacy estates
concepts.summary: Judge sequencing, risk and tooling for bringing a large manually built estate under code incrementally.

misconceptions.text: Automatic remediation of all drift is always desirable.
Adopting one IaC tool across the whole organisation removes the need for governance and conventions.
Legacy estates should be imported in one big-bang effort to reach full coverage quickly.

concepts.name: Agile Manifesto values
concepts.summary: Recall the four Agile values and explain that they favour individuals, working software, collaboration and responding to change while still valuing the items on the right.

concepts.name: Twelve Agile principles
concepts.summary: Explain key principles such as early and continuous delivery, welcoming changing requirements and sustainable pace.

concepts.name: Iterative incremental delivery
concepts.summary: Describe how delivering work in small time-boxed increments allows feedback and adaptation, in contrast to a single big-bang delivery.

concepts.name: Scrum roles
concepts.summary: Name the three Scrum accountabilities and state what each is responsible for.

concepts.name: Scrum events
concepts.summary: List the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective and state the purpose of each.

concepts.name: Scrum artifacts
concepts.summary: Explain the Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog and Increment and how each relates to a commitment.

concepts.name: Time-boxing
concepts.summary: Understand that Scrum events and sprints have fixed maximum durations and why fixed length supports rhythm and focus.

misconceptions.text: Agile means no planning and no documentation.
The Scrum Master is the project manager who assigns tasks to the team.
Scrum is a methodology that prescribes every practice in detail.

concepts.name: Writing user stories
aliases: As a, I want, so that
concepts.summary: Write user stories in the role-goal-benefit format that describe value from a user's perspective.

concepts.name: Acceptance criteria
concepts.summary: Write testable criteria that define when a story meets expectations.

concepts.name: Product backlog ordering
concepts.summary: Order backlog items by value, risk and dependencies so the most important work is at the top.

concepts.name: Sprint planning steps
concepts.summary: Run planning by agreeing a sprint goal, selecting backlog items and breaking them into tasks in the sprint backlog.

concepts.name: Daily Scrum conduct
concepts.summary: Use the 15-minute Daily Scrum to inspect progress toward the sprint goal and adapt the plan for the next day.

concepts.name: Story point estimation
concepts.summary: Estimate items relatively in story points using techniques such as planning poker.

concepts.name: Kanban board basics
concepts.summary: Use a board with columns for workflow states to visualise work and its status.

misconceptions.text: Story points measure the number of hours a task will take.
The Daily Scrum is a status report to the Scrum Master or manager.
A user story is a detailed specification written once and then frozen.

concepts.name: Velocity-based forecasting
concepts.summary: Use average completed points per sprint to forecast how much work and how many sprints a backlog needs.

concepts.name: Burndown and burnup charts
concepts.summary: Read burndown and burnup charts to diagnose scope change, slippage and risk to the sprint goal.

concepts.name: Definition of Done
concepts.summary: Analyse how a shared quality standard makes the Increment transparent and prevents hidden unfinished work.

concepts.name: Backlog refinement
concepts.summary: Break down, clarify and estimate upcoming items so they are ready for planning, applying splitting patterns such as INVEST.

concepts.name: Effective retrospectives
concepts.summary: Analyse sprint problems, find root causes and turn them into a small number of actionable improvements.

concepts.name: Sprint review feedback
concepts.summary: Demonstrate the Increment to stakeholders and turn feedback into backlog changes.

concepts.name: WIP limits and flow
concepts.summary: Analyse how limiting work in progress improves flow and exposes bottlenecks on a Kanban board.

concepts.name: Scrum Master servant leadership
concepts.summary: Apply coaching, facilitation and impediment removal to help the team self-manage.

misconceptions.text: A higher velocity means a team is more productive and teams can be compared by velocity.
Partially finished stories count toward velocity or the sprint review.
Retrospectives are for blaming individuals and do not need follow-up actions.

concepts.name: Scaling Agile approaches
concepts.summary: Analyse coordination needs across multiple teams and compare scaling approaches and their trade-offs.

concepts.name: Value-driven prioritisation
concepts.summary: Evaluate prioritisation techniques and select one fitting the context of value, cost of delay and uncertainty.

concepts.name: Agile metrics evaluation
concepts.summary: Judge which metrics such as cycle time, throughput and escaped defects give useful signals and which invite gaming.

concepts.name: Scrumban hybrid
concepts.summary: Assess when to combine Scrum's cadence with Kanban's flow practices and adapt the process accordingly.

concepts.name: Team dynamics and conflict
concepts.summary: Diagnose issues such as low trust, dominant members or weak ownership and select interventions.

concepts.name: Release and roadmap planning
concepts.summary: Evaluate release plans and outcome-based roadmaps that balance commitment and uncertainty.

concepts.name: Technical practices for agility
concepts.summary: Analyse how engineering practices enable frequent, sustainable delivery of a Done increment.

misconceptions.text: Scaling frameworks can be adopted wholesale to make a large organisation agile.
Scrumban or Kanban means abandoning planning and improvement events.
Agile metrics should be used as targets to evaluate individual performance.

concepts.name: Designing tailored Agile systems
concepts.summary: Create a working approach for an organisation by composing practices while preserving core Agile principles.

concepts.name: Agile transformation strategy
concepts.summary: Design a staged change plan addressing structure, incentives, leadership behaviour and culture.

concepts.name: Critiquing Agile dogma
concepts.summary: Evaluate Agile practices critically against evidence, identifying ritual without purpose and when plan-driven methods suit better.

concepts.name: Outcome-oriented product governance
concepts.summary: Create governance and funding models that steer by outcomes and validated learning rather than output and fixed scope.

concepts.name: Agile in regulated contexts
concepts.summary: Judge how to meet audit, safety and contractual demands while keeping iterative delivery.

concepts.name: Coaching teams and leaders
concepts.summary: Develop coaching approaches that grow team maturity and shift leaders from directing to enabling.

concepts.name: Empirical process control theory
concepts.summary: Evaluate how empiricism underpins Scrum and use it to judge whether adaptations preserve its feedback loops.

misconceptions.text: A transformation is complete once all teams follow Scrum events correctly.
Agile cannot be used in regulated or fixed-contract environments.
Experts should enforce the framework exactly as written regardless of context.

concepts.name: Story elements
concepts.summary: Name and recognise the core parts of a story: character, setting, conflict, plot and ending.

concepts.name: Sensory detail
concepts.summary: Explain how details of sight, sound, smell, taste and touch make a scene feel real to the reader.

concepts.name: Show versus tell
concepts.summary: Understand the difference between stating an emotion or fact and conveying it through action, detail and dialogue.

concepts.name: Point of view basics
concepts.summary: Distinguish first-person and third-person narration and describe how each changes what the reader knows.

concepts.name: Concrete versus abstract language
concepts.summary: Understand why specific, concrete nouns and verbs create clearer images than vague abstractions.

concepts.name: Simile and metaphor
concepts.summary: Recall and identify similes and metaphors as comparisons that describe one thing in terms of another.

concepts.name: Freewriting habit
concepts.summary: Understand that writing a rough first draft without self-editing generates raw material to refine later.

misconceptions.text: Good writing should come out polished on the first try.
Showing means never stating anything directly.
Using more adjectives and fancy words always makes description better.

concepts.name: Scene construction
concepts.summary: Write a scene with a clear setting, a character who wants something, an obstacle and a shift by the end.

concepts.name: Character desire and flaw
concepts.summary: Give a character a concrete want and a limiting flaw that drive their choices on the page.

concepts.name: Dialogue that reveals
concepts.summary: Write dialogue that sounds natural, carries subtext and reveals character, with correct punctuation and tags.

concepts.name: Plot structure arc
concepts.summary: Explain how setup, rising action, climax and resolution shape a short story's progression.

concepts.name: Setting as atmosphere
concepts.summary: Use selected details of place and weather to establish mood rather than listing everything visible.

concepts.name: Imagery in poetry
concepts.summary: Write short poems built on fresh, concrete images instead of stated feelings.

concepts.name: Line breaks and rhythm
concepts.summary: Use line breaks, stress and sound patterns such as alliteration to control pace and emphasis in a poem.

concepts.name: Self-editing pass
concepts.summary: Reread a draft to cut filler, fix clichés and tighten sentences.

misconceptions.text: Dialogue should copy real speech exactly, including every filler word and pleasantry.
Every story needs a big dramatic event or twist to work.
A poem must rhyme to be a poem.

concepts.name: Point of view control
concepts.summary: Choose a viewpoint and maintain consistent narrative distance, avoiding head-hopping and knowledge the narrator lacks.

concepts.name: Subtext and implication
concepts.summary: Analyse and craft passages where the meaning lies beneath what characters say or do.

concepts.name: Pacing and scene-summary balance
concepts.summary: Decide when to dramatise in scene and when to compress in summary to control tempo.

concepts.name: Character arc and change
concepts.summary: Analyse how events pressure a character's belief so they change, or fail to change, across a story.

concepts.name: Theme through motif
concepts.summary: Develop theme implicitly through recurring images, objects and patterns rather than stated morals.

concepts.name: Poetic form and device
concepts.summary: Apply forms and devices such as free verse, enjambment, volta and repetition deliberately to serve meaning.

concepts.name: Structured revision
concepts.summary: Revise in layers, from structure and character to paragraph and word level, diagnosing what each draft needs.

concepts.name: Giving and using feedback
concepts.summary: Analyse peer critique to separate the reader's symptoms from proposed fixes and decide what to act on.

misconceptions.text: Revision means correcting typos and grammar.
Theme is a moral the story should state clearly at the end.
Every piece of feedback must be followed to improve the work.

concepts.name: Distinctive voice
concepts.summary: Evaluate how diction, syntax, rhythm and attitude combine into a voice, and tune it to the piece.

concepts.name: Unreliable and layered narration
concepts.summary: Analyse how gaps between narrator and reader knowledge create irony and tension.

concepts.name: Structural experiment
concepts.summary: Judge when nonlinear, braided or fragmentary structures serve a story's meaning and when they distract.

concepts.name: Sound and syntax control
concepts.summary: Analyse and shape sentence length, cadence and sound to produce effect in prose and poetry.

concepts.name: Genre conventions and subversion
concepts.summary: Evaluate how a genre's conventions shape reader expectation and when to honour or subvert them.

concepts.name: Personal prose craft
concepts.summary: Evaluate how reflection, selection and honesty turn lived experience into shaped narrative with a larger point.

concepts.name: Critical reading as a writer
concepts.summary: Analyse published work to identify techniques and judge which are worth adapting.

misconceptions.text: Voice is a quirky style you add on top, such as slang or odd punctuation.
Experimental structure automatically makes writing more original.
Personal writing only needs to be true to events, not shaped like a story.

concepts.name: Original aesthetic vision
concepts.summary: Develop a coherent personal aesthetic and obsessions that unify a body of work.

concepts.name: Form invention and hybridity
concepts.summary: Create new or hybrid forms that fuse prose, poetry and other modes so form carries meaning.

concepts.name: Evaluating craft decisions
concepts.summary: Judge the trade-offs of craft choices against the intended effect and defend them.

concepts.name: Tradition and intertextuality
concepts.summary: Evaluate how a work converses with earlier texts and movements, using influence without imitation.

concepts.name: Ethics of representation
concepts.summary: Weigh the ethical and artistic consequences of depicting real people, other cultures and trauma.

concepts.name: Sustained long-form architecture
concepts.summary: Design the architecture of a collection, novella or sequence so pieces build cumulative meaning.

concepts.name: Mentoring and editorial judgement
concepts.summary: Assess others' drafts and guide revision toward the writer's own aims rather than imposing taste.

misconceptions.text: Originality means avoiding all influence and convention.
Breaking formal rules is always a sign of artistic mastery.
A collection is simply the best individual pieces gathered in any order.

concepts.name: JDK, JRE and JVM roles
concepts.summary: Explain that the JDK provides tools like javac, the JRE provides what is needed to run programs, and the JVM executes bytecode.

concepts.name: Compile and run cycle
concepts.summary: Describe how javac turns .java source into .class bytecode that the java launcher runs on a JVM.

concepts.name: Primitive and reference types
concepts.summary: Distinguish primitives such as int and boolean from reference types such as String and understand that variable types are fixed at compile time.

concepts.name: Class structure and main method
concepts.summary: Recall how a class is declared in a file of the same name and how main serves as the program entry point.

concepts.name: Objects and constructors
concepts.summary: Understand that a class is a blueprint, and new calls a constructor to create an object with its own fields.

concepts.name: Methods, fields and access modifiers
concepts.summary: Understand how instance members hold state and behaviour and how public and private control visibility.

concepts.name: Compiler error reading
concepts.summary: Interpret common javac messages such as missing symbol or incompatible types to locate the cause.

misconceptions.text: Java source code is run directly by the computer's processor after compiling.
The JVM and the JDK are the same thing.
Assigning one object variable to another copies the object itself.

concepts.name: Inheritance and method overriding
concepts.summary: Use extends, super and @Override to specialise a class and reuse behaviour from a superclass.

concepts.name: Interfaces and implementation
concepts.summary: Define an interface and implement it in classes, programming against the interface type.

concepts.name: Abstract classes
concepts.summary: Use abstract classes to share partial implementation while forcing subclasses to supply abstract methods.

concepts.name: Polymorphism and dynamic dispatch
concepts.summary: Apply a supertype reference to hold subclass objects and predict which overridden method runs.

concepts.name: ArrayList usage
concepts.summary: Add, get, remove and iterate over an ArrayList, including with the enhanced for loop.

concepts.name: HashMap usage
concepts.summary: Store, look up and iterate key-value pairs in a HashMap and handle missing keys.

concepts.name: Equals and hashCode contract
concepts.summary: Use equals to compare content instead of ==, and see why equal objects need equal hash codes in HashMap keys.

concepts.name: Try-catch and checked exceptions
concepts.summary: Handle or declare checked exceptions with try, catch, finally and throws.

misconceptions.text: Using == on two Strings or objects compares their contents.
A class can extend several classes as long as it is careful.
The method that runs is chosen by the declared type of the variable rather than the actual object.

concepts.name: Generic classes and methods
concepts.summary: Write and use generic types and methods so type errors are caught at compile time without casts.

concepts.name: Bounded types and wildcards
concepts.summary: Analyse when to use bounded type parameters and ? extends or ? super wildcards for flexible APIs.

concepts.name: Lambdas and functional interfaces
concepts.summary: Write lambdas and method references that target functional interfaces such as Predicate and Function.

concepts.name: Stream pipelines
concepts.summary: Decompose data processing into source, intermediate operations and a terminal operation, including collectors like groupingBy.

concepts.name: Collections framework selection
concepts.summary: Choose between ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeMap and others based on ordering, uniqueness and performance.

concepts.name: Custom and unchecked exceptions
concepts.summary: Distinguish checked from unchecked exceptions and design custom exceptions with try-with-resources for cleanup.

concepts.name: Maven or Gradle project builds
concepts.summary: Use a build tool to declare dependencies, run the build lifecycle and tests, and package a JAR.

concepts.name: Immutability and Optional
concepts.summary: Analyse how immutable classes and Optional reduce null-related errors and shared-state bugs.

misconceptions.text: A List<Dog> can be passed where a List<Animal> is expected because Dog extends Animal.
Streams store data like a collection and can be reused after a terminal operation.
Generic type information is fully available at runtime.

concepts.name: Type erasure consequences
concepts.summary: Analyse how erasure limits generic arrays, instanceof checks and overloads, and why bridge methods and unchecked warnings appear.

concepts.name: Class loading and bytecode structure
concepts.summary: Analyse how class loaders load, link and initialise classes and read bytecode with javap to explain behaviour.

concepts.name: Garbage collection and memory model
concepts.summary: Reason about heap versus stack, object reachability, and how collector choice and allocation patterns affect latency and throughput.

concepts.name: Stream performance and parallelism
concepts.summary: Evaluate when sequential, parallel or plain loop approaches are appropriate given statefulness, side effects and workload.

concepts.name: API and class design tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Evaluate choices between inheritance, composition, interfaces with default methods and sealed hierarchies.

concepts.name: Concurrency primitives and visibility
concepts.summary: Analyse race conditions and visibility problems and apply synchronized, volatile, atomics and concurrent collections.

concepts.name: Multi-module dependency management
concepts.summary: Evaluate dependency scopes, transitive conflicts and version management in multi-module Maven or Gradle builds.

concepts.name: Profiling and diagnosing performance
concepts.summary: Use profilers, thread dumps and heap dumps to find the cause of slowness, leaks and deadlocks.

misconceptions.text: Parallel streams always make processing faster.
Garbage collection means memory leaks are impossible in Java.
Synchronizing every method makes a class thread-safe and efficient.

concepts.name: JIT compilation and optimisation
concepts.summary: Evaluate how JIT inlining, escape analysis and warm-up shape performance and the validity of benchmarks.

concepts.name: Java Memory Model happens-before
concepts.summary: Judge the correctness of concurrent code by reasoning with happens-before rules, safe publication and reordering.

concepts.name: Microbenchmark design
concepts.summary: Assess and design benchmarks that avoid dead-code elimination, constant folding and warm-up artefacts.

concepts.name: Designing library and framework APIs
concepts.summary: Create APIs that remain binary and source compatible, using generics, interfaces, sealed types and modules deliberately.

concepts.name: Bytecode manipulation and reflection
concepts.summary: Design solutions using reflection, annotation processors, proxies or agents, weighing their cost and safety.

concepts.name: Concurrency architecture choices
concepts.summary: Design concurrent systems choosing among platform threads, virtual threads, executors and async composition for a workload.

concepts.name: Reproducible build and release engineering
concepts.summary: Create reproducible, cached builds with custom plugins, versioning and release pipelines across large codebases.

concepts.name: JVM tuning and production diagnostics
concepts.summary: Evaluate GC selection and JVM flag settings against production metrics and justify tuning decisions.

misconceptions.text: Java benchmark results from a single short run reflect steady-state performance.
Tuning JVM flags is a reliable substitute for fixing allocation or design problems.
Virtual threads speed up CPU-bound work.

concepts.name: Set notation and membership
concepts.summary: Read and write sets using roster and set-builder notation and decide whether an element belongs to a set or a set is a subset of another.

concepts.name: Set operations and Venn diagrams
concepts.summary: Compute and explain union, intersection, difference and complement and represent them with Venn diagrams.

concepts.name: Propositions and logical connectives
concepts.summary: Identify statements that are true or false and explain the meaning of AND, OR, NOT, implication and biconditional.

concepts.name: Truth tables
concepts.summary: Build a truth table for a compound proposition and read off when it is true or false.

concepts.name: Functions as mappings
concepts.summary: Explain a function as a rule assigning each domain element exactly one codomain element, distinguishing domain, codomain and range.

concepts.name: Counting by sum and product
concepts.summary: Explain when to add and when to multiply counts of choices in simple counting problems.

misconceptions.text: The empty set and the set containing the empty set are the same thing.
The implication 'if P then Q' is false whenever P is false.
In ordinary logic, 'or' means exactly one of the two is true.

concepts.name: Logical equivalence and De Morgan
concepts.summary: Apply equivalences such as De Morgan's laws and the contrapositive to rewrite statements and recognize tautologies and contradictions.

concepts.name: Quantifiers and negation
concepts.summary: Translate statements into predicates with for-all and there-exists and correctly negate them.

concepts.name: Relations and their properties
concepts.summary: Represent relations as sets of pairs and test them for reflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry and transitivity.

concepts.name: Injective, surjective and bijective functions
concepts.summary: Classify functions as one-to-one, onto or both and use composition and inverses of bijections.

concepts.name: Permutations and combinations
concepts.summary: Compute counts of ordered and unordered selections with and without repetition and choose the right formula.

concepts.name: Direct proof
concepts.summary: Write a direct proof of a simple statement from definitions, such as properties of even and odd integers.

concepts.name: Divisibility and modular congruence
concepts.summary: Use divisibility, remainders and congruence mod n to compute sums, products and powers of residues.

misconceptions.text: The negation of 'for all x, P(x)' is 'for all x, not P(x)'.
A relation that is symmetric and transitive must also be reflexive.
Order matters in combinations just as it does in permutations.

concepts.name: Proof by contradiction and contrapositive
concepts.summary: Choose and carry out contrapositive or contradiction proofs, such as irrationality of the square root of 2.

concepts.name: Mathematical induction
concepts.summary: Prove statements over the natural numbers with a base case and an inductive step using the inductive hypothesis.

concepts.name: Strong induction
concepts.summary: Decide when strong induction is needed and use several earlier cases in the inductive step.

concepts.name: Equivalence relations and partitions
concepts.summary: Analyse how an equivalence relation splits a set into classes and connect it to partitions, including congruence classes.

concepts.name: Inclusion-exclusion principle
concepts.summary: Count elements of unions of overlapping sets by alternating sums of intersection sizes.

concepts.name: Pigeonhole principle
concepts.summary: Identify the pigeons and holes in a problem and apply basic and generalized pigeonhole arguments.

concepts.name: Solving linear recurrences
concepts.summary: Set up recurrences from problems and solve first-order and linear homogeneous second-order ones by iteration or characteristic roots.

concepts.name: Modular inverses and the Euclidean algorithm
concepts.summary: Compute gcds and modular inverses and solve linear congruences.

misconceptions.text: In an induction proof, the inductive step may assume the statement for all n, including the one being proved.
The base case is a formality and can be skipped when the inductive step works.
The pigeonhole principle tells you which hole holds multiple pigeons.

concepts.name: Nested quantifiers and proof strategy
concepts.summary: Analyse how the order of nested quantifiers changes meaning and pick proof strategies for statements with several quantifiers.

concepts.name: Structural induction
concepts.summary: Prove properties of recursively defined sets, strings and trees by induction over their construction.

concepts.name: Generating functions for counting
concepts.summary: Use generating functions to count selections with constraints and to solve recurrences, judging when they beat direct methods.

concepts.name: Non-homogeneous recurrences and divide-and-conquer
concepts.summary: Solve recurrences with forcing terms and evaluate solution methods for divide-and-conquer cost recurrences.

concepts.name: Binomial identities and combinatorial proof
concepts.summary: Establish identities by counting one set in two ways or by building a bijection, and compare with algebraic proofs.

concepts.name: Cardinality and countability
concepts.summary: Compare sizes of sets via bijections, show sets are countable, and use the diagonal argument to show uncountability.

concepts.name: Number-theoretic theorems and applications
concepts.summary: Apply Fermat, Euler and the Chinese remainder theorem and evaluate their use in modular computation and RSA-style cryptography.

concepts.name: Partial orders and lattices
concepts.summary: Analyse partial orders using Hasse diagrams, extremal elements, chains and antichains.

misconceptions.text: For all x there exists y is logically the same as there exists y for all x.
All infinite sets have the same size.
Fermat's little theorem holds for any modulus, not only primes.

concepts.name: Formal proof design and evaluation
concepts.summary: Judge the validity, rigour and elegance of proofs, spot subtle flaws, and select the most suitable technique for a new claim.

concepts.name: Asymptotic analysis of recurrences
concepts.summary: Derive and justify tight bounds for irregular recurrences and compare methods such as substitution, recursion trees and generating functions.

concepts.name: Probabilistic and extremal methods
concepts.summary: Design existence arguments using expected values or extremal choices to prove combinatorial results without construction.

concepts.name: Generalized pigeonhole and Ramsey theory
concepts.summary: Evaluate Ramsey-type guarantees of structure in large systems and construct arguments or bounds for small cases.

concepts.name: Inclusion-exclusion with Möbius inversion
concepts.summary: Generalize inclusion-exclusion to posets and use it for derangements, sieve counts and inversion formulas.

concepts.name: Formal logic and decidability limits
concepts.summary: Evaluate the expressive power and limits of propositional and first-order logic, including satisfiability, completeness and undecidability.

concepts.name: Modelling problems discretely
concepts.summary: Create discrete models of real problems by choosing sets, relations, recurrences or counting structures and justify the choice.

misconceptions.text: A probabilistic existence proof gives an efficient way to construct the object.
Ramsey numbers are easy to compute exactly once the general bounds are known.
Any true statement in first-order arithmetic can be proven from a fixed axiom system.

concepts.name: Role of the kernel
concepts.summary: Explain that the kernel manages CPU, memory, and devices on behalf of programs and provides a protected abstraction layer over hardware.

concepts.name: User mode versus kernel mode
concepts.summary: Describe why the CPU runs user code with restricted privileges and kernel code with full privileges, and how this protects the system.

concepts.name: Process as running program
concepts.summary: Distinguish a program on disk from a process, which has its own address space, state, and resources.

concepts.name: Process states
concepts.summary: Recall the main process states (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated) and what causes transitions between them.

concepts.name: System call interface
concepts.summary: Explain that programs request kernel services such as file I/O or process creation through system calls rather than direct hardware access.

concepts.name: Threads within a process
concepts.summary: Explain that a thread is an execution path inside a process sharing its address space while having its own stack and registers.

concepts.name: Files and directories abstraction
concepts.summary: Understand files as named byte sequences organised in a directory tree, hiding physical disk layout.

concepts.name: Virtual memory idea
concepts.summary: Explain that each process sees its own private virtual address space which the OS maps onto physical memory.

misconceptions.text: The operating system is just the graphical desktop and bundled applications.
A process and a program are the same thing.
Threads of the same process have completely separate memory.

concepts.name: Process creation with fork and exec
concepts.summary: Use fork, exec, wait, and exit to create, replace, and reap child processes in a Unix-like system.

concepts.name: Context switch mechanics
concepts.summary: Explain how the kernel saves and restores register state and process control block data to switch the CPU between processes.

concepts.name: Basic CPU scheduling policies
concepts.summary: Apply first-come-first-served, shortest-job-first, and round-robin to a set of jobs and compute waiting and turnaround times.

concepts.name: Interrupts and handlers
concepts.summary: Explain how devices signal the CPU via interrupts and how the handler runs and returns control.

concepts.name: Paging and page tables
concepts.summary: Translate a virtual address into a physical address using page number, offset, and a page table.

concepts.name: File descriptors and open files
concepts.summary: Use file descriptors, including standard streams, redirection, and pipes, and relate them to kernel open-file structures.

concepts.name: Race conditions
concepts.summary: Identify a race condition on shared data between threads and locate the critical section.

concepts.name: Inter-process communication basics
concepts.summary: Describe pipes, signals, and shared memory as ways for processes to exchange data or notifications.

misconceptions.text: fork starts a brand new program in the child process.
A context switch is free and has no performance cost.
Shortest-job-first is always practical because the OS knows each job's run time in advance.

concepts.name: Mutexes and locking discipline
concepts.summary: Protect critical sections with mutexes, choosing between blocking locks and spinlocks and avoiding lock misuse.

concepts.name: Semaphores and condition variables
concepts.summary: Coordinate threads with semaphores and condition variables to solve producer-consumer and readers-writers problems.

concepts.name: Deadlock conditions and handling
concepts.summary: Analyse a system for the four necessary deadlock conditions and compare prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.

concepts.name: Page replacement algorithms
concepts.summary: Compare FIFO, LRU, and clock replacement on reference strings and analyse page fault behaviour.

concepts.name: Demand paging and page faults
concepts.summary: Trace how a page fault is handled and how demand paging, copy-on-write, and swap affect performance.

concepts.name: TLB and translation cost
concepts.summary: Analyse how the TLB hit rate affects effective memory access time and why multi-level page tables save space.

concepts.name: Priority and multilevel feedback scheduling
concepts.summary: Analyse priority-based and multilevel feedback schedulers, including starvation, aging, and priority inversion.

concepts.name: File system structures
concepts.summary: Apply inode, directory, and block allocation structures to explain how files are located, linked, and read.

misconceptions.text: Deadlock occurs whenever a program is slow or waits for a lock.
A mutex and a binary semaphore are identical, including ownership semantics.
LRU replacement always gives fewer page faults than FIFO on any reference string.

concepts.name: Multiprocessor scheduling and affinity
concepts.summary: Analyse trade-offs of per-core run queues, load balancing, and CPU affinity on cache locality and fairness.

concepts.name: Memory consistency and atomics
concepts.summary: Explain how atomic instructions and memory ordering enable lock-free structures and why naive code breaks on modern CPUs.

concepts.name: Thrashing and working set
concepts.summary: Diagnose thrashing and evaluate working-set or page-fault-frequency policies for memory allocation.

concepts.name: File system consistency and journaling
concepts.summary: Evaluate journaling, copy-on-write, and fsck approaches for keeping file systems consistent after crashes.

concepts.name: Device drivers and I/O paths
concepts.summary: Trace an I/O request through the VFS, block layer, driver, DMA, and interrupt completion, including top and bottom halves.

concepts.name: Linux process and scheduler internals
concepts.summary: Analyse how Linux represents tasks and uses a fair scheduler with virtual runtime and cgroups to share CPU.

concepts.name: Isolation with namespaces and cgroups
concepts.summary: Evaluate how namespaces and control groups provide process isolation and resource limits without virtualising hardware.

concepts.name: Performance diagnosis with tracing
concepts.summary: Use syscall tracing, profiling, and kernel counters to judge whether a bottleneck is CPU, memory, I/O, or locking.

misconceptions.text: Lock-free code is always faster than lock-based code.
Journaling guarantees no data loss for any application write.
Containers are lightweight virtual machines with their own kernel.

concepts.name: Designing kernel synchronization schemes
concepts.summary: Design synchronization for kernel data structures that balances scalability, latency, and correctness using fine-grained locks, RCU, or per-CPU data.

concepts.name: Evaluating scheduler designs
concepts.summary: Judge scheduler designs against throughput, latency, fairness, and real-time guarantees such as EDF or rate-monotonic analysis.

concepts.name: Virtualization and hypervisor support
concepts.summary: Evaluate how hypervisors use trap-and-emulate, hardware extensions, and nested page tables to share hardware among guest kernels.

concepts.name: Kernel security and isolation design
concepts.summary: Assess mitigations such as ASLR, capabilities, seccomp, and speculative-execution defences, including their performance and coverage limits.

concepts.name: Designing a file system or storage stack
concepts.summary: Create a file system design choosing on-disk layout, caching, and consistency strategy for given workloads and media such as SSDs.

concepts.name: Kernel architecture trade-offs
concepts.summary: Compare monolithic, microkernel, and hybrid structures such as Linux and Windows NT for performance, reliability, and security.

concepts.name: Debugging kernel failures
concepts.summary: Devise a method to diagnose panics, deadlocks, and memory corruption using dumps, tracing, and debuggers in a live or post-mortem kernel.

concepts.name: Memory management subsystem design
concepts.summary: Design memory policies for allocators, NUMA placement, and huge pages that fit specific workloads.

misconceptions.text: Microkernels are always slower and therefore never used in practice.
Hardware virtualization removes any need for the host kernel to manage guest memory.
Fine-grained locking always improves scalability over coarse locking.

concepts.name: Function as input-output rule
concepts.summary: Explain that a function assigns exactly one output to each input and describe it as a rule, table, or mapping.

concepts.name: Function notation f(x)
concepts.summary: Read and interpret f(x) as the output for input x and evaluate f(3) by substitution.

concepts.name: Coordinate plane and ordered pairs
concepts.summary: Recall how to name and locate points (x, y) using the axes and quadrants.

concepts.name: Table of values plotting
concepts.summary: Build a table of input-output values and plot the points to show the shape of a graph.

concepts.name: Domain and range meaning
concepts.summary: Describe domain as the set of allowed inputs and range as the set of resulting outputs.

concepts.name: Vertical line test
concepts.summary: Use the vertical line test to decide whether a graph represents a function.

misconceptions.text: f(x) means f multiplied by x.
A function can give two different outputs for the same input as long as the rule is consistent.
In an ordered pair (x, y), the y-value is plotted first along the horizontal axis.

concepts.name: Linear function graphs
concepts.summary: Sketch a linear function from its gradient and y-intercept and read these from its equation.

concepts.name: Intercepts of a graph
concepts.summary: Find x-intercepts by setting f(x)=0 and the y-intercept by evaluating f(0).

concepts.name: Finding domain and range
concepts.summary: Determine domain and range from an equation or graph, including restrictions such as division by zero and square roots of negatives.

concepts.name: Quadratic graph features
concepts.summary: Sketch a parabola identifying its vertex, axis of symmetry, intercepts and direction of opening.

concepts.name: Translations of graphs
concepts.summary: Apply y = f(x) + k and y = f(x - h) to shift a graph and describe the resulting movement.

concepts.name: Interval notation
concepts.summary: Write domains and ranges using inequalities and interval notation with correct open and closed ends.

concepts.name: Evaluating and interpreting graphs
concepts.summary: Read function values, solve f(x)=k and identify where a function is increasing or decreasing from its graph.

misconceptions.text: y = f(x - 2) moves the graph 2 units to the left.
The range of a function is always all real numbers.
A graph only has an x-intercept if it also has a y-intercept.

concepts.name: Stretches and reflections
concepts.summary: Apply y = af(x), y = f(bx), y = -f(x) and y = f(-x) and describe their effect on key points.

concepts.name: Combining graph transformations
concepts.summary: Determine the correct order of multiple transformations and deduce the equation of a transformed graph.

concepts.name: Composite functions
concepts.summary: Form and evaluate f(g(x)), recognise that fg differs from gf, and find the domain of the composite.

concepts.name: Inverse functions
concepts.summary: Find f⁻¹ algebraically, link its graph to a reflection in y = x and explain the swap of domain and range.

concepts.name: One-to-one and restricted domains
concepts.summary: Use the horizontal line test to decide if an inverse exists and restrict the domain to create one.

concepts.name: Piecewise-defined functions
concepts.summary: Evaluate and sketch piecewise functions, including absolute value, handling endpoints and continuity.

concepts.name: Exponential function graphs
concepts.summary: Sketch y = a^x for a>1 and 0<a<1, showing the y-intercept, horizontal asymptote and growth or decay.

misconceptions.text: f(g(x)) is always the same as g(f(x)).
The inverse function f⁻¹(x) means 1/f(x).
y = f(2x) stretches the graph horizontally by a factor of 2.

concepts.name: Logarithmic functions as inverses
concepts.summary: Analyse y = log_a x as the inverse of y = a^x and derive its domain, range, vertical asymptote and intercept.

concepts.name: Rational function structure
concepts.summary: Analyse how factors of numerator and denominator determine zeros, vertical asymptotes and holes.

concepts.name: Asymptote determination
concepts.summary: Find vertical, horizontal and oblique asymptotes using denominator zeros and degree comparison, and explain end behaviour.

concepts.name: Sketching from key features
concepts.summary: Combine intercepts, asymptotes, sign analysis and symmetry to produce and justify a sketch of a rational graph.

concepts.name: Even and odd symmetry
concepts.summary: Test f(-x) to classify functions as even, odd or neither and link this to reflective or rotational symmetry.

concepts.name: Transformations of log and exponential
concepts.summary: Determine how transformations move asymptotes, intercepts and domain or range of exponential and log graphs.

concepts.name: Modelling with function graphs
concepts.summary: Evaluate which function family fits a context, and interpret parameters and limitations of the fitted graph.

misconceptions.text: A common factor cancelled from a rational function leaves no trace on the graph.
A graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote.
Every function that is not even must be odd.

concepts.name: Function behaviour near singularities
concepts.summary: Evaluate behaviour on each side of a discontinuity or asymptote and justify classification as hole, jump or infinite.

concepts.name: Domain-aware inverse and composition
concepts.summary: Evaluate when compositions and inverses are valid, including the identity (f∘g)⁻¹ = g⁻¹∘f⁻¹ and domain consequences.

concepts.name: Designing functions to specification
concepts.summary: Create a function with prescribed intercepts, asymptotes, symmetry and domain, and verify it meets them.

concepts.name: Comparing growth rates
aliases: polynomial vs exponential vs log growth
concepts.summary: Judge relative long-run growth of logarithmic, polynomial and exponential functions and justify with graphs.

concepts.name: Linearising data by transformation
concepts.summary: Design log or semi-log transformations that turn power and exponential relationships into straight lines to estimate parameters.

concepts.name: Parametric families of graphs
concepts.summary: Evaluate how changing a parameter alters the qualitative features and number of intercepts or asymptotes in a family of functions.

concepts.name: Critiquing graphical arguments
concepts.summary: Assess when a graph, window or technology output misleads about domain, asymptotes or solutions and correct it.

misconceptions.text: Exponential growth with a small base multiplier will eventually be overtaken by any polynomial.
If a graphing tool shows a smooth line through a point, the function is defined and continuous there.
The inverse of a composite fg is f⁻¹g⁻¹ in the same order.

issues: nov-5 'Domain and range meaning' and adb-3 'Finding domain and range' overlap; adb-3 should be about determining restrictions, and nov-5 should be clearly the definition.
novice misconception 'f(x) means f multiplied by x' is thin and only loosely tied to a concept; fine but the novice prereq ordering has odd links.
nov-6 vertical line test depends on graphs (nov-4) but also the misconception about two outputs is stated as a correct-sounding belief; rephrase as a clear wrong belief.
Prerequisite [nov-4, nov-6] present but nov-3 prerequisite of nov-4 ok; adb-6 interval notation at C2 is allowed in band.
cmp-1 misconception about f(2x) is attached to cmp-2 unnecessarily; cmp-2 should depend on adb-5 too.
cmp-4 inverse is missing dependency on nov-5/adb-3 domain-range and cmp-5 should precede cmp-4 (present) but cmp-5 lacks dependency on cmp-3 irrelevant; fine.
cmp-7 exponential depends on quadratic graph features (adb-4), which is not a genuine dependency; should depend on adb-1/adb-5 instead.
prf-1 depends on cmp-7 and cmp-4 correctly; prf-3 asymptote determination overlaps with prf-2 but is acceptable; prf-4 lacks dependency on prf-5 symmetry, and prf-4 should depend on adb-2 (present).
exp-4 misconception is incorrectly worded ('small base multiplier'): the wrong belief should be stated as a polynomial eventually overtaking any exponential with base greater than 1.
exp-2 is partly a repeat of cmp-3/cmp-4 but extends with domain consequences; acceptable. exp-4 lacks dependency on cmp-7.
