concepts.name: Income versus expenses
concepts.summary: Distinguish gross from net income and fixed from variable expenses, and recognise that money in minus money out determines whether you save or borrow.

concepts.name: Needs versus wants
concepts.summary: Explain why spending is sorted into essentials and discretionary items and classify everyday purchases accordingly.

concepts.name: Monthly budget structure
concepts.summary: Describe how a budget assigns expected income to categories such as housing, food, savings and debt payments for a month.

concepts.name: Emergency fund purpose
concepts.summary: Explain why a cash reserve for unexpected costs prevents borrowing and covers job loss or repairs.

concepts.name: How credit cards charge interest
concepts.summary: Understand that carrying a balance incurs interest at an annual percentage rate, making purchases cost more than their price.

concepts.name: Paycheck deductions
concepts.summary: Identify the items on a pay stub, such as income tax withholding, payroll taxes and benefit contributions, that explain gross versus take-home pay.

concepts.name: Credit score meaning
concepts.summary: Recall that a credit score summarises borrowing history and influences loan approval and interest rates.

misconceptions.text: Gross pay is the amount you have available to spend each month.
Paying only the minimum on a credit card is a fine way to pay it off.
A budget is a restriction that leaves no room for any wants.

concepts.name: Building a zero-based budget
concepts.summary: Create a monthly budget from your own net income that assigns every dollar to a category, using a framework such as 50/30/20 as a starting point.

concepts.name: Tracking spending
concepts.summary: Record and categorise actual transactions using statements or an app and compare them to the budget to find gaps.

concepts.name: Sizing an emergency fund
concepts.summary: Calculate a target of roughly three to six months of essential expenses and set a monthly contribution to reach it.

concepts.name: Paying credit cards in full
concepts.summary: Apply the statement balance, due date and grace period to avoid interest, and compute how long minimum payments take to clear a balance.

concepts.name: Credit score factors
concepts.summary: Explain how payment history, utilisation, account age, mix and new inquiries affect a score, and act on them.

concepts.name: Basic tax filing
concepts.summary: Use a W-2 and the standard deduction to complete a simple return and determine a refund or amount owed.

concepts.name: Employer retirement match
concepts.summary: Understand that contributing enough to earn an employer match gives an immediate return on those contributions.

misconceptions.text: A tax refund is a bonus rather than a return of your own overpaid money.
Carrying a small credit card balance month to month improves your credit score.
Checking your own credit score lowers it.

concepts.name: Debt payoff strategies
concepts.summary: Compare the avalanche and snowball methods for multiple debts by total interest paid and motivation, and choose one for a given situation.

concepts.name: Student loan repayment options
concepts.summary: Analyse loan types, interest accrual and repayment plans to see how each affects monthly payment and total cost.

concepts.name: Marginal tax brackets
concepts.summary: Calculate tax under progressive brackets and distinguish marginal from effective rates when evaluating extra income.

concepts.name: Tax deductions versus credits
concepts.summary: Analyse how deductions reduce taxable income while credits reduce tax owed, and decide between standard and itemised deductions.

concepts.name: Traditional versus Roth accounts
concepts.summary: Compare when taxes are paid, contribution limits and withdrawal rules across 401(k), traditional IRA and Roth IRA accounts.

concepts.name: Insurance deductibles and premiums
concepts.summary: Analyse how premium, deductible, copay, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximum trade off when comparing plans.

concepts.name: Compound growth in saving
concepts.summary: Apply compounding to project savings and loan balances, showing why starting early and paying interest early matter.

concepts.name: Prioritising financial goals
concepts.summary: Sequence goals such as starter emergency fund, match, high-interest debt and retirement saving by their relative returns and risk.

misconceptions.text: Moving into a higher tax bracket makes all of your income taxed at the higher rate.
A tax deduction cuts your tax bill dollar for dollar.
The cheapest premium is always the cheapest insurance plan overall.

concepts.name: Tax-location of retirement savings
concepts.summary: Evaluate how to split contributions between pre-tax, Roth and taxable accounts based on current versus expected future marginal rates.

concepts.name: Retirement savings adequacy
concepts.summary: Judge whether a savings rate and balance can fund retirement using income replacement targets, inflation and sustainable withdrawal assumptions.

concepts.name: Refinancing and consolidation decisions
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether refinancing, consolidating or transferring a balance saves money after fees, rate changes and lost protections.

concepts.name: Insurance coverage gap analysis
concepts.summary: Analyse household exposures to find which risks to insure, retain or reduce, and size coverage such as term life and disability.

concepts.name: Risk and diversification in investing
concepts.summary: Analyse how asset allocation, diversification and fees shape risk and long-run returns within retirement accounts.

concepts.name: Tax-aware income planning
concepts.summary: Analyse income sources and adjust withholding or estimated payments to avoid penalties and surprises.

concepts.name: Behavioural money biases
concepts.summary: Evaluate how biases distort spending and saving decisions and judge which automation or commitment devices counter them.

misconceptions.text: Roth accounts are always better than traditional accounts regardless of your tax rate.
Refinancing to a lower monthly payment always saves money.
Insurance should cover every possible loss, however small.

concepts.name: Lifetime household financial plan
concepts.summary: Design a multi-decade plan that integrates cash flow, debt, insurance, taxes, investing and retirement for a specific household.

concepts.name: Retirement drawdown sequencing
concepts.summary: Create a withdrawal plan that sequences taxable, pre-tax and Roth accounts and manages sequence-of-returns risk, required distributions and Social Security timing.

concepts.name: Evaluating financial advice
concepts.summary: Assess advisors, products and media claims by incentives, fees and fiduciary duty, and decide when professional help is worth its cost.

concepts.name: Multi-year tax strategy
concepts.summary: Design multi-year moves such as Roth conversions, loss harvesting and income timing that lower lifetime rather than single-year tax.

concepts.name: Stress testing household resilience
concepts.summary: Evaluate how a plan holds up under job loss, illness, inflation or market decline and judge buffers and insurance accordingly.

concepts.name: Estate and beneficiary planning
concepts.summary: Evaluate wills, beneficiary designations and powers of attorney so assets pass as intended and dependents are protected.

concepts.name: Adapting plans to life events
concepts.summary: Create revised plans for events such as marriage, children, home purchase, career change or divorce, tracing the effects on every part of the plan.

misconceptions.text: A good financial plan is set once and then left unchanged.
Beneficiary designations on retirement accounts are overridden by what a will says.
A paid advisor is automatically obliged to act in your best interest.

concepts.name: Contiguous array storage and indexing
concepts.summary: Explain that an array stores elements contiguously so any element is reached by index in constant time, and that its size is fixed once allocated.

concepts.name: Linked list nodes and pointers
concepts.summary: Describe a singly linked list as nodes holding a value and a reference to the next node, reached only by following links from the head.

concepts.name: Stack last-in first-out
concepts.summary: Explain that a stack adds and removes only at one end, so the most recently pushed item is the first popped.

concepts.name: Queue first-in first-out
concepts.summary: Explain that a queue adds at the back and removes from the front, so items leave in arrival order.

concepts.name: Cost of insertion and lookup
concepts.summary: Recall in rough terms that array indexing is constant time while searching an unsorted sequence or inserting in the middle takes time proportional to the number of elements.

concepts.name: Key-value lookup with hash tables
concepts.summary: Recall that a hash table stores key-value pairs and finds a value by its key without scanning all entries.

misconceptions.text: A linked list lets you reach the nth element as fast as an array does.
A stack and a queue are the same structure because both hold items in order.
A hash table keeps its keys in sorted order.

concepts.name: Dynamic array resizing
concepts.summary: Implement an array that doubles its capacity when full and explain why appends are cheap on average.

concepts.name: Linked list insertion and deletion
concepts.summary: Insert and delete nodes in singly linked lists by rewiring references, handling head and empty-list cases.

concepts.name: Doubly linked lists and tail pointers
concepts.summary: Use previous links and a tail reference to make removal at a known node and appends at the end constant time.

concepts.name: Stack and queue implementations
concepts.summary: Build stacks and queues on arrays or linked lists, including a circular buffer, with constant-time operations.

concepts.name: Deque operations
concepts.summary: Use a deque to add and remove at both ends and recognise when it replaces a stack or queue.

concepts.name: Hashing and collision handling
concepts.summary: Apply a hash function to map keys to buckets and resolve collisions with chaining or probing.

concepts.name: Choosing a structure by operation costs
concepts.summary: Pick between array, linked list, stack, queue and hash table for a small task by comparing the costs of its main operations.

misconceptions.text: Appending to a dynamic array is always constant time in the worst case.
Deleting a node from a singly linked list is constant time given only the node's value.
A good hash function eliminates collisions entirely.

concepts.name: Hash table load factor and rehashing
concepts.summary: Analyse how load factor affects probe lengths and chain lengths, and why tables rehash into a larger array to keep operations near constant time.

concepts.name: Binary search tree operations
concepts.summary: Implement search, insertion and deletion in a binary search tree, including the cases for deleting nodes with zero, one or two children.

concepts.name: Tree traversal orders
concepts.summary: Perform in-order, pre-order, post-order and level-order traversals and state what each is useful for, such as in-order yielding sorted keys.

concepts.name: Binary heap and priority queue
concepts.summary: Implement a binary heap in an array with sift-up and sift-down to support insertion and extraction of the extreme element in logarithmic time.

concepts.name: Graph adjacency list and matrix
concepts.summary: Compare adjacency lists and matrices in memory use and in the cost of edge lookup and neighbour iteration for sparse and dense graphs.

concepts.name: Trie prefix storage
concepts.summary: Build a trie that stores strings by character along paths and use it for lookup and prefix queries in time proportional to key length.

concepts.name: Tree height and degeneration
concepts.summary: Analyse how insertion order determines binary search tree height and why sorted insertions degrade operations to linear time.

misconceptions.text: A binary search tree always gives logarithmic-time search.
A heap keeps all its elements in sorted order, so iterating its array gives sorted output.
An adjacency matrix is always the better graph representation because edge lookup is constant time.

concepts.name: AVL rotations and balance factors
concepts.summary: Analyse how balance factors detect imbalance after updates and how single and double rotations restore height balance while preserving order.

concepts.name: Red-black tree invariants
concepts.summary: Explain the colour and black-height invariants of red-black trees and how recolouring and rotations maintain them, bounding height at about twice the optimum.

concepts.name: Amortised analysis of structures
concepts.summary: Use amortised reasoning to justify costs of dynamic array growth and hash table rehashing, distinguishing them from worst-case and average-case bounds.

concepts.name: Collision strategy trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate linear probing, double hashing and chaining by clustering, deletion handling, memory overhead and cache locality.

concepts.name: Heap construction and heapsort
concepts.summary: Analyse why bottom-up heap construction takes linear time and how it supports in-place heapsort and top-k selection.

concepts.name: Memory layout and cache effects
concepts.summary: Evaluate how contiguity and pointer chasing affect real performance so that an array can beat a linked list despite equal asymptotic costs.

concepts.name: Balanced tree versus hash table choice
concepts.summary: Judge when ordered operations such as range queries and predecessor lookup justify balanced trees over hash tables, given worst-case guarantees and memory.

misconceptions.text: AVL and red-black trees are equally strictly balanced, so they perform identically.
Amortised constant time means every single operation is fast.
Two structures with the same Big-O costs will perform the same in practice.

concepts.name: Designing structures for workload
concepts.summary: Design or compose a structure from an access pattern, such as combining a hash table with a linked list to get constant-time least-recently-used eviction.

concepts.name: Evaluating adversarial and worst-case inputs
concepts.summary: Evaluate structures against adversarial input, including hash collision attacks, and choose randomised hashing or balanced trees to bound worst-case behaviour.

concepts.name: Cache-aware and external-memory trees
concepts.summary: Assess why wide-node trees such as B-trees minimise block transfers and when they beat binary trees in memory hierarchies.

concepts.name: Probabilistic and approximate structures
concepts.summary: Evaluate skip lists and Bloom filters by their expected costs, error rates and memory use against deterministic structures.

concepts.name: Concurrent and persistent structures
concepts.summary: Design or select structures that stay correct under concurrent access or keep older versions via structural sharing, weighing the overhead against simpler locking.

concepts.name: Graph representation for large-scale use
concepts.summary: Create a graph storage scheme such as compressed sparse rows that fits the graph's density, update rate and traversal pattern.

concepts.name: Proving invariants and bounds
concepts.summary: Evaluate and justify a structure's correctness and complexity bounds by stating invariants and using potential-function arguments.

misconceptions.text: Expected-case guarantees are enough in every deployment, so worst-case behaviour can be ignored.
Lock-free structures are always faster than lock-based ones.
Binary trees are optimal for any large dataset, so B-trees are only a database detail.

concepts.name: Right triangle side labels
concepts.summary: Identify the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides relative to a chosen acute angle in a right triangle.

concepts.name: Sine cosine tangent ratios
concepts.summary: Explain sine, cosine and tangent as ratios of side lengths that depend only on the angle, and recall SOH-CAH-TOA.

concepts.name: Reciprocal trig functions
concepts.summary: Recall that cosecant, secant and cotangent are the reciprocals of sine, cosine and tangent respectively.

concepts.name: Degree measure of angles
concepts.summary: Describe angles in degrees as fractions of a full 360° turn and recognise standard angles such as 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°.

concepts.name: Special right triangle ratios
concepts.summary: Understand how the 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles give exact sine, cosine and tangent values for standard angles.

concepts.name: Calculator trig evaluation
concepts.summary: Understand that a calculator must be in the correct angle mode to evaluate trig functions and read the results sensibly.

misconceptions.text: Sine, cosine and tangent depend on the size of the triangle rather than only on the angle.
The opposite and adjacent sides are fixed features of the triangle regardless of which angle is being used.
Secant is the reciprocal of sine and cosecant is the reciprocal of cosine.

concepts.name: Solving right triangles
concepts.summary: Use trig ratios and the Pythagorean theorem to find all unknown sides and angles of a right triangle.

concepts.name: Angles of elevation and depression
concepts.summary: Model real situations such as heights and distances with right triangles and solve them using trig ratios.

concepts.name: Radian measure
concepts.summary: Define a radian as the angle subtending an arc equal to the radius and convert between radians and degrees.

concepts.name: Unit circle coordinates
concepts.summary: Use the point (cos θ, sin θ) on the unit circle to evaluate trig functions at standard angles.

concepts.name: Reference angles and quadrant signs
concepts.summary: Find trig values of angles beyond 90° using reference angles and the sign of each function in each quadrant.

concepts.name: Inverse trig for angles
concepts.summary: Apply inverse sine, cosine and tangent to find an acute angle from a known ratio.

concepts.name: Pythagorean identity basics
concepts.summary: Use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 to find one function value from another given the quadrant.

misconceptions.text: Radians and degrees are different kinds of quantities, so a radian value cannot be compared with a degree value.
Trig functions of angles larger than 90° are undefined because there is no right triangle.
sin⁻¹(x) means 1/sin(x).

concepts.name: Law of sines
concepts.summary: Apply a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C to find missing sides or angles in non-right triangles.

concepts.name: Law of cosines
concepts.summary: Apply c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C to triangles given SAS or SSS information.

concepts.name: Ambiguous SSA case
concepts.summary: Analyse SSA data to decide whether it yields zero, one or two triangles.

concepts.name: Graphs of sine and cosine
concepts.summary: Sketch y = sin x and y = cos x and read zeros, maxima, minima and periodicity from them.

concepts.name: Amplitude period and phase shift
concepts.summary: Analyse how A, B, C and D transform a sinusoid and write an equation from a graph.

concepts.name: Angle-sum and difference identities
concepts.summary: Apply the sum and difference formulas for sine, cosine and tangent to evaluate exact values and simplify expressions.

concepts.name: Basic trig equations
concepts.summary: Solve equations like 2sin x = 1 over a given interval by finding all solutions using symmetry and periodicity.

concepts.name: Domain and range of inverses
concepts.summary: Analyse why inverse trig functions need restricted domains and state their principal value ranges.

misconceptions.text: The law of sines can be used with any three given pieces of a triangle.
sin(A+B) equals sin A + sin B.
In y = sin(Bx − C), the phase shift is C rather than C/B.

concepts.name: Double and half-angle identities
concepts.summary: Derive double and half-angle formulas from the sum identities and choose among cos 2θ forms strategically.

concepts.name: Proving trig identities
concepts.summary: Analyse both sides of an identity and select substitutions such as Pythagorean, reciprocal and quotient forms to prove it rigorously.

concepts.name: Product-to-sum and sum-to-product
concepts.summary: Use product-to-sum and sum-to-product identities to transform expressions for simplification or solving.

concepts.name: Complex trig equations
concepts.summary: Solve equations needing factoring, quadratic substitution, multiple angles or identities, and check for extraneous solutions.

concepts.name: Harmonic form conversion
aliases: a sin x + b cos x
concepts.summary: Rewrite a sin x + b cos x as a single sinusoid and judge when this form simplifies a problem.

concepts.name: Graphs of other trig functions
concepts.summary: Analyse the graphs of tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant, including asymptotes, periods and links to sine and cosine.

concepts.name: Sinusoidal modelling
concepts.summary: Fit and evaluate sinusoidal models for periodic data and judge their validity and limitations.

misconceptions.text: To prove an identity you may apply operations to both sides, such as cross-multiplying, as with solving an equation.
Squaring both sides or dividing by a trig factor is always safe when solving trig equations.
cos 2θ has only one correct form, 2cos²θ − 1.

concepts.name: Euler's formula connection
aliases: e^{iθ} = cos θ + i sin θ
concepts.summary: Evaluate how Euler's formula unifies trig identities and derives angle-sum and multiple-angle results.

concepts.name: De Moivre's theorem applications
concepts.summary: Use de Moivre's theorem to derive multiple-angle formulas and roots of unity, judging when it beats real identities.

concepts.name: Trig substitution strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate when substituting sin, tan or sec simplifies radicals and constraints, and justify the chosen domain.

concepts.name: Small-angle approximation analysis
concepts.summary: Assess the accuracy and error of approximations such as sin x ≈ x and cos x ≈ 1 − x²/2.

concepts.name: Fourier series intuition
concepts.summary: Judge how periodic functions can be built from sums of sinusoids of different frequencies, and what amplitude and phase represent.

concepts.name: Designing trig-based models
concepts.summary: Design and justify trigonometric models or solution methods for novel problems in surveying, navigation or oscillation.

concepts.name: Constructing original identity proofs
concepts.summary: Create new proofs of identities and laws, such as the law of cosines from coordinates or sum formulas from geometry.

misconceptions.text: The small-angle approximation sin x ≈ x holds for angles in degrees as well as radians.
A trig substitution works over any domain without needing to check the sign of the resulting root.
Euler's formula is just a notational convenience and gives no new way to derive trig identities.

issues: Advanced beginner misconception "sin⁻¹(x) means 1/sin(x)" is a real misconception but is thin: it is stated as a bare notation claim, with no wrong belief about what the inverse does.
Novice nov-6 "Calculator trig evaluation" is a tool skill rather than a trig concept, and sits oddly at the novice stage.
Novice nov-4 degree measure is a prerequisite-level geometry idea (angles in degrees), and nov-5 special triangles is a geometry topic repeated here.
Prerequisite nov-2 -> nov-3 is fine, but nov-3 reciprocal functions has no dependency link to later stages; nov-3 is never used, though prf-6 needs it.

cmp-8 domain and range of inverses depends on the unit circle and graphs, but adb-6 inverses for angles (cmp-7 uses them) is fine; cmp-7 should depend on cmp-8 for principal values and cmp-8 should not be skipped.

Pythagorean identity (adb-7) is at advanced_beginner but the sum identities at competent depend on it; this is acceptable, but prf-2 proving identities needs the reciprocal functions (nov-3) and prf-6 needs nov-3.
Expert exp-1 summary and exp-2 near-overlap (Euler's formula and de Moivre's both derive multiple-angle results), and misconception 3 spans both concepts.
Expert exp-4 small-angle approximation cites Taylor approximation, a calculus topic; the concept remains legitimate but should be stated without needing calculus.
Proficient prf-6 graphs of other trig functions is a standard topic that fits earlier (competent) stage alongside graphs of sine and cosine, though proficient is tolerable.

concepts.name: Node as server-side runtime
concepts.summary: Recall that Node.js runs JavaScript on the V8 engine outside the browser and exposes system APIs such as files and networking instead of the DOM.

concepts.name: Running scripts from terminal
concepts.summary: Run a file with the node command and use the REPL to try out expressions.

concepts.name: CommonJS require and exports
concepts.summary: Explain how require loads another file or built-in module and how module.exports determines what a file shares.

concepts.name: package.json and dependencies
concepts.summary: Understand that package.json describes a project and its dependencies, and that npm install fetches them into node_modules.

concepts.name: npm scripts
concepts.summary: Explain that the scripts field names shell commands that can be run with npm run, such as start and test.

concepts.name: Built-in core modules
concepts.summary: Name core modules such as fs, path, http and os that ship with Node and need no installation.

concepts.name: The process object basics
concepts.summary: Understand that process gives access to command-line arguments, environment variables and the current working directory.

misconceptions.text: Node.js is a programming language rather than a runtime for JavaScript.
Browser globals like window and document are available in Node.
Core modules like fs must be installed with npm before use.

concepts.name: Reading and writing files with fs
concepts.summary: Read, write and append files using callback, promise and sync variants of fs and choose the non-blocking form in servers.

concepts.name: Portable paths with path
concepts.summary: Build file paths with path.join and path.resolve and __dirname rather than concatenating strings.

concepts.name: ES modules in Node
concepts.summary: Write import and export syntax and enable ES modules through the .mjs extension or the type field, noting differences from CommonJS.

concepts.name: Semantic versioning and lockfiles
concepts.summary: Interpret version ranges such as ^ and ~ and explain why a lockfile pins exact installed versions.

concepts.name: Dev versus runtime dependencies
concepts.summary: Place packages in dependencies or devDependencies according to whether production code needs them.

concepts.name: Basic HTTP server
concepts.summary: Create a server with http.createServer that reads the request method and URL and writes a status, headers and body.

concepts.name: Buffers and binary data
concepts.summary: Create Buffers from strings and convert them back with an encoding such as utf8 or base64.

concepts.name: Event loop ordering basics
concepts.summary: Predict the order of synchronous code, timers, promises and I/O callbacks at a basic level.

misconceptions.text: Relative paths in fs calls resolve from the script's folder rather than the current working directory.
Using readFileSync is fine in a request handler because it is simpler.
require and import can be mixed freely in any file with no restrictions.

concepts.name: Express routing
concepts.summary: Define routes by method and path, read params, query and body, and organise them with Router.

concepts.name: Middleware chain and next
concepts.summary: Analyse how middleware runs in registration order and how calling next, responding or throwing controls the flow.

concepts.name: Express error handling
concepts.summary: Centralise errors with four-argument middleware and forward async failures to it correctly.

concepts.name: REST API design
concepts.summary: Model resources with nouns, correct methods and meaningful status codes, and validate input before use.

concepts.name: EventEmitter pattern
concepts.summary: Register listeners with on and once, emit events with arguments, and handle the special error event.

concepts.name: Streams and piping
concepts.summary: Process large data in chunks with readable and writable streams and connect them with pipe or pipeline.

concepts.name: Environment configuration
concepts.summary: Keep ports, credentials and settings in environment variables rather than in source code.

concepts.name: Building CLI tools
concepts.summary: Build a command-line tool that parses arguments, sets exit codes and is exposed through the bin field with a shebang.

misconceptions.text: Middleware order does not matter in Express.
Throwing inside an async route handler is always caught by Express error middleware.
Reading a whole file into memory is equivalent to streaming it for large files.

concepts.name: Event loop phases
concepts.summary: Analyse how libuv phases, the microtask queue and process.nextTick determine callback ordering and starvation.

concepts.name: Backpressure in streams
concepts.summary: Diagnose memory growth caused by ignoring write return values and apply drain handling or pipeline to fix it.

concepts.name: Worker threads and clustering
concepts.summary: Choose between worker threads, cluster and child processes for CPU-bound work or multi-core scaling.

concepts.name: Authentication and security middleware
concepts.summary: Evaluate session and token authentication, input validation and header and rate-limit protections for an API.

concepts.name: Testing Node services
concepts.summary: Design unit and HTTP integration tests that isolate I/O with mocks or test servers.

concepts.name: Profiling and memory leaks
concepts.summary: Use the inspector, CPU profiles and heap snapshots to locate blocking code and leaks.

concepts.name: Graceful shutdown and process signals
concepts.summary: Judge how to handle signals, close servers and drain connections, and why to restart after uncaught exceptions.

concepts.name: Module resolution and interop
concepts.summary: Analyse how Node resolves modules and how the exports map, dynamic import and CJS-ESM interop affect packages.

misconceptions.text: Node.js is single-threaded in every respect, so it cannot use multiple cores or threads.
Async functions make CPU-heavy work non-blocking.
Catching uncaughtException and carrying on keeps the process safe.

concepts.name: Scalable service architecture
concepts.summary: Design stateless Node services with queues, caching and load balancing that scale and fail gracefully.

concepts.name: Performance tradeoff evaluation
concepts.summary: Evaluate frameworks, serialization and concurrency choices using reproducible benchmarks and latency percentiles.

concepts.name: Native addons and N-API
concepts.summary: Judge when native addons or WebAssembly justify their build and portability costs.

concepts.name: Custom stream implementations
concepts.summary: Create Transform and custom streams that respect backpressure and error propagation for data pipelines.

concepts.name: Observability design
concepts.summary: Build logging, metrics and distributed tracing, including AsyncLocalStorage context, into services.

concepts.name: Package publishing and supply chain
concepts.summary: Design and publish reusable packages with sound versioning, exports and dependency vetting.

concepts.name: V8 and runtime internals
concepts.summary: Evaluate how V8 compilation, hidden classes and garbage collection affect code performance and memory.

misconceptions.text: Rewriting hot paths in native code always yields net speedups.
Adding more Node processes always improves throughput linearly.
Micro-benchmarks of isolated functions reliably predict production performance.

concepts.name: Leadership versus management
concepts.summary: Explain how leadership (setting direction, influencing people) differs from and overlaps with management (planning, organising, controlling work).

concepts.name: Formal and informal leadership
concepts.summary: Distinguish leadership that comes from a position from leadership that comes from influence and recognise that both exist in teams.

concepts.name: Core leadership styles
concepts.summary: Name and describe the classic styles such as autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire.

concepts.name: Transformational, servant and situational leadership
concepts.summary: Recall the central idea of each of the three named theories in one sentence.

concepts.name: Purpose of a vision
concepts.summary: Explain that a vision describes a desired future that gives a team direction and meaning.

concepts.name: Trust as foundation
concepts.summary: Explain why followers need to trust a leader's competence, intentions and consistency before they willingly follow.

concepts.name: Leading by example
concepts.summary: Understand that a leader's observable behaviour sets the standard a team actually follows.

misconceptions.text: Leaders are born with charisma and leadership cannot be learned.
Leadership is the same thing as holding a senior job title.
A good leader is simply the one who gives the best orders.

concepts.name: Transformational leadership components
concepts.summary: Describe idealised influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration and recognise each in behaviour.

concepts.name: Servant leadership principles
concepts.summary: Explain how putting followers' growth and needs first, through listening, empathy and stewardship, shapes a leader's actions.

concepts.name: Situational leadership matching
concepts.summary: Choose directing, coaching, supporting or delegating according to a person's competence and commitment on a given task.

concepts.name: Writing a clear vision
concepts.summary: Draft a concise, concrete and inspiring vision for a small team that links to its purpose and values.

concepts.name: Basic influence methods
concepts.summary: Apply simple influence tactics such as rational persuasion, consultation and inspirational appeals to gain support without relying on authority.

concepts.name: Trust-building behaviours
concepts.summary: Use consistent behaviours such as keeping promises, being open and admitting mistakes to build trust with a team.

concepts.name: Power bases
concepts.summary: Identify legitimate, reward, coercive, expert and referent power and explain how each affects followers.

misconceptions.text: Servant leadership means the leader is weak and does whatever followers ask.
Situational leadership means a leader should change their personality to suit each person.
A vision statement is just a slogan, and writing it is the whole job of creating a vision.

concepts.name: Diagnosing readiness for style choice
concepts.summary: Analyse a team member's skill and motivation per task and justify the leadership style adjustment that results.

concepts.name: Communicating vision across audiences
concepts.summary: Adapt and repeat a vision through stories, symbols and concrete goals so that different audiences understand why it matters to them.

concepts.name: Contingency and path-goal thinking
concepts.summary: Analyse how task structure, follower traits and context determine which leader behaviour is effective.

concepts.name: Leader-member exchange
concepts.summary: Analyse how differing relationship quality with individual followers creates in-groups and out-groups and affects fairness and performance.

concepts.name: Motivating through autonomy and purpose
concepts.summary: Design work, goals and recognition that build autonomy, mastery and purpose rather than relying only on rewards.

concepts.name: Trust repair after breaches
concepts.summary: Analyse the cause of a trust breach (competence versus integrity) and select actions to repair it.

concepts.name: Coaching conversations
concepts.summary: Run structured conversations that use questions and feedback to build another person's capability rather than giving answers.

misconceptions.text: A leader should treat everyone identically to be fair.
Announcing the vision once, clearly, is enough to get people to adopt it.
Trust broken by a leader is restored by a sincere apology alone.

concepts.name: Integrating leadership theories critically
concepts.summary: Evaluate the evidence and limits of transformational, servant and situational models and combine them to suit a context.

concepts.name: Leading change
concepts.summary: Judge and sequence actions to create urgency, build a coalition, anchor change and handle resistance.

concepts.name: Shaping organisational culture
concepts.summary: Analyse how artefacts, espoused values and underlying assumptions form a culture and how leader behaviour, rewards and rituals reinforce it.

concepts.name: Leader development pipelines
concepts.summary: Evaluate stretch assignments, mentoring and feedback systems for their ability to grow leaders at multiple levels.

concepts.name: Psychological safety and dissent
concepts.summary: Analyse how leader behaviour creates or erodes safety for candour, and assess its effect on learning and decisions.

concepts.name: Influence without authority
concepts.summary: Evaluate stakeholder interests and choose coalition and negotiation strategies to lead across teams where there is no formal power.

concepts.name: Ethical and values-based leadership
concepts.summary: Judge leadership decisions against ethical principles and the leader's stated values, including the risk of manipulative charisma.

misconceptions.text: A strong inspirational vision overcomes the need to manage resistance to change.
Culture is set by posters and value statements rather than by what leaders reward and tolerate.
Psychological safety means lowering standards and avoiding conflict.

concepts.name: Designing leadership systems
concepts.summary: Create structures, roles and decision rights that spread leadership across the organisation and reduce dependence on individuals.

concepts.name: Culture transformation strategy
concepts.summary: Design a multi-year plan that aligns incentives, rituals, hiring and leader behaviour to shift a culture and measure that it holds.

concepts.name: Evaluating leadership effectiveness
concepts.summary: Judge the validity of measures such as 360 feedback, engagement data and outcomes when assessing a leader or program.

concepts.name: Leading through crisis and ambiguity
concepts.summary: Evaluate decisions and communications under pressure, balancing speed, transparency and the maintenance of trust.

concepts.name: Building a leadership philosophy
concepts.summary: Synthesise theory, experience and values into a coherent, testable personal approach to leading that evolves with feedback.

concepts.name: Leadership across cultures and contexts
concepts.summary: Evaluate how national, industry and organisational cultures change which leadership behaviours are effective and adapt accordingly.

concepts.name: Leadership succession and legacy
concepts.summary: Create succession approaches that preserve purpose and culture while letting new leaders reshape direction.

misconceptions.text: A culture change succeeds once top leaders announce new values and a few role models adopt them.
Leadership effectiveness can be read directly from financial results or from popularity scores.
Best-practice leadership behaviours from one culture transfer unchanged to any other.

concepts.name: Biomolecule classes and monomers
concepts.summary: Recall the four major classes (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids) and their building blocks.

concepts.name: Amino acid structure
concepts.summary: Describe the common alpha-carbon, amino group, carboxyl group and variable side chain of amino acids.

concepts.name: Peptide bond and primary structure
concepts.summary: Explain how amino acids link by condensation into a polypeptide whose sequence is its primary structure.

concepts.name: Enzymes as biological catalysts
concepts.summary: Explain that enzymes speed up reactions by lowering activation energy at an active site without being consumed.

concepts.name: ATP as energy currency
concepts.summary: Explain that ATP hydrolysis releases usable energy that is coupled to cellular work.

concepts.name: Monosaccharides and fatty acids
concepts.summary: Recognise glucose as a key sugar and fatty acids as long hydrocarbon chains with a carboxyl group.

concepts.name: Metabolism overview: catabolism and anabolism
concepts.summary: Distinguish pathways that break down fuels to release energy from those that build molecules using energy.

misconceptions.text: Enzymes are used up in the reactions they catalyse.
ATP stores energy in a stable form that the cell keeps in large reserves.
Energy is stored in the phosphate bond itself and released simply by breaking it.

concepts.name: Amino acid side chain properties
concepts.summary: Classify side chains as nonpolar, polar, acidic or basic and predict their charge and behaviour at physiological pH.

concepts.name: Levels of protein structure
concepts.summary: Describe alpha helices, beta sheets, tertiary folding and quaternary assembly and the bonds stabilising each.

concepts.name: Michaelis-Menten parameters
concepts.summary: Interpret Vmax and Km on a saturation curve and read their values from rate data.

concepts.name: Glycolysis stages and net yield
concepts.summary: Trace glucose to pyruvate through the investment and payoff phases and compute net ATP and NADH.

concepts.name: Citric acid cycle inputs and outputs
concepts.summary: Follow acetyl-CoA through the cycle and account for CO2, NADH, FADH2 and GTP/ATP produced per turn.

concepts.name: Electron transport and ATP synthase
concepts.summary: Explain how NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to drive a proton gradient that powers ATP synthase.

concepts.name: Redox coenzymes NAD and FAD
concepts.summary: Apply the oxidised and reduced forms of NAD+/NADH and FAD/FADH2 when following metabolic reactions.

concepts.name: Glycosidic bonds and nucleotide components
concepts.summary: Describe glycosidic linkages in disaccharides and polysaccharides and the base-sugar-phosphate makeup of nucleotides.

misconceptions.text: Km is the maximum rate of an enzyme reaction.
Glycolysis requires oxygen.
The citric acid cycle produces most ATP directly by substrate-level phosphorylation.

concepts.name: Lineweaver-Burk analysis
concepts.summary: Linearise kinetic data to determine Km and Vmax and compare enzyme behaviour.

concepts.name: Reversible inhibition types
concepts.summary: Distinguish competitive, noncompetitive and uncompetitive inhibition by their effects on apparent Km and Vmax.

concepts.name: Allosteric regulation and cooperativity
concepts.summary: Analyse how effectors and subunit cooperativity produce sigmoidal curves and shift enzyme activity.

concepts.name: Free energy of metabolic reactions
concepts.summary: Use standard versus actual free energy change to decide reaction direction and how coupling drives unfavourable steps.

concepts.name: Beta-oxidation of fatty acids
concepts.summary: Follow the repeated cycle of oxidation, hydration, oxidation and thiolysis and calculate acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH2 from a given chain.

concepts.name: Gluconeogenesis and bypass reactions
concepts.summary: Explain how gluconeogenesis circumvents the three irreversible glycolytic steps with distinct enzymes.

concepts.name: Regulation of glycolysis
concepts.summary: Analyse control of hexokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 and pyruvate kinase by energy charge and metabolites.

concepts.name: Chemiosmotic coupling and P/O ratios
concepts.summary: Relate proton gradient magnitude to ATP synthesis and estimate ATP yield from glucose oxidation.

misconceptions.text: A competitive inhibitor lowers Vmax.
A reaction with a negative standard free energy always proceeds in the cell.
Gluconeogenesis is simply glycolysis run in reverse with the same enzymes.

concepts.name: Mechanisms of enzymatic catalysis
concepts.summary: Analyse how acid-base, covalent, metal-ion and proximity effects and transition-state binding produce rate enhancement.

concepts.name: Multisubstrate and irreversible inhibition
concepts.summary: Distinguish sequential from ping-pong kinetics and interpret mechanism-based inactivation from kinetic patterns.

concepts.name: Protein folding energetics
concepts.summary: Evaluate how hydrophobic effect, entropy and chaperones shape folding and how misfolding leads to disease.

concepts.name: Integration of fuel metabolism
concepts.summary: Evaluate how insulin, glucagon and tissue-specific pathways coordinate fuel use across fed and fasting states.

concepts.name: Metabolic control analysis
concepts.summary: Judge which steps control pathway flux using ideas such as near-equilibrium versus irreversible reactions and flux control.

concepts.name: Shuttles and mitochondrial transport
concepts.summary: Analyse how reducing equivalents and fatty acyl groups cross the inner mitochondrial membrane and affect ATP yield.

concepts.name: Respiratory control and uncoupling
concepts.summary: Evaluate how ADP availability, inhibitors and uncouplers alter oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis.

concepts.name: Ketone bodies and amino acid catabolism
concepts.summary: Analyse how fatty acid and amino acid carbon and nitrogen are routed to ketones, glucose or urea during fasting.

misconceptions.text: Enzymes work by changing the equilibrium of a reaction.
The rate-limiting enzyme is always the slowest step and alone determines pathway flux.
Fatty acids can be converted to glucose in animals via acetyl-CoA.

concepts.name: Critique of kinetic models
concepts.summary: Evaluate when Michaelis-Menten assumptions fail, such as tight-binding inhibitors, enzyme concentration comparable to substrate, or product inhibition, and choose a suitable model.

concepts.name: Systems-level flux analysis
concepts.summary: Assess flux distributions with stoichiometric models and isotope labelling and judge their limitations.

concepts.name: Design of enzyme inhibitors
concepts.summary: Design inhibitors using mechanism, kinetics and transition-state analogy and justify selectivity and potency measures.

concepts.name: Enzyme and pathway engineering
concepts.summary: Devise strategies to modify enzymes or reconstruct pathways to alter specificity, yield or regulation.

concepts.name: Metabolic reprogramming in disease
concepts.summary: Evaluate how altered glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation and lipid metabolism drive cancer, diabetes and inborn errors.

concepts.name: Thermodynamic and evolutionary constraints
concepts.summary: Judge why pathways have their observed structure, balancing yield, rate, thermodynamic feasibility and regulation.

concepts.name: Experimental design in bioenergetics
concepts.summary: Create experiments with appropriate assays, controls and inhibitors to test hypotheses about enzyme mechanism or mitochondrial function.

misconceptions.text: Michaelis-Menten kinetics apply universally to all enzymes under any conditions.
Inhibiting the rate-limiting enzyme of a pathway will always produce a proportionate drop in flux.
Cancer cells use aerobic glycolysis because their mitochondria are nonfunctional.

issues: Flag confirmed: the advanced_beginner misconception 'Glycolysis requires oxygen' is a real, common error but is the only one tied to a single concept; the stage's misconceptions are otherwise fine, so the thin flag is mostly harmless.
nov-4 depends on nov-3 (peptide bond) in a way that is weak; enzymes as catalysts do not require knowing peptide bonds in detail, and the novice stage has no link from nov-1 to nov-2.
Missing dependency: nov-6 (monosaccharides) is not linked into glycolysis; adb-4 has no prerequisite from nov-6 or nov-7.
adb-4 and adb-5 depend on adb-7 only partly: adb-5 (citric acid cycle) also needs adb-7 for NADH/FADH2, which is missing.
adb-8 (glycosidic bonds and nucleotide components) merges two unrelated ideas and is not linked to anything; it should be split or narrowed.

adb-1 to adb-3 prerequisite chain: Levels of protein structure does not depend on Michaelis-Menten in the way adb-2 -> adb-3 implies; protein structure is not needed for Km/Vmax interpretation, and adb-3 lacks a link from nov-4.
adb-6 is Bloom C2 and fits, but adb-7 'Redox coenzymes' at C3 duplicates prerequisites too late: NAD/FAD are needed before glycolysis, which is already encoded.
cmp-5 (beta-oxidation) depends on cmp-4 and adb-7 but not on nov-6/fatty acid activation; acceptable. cmp-1 (Lineweaver-Burk) at C3 is fine.
cmp-7 -> cmp-6 is reasonable, but cmp-6 also needs cmp-4 for irreversibility; edge from cmp-4 to cmp-6 is missing.

Misconception 'Fatty acids can be converted to glucose via acetyl-CoA' is correct but is stated against prf-4 and prf-8 where the underlying reaction (pyruvate dehydrogenase irreversibility) is covered by cmp-6; fine.
prf-8 'Ketone bodies and amino acid catabolism' combines two ideas and leans on the urea cycle; acceptable but broad. prf-5 misconception is fine.
exp-3 misconception link to exp-2 is odd: the 'rate-limiting enzyme inhibition' misconception belongs to exp-2 and prf-5 rather than exp-3 (drug design).
exp-1 and exp-7 overlap in 'assumption critique' vs 'assay design' but are distinct enough.

concepts.name: Reaction rate meaning
concepts.summary: State that reaction rate is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

concepts.name: Collision theory
concepts.summary: Explain that reactions occur when particles collide with sufficient energy and proper orientation.

concepts.name: Factors affecting rate
concepts.summary: Describe how concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts change reaction rate and why.

concepts.name: Activation energy
concepts.summary: Understand activation energy as the minimum energy needed for a collision to lead to reaction.

concepts.name: Reversible reactions
concepts.summary: Recognise that some reactions proceed in both directions and are written with a double arrow.

concepts.name: Dynamic equilibrium
concepts.summary: Explain that at equilibrium forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant while reactions continue.

concepts.name: Le Chatelier's principle
concepts.summary: State qualitatively that a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by partly counteracting it.

misconceptions.text: At equilibrium the reaction has stopped.
At equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.
A catalyst makes a reaction go faster because it adds energy to the molecules.

concepts.name: Average and instantaneous rate
concepts.summary: Calculate average rates from data and estimate instantaneous rates from the slope of a concentration-time curve.

concepts.name: Rate law and rate constant
concepts.summary: Write a rate law of the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n and identify the roles of k and the orders.

concepts.name: Reaction order from data
concepts.summary: Determine orders and k from initial-rate experiments.

concepts.name: Equilibrium constant expression
concepts.summary: Write Kc and Kp expressions from balanced equations, omitting pure solids and liquids.

concepts.name: Magnitude of K
concepts.summary: Interpret large and small K values as favouring products or reactants at equilibrium.

concepts.name: Reaction quotient comparison
concepts.summary: Compute Q and compare it with K to predict the direction a reaction proceeds.

concepts.name: Applying Le Chatelier shifts
concepts.summary: Predict shifts from changes in concentration, pressure, volume and temperature.

misconceptions.text: Reaction orders can be read directly from the coefficients of the balanced equation.
A large K means the reaction is fast.
Adding a catalyst or a pure solid shifts the equilibrium position.

concepts.name: Integrated rate laws
concepts.summary: Use zero-, first- and second-order integrated laws to find concentrations and times.

concepts.name: Half-life analysis
concepts.summary: Relate half-life to k and order, and recognise when it is concentration independent.

concepts.name: Graphical order determination
concepts.summary: Analyse plots of [A], ln[A] and 1/[A] against time to identify order and k.

concepts.name: Arrhenius equation
concepts.summary: Use the Arrhenius equation and its linear form to relate k, temperature and activation energy.

concepts.name: ICE table calculations
concepts.summary: Set up initial, change and equilibrium quantities to solve for unknown equilibrium concentrations.

concepts.name: Approximation validity
concepts.summary: Judge when x can be neglected and when a quadratic must be solved.

concepts.name: K manipulation and Kp-Kc
concepts.summary: Adjust K for reversed, scaled or summed reactions and convert between Kc and Kp using Δn.

concepts.name: Thermodynamic link to K
concepts.summary: Relate K to ΔG° and explain how temperature changes K according to ΔH°.

misconceptions.text: Half-life is constant for every reaction regardless of order.
Changing temperature shifts equilibrium but leaves K unchanged.
The small-x approximation is always valid when K is small, regardless of initial concentration.

concepts.name: Elementary steps and molecularity
concepts.summary: Distinguish elementary steps from overall reactions and derive rate laws for elementary steps from molecularity.

concepts.name: Rate-determining step analysis
concepts.summary: Analyse a mechanism to derive a rate law consistent with its slowest step.

concepts.name: Steady-state and pre-equilibrium
concepts.summary: Apply pre-equilibrium and steady-state approximations to eliminate intermediates from rate laws.

concepts.name: Evaluating proposed mechanisms
concepts.summary: Judge whether a mechanism fits stoichiometry and observed rate law, recognising that data cannot prove it.

concepts.name: Catalysis and energy profiles
concepts.summary: Interpret reaction profiles to show catalysts lower barriers of both directions without changing K.

concepts.name: Simultaneous equilibria
concepts.summary: Analyse systems with multiple coupled equilibria, such as solubility with complexation or acid-base buffers.

concepts.name: Kinetic versus thermodynamic control
concepts.summary: Evaluate how rates and stabilities determine product distributions under different conditions.

misconceptions.text: The rate law of a multistep reaction follows from its overall stoichiometry.
A rate law matching experiment proves the proposed mechanism is correct.
A catalyst increases the equilibrium yield of products.

concepts.name: Design of kinetic experiments
concepts.summary: Design experiments such as isolation and flooding to separate orders and minimise confounding effects.

concepts.name: Error analysis in kinetic fits
concepts.summary: Evaluate uncertainty in k and Ea from linear and nonlinear fits and judge model adequacy.

concepts.name: Transition state theory
concepts.summary: Evaluate rate behaviour using activation enthalpy and entropy and compare with Arrhenius and collision models.

concepts.name: Complex kinetic schemes
concepts.summary: Build and solve models of consecutive, parallel and reversible-approach reactions, including numerical solution.

concepts.name: Enzyme and surface catalysis models
concepts.summary: Evaluate saturation kinetics models and their limiting rate behaviours.

concepts.name: Relaxation and perturbation methods
concepts.summary: Judge how perturbation techniques measure fast kinetics and extract rate constants from relaxation to equilibrium.

concepts.name: Detailed balance and microscopic reversibility
concepts.summary: Use detailed balance to link forward and reverse rate constants to K and test mechanisms for consistency.

concepts.name: Nonideal and open systems
concepts.summary: Design treatments using activities, fugacities and steady flow where ideal concentration-based K and batch assumptions fail.

misconceptions.text: Thermodynamic K alone tells you how quickly a system approaches equilibrium.
Activation energy from an Arrhenius plot is a fixed property valid across any temperature range and mechanism change.
Equilibrium constants defined with concentrations remain exact at high ionic strength or pressure.

concepts.name: Defining mindfulness
concepts.summary: Can state that mindfulness is paying attention to present experience on purpose and without judgment.

concepts.name: Posture and setup
concepts.summary: Can explain how an alert, comfortable posture and quiet setting support practice.

concepts.name: Breath as anchor
concepts.summary: Understands why the breath serves as a neutral, always-available object for attention.

concepts.name: Noticing wandering mind
concepts.summary: Understands that the mind wandering is normal and that noticing it is the core moment of practice.

concepts.name: Gentle return of attention
concepts.summary: Can describe returning attention kindly without self-criticism each time it drifts.

concepts.name: Short daily sessions
concepts.summary: Can recall that short, regular sessions of a few minutes are enough to begin.

misconceptions.text: Meditation means emptying the mind of all thoughts.
If my mind wanders, I am failing at meditation.
You must sit cross-legged on the floor to meditate properly.

concepts.name: Counting and labeling breaths
concepts.summary: Can apply counting or silent labeling to stabilise attention during a sitting.

concepts.name: Body scan sequence
concepts.summary: Can guide attention systematically through body regions, noticing sensations without trying to change them.

concepts.name: Distinguishing sensation from story
concepts.summary: Can separate raw physical sensations from thoughts and interpretations about them.

concepts.name: Loving-kindness phrases
concepts.summary: Can practise silently repeating kind phrases toward self and then others.

concepts.name: Handling sleepiness and restlessness
concepts.summary: Can apply simple adjustments such as posture, eyes open or shorter sits when drowsy or restless.

concepts.name: Informal mindfulness
concepts.summary: Can bring mindful attention to routine activities like eating or walking.

misconceptions.text: The body scan is a relaxation technique meant to make you feel calm every time.
Loving-kindness only works if you genuinely feel warmth during the phrases.
Mindfulness only happens during formal sitting sessions.

concepts.name: Open monitoring practice
concepts.summary: Can sustain receptive awareness of whatever arises without fixating on a single object.

concepts.name: Focused versus open attention
concepts.summary: Can compare the two meditation styles and choose one to fit a goal or state of mind.

concepts.name: Building a daily routine
concepts.summary: Can design a realistic routine using fixed time, place and cues to sustain practice.

concepts.name: Working with difficult emotions
concepts.summary: Can analyse an arising emotion and respond with recognising, allowing and investigating rather than suppressing or reacting.

concepts.name: Stress response and pausing
concepts.summary: Can analyse how stress reactions unfold and use a brief mindful pause to interrupt them.

concepts.name: Equanimity and non-striving
concepts.summary: Can practise meeting pleasant, unpleasant and neutral experience with even-minded acceptance.

concepts.name: Practice journaling and review
concepts.summary: Can examine practice notes to identify patterns, obstacles and progress.

misconceptions.text: Mindfulness is meant to eliminate stress and unpleasant emotions.
Open monitoring is just daydreaming with no structure.
Acceptance means passively putting up with everything and not acting.

concepts.name: Tailoring practice to attention goals
concepts.summary: Can evaluate which practices best train sustained focus, meta-awareness or cognitive flexibility and adapt a program accordingly.

concepts.name: Meta-awareness and decentering
concepts.summary: Can analyse thoughts as mental events rather than facts and shift into an observing stance.

concepts.name: Practice during daily demands
concepts.summary: Can judge where and how to apply mindful techniques to meetings, workload and digital distraction.

concepts.name: Compassion and self-compassion
concepts.summary: Can analyse self-criticism patterns and apply compassion practices to relate to them differently.

concepts.name: Recognising meditation difficulties
concepts.summary: Can evaluate when practice is causing distress such as dissociation or rumination and modify or seek support.

concepts.name: Appraising evidence for mindfulness
concepts.summary: Can critically appraise claims about mindfulness benefits, noting effect sizes, controls and limits of studies.

misconceptions.text: Meditation is always safe and beneficial for everyone, with no possible downsides.
Self-compassion is just self-indulgence that lowers motivation.
Research has proven mindfulness works equally well as a treatment for all conditions.

concepts.name: Designing personalised practice programs
concepts.summary: Can create a tailored, progressive practice plan integrating focus, open monitoring, body-based and compassion practices for an individual's needs.

concepts.name: Guiding others in meditation
concepts.summary: Can create and deliver clear guided instructions with appropriate pacing, language and inquiry.

concepts.name: Contemplative traditions and secular adaptation
concepts.summary: Can evaluate how secular programs differ from and draw on traditional contemplative frameworks.

concepts.name: Trauma-sensitive adaptation
concepts.summary: Can design practice and instruction choices that offer safety, choice and alternatives to internal focus for vulnerable participants.

concepts.name: Evaluating practice outcomes
concepts.summary: Can assess the effects of practice using sound criteria, self-report limits and behavioural indicators.

concepts.name: Integrating insight into conduct
concepts.summary: Can judge how awareness, ethics and compassion translate into skilful action and avoid spiritual bypassing.

misconceptions.text: A single standard technique suits every person and context.
Secular mindfulness programs are identical to traditional Buddhist practice.
Feeling calm and detached is proof that practice is working and insight has been gained.

concepts.name: Firm's financial objective
concepts.summary: Explain that corporate finance decisions aim to maximise firm value for owners, and distinguish this from maximising accounting profit.

concepts.name: Three core financial decisions
concepts.summary: Recall the investment, financing and payout decisions and what each asks a manager to decide.

concepts.name: Time value of money
concepts.summary: Explain why a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later because of earning capacity and risk.

concepts.name: Present and future value
concepts.summary: Describe how compounding moves a sum forward and discounting brings it back to today at a given rate.

concepts.name: Risk and required return
concepts.summary: Explain that riskier cash flows demand higher expected returns from investors.

concepts.name: Debt versus equity
concepts.summary: Recall that debt is a contractual borrowing with interest while equity is ownership with residual claims.

concepts.name: Cash flow versus profit
concepts.summary: Explain why finance values cash flows rather than accounting earnings.

misconceptions.text: A company's goal is to maximise its accounting profit each year.
Money's value over time changes only because of inflation.
Debt is always cheaper and therefore always better than equity.

concepts.name: Annuities and perpetuities
concepts.summary: Compute present and future values of level and growing payment streams using standard formulas.

concepts.name: Net present value calculation
concepts.summary: Discount a project's forecast cash flows at the required return and accept it when the NPV is positive.

concepts.name: Internal rate of return
concepts.summary: Find the discount rate that sets NPV to zero and compare it to the required return.

concepts.name: Payback and simple rules
concepts.summary: Calculate payback periods and explain why they ignore value beyond the cutoff or the time value.

concepts.name: Incremental project cash flows
concepts.summary: Build project cash flows from only incremental items, including working capital, capex and after-tax operating flows, and ignore sunk costs.

concepts.name: Cost of debt and equity
concepts.summary: Compute the after-tax cost of debt and a basic cost of equity from observed yields or dividends.

concepts.name: Working capital cycle
concepts.summary: Calculate days inventory, receivables and payables and combine them into the cash conversion cycle.

misconceptions.text: Sunk costs and allocated overhead should be included in a project's cash flows.
A project with a short payback period is always a good investment.
IRR is the return the firm will actually earn on reinvested cash flows.

concepts.name: NPV versus IRR conflicts
concepts.summary: Diagnose when IRR and NPV disagree because of scale, timing or non-conventional cash flows and resolve it in favour of NPV.

concepts.name: Capital rationing and comparison
concepts.summary: Rank projects under a budget constraint or unequal lives using profitability index and equivalent annual annuity.

concepts.name: CAPM and beta
concepts.summary: Estimate cost of equity from the risk-free rate, equity beta and market risk premium and explain systematic risk.

concepts.name: Weighted average cost of capital
concepts.summary: Compute WACC using market-value weights and after-tax debt cost, and use it as the discount rate for average-risk projects.

concepts.name: Sensitivity and scenario analysis
concepts.summary: Test how NPV changes with key assumptions to identify the drivers of project risk.

concepts.name: Tax shield and leverage
concepts.summary: Analyse why capital structure is irrelevant without frictions and how interest tax shields change value.

concepts.name: Working capital financing policy
concepts.summary: Compare aggressive and conservative funding of current assets and the trade-off of cost, liquidity and risk.

concepts.name: Dividend and repurchase choices
concepts.summary: Describe how dividends and buybacks distribute cash and evaluate their effect on shareholders' wealth.

misconceptions.text: The project with the highest IRR is always the one that adds the most value.
A firm's WACC is the correct discount rate for every project it undertakes.
Equity is free or cheaper than debt because dividends are optional.

concepts.name: Project-specific discount rates
concepts.summary: Unlever and relever comparable-firm betas to set discount rates that match each project's business risk.

concepts.name: Trade-off and pecking order
concepts.summary: Evaluate a firm's leverage using tax benefits, distress costs, agency costs and information asymmetry.

concepts.name: Adjusted present value
concepts.summary: Value a project by adding financing side effects to its all-equity NPV when capital structure changes.

concepts.name: Real options in investment
concepts.summary: Judge how options to delay, expand or abandon add value that static NPV misses.

concepts.name: Simulation and risk-adjusted valuation
concepts.summary: Assess project risk using probabilistic simulation and decide how to treat it in rates versus cash flows.

concepts.name: Agency problems in finance
concepts.summary: Analyse how conflicts among managers, shareholders and creditors distort investment and financing choices.

concepts.name: Capital issuance and signalling
concepts.summary: Interpret issuance costs and market reactions to debt, equity and payout announcements.

concepts.name: Optimal cash management
concepts.summary: Evaluate credit terms, inventory and cash holdings by weighing carrying costs against shortage costs.

misconceptions.text: Using the firm's WACC is fine even when a project's risk differs sharply from the firm's.
Static NPV already captures the value of managerial flexibility.
Raising leverage always lowers WACC and so always raises firm value.

concepts.name: Designing capital allocation frameworks
concepts.summary: Create a firm-wide process for generating, screening, approving and auditing investments that limits bias and gaming.

concepts.name: Critiquing valuation assumptions
aliases: terminal value and discount rate scrutiny
concepts.summary: Evaluate forecasts, terminal values and discount rates in a valuation to expose where most value is concentrated.

concepts.name: Optimal capital structure design
concepts.summary: Construct a financing policy that sets target leverage, debt maturity and covenants for a specific firm's risks and growth options.

concepts.name: Financial flexibility and risk management
concepts.summary: Judge when hedging and liquidity reserves protect investment capacity and when they destroy value.

concepts.name: Corporate restructuring and M&A valuation
concepts.summary: Appraise acquisitions, spin-offs and leveraged buyouts by separating synergies, control premia and financing effects.

concepts.name: Payout policy under uncertainty
concepts.summary: Design payout policy that balances investment needs, signalling, taxes and investor clienteles.

concepts.name: International corporate finance
concepts.summary: Evaluate foreign projects by handling exchange rates, country risk and differing tax regimes consistently in cash flows and discount rates.

misconceptions.text: A sophisticated valuation model gives a precise answer, so the judgement behind inputs matters little.
Hedging always creates value for shareholders because it reduces volatility.
Acquisitions create value whenever the target is profitable or earnings per share rises.

concepts.name: Nature of conflict
concepts.summary: Recognise conflict as a perceived incompatibility of needs, goals or values between people, and that it is normal and can be constructive or destructive.

concepts.name: Common sources of conflict
concepts.summary: Explain how scarce resources, unclear roles, differing values, poor communication and personality clashes commonly spark disputes.

concepts.name: Conflict escalation signs
concepts.summary: Spot early signs such as raised voices, withdrawal, sarcasm and blaming that show a disagreement is intensifying.

concepts.name: Five conflict styles
concepts.summary: Name the avoiding, accommodating, competing, compromising and collaborating styles and describe each in a sentence.

concepts.name: Listening before responding
concepts.summary: Understand why letting the other person finish and paying attention to them, without planning a rebuttal, lowers tension.

concepts.name: Calm-down pause
concepts.summary: Explain why stepping away briefly when emotions run high helps a discussion resume productively.

misconceptions.text: Conflict is always bad and a sign that a relationship or team is failing.
Listening just means staying quiet until it is your turn to talk.
Avoiding a disagreement makes it go away on its own.

concepts.name: Active listening techniques
concepts.summary: Apply paraphrasing, open questions, summarising and nonverbal attentiveness to show and check understanding in a real disagreement.

concepts.name: I-statements
concepts.summary: Construct statements describing behaviour, your feeling and its impact without accusing, instead of using you-statements.

concepts.name: Positions versus interests
concepts.summary: Distinguish what someone says they want (position) from the underlying needs and concerns (interests) that drive it.

concepts.name: Matching styles to situations
concepts.summary: Pick a conflict style suited to simple situations, such as accommodating on trivial issues or competing in an emergency.

concepts.name: De-escalation phrases
concepts.summary: Use calm tone, acknowledgement of feelings and lowered pace to reduce intensity when someone is angry.

concepts.name: Asking clarifying questions
concepts.summary: Ask neutral, open questions to uncover facts and needs rather than assuming the other's motives.

misconceptions.text: An I-statement is just a you-accusation with 'I feel' placed in front of it.
Paraphrasing what someone said means you agree with them.
The other person's stated demand is what they truly need.

concepts.name: Root cause analysis of disputes
concepts.summary: Separate triggers from deeper causes such as structural, relational, data or value issues by examining a conflict's history and context.

concepts.name: Interest mapping
concepts.summary: Analyse each party's interests to find common, compatible and conflicting ones as the basis for solutions.

concepts.name: Win-win option generation
concepts.summary: Generate multiple options that meet both parties' interests, using brainstorming before judging proposals.

concepts.name: Structured difficult conversation
concepts.summary: Prepare and run a conversation by setting purpose, describing facts, sharing impact, inviting the other view and agreeing next steps.

concepts.name: Workplace dispute dynamics
concepts.summary: Analyse how hierarchy, role ambiguity, policy and escalation channels such as HR shape disputes at work.

concepts.name: Family conflict patterns
concepts.summary: Identify recurring cycles such as pursue-withdraw, triangulation and old grievances in family disputes.

concepts.name: Objective criteria for fairness
concepts.summary: Use external standards such as market rates, precedent or policy to judge proposals instead of contests of will.

misconceptions.text: Compromise is the best outcome because both sides give something up equally.
The event that set off the argument is its root cause.
Every interest conflict is zero-sum, so one side must lose for the other to win.

concepts.name: Mediation process stages
concepts.summary: Analyse the phases of mediation, from opening and storytelling through issue framing, option generation and agreement, and what each accomplishes.

concepts.name: Mediator neutrality and impartiality
concepts.summary: Judge whether a mediator's conduct preserves impartiality, confidentiality and party self-determination.

concepts.name: Choosing intervention level
aliases: when to bring in a third party
concepts.summary: Evaluate when to self-resolve, facilitate, mediate, arbitrate or escalate, given the stakes, power balance and relationship.

concepts.name: Power imbalance management
concepts.summary: Assess how unequal power distorts negotiation and decide on safeguards or whether mediation is appropriate.

concepts.name: Reframing and caucusing
concepts.summary: Analyse how reframing accusations into shared problems and separate private meetings unlock stalled talks.

concepts.name: Evaluating settlement durability
concepts.summary: Assess whether an agreement is specific, realistic, mutually owned and equipped with follow-up so it will hold.

misconceptions.text: A mediator decides who is right and imposes the outcome.
A signed agreement means the conflict is resolved.
Mediation works equally well in every dispute regardless of power or safety concerns.

concepts.name: Designing dispute resolution systems
concepts.summary: Create a tiered system of negotiation, mediation and arbitration channels that fits an organisation's culture and prevents disputes from escalating.

concepts.name: Cultural variation in conflict
concepts.summary: Evaluate how culture shapes norms about directness, face, authority and emotion, and adapt approach accordingly.

concepts.name: Entrenched conflict transformation
concepts.summary: Devise strategies for long-running disputes involving identity, history and trust damage, going beyond settlement to relational change.

concepts.name: Multi-party dispute facilitation
concepts.summary: Design processes for disputes with many stakeholders, managing coalitions, representation and sequencing of issues.

concepts.name: Critiquing resolution approaches
concepts.summary: Weigh interest-based, transformative, narrative and rights-based approaches against their assumptions and fit for a dispute.

concepts.name: Own bias and role reflection
concepts.summary: Evaluate your own triggers, biases and habitual style to improve practice and coach others.

misconceptions.text: Interest-based negotiation works the same way in every culture.
Every long-running conflict can be resolved by finding the right win-win deal.
An experienced practitioner is free of bias in the disputes they handle.

concepts.name: Continuous versus discrete-time signals
concepts.summary: Distinguish signals defined for all real time x(t) from sequences x[n] defined only at integer indices, and give examples of each.

concepts.name: Basic signal operations
concepts.summary: Explain how shifting, reversing and scaling the time axis and scaling amplitude change the graph of a signal.

concepts.name: Standard test signals
concepts.summary: Recognise and sketch the unit step, ramp, rectangular pulse, real and complex exponentials and sinusoids.

concepts.name: Unit impulse function
concepts.summary: Explain the continuous delta and discrete unit sample and the sifting property that lets a signal be built from shifted impulses.

concepts.name: Even, odd and periodic signals
concepts.summary: Classify a signal as even, odd or periodic and identify its period or fundamental frequency.

concepts.name: System as input-output mapping
concepts.summary: Describe a system as a rule that maps an input signal to an output signal, with examples such as an RC circuit or a moving average.

concepts.name: Energy and power of signals
concepts.summary: Explain energy and average power of a signal and distinguish energy signals from power signals.

misconceptions.text: A discrete-time signal is just a continuous signal with small steps, so it is defined between the integer sample points.
The unit impulse is a very tall pulse whose value at zero is simply infinity, so it has no defined meaning.
The sum of any two periodic signals is always periodic.

concepts.name: Linearity and time invariance
concepts.summary: Test a given system for linearity and time invariance by applying superposition and input shifts.

concepts.name: Causality and stability of systems
concepts.summary: Determine whether a system is causal, memoryless or BIBO stable from its equation or response.

concepts.name: Impulse response
concepts.summary: Explain that the response of an LTI system to a unit impulse fully characterises the system.

concepts.name: Convolution integral and sum
concepts.summary: Compute the output of an LTI system by flipping, shifting, multiplying and integrating or summing for simple signals.

concepts.name: Convolution properties
concepts.summary: Apply commutativity, associativity and distributivity of convolution to combine cascaded and parallel systems.

concepts.name: Step response
concepts.summary: Obtain the step response as the running integral or sum of the impulse response and read off settling behaviour.

concepts.name: Difference and differential equations
concepts.summary: Describe simple LTI systems with linear constant-coefficient equations and find homogeneous and particular solutions.

concepts.name: Complex exponentials as eigenfunctions
concepts.summary: Explain that an LTI system maps e^{st} or z^n to a scaled copy of itself, motivating frequency-domain analysis.

misconceptions.text: A system whose output is a straight line in the input, such as y = 2x + 3, is linear.
Convolution is just pointwise multiplication of the input and the impulse response.
A bounded impulse response is enough for BIBO stability.
