concepts.name: Fourier series representation
concepts.summary: Compute Fourier series coefficients of periodic signals and reconstruct them from harmonics.

concepts.name: Continuous-time Fourier transform
concepts.summary: Compute and interpret the Fourier transform of common aperiodic signals using the definition and tables.

concepts.name: Fourier transform properties
concepts.summary: Use linearity, time shift, modulation, scaling, differentiation and the convolution theorem to find transforms and outputs.

concepts.name: Frequency response of LTI systems
concepts.summary: Relate the frequency response to the impulse response and predict the output of a system for sinusoidal inputs.

concepts.name: Laplace transform and ROC
concepts.summary: Compute Laplace transforms and inverse transforms, tracking the region of convergence for causal and anticausal signals.

concepts.name: Transfer function poles and zeros
concepts.summary: Derive a transfer function from a differential equation and infer stability and causality from pole locations and ROC.

concepts.name: Discrete-time Fourier transform
concepts.summary: Compute the DTFT of sequences and explain why it is periodic in frequency with period 2π.

concepts.name: z-transform and ROC
concepts.summary: Compute z-transforms and inverses, link pole positions relative to the unit circle to stability, and solve difference equations.

misconceptions.text: The Fourier transform of a signal exists for every signal, including growing exponentials.
The Laplace transform expression alone identifies the signal, without specifying the region of convergence.
A system with a pole in the right half-plane is always unstable, regardless of the ROC.

concepts.name: Sampling theorem and aliasing
concepts.summary: Analyse the spectrum of an impulse-sampled signal to show when reconstruction is possible and how aliasing arises.

concepts.name: Ideal and practical reconstruction
concepts.summary: Compare sinc interpolation with zero-order hold and quantify the distortion each introduces.

concepts.name: Discrete Fourier transform and FFT
concepts.summary: Relate the DFT to samples of the DTFT and analyse leakage, resolution and zero padding in spectral estimates.

concepts.name: Circular versus linear convolution
concepts.summary: Analyse when DFT multiplication yields linear convolution and choose transform lengths to avoid wraparound.

concepts.name: Filter specification and design
concepts.summary: Evaluate trade-offs among passband ripple, transition width and stopband attenuation when choosing a filter.

concepts.name: FIR and IIR filter structures
concepts.summary: Compare FIR and IIR filters in terms of stability, phase linearity, order and computational cost.

concepts.name: Group delay and phase distortion
concepts.summary: Analyse how nonlinear phase response distorts waveforms through group delay variation.

concepts.name: Bode plots and system response
concepts.summary: Sketch and interpret Bode plots for first- and second-order systems and relate them to time-domain response.

misconceptions.text: Sampling at exactly twice the highest frequency always guarantees perfect reconstruction.
Aliasing can be removed digitally after sampling.
Zero padding before a DFT increases the true frequency resolution.

concepts.name: Time-frequency uncertainty trade-off
concepts.summary: Evaluate how limits on joint time and frequency localisation constrain analysis, windowing and filter design.

concepts.name: Optimal filter design methods
concepts.summary: Design FIR and IIR filters to meet specifications using equiripple, window and bilinear methods and justify the choice.

concepts.name: Multirate signal processing
concepts.summary: Evaluate and design sample-rate conversion systems, including anti-aliasing and anti-imaging filters.

concepts.name: State-space representation
concepts.summary: Model LTI systems in state-space form and relate eigenvalues of the state matrix to transfer function poles and stability.

concepts.name: Stochastic signals and spectra
concepts.summary: Evaluate how random signals and noise are shaped by LTI systems using autocorrelation and power spectral density.

concepts.name: Matched and Wiener filtering
concepts.summary: Design filters that maximise signal-to-noise ratio or minimise mean-square error for a stated signal and noise model.

concepts.name: Time-frequency and wavelet analysis
concepts.summary: Judge when short-time Fourier or wavelet methods are more appropriate than global Fourier analysis for nonstationary signals.

concepts.name: Finite word-length effects
concepts.summary: Assess how quantisation of coefficients and arithmetic affects filter performance and choose structures to mitigate it.

misconceptions.text: A transform that is sharper in both time and frequency can always be obtained with a better window.
Decimating a signal by M is just discarding samples, with no need for prior filtering.
A filter designed with infinite-precision coefficients will behave identically when implemented in fixed-point arithmetic.

issues: Flags on cmp-2/cmp-7 and cmp-5/cmp-8 are harmless: CTFT vs DTFT and Laplace vs z-transform are distinct concepts with parallel names.
Minor: nov-3 is C1 and nov-4 C2, both within the novice band; all Bloom levels sit inside their stage bands.
Prerequisite pairs are genuine dependencies and acyclic; ids refer only to the same or lower stages.

concepts.name: Project versus ongoing operations
concepts.summary: Explain that a project is temporary, has a unique outcome and a defined end, unlike repeating day-to-day operations.

concepts.name: Triple constraint
concepts.summary: Describe how scope, time and cost are linked so that changing one usually affects the others and quality.

concepts.name: Project life cycle phases
concepts.summary: Recall the phases of a waterfall-style project: initiating, planning, executing, monitoring and controlling, and closing.

concepts.name: Project roles
concepts.summary: Identify what the sponsor, project manager, team members and other stakeholders do on a project.

concepts.name: Project charter purpose
concepts.summary: Explain that a charter formally authorises the project and records its purpose, objectives, sponsor and the manager's authority.

concepts.name: Tasks, deliverables and milestones
concepts.summary: Distinguish work activities from the tangible outputs they produce and from zero-duration checkpoints.

concepts.name: Stakeholders
concepts.summary: Define stakeholders as people or groups affected by or able to influence the project, and name typical examples.

misconceptions.text: A project is any work the team does repeatedly, such as monthly reporting.
A project manager personally does most of the project's technical work.
Stakeholders are only the people who work on the project team.

concepts.name: Writing a scope statement
concepts.summary: Write a scope statement listing deliverables, boundaries, exclusions, assumptions and acceptance criteria for a small project.

concepts.name: Building a work breakdown structure
concepts.summary: Decompose project deliverables into hierarchical work packages that cover all the scope and nothing more.

concepts.name: Estimating task durations
concepts.summary: Produce duration estimates for work packages using expert judgement, analogous comparison and simple three-point estimates.

concepts.name: Task dependencies
concepts.summary: Sequence activities using finish-to-start, start-to-start, finish-to-finish and start-to-finish links, with lead and lag.

concepts.name: Reading and drawing Gantt charts
concepts.summary: Build and interpret a Gantt chart showing task bars, dependencies, milestones and progress against a timeline.

concepts.name: Basic cost estimation
concepts.summary: Estimate costs for labour, materials and other items from the WBS and total them into a simple budget.

concepts.name: Simple risk identification
concepts.summary: Identify uncertain events that could help or harm objectives and distinguish them from issues already occurring.

misconceptions.text: A WBS is a list of tasks in time order, like a schedule.
If a task is not mentioned in the scope statement, the team should do it anyway to please the client.
A risk is the same thing as a problem that is already happening.

concepts.name: Critical path analysis
concepts.summary: Compute forward and backward passes to find the longest path and determine the minimum project duration.

concepts.name: Float and slack
concepts.summary: Calculate total and free float and analyse which tasks can slip without delaying the finish date.

concepts.name: Resource allocation and levelling
concepts.summary: Analyse resource loads across the schedule, resolve overallocation and understand the effect on the end date.

concepts.name: Risk register and scoring
concepts.summary: Maintain a register that scores risks by probability and impact, assigns owners and records responses.

concepts.name: Risk response strategies
concepts.summary: Select and justify avoid, transfer, mitigate or accept responses for individual risks.

concepts.name: Budget baseline and contingency
concepts.summary: Build a time-phased budget with contingency from the cost estimates and schedule.

concepts.name: Stakeholder analysis and communication plan
concepts.summary: Analyse stakeholders' influence and interest and design who receives which information, how and how often.

concepts.name: Status tracking and reporting
concepts.summary: Track percent complete and actual versus planned dates and cost and report variances clearly.

misconceptions.text: The critical path is the path with the most important or most expensive tasks.
Tasks with float can be delayed indefinitely without consequence.
Adding more people to a late task always shortens it proportionally.

concepts.name: Earned value analysis
concepts.summary: Use planned value, earned value and actual cost to compute schedule and cost variances and performance indices.

concepts.name: Forecasting completion
concepts.summary: Evaluate which estimate-at-completion formula fits the situation and judge whether the budget and deadline are achievable.

concepts.name: Schedule compression
concepts.summary: Evaluate crashing and fast-tracking options for recovering schedule against their cost and risk impact.

concepts.name: Integrated change control
concepts.summary: Run changes through a formal process that assesses impact on scope, schedule, cost and risk before approval and updates the baselines.

concepts.name: Quantitative schedule risk
concepts.summary: Evaluate schedule confidence using PERT estimates and simulation rather than single-point durations.

concepts.name: Scope creep control
concepts.summary: Analyse how uncontrolled additions arise and apply baselines and acceptance criteria to contain them.

concepts.name: Managing stakeholder expectations
concepts.summary: Judge engagement approaches for resistant or conflicting stakeholders and negotiate trade-offs among priorities.

concepts.name: Issue and escalation management
concepts.summary: Analyse issues, assign owners and decide when and how to escalate beyond the project manager's authority.

misconceptions.text: A positive cost variance alone means the project is healthy.
Crashing and fast-tracking are the same and both only cost money.
Small change requests can be accepted informally if the sponsor asks.

concepts.name: Tailoring the planning approach
concepts.summary: Judge when a plan-driven approach, a hybrid or an adaptive one suits a project's uncertainty, constraints and governance.

concepts.name: Critical chain and buffer management
concepts.summary: Evaluate critical chain scheduling, with resource constraints and shared buffers, against traditional critical path control.

concepts.name: Designing project controls
concepts.summary: Design governance, stage gates, thresholds and reporting that fit the project's size, risk and organisational context.

concepts.name: Portfolio-level trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate competing projects' priorities and shared resources to make defensible trade-offs and recommendations.

concepts.name: Recovering a failing project
concepts.summary: Diagnose root causes of failure and create a recovery plan, including re-baselining, descoping or termination.

concepts.name: Contract and procurement risk
aliases: fixed price vs time and materials
concepts.summary: Evaluate contract types and vendor arrangements for how they allocate cost and schedule risk.

concepts.name: Benefits realisation and lessons learned
concepts.summary: Create closure practices that confirm acceptance, transfer handover, measure benefits and feed lessons into future planning.

misconceptions.text: A project delivered on time and on budget is automatically a success.
Adding more reporting and controls always improves project performance.
Re-baselining a late project resolves the underlying problems.

concepts.name: Negotiation as joint decision
concepts.summary: Explain that negotiation is two parties seeking agreement on price or terms where each can say no, and that both must accept the result.

concepts.name: Interests versus positions
concepts.summary: Distinguish what a party asks for (position) from the underlying reason or need (interest) it serves.

concepts.name: BATNA
aliases: best alternative to a negotiated agreement
concepts.summary: Define a BATNA as your best option if no deal is reached and explain why it sets your real bargaining strength.

concepts.name: Reservation point
concepts.summary: Recall that the reservation point is the worst deal you would still accept, beyond which you prefer your alternative.

concepts.name: Target and aspiration
concepts.summary: Understand that a target is the ambitious but realistic outcome you aim for, set above your reservation point.

concepts.name: Offer and counteroffer
concepts.summary: Recognise the basic move sequence in which one side proposes terms and the other accepts, rejects or answers with a different proposal.

concepts.name: Preparation before talking
concepts.summary: Explain why researching market values, the other side and your own priorities before the meeting improves outcomes.

misconceptions.text: Negotiation is a fight in which one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss.
Your reservation point is the same as your target.
You can negotiate well without any preparation if you are confident and quick.

concepts.name: Setting a reservation point from BATNA
concepts.summary: Calculate a reservation point by valuing your BATNA and adjusting for costs, risks and non-price factors.

concepts.name: Zone of possible agreement
concepts.summary: Identify the overlap between both sides' reservation points, and recognise that no overlap means no deal is possible.

concepts.name: Anchoring
concepts.summary: Apply the effect that an early number pulls the final outcome toward it, by making a well-justified first offer.

concepts.name: Making concessions
concepts.summary: Make concessions that are gradual, reciprocal and shrinking in size so they signal limits without giving away value.

concepts.name: Multiple issues in a deal
concepts.summary: Recognise that deals include price plus terms such as timing, scope, benefits and risk that can all be negotiated.

concepts.name: Justifying with objective criteria
concepts.summary: Support a request with external standards such as market data or precedent rather than preference alone.

concepts.name: Active listening and questions
concepts.summary: Use open questions and paraphrasing to uncover the other side's priorities and constraints.

misconceptions.text: Whoever makes the first offer always loses because they reveal too much.
Agreement is possible whenever both sides keep talking long enough.
Large early concessions build goodwill and are returned automatically.

concepts.name: Estimating the other side's BATNA
concepts.summary: Infer the counterpart's alternatives and likely reservation point from market evidence and their behaviour to judge the ZOPA.

concepts.name: Trading issues through logrolling
concepts.summary: Analyse differing priorities across issues and trade what you value less for what you value more to create joint gain.

concepts.name: Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers
concepts.summary: Present several packages of equal value to you to learn which the counterpart prefers.

concepts.name: Responding to anchors
concepts.summary: Assess an extreme first offer and respond by rejecting its basis, re-anchoring with data or refocusing on criteria.

concepts.name: Concession pattern analysis
concepts.summary: Interpret the size and timing of the counterpart's concessions to estimate how close they are to their limit.

concepts.name: Separating people from the problem
concepts.summary: Handle emotion and relationship concerns separately from the substantive issues so they do not distort the terms.

concepts.name: Closing and documenting agreement
concepts.summary: Summarise agreed terms, test for unresolved points, and put them in writing so both parties can sign.

misconceptions.text: Trading issues means splitting every difference down the middle.
Ignoring an extreme anchor is enough to neutralise its influence.
A verbal handshake means the deal is closed and details can be sorted out later.

concepts.name: Evaluating package value
concepts.summary: Judge competing packages by weighting issues with a scoring model that includes risk and time value, not price alone.

concepts.name: Improving BATNA and reframing leverage
concepts.summary: Evaluate ways to strengthen your alternatives or weaken the counterpart's, and choose the one worth the cost.

concepts.name: Contingent and risk-sharing terms
concepts.summary: Analyse when differing beliefs about the future can be bridged by terms such as bonuses, earn-outs or price adjustments.

concepts.name: Deadlock diagnosis
concepts.summary: Diagnose whether a stalemate stems from no ZOPA, hidden interests, face-saving or process, and select a remedy.

concepts.name: Negotiating with multiple parties
concepts.summary: Analyse hidden decision makers, agents and coalitions and adapt the approach to each.

concepts.name: Hardball tactics and responses
concepts.summary: Judge tactics such as deadlines, good cop/bad cop and nibbling, and decide whether to name, ignore or counter them.

concepts.name: Ethics and trust in bargaining
concepts.summary: Evaluate the line between acceptable withholding or puffery and deception, and its effect on reputation and enforceability.

misconceptions.text: Lying about your reservation point is a normal and harmless part of negotiating.
Every tactic from a counterpart should be met with matching toughness.
An impasse always means the other side is being unreasonable.

concepts.name: Designing negotiation strategy
concepts.summary: Design a negotiation plan across sequence, venue, coalition and timing that fits the power balance and the relationship horizon.

concepts.name: Creating new value structures
concepts.summary: Invent deal structures such as bundled long-term contracts or option rights that open gains neither side initially saw.

concepts.name: Judging fairness and sustainability of deals
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a deal will hold by assessing perceived fairness, enforcement and incentives to renege.

concepts.name: Adapting across cultures and contexts
concepts.summary: Assess how culture, hierarchy and communication norms alter the meaning of offers, silence and concessions, and adjust.

concepts.name: Behavioural bias management
concepts.summary: Evaluate and counter biases such as overconfidence, fixed-pie thinking and escalation of commitment in yourself and others.

concepts.name: Mediating and coaching negotiations
concepts.summary: Create a process in which a third party or team negotiates well, including mandates, authority limits and debriefs.

concepts.name: Portfolio and repeated-game negotiation
concepts.summary: Evaluate how a deal sets precedent and shapes future bargaining, and trade single-deal gains against long-term position.

misconceptions.text: Expert negotiators succeed mainly through charisma and instinct rather than structured preparation.
The same tactics work equally well in every culture and context.
Maximising the result of each single deal is always the best long-term strategy.

concepts.name: Wave Parameters and Terminology
concepts.summary: Identify and define wavelength, frequency, period and amplitude on a wave diagram.

concepts.name: Transverse versus Longitudinal Waves
concepts.summary: Distinguish waves by the direction of particle oscillation relative to the direction of energy travel, with examples such as light and sound.

concepts.name: Wave Speed Relation
concepts.summary: Explain and use that wave speed equals frequency times wavelength, and that period is the inverse of frequency.

concepts.name: Waves Transfer Energy Not Matter
concepts.summary: Explain that a wave carries energy through a medium while the medium's particles only oscillate about equilibrium.

concepts.name: Reflection and Law of Reflection
concepts.summary: State and explain that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal.

concepts.name: Refraction as Change of Speed
concepts.summary: Describe how a wave changes speed and direction on entering a different medium while its frequency stays the same.

concepts.name: Sound as a Pressure Wave
concepts.summary: Describe sound as longitudinal compressions and rarefactions, with pitch tied to frequency and loudness to amplitude.

misconceptions.text: The particles of the medium travel along with the wave from source to receiver.
A wave's speed depends on its frequency or amplitude rather than on the medium.
Sound can travel through a vacuum just as light does.

concepts.name: Snell's Law Calculations
aliases: n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2
concepts.summary: Use refractive index and Snell's law to compute refraction angles at an interface, with angles measured from the normal.

concepts.name: Total Internal Reflection and Critical Angle
concepts.summary: Determine the critical angle from the indices and predict when light is totally reflected, as in optical fibres.

concepts.name: Ray Diagrams for Thin Lenses
concepts.summary: Draw principal rays through converging and diverging lenses to locate and characterise images as real or virtual.

concepts.name: Plane and Curved Mirror Images
concepts.summary: Construct ray diagrams for plane, concave and convex mirrors and describe the resulting image.

concepts.name: Superposition and Interference of Waves
concepts.summary: Explain how overlapping waves add to give constructive or destructive interference depending on phase.

concepts.name: Standing Waves on Strings and Pipes
concepts.summary: Find nodes, antinodes and harmonic frequencies for strings and open or closed pipes from boundary conditions.

concepts.name: Sound Intensity Level in Decibels
concepts.summary: Compute intensity levels using the logarithmic decibel scale and relate intensity to power and distance.

misconceptions.text: Light bends toward the normal when it enters any new medium.
Total internal reflection can occur when light passes from a lower-index to a higher-index medium.
Doubling the decibel level means doubling the sound intensity.

concepts.name: Thin Lens and Mirror Equations
concepts.summary: Apply the lens and mirror equations with a consistent sign convention to compute image distance, magnification and orientation.

concepts.name: Doppler Effect Calculations
concepts.summary: Calculate observed frequency for moving sources and observers and reason about the direction of shift.

concepts.name: Resonance and Driven Oscillation
concepts.summary: Analyse how a driving frequency matching a natural frequency produces large amplitude, and how damping limits it.

concepts.name: Double-Slit Interference Pattern
concepts.summary: Analyse path difference to derive fringe positions d sin theta = m lambda and fringe spacing for coherent light.

concepts.name: Single-Slit Diffraction Pattern
concepts.summary: Locate minima with a sin theta = m lambda and explain how slit width controls central maximum width.

concepts.name: Diffraction Gratings
concepts.summary: Use the grating equation to find the angles of sharp maxima and to separate wavelengths.

concepts.name: Polarization and Malus's Law
concepts.summary: Compute transmitted intensity through polarizers with I = I0 cos^2 theta and explain why only transverse waves polarize.

concepts.name: Wave Phase Change on Reflection
concepts.summary: Analyse when reflection introduces a half-wavelength shift and how it affects interference and standing wave ends.

misconceptions.text: In the double-slit pattern the bright fringes are caused by light from each slit simply adding as separate beams without regard to phase.
A narrower slit gives a narrower diffraction pattern.
The Doppler effect arises because the source changes the frequency it emits when it moves.

concepts.name: Thin-Film Interference
concepts.summary: Combine optical path difference and reflection phase shifts to predict constructive and destructive conditions in films.

concepts.name: Resolution and Rayleigh Criterion
concepts.summary: Evaluate the resolving power of apertures and instruments using theta ≈ 1.22 lambda / D.

concepts.name: Intensity Distribution of Interference Patterns
concepts.summary: Analyse how the single-slit envelope modulates double-slit fringes and why some orders are missing.

concepts.name: Lens Combinations and Optical Instruments
concepts.summary: Analyse multi-lens systems by treating each image as the next object, and derive angular magnification.

concepts.name: Brewster Angle and Polarization by Reflection
concepts.summary: Analyse polarization on reflection and scattering and determine Brewster's angle from tan theta = n2/n1.

concepts.name: Dispersion and Aberrations
concepts.summary: Explain how wavelength-dependent index causes dispersion and lens defects, and evaluate corrections.

concepts.name: Group and Phase Velocity
concepts.summary: Distinguish phase velocity from group velocity in dispersive media and evaluate which carries energy and information.

misconceptions.text: Better magnification alone always lets an instrument reveal finer detail, regardless of aperture or wavelength.
Phase velocity is the speed at which energy and information travel in all cases.
A coating can eliminate reflection for all wavelengths at once.

concepts.name: Wave Equation and Superposition Derivations
concepts.summary: Derive the wave equation for a medium and construct solutions for travelling and standing waves from boundary conditions.

concepts.name: Fourier Decomposition of Waveforms
concepts.summary: Evaluate how complex waves decompose into harmonics and how this explains timbre and bandwidth limits.

concepts.name: Coherence and Fringe Visibility
concepts.summary: Evaluate how source bandwidth and size limit interference visibility and design setups accordingly.

concepts.name: Fresnel and Fraunhofer Diffraction Regimes
concepts.summary: Judge which diffraction regime applies from the Fresnel number and choose appropriate models.

concepts.name: Fermat's Principle and Ray Optics Limits
concepts.summary: Derive reflection and refraction laws from stationary optical path and assess when the ray model fails.

concepts.name: Interferometer Design
concepts.summary: Design interferometric measurements and predict fringe behaviour, resolution and sensitivity.

concepts.name: Optical System Design Trade-offs
concepts.summary: Create and justify a system design balancing aberrations, diffraction limit, aperture, and cost.

misconceptions.text: Geometric ray optics remains valid at any scale, so rays accurately predict focused spot sizes.
Any light source of a single colour produces sharp interference fringes.
Only sinusoidal waves are physically meaningful, so non-sinusoidal waves cannot be analysed with superposition.

concepts.name: Layers of the Earth
concepts.summary: Name and describe the crust, mantle, outer core and inner core and say which are solid or liquid.

concepts.name: Mineral definition and properties
concepts.summary: Explain that a mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic, crystalline solid with a definite chemical composition.

concepts.name: Three rock types
concepts.summary: Distinguish igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks by how they form.

concepts.name: The rock cycle
concepts.summary: Describe how rocks change from one type to another through melting, cooling, weathering, burial and heat and pressure.

concepts.name: Tectonic plates and boundaries
concepts.summary: Describe that the lithosphere is broken into moving plates and name the three boundary types and their motion.

concepts.name: Volcanoes and earthquakes basics
concepts.summary: Explain in simple terms that volcanoes release magma and earthquakes release energy from sudden movement on faults.

concepts.name: Weathering versus erosion
concepts.summary: Tell apart weathering as breakdown in place from erosion as removal and transport of material.

misconceptions.text: The Earth's mantle is a sea of liquid magma.
Any hard solid found in nature, such as coal or glass, counts as a mineral.
Weathering and erosion are the same thing.

concepts.name: Mineral identification tests
concepts.summary: Use hardness, streak, luster, cleavage and fracture to identify common minerals such as quartz, feldspar, calcite and mica.

concepts.name: Igneous texture and composition
concepts.summary: Relate grain size to cooling rate and classify rocks like granite and basalt by texture and felsic or mafic composition.

concepts.name: Clastic and chemical sedimentary rocks
concepts.summary: Identify common sedimentary rocks by grain size and composition and explain how compaction and cementation form them.

concepts.name: Metamorphic grade and foliation
concepts.summary: Identify metamorphic rocks by foliation and relate them to increasing heat and pressure.

concepts.name: Relative dating principles
concepts.summary: Apply superposition, original horizontality and cross-cutting relationships to order events in a simple rock sequence.

concepts.name: Earthquake waves and measurement
concepts.summary: Describe P, S and surface waves, locate focus and epicenter, and distinguish magnitude from intensity.

concepts.name: Volcano types and eruption styles
concepts.summary: Match volcano shapes and eruption styles to magma viscosity and gas content.

misconceptions.text: Color is a reliable way to identify a mineral.
Metamorphic rocks form when rock melts and recrystallizes.
The Richter magnitude and the shaking felt at a place measure the same thing.

concepts.name: Plate tectonic evidence
concepts.summary: Analyse fossil, rock-match, magnetic stripe and seafloor age evidence supporting plate motion.

concepts.name: Boundary settings and associated hazards
concepts.summary: Explain how each boundary type controls the distribution of volcanoes, earthquakes, trenches and mountain belts.

concepts.name: Fault types and stress
concepts.summary: Link tension, compression and shear to normal, reverse and strike-slip faults and recognise them in cross-section.

concepts.name: Folds and geologic structures
concepts.summary: Identify folds, dip and strike and describe how rock layers deform.

concepts.name: Reading geologic maps
concepts.summary: Interpret map units, contacts, symbols and outcrop patterns to infer structure and a cross-section.

concepts.name: Absolute dating and radiometric decay
concepts.summary: Use half-lives and parent-daughter ratios to calculate ages and choose suitable isotopes.

concepts.name: Weathering processes and soils
concepts.summary: Compare physical and chemical weathering and analyse how climate, rock type and time shape soils.

concepts.name: Depositional environments and facies
concepts.summary: Infer ancient environments from sedimentary structures, grain size and fossils.

misconceptions.text: Continents plow through the ocean floor as they move.
Radiometric dating of a sedimentary rock directly dates when its grains were deposited.
Contacts on a geologic map show the rocks' ages only, not their three-dimensional geometry.

concepts.name: Mantle convection and plate driving forces
concepts.summary: Analyse slab pull, ridge push and mantle convection as drivers of plate motion and assess hotspot models.

concepts.name: Magma generation and differentiation
concepts.summary: Explain how decompression, flux and heating produce melts and how crystallization changes magma composition.

concepts.name: Metamorphic facies and P-T paths
concepts.summary: Use mineral assemblages to infer pressure-temperature conditions and tectonic setting.

concepts.name: Stratigraphic correlation and sequence stratigraphy
concepts.summary: Evaluate correlations using fossils, markers and unconformities and interpret sea-level change in stratigraphic records.

concepts.name: Seismic hazard assessment
concepts.summary: Evaluate fault slip rates, recurrence intervals and site effects to judge earthquake hazard.

concepts.name: Landscape evolution and geomorphic processes
concepts.summary: Explain how rivers, glaciers, slopes and tectonics together shape landforms and drainage patterns.

concepts.name: Geochemical and isotopic tracers
concepts.summary: Judge what oxygen isotopes, trace elements and radiogenic isotopes reveal about source, climate and process.

misconceptions.text: Plates are pushed along by convection currents dragging them like a conveyor belt, with no role for slab pull.
Unconformities and missing layers mean the stratigraphic record is a continuous clock.
Earthquake recurrence intervals are regular, so a quake is not due until the mean interval has passed.

concepts.name: Integrating multi-method geologic syntheses
concepts.summary: Combine structural, stratigraphic, geochemical and geochronologic data into a coherent regional history.

concepts.name: Competing tectonic model evaluation
concepts.summary: Weigh alternative models of orogeny, rifting and plume activity against field and geophysical evidence.

concepts.name: Uncertainty in geochronology
concepts.summary: Assess closure temperatures, decay constant errors and sample quality to judge the reliability of an age.

concepts.name: Designing field investigations
concepts.summary: Plan mapping and sampling campaigns that test specific hypotheses within logistical limits.

concepts.name: Deep time and mass extinction causes
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence for large volcanism, impacts and ocean chemistry change as drivers of major biotic and environmental shifts.

concepts.name: Geohazard risk communication and mitigation
concepts.summary: Create hazard models and communicate probabilistic risk to guide land use and emergency planning.

concepts.name: Resource formation and geologic constraints
concepts.summary: Evaluate how tectonic setting, fluids and structure control where ore, hydrocarbons and groundwater accumulate.

misconceptions.text: A single well-dated sample settles the age of a geologic event.
One mass extinction cause must be correct, so competing hypotheses are mutually exclusive.
A hazard probability model removes uncertainty so that communication of risk is simply stating one number.

concepts.name: Population-level health thinking
concepts.summary: Explain that epidemiology studies patterns of disease in groups rather than diagnosing or treating individuals.

concepts.name: Person, place, time
concepts.summary: Recall that disease distribution is described by who is affected, where, and when.

concepts.name: Incidence and prevalence
concepts.summary: Distinguish new cases arising over time from all existing cases at a point or period.

concepts.name: Risk factors and exposures
concepts.summary: Identify exposures and outcomes and explain that a risk factor raises the probability of disease without guaranteeing it.

concepts.name: Epidemic, endemic, pandemic
concepts.summary: Recall the definitions of endemic, outbreak, epidemic and pandemic by comparison with expected frequency and spread.

concepts.name: Association versus causation
concepts.summary: Explain that an observed link between exposure and disease does not by itself show that the exposure causes it.

misconceptions.text: Prevalence and incidence mean the same thing.
If two things occur together, one must cause the other.
Epidemiology is only about infectious disease outbreaks.

concepts.name: Rates, risks and proportions
concepts.summary: Calculate incidence proportion, incidence rate with person-time, and point prevalence from data.

concepts.name: Relative risk and odds ratio
concepts.summary: Compute and interpret risk ratio and odds ratio from a 2x2 table.

concepts.name: Risk difference and attributable risk
concepts.summary: Calculate risk difference and attributable fraction and interpret the absolute impact of an exposure.

concepts.name: Cohort and case-control designs
concepts.summary: Describe how cohort and case-control studies select participants and which measures each can estimate.

concepts.name: Cross-sectional studies
concepts.summary: Explain how a single-time survey measures prevalence and why it struggles to establish temporality.

concepts.name: Randomized controlled trials
concepts.summary: Explain how randomization and a control group allow comparison of an intervention's effect.

concepts.name: Standardization of rates
concepts.summary: Apply age adjustment to compare rates between populations with different age structures.

misconceptions.text: The odds ratio is always interchangeable with the relative risk.
A high relative risk always means a large number of cases is attributable to the exposure.
Comparing crude rates between populations is always fair.

concepts.name: Selection bias mechanisms
concepts.summary: Analyse how participant selection, loss to follow-up and nonresponse distort associations.

concepts.name: Information bias and misclassification
concepts.summary: Distinguish differential from nondifferential misclassification and predict their effects on estimates.

concepts.name: Confounding identification
concepts.summary: Identify a confounder by its association with both exposure and outcome and its absence from the causal pathway.

concepts.name: Stratification and adjustment
concepts.summary: Control confounding through restriction, stratified analysis or multivariable regression.

concepts.name: Effect modification
concepts.summary: Distinguish effect modification from confounding by examining whether stratum-specific effects differ.

concepts.name: Confidence intervals and p-values
concepts.summary: Interpret confidence intervals around risk measures and separate statistical from clinical significance.

concepts.name: Outbreak investigation steps
concepts.summary: Apply the sequence of verifying the diagnosis, defining cases, finding cases, generating hypotheses and testing them.

concepts.name: Epidemic curves
concepts.summary: Interpret the shape of an epidemic curve to infer point-source versus propagated spread.

misconceptions.text: Any variable that changes the estimate when adjusted for is a confounder.
Misclassification always biases results toward the null.
A statistically significant result proves the association is causal and important.

concepts.name: Causal inference frameworks
concepts.summary: Evaluate causal claims using the counterfactual framework and Bradford Hill considerations.

concepts.name: Directed acyclic graphs
concepts.summary: Use DAGs to identify confounders, mediators and colliders and choose adjustment sets.

concepts.name: Collider and mediator bias
concepts.summary: Analyse how adjusting for mediators or colliders creates bias.

concepts.name: Survival and time-to-event analysis
concepts.summary: Interpret hazard ratios and censoring in time-to-event analyses.

concepts.name: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis
concepts.summary: Appraise pooled estimates, heterogeneity and publication bias in a body of evidence.

concepts.name: Screening and diagnostic accuracy
concepts.summary: Analyse how sensitivity, specificity and prevalence determine predictive values and screening biases like lead time.

concepts.name: Critical appraisal of studies
concepts.summary: Judge a study's validity by assessing design, bias, confounding, precision and generalizability.

misconceptions.text: Adjusting for more variables always gives a less biased estimate.
A test with high sensitivity and specificity has a high positive predictive value in any population.
Meta-analysis of many studies removes the biases in the individual studies.

concepts.name: Target trial emulation
concepts.summary: Design observational analyses that explicitly emulate a hypothetical randomized trial to avoid time-related biases.

concepts.name: Quasi-experimental methods
concepts.summary: Evaluate when natural experiments and instruments support causal estimates and which assumptions they require.

concepts.name: Mendelian randomization
concepts.summary: Appraise genetic-instrument analyses by testing relevance, independence and exclusion assumptions including pleiotropy.

concepts.name: Quantitative bias analysis
concepts.summary: Assess how strong unmeasured confounding or misclassification would have to be to explain a result.

concepts.name: Transmission modelling
concepts.summary: Evaluate compartmental models and reproduction numbers to project epidemics and compare interventions.

concepts.name: Surveillance system design
concepts.summary: Design a surveillance system that balances sensitivity, timeliness, representativeness and cost.

concepts.name: Study protocol design
concepts.summary: Create a protocol with a defensible design, power calculation, bias controls and pre-specified analysis plan.

concepts.name: Translating evidence into policy
concepts.summary: Weigh uncertain, conflicting evidence together with harms, equity and feasibility to recommend public health action.

misconceptions.text: An instrumental variable or Mendelian randomization analysis guarantees causal estimates regardless of assumptions.
The basic reproduction number is a fixed biological constant of a pathogen.
Sophisticated statistical modelling can fully compensate for a poorly designed study.

concepts.name: Purpose of a message
concepts.summary: State in one sentence why you are writing and what you want the reader to know or do.

concepts.name: Audience awareness
concepts.summary: Explain how the reader's role, knowledge and needs shape what you include and how you say it.

concepts.name: Common workplace document types
concepts.summary: Recognise what emails, memos, reports and proposals are each used for and when each fits.

concepts.name: Clear subject lines
concepts.summary: Write a specific subject line that tells the reader the topic and any needed action.

concepts.name: Plain, concise wording
concepts.summary: Choose short, familiar words and cut filler so each sentence carries one clear point.

concepts.name: Professional tone basics
concepts.summary: Distinguish a polite, respectful, neutral workplace tone from slang, rudeness or over-casual phrasing.

concepts.name: Opening and closing conventions
concepts.summary: Use appropriate greetings and sign-offs and include a clear closing line.

misconceptions.text: Longer, more formal wording sounds more professional and is therefore better.
A subject line is optional because the reader will open the email anyway.
Every workplace message should be written the same way regardless of who reads it.

concepts.name: Lead with the main point
concepts.summary: Open a message with the conclusion, request or decision before giving supporting detail.

concepts.name: Paragraph structure
concepts.summary: Build short paragraphs that each start with a topic sentence and develop a single idea.

concepts.name: Active voice and strong verbs
concepts.summary: Rewrite passive, noun-heavy sentences so the actor and action are clear and direct.

concepts.name: Clear requests and deadlines
concepts.summary: Phrase a request so it states who should do what by when.

concepts.name: Formatting for scanning
concepts.summary: Use headings, bullets, numbered lists and white space to make content easy to scan.

concepts.name: Adjusting formality
concepts.summary: Adapt formality and warmth to the relationship and situation, such as a manager versus a client.

concepts.name: Proofreading routine
concepts.summary: Check for errors, names, attachments and facts systematically before sending.

misconceptions.text: Building up background first is more polite than stating the main point at the start.
Passive voice is always more professional and should be used in business writing.
Hinting at what you need is enough; readers will work out the request.

concepts.name: Audience analysis for design
concepts.summary: Analyse a reader's knowledge, priorities, objections and decision power to decide content, depth and order.

concepts.name: Direct versus indirect structure
concepts.summary: Choose between leading with the point or building toward it, based on expected reader reaction, especially for bad news.

concepts.name: Report structure and executive summary
concepts.summary: Organise a report into purpose, findings, analysis and recommendations with a standalone summary.

concepts.name: Evidence and recommendations
concepts.summary: Link data and findings logically to conclusions and specific recommendations.

concepts.name: Structural editing
concepts.summary: Revise a draft for order, completeness and relevance before polishing sentences.

concepts.name: Tone and emotional impact
concepts.summary: Analyse how word choice conveys attitude and rework phrasing to be reader-centred and constructive.

concepts.name: Email threads and recipients
concepts.summary: Manage recipients, threads and forwarding so the right people get the right information.

misconceptions.text: Bad news should always be stated bluntly first, whatever the reader's situation.
An executive summary is just the introduction copied shorter.
Editing means fixing grammar and wording; reorganising is rewriting, not editing.

concepts.name: Persuasive proposal design
concepts.summary: Build a proposal that frames the problem, justifies the solution, addresses costs and risks, and fits the decision-maker's criteria.

concepts.name: Writing for mixed audiences
concepts.summary: Layer a document so executives, specialists and implementers each find what they need.

concepts.name: Evaluating argument strength
concepts.summary: Judge whether claims, evidence and assumptions in a draft are sufficient and fair, and fix weak points.

concepts.name: Handling sensitive messages
concepts.summary: Judge when and how to write about complaints, refusals or conflict, and when written form is the wrong channel.

concepts.name: Data presentation in text
concepts.summary: Select and caption tables or charts and write the interpretation that makes the numbers meaningful.

concepts.name: Style consistency and templates
concepts.summary: Apply and adapt organisational style guides and templates while keeping content clear.

concepts.name: Peer review and feedback
concepts.summary: Give prioritised, actionable feedback on a colleague's writing and judge feedback you receive.

misconceptions.text: A strong proposal mainly lists the features and credentials of the writer's own solution.
Charts and tables speak for themselves and need no written interpretation.
Written messages are always the best way to handle a sensitive issue because they create a record.

concepts.name: Communication strategy design
concepts.summary: Design a coordinated set of written communications that sequences messages, channels and timing to achieve organisational goals.

concepts.name: Cross-cultural writing judgement
concepts.summary: Evaluate how directness, hierarchy, idiom and politeness norms affect understanding across cultures and adapt accordingly.

concepts.name: Creating writing standards
concepts.summary: Create guidelines, templates and review processes that raise writing quality across a team or organisation.

concepts.name: Risk, legal and ethical review
concepts.summary: Evaluate written communications for legal exposure, confidentiality, bias and misleading framing.

concepts.name: Coaching writers
concepts.summary: Develop others' writing by diagnosing patterns and designing targeted practice and feedback.

concepts.name: Voice and narrative in leadership
concepts.summary: Craft messages that use narrative and a consistent voice to build trust and motivate change.

concepts.name: Measuring communication effectiveness
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether writing achieved its goals using response, action and comprehension evidence and refine accordingly.

misconceptions.text: One well-written message is enough to drive organisational change.
Plain, direct English works equally well in every culture.
A strict style guide alone guarantees good writing across a team.

concepts.name: Tables, rows and columns
concepts.summary: Recognise that a relational schema stores each kind of thing in a table whose rows are records and whose columns are typed attributes.

concepts.name: Entities and attributes
concepts.summary: Identify the real-world entities in a set of requirements and the attributes that describe each one.

concepts.name: Primary keys
concepts.summary: Explain that a primary key uniquely identifies each row and must be unique and never null.

concepts.name: Foreign keys
concepts.summary: Explain that a foreign key stores another table's key value to link rows across tables.

concepts.name: Relationship cardinality
concepts.summary: Distinguish one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships between entities.

concepts.name: Redundancy and anomalies
concepts.summary: Describe how repeating the same facts in many rows leads to inconsistencies when data is changed.

misconceptions.text: A database table is just like a spreadsheet, so putting everything into one wide table is fine.
A primary key must be a single meaningful value like a name or email.
A foreign key is just a column with the same name as another table's column.

concepts.name: Entity-relationship diagrams
concepts.summary: Draw an ER diagram from a requirements description showing entities, attributes and relationships with cardinality.

concepts.name: Junction tables
concepts.summary: Resolve a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships using a junction table, including attributes of the relationship.

concepts.name: Mapping ER to tables
concepts.summary: Translate an ER diagram into tables with keys and foreign keys placed on the correct side of each relationship.

concepts.name: Natural versus surrogate keys
concepts.summary: Compare keys derived from real data with generated identifiers and pick one for simple cases.

concepts.name: Column data types
concepts.summary: Choose suitable data types for columns such as exact decimals for money, dates for dates and text lengths.

concepts.name: Basic column constraints
concepts.summary: Apply NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints to enforce simple rules in the schema.

concepts.name: First normal form
concepts.summary: Remove repeating groups and multi-valued columns so each cell holds one atomic value.

misconceptions.text: Storing a comma-separated list of IDs in one column is a fine way to model a many-to-many relationship.
In a one-to-many relationship the foreign key goes on the 'one' side.
Prices are best stored in floating-point columns.

concepts.name: Functional dependencies
concepts.summary: Identify which attributes determine others in a table and use that to find candidate keys.

concepts.name: Second and third normal form
concepts.summary: Detect partial and transitive dependencies in a table and decompose it into 2NF and 3NF.

concepts.name: Boyce-Codd normal form
concepts.summary: Decide whether every determinant is a candidate key and decompose when it is not.

concepts.name: Referential actions
concepts.summary: Select cascade, restrict or set-null behaviour for foreign keys according to the lifecycle of the data.

concepts.name: Composite keys
concepts.summary: Use multi-column keys where the identity of a row depends on several attributes, and reference them correctly.

concepts.name: Index fundamentals for schemas
concepts.summary: Choose indexes for foreign keys and frequent filters, weighing read speed against write cost and storage.

concepts.name: Modeling hierarchies and optional data
concepts.summary: Represent trees, optional attributes and subtypes using self-referencing keys, nullable columns or separate tables.

misconceptions.text: A table with a single-column primary key is automatically in third normal form.
ON DELETE CASCADE is a safe default for every foreign key.
Adding an index to every column makes the database faster.

concepts.name: Lossless and dependency-preserving decomposition
concepts.summary: Evaluate a decomposition for whether it reconstructs the original data exactly and keeps constraints enforceable.

concepts.name: Higher normal forms
concepts.summary: Recognise multivalued and join dependencies and decide when fourth or fifth normal form is warranted.

concepts.name: Deliberate denormalization
concepts.summary: Judge when adding redundancy or summary data is justified by read patterns and how to keep it consistent.

concepts.name: Composite and covering indexes
concepts.summary: Design multicolumn, covering and partial indexes by assessing column order and query patterns.

concepts.name: Surrogate key trade-offs
concepts.summary: Evaluate integer, UUID and natural keys regarding index size, locality, portability and uniqueness guarantees.

concepts.name: Temporal and history modeling
concepts.summary: Choose among versioned rows, effective-date ranges, audit tables and soft deletes to retain history.

concepts.name: Integrity beyond declared constraints
concepts.summary: Analyse rules that simple constraints cannot express and decide between triggers, deferred checks and application logic.

misconceptions.text: Denormalization is always a sign of poor design.
Any decomposition into smaller tables is safe as long as each table is in normal form.
A composite index on (a, b) serves queries filtering on b alone equally well.

concepts.name: Workload-driven schema evaluation
concepts.summary: Critique a schema against realistic read and write workloads, data volumes and growth, and prioritise changes by impact.

concepts.name: Schema evolution strategy
concepts.summary: Plan staged, backward-compatible schema migrations that avoid downtime and data loss on live systems.

concepts.name: Partitioning and sharding design
concepts.summary: Design partition or shard keys and schema layout that scale while keeping keys, constraints and joins workable.

concepts.name: Multi-tenant schema patterns
concepts.summary: Create a tenancy model by weighing shared tables, separate schemas and separate databases for isolation, cost and complexity.

concepts.name: Flexible and semi-structured columns
concepts.summary: Evaluate when JSON columns or EAV beat relational modeling and what integrity and query power is lost.

concepts.name: Relational versus analytical modeling
concepts.summary: Judge how transactional normalized designs differ from dimensional models and when each fits.

concepts.name: Design standards and governance
concepts.summary: Establish conventions, documentation and review practices so a team's schemas stay consistent and maintainable.

misconceptions.text: Storing everything in JSON columns removes the need for schema design.
Sharding is a free way to scale that leaves queries and constraints unchanged.
A star schema is just a more normalized version of the transactional schema.

concepts.name: Binary signals and logic levels
concepts.summary: Recall that digital circuits represent information as two levels, 0 and 1, and relate them to voltage ranges.

concepts.name: Basic gate functions
concepts.summary: Explain what AND, OR and NOT gates output for each input combination and recognise their symbols.

concepts.name: Truth tables
concepts.summary: Write and read a truth table listing every input combination and the resulting output of a gate or small circuit.

concepts.name: Derived gates NAND NOR XOR
concepts.summary: Describe the behaviour of NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR gates and how they relate to the basic gates.

concepts.name: Boolean expressions
concepts.summary: Interpret expressions using AND, OR and complement notation as descriptions of gate networks.

concepts.name: Number systems for logic
concepts.summary: Convert between binary, decimal and hexadecimal to label input and output patterns.

misconceptions.text: The logic value 1 always means exactly 5 volts.
An OR gate outputs 1 only when exactly one input is 1.
A NAND gate is simply an AND gate with the inputs inverted.

concepts.name: Boolean algebra laws
concepts.summary: Apply identity, complement, distributive and absorption laws to rewrite expressions.

concepts.name: De Morgan's theorems
concepts.summary: Use De Morgan's theorems to convert between AND-type and OR-type forms and to push inversions through gates.

concepts.name: Sum of products and product of sums
concepts.summary: Derive canonical SOP and POS expressions from a truth table using minterms and maxterms.

concepts.name: Circuit from expression
concepts.summary: Draw a gate network from a Boolean expression and evaluate its output for given inputs.

concepts.name: NAND-only and NOR-only implementation
concepts.summary: Rebuild a network using only NAND or only NOR gates.

concepts.name: Karnaugh maps up to four variables
concepts.summary: Fill a K-map from a truth table and group adjacent ones in powers of two to get a minimal SOP.

concepts.name: Don't-care conditions
concepts.summary: Use don't-care entries in K-maps to enlarge groups and simplify the result.

misconceptions.text: De Morgan's theorem says the complement of A AND B equals the complement of A AND the complement of B.
K-map groups can be any size as long as they contain only ones.
K-map rows and columns are ordered in plain binary counting order.

concepts.name: Quine-McCluskey minimisation
concepts.summary: Find prime and essential prime implicants systematically for functions with many variables.

concepts.name: Multiplexers and decoders
concepts.summary: Design and use multiplexers, decoders and encoders, including implementing functions with a MUX.

concepts.name: Half and full adders
concepts.summary: Build half and full adders and chain them into a multi-bit ripple-carry adder.

concepts.name: Two's complement arithmetic circuits
concepts.summary: Analyse how adders perform signed addition and subtraction and detect overflow.

concepts.name: Propagation delay and hazards
concepts.summary: Analyse how gate delays create glitches and how redundant terms remove static hazards.

concepts.name: SR and D latches
concepts.summary: Explain and trace cross-coupled gate latches and the transparent D latch, including the forbidden SR state.

concepts.name: Edge-triggered flip-flops
concepts.summary: Distinguish latches from edge-triggered D, JK and T flip-flops and predict outputs from timing diagrams.

concepts.name: Combinational HDL description
concepts.summary: Describe combinational circuits in Verilog or VHDL using continuous assignments and simple processes.

misconceptions.text: A latch and a flip-flop are the same thing.
A hazard-free minimal SOP is always obtained by choosing the fewest terms.
Carry out of the top bit always signals overflow in signed addition.

concepts.name: Synchronous counter design
concepts.summary: Design synchronous counters from flip-flop excitation tables and compare them with ripple counters.

concepts.name: Registers and shift registers
concepts.summary: Analyse register structures with load, enable and shift control, and their use in data paths.

concepts.name: Finite state machine modelling
concepts.summary: Model sequential behaviour as Moore or Mealy machines with state diagrams and transition tables.

concepts.name: State assignment and implementation
concepts.summary: Choose state encodings and derive next-state and output logic, evaluating cost and speed trade-offs.

concepts.name: Setup hold and clock timing
concepts.summary: Calculate setup and hold slack and maximum clock frequency from flip-flop and logic delays.

concepts.name: Synthesisable sequential HDL
concepts.summary: Write and evaluate HDL for registers and FSMs that synthesise to the intended hardware, avoiding inferred latches.

concepts.name: Testbenches and simulation
concepts.summary: Build testbenches that exercise a design and judge correctness from simulated waveforms.

misconceptions.text: A Mealy machine and a Moore machine always need the same number of states and respond at the same time.
Lowering the clock frequency fixes both setup and hold violations.
Blocking and nonblocking assignments are interchangeable in clocked HDL code.

concepts.name: Metastability and synchronisers
concepts.summary: Evaluate metastability risk and design safe clock domain crossings using synchronisers and handshakes.

concepts.name: Fast adder architectures
concepts.summary: Compare carry-lookahead, carry-select and prefix adders on delay and area.

concepts.name: Datapath and control partitioning
concepts.summary: Design a system by separating datapath and FSM controller from an algorithmic specification.

concepts.name: Pipelining and retiming
concepts.summary: Insert pipeline stages and retime logic to raise clock rate while weighing latency, area and hazards.

concepts.name: Clocking and power trade-offs
concepts.summary: Assess clock skew, gating and dynamic power effects on timing and reliability.

concepts.name: Design for testability and verification
concepts.summary: Plan scan, assertions and coverage-driven verification so that a design can be tested and proven correct.

concepts.name: Synthesis and implementation trade-offs
concepts.summary: Judge how synthesis constraints and target technology affect area, speed and structure, and restructure RTL accordingly.

misconceptions.text: A two-flop synchroniser eliminates metastability completely.
Pipelining always improves overall performance because it shortens the clock period.
Passing simulation proves a design is correct and ready for hardware.

concepts.name: Resistance and muscle adaptation
concepts.summary: Explain that muscles adapt to challenging loads by getting stronger and larger over time, with the nervous system driving early strength gains.

concepts.name: Core compound lifts
concepts.summary: Name the main compound movements such as squat, deadlift, bench press, overhead press and row, and the muscles each trains.

concepts.name: Sets, reps and load
concepts.summary: Define a repetition, a set, the load lifted and rest between sets, and read a basic workout written in those terms.

concepts.name: Neutral spine and bracing
concepts.summary: Explain why keeping a neutral spine and bracing the trunk protects the back and transfers force during lifts.

concepts.name: Warm-up routine
concepts.summary: Describe why a general warm-up and lighter ramp-up sets prepare the body before heavy work.

concepts.name: Gym safety essentials
concepts.summary: Understand how to use spotters, safety bars, collars and sensible loading to lift without injury.

concepts.name: Rest and sleep basics
concepts.summary: Understand that muscles recover and grow between sessions through rest, sleep and adequate food, not during the workout itself.

misconceptions.text: Lifting weights makes you bulky quickly, especially for women.
Muscle grows during the workout itself rather than during recovery afterwards.
Lifting with a rounded back is fine as long as the weight feels manageable.

concepts.name: Technique for each core lift
concepts.summary: Perform the squat, hip hinge, press and row with correct bar path, joint positions and depth using light to moderate loads.

concepts.name: Progressive overload
concepts.summary: Apply small, regular increases in weight, reps or sets so that training stays challenging as the body adapts.

concepts.name: Rep ranges and goals
concepts.summary: Explain how lower rep ranges favour maximal strength while moderate ranges suit muscle size, and choose a range for a goal.

concepts.name: Effort and proximity to failure
concepts.summary: Use reps in reserve or perceived exertion to judge how hard a set is and stop short of form breakdown.

concepts.name: Basic weekly split
concepts.summary: Arrange a simple full-body or upper/lower weekly schedule that trains each muscle group about twice a week.

concepts.name: Training log keeping
concepts.summary: Record exercises, loads, reps and effort each session and use the record to choose the next workout.

concepts.name: Protein and energy intake
concepts.summary: Explain that adequate protein and enough total calories support muscle gain and recovery.

misconceptions.text: Adding weight every session is the only way to progress, regardless of form.
Light weights for high reps will tone muscle while heavy weights only build bulk.
Every set must go to complete failure to be effective.

concepts.name: Weekly volume management
concepts.summary: Plan and adjust the number of hard sets per muscle group each week to fall between productive minimum and recoverable maximum.

concepts.name: Exercise selection and balance
concepts.summary: Choose main lifts and accessories that cover all movement patterns and balance pushing, pulling and leg work for a given goal.

concepts.name: Periodised programme structure
concepts.summary: Organise training into blocks with planned changes in volume and intensity, including a scheduled easier week.

concepts.name: Plateau diagnosis
concepts.summary: Analyse a stall by examining recovery, nutrition, volume, technique and programming to find the likely cause.

concepts.name: Fatigue and deloads
concepts.summary: Recognise accumulated fatigue from performance, sleep and joint signs and decide when to reduce load or volume.

concepts.name: Injury versus soreness
concepts.summary: Distinguish normal muscle soreness from pain signalling injury and adapt exercises to train around a problem.

concepts.name: Range of motion and tempo
concepts.summary: Control tempo and use full, controlled ranges of motion to deliver tension to the target muscle.

misconceptions.text: More volume is always better, so adding sets endlessly speeds up growth.
Muscle soreness is a reliable measure of how effective a workout was.
Changing exercises every session keeps muscles guessing and is needed for progress.

concepts.name: Autoregulated load selection
concepts.summary: Adjust daily loads and sets from readiness and effort ratings instead of fixed percentages alone.

concepts.name: Individualising programme variables
concepts.summary: Evaluate how a lifter's training age, recovery capacity, schedule and response should shape frequency, volume and intensity.

concepts.name: Biomechanics and leverages
concepts.summary: Analyse how body proportions affect lift mechanics and adjust stance, grip and bar position to suit them.

concepts.name: Periodisation model comparison
concepts.summary: Compare linear, undulating and block models and judge which suits a given goal, level and timeline.

concepts.name: Specificity and peaking
concepts.summary: Evaluate how to bias training toward specific lifts and taper fatigue to express maximal strength on a target date.

concepts.name: Weak point analysis
concepts.summary: Identify the phase or muscle limiting a lift and select targeted variations or accessories to address it.

concepts.name: Evidence quality appraisal
concepts.summary: Judge fitness claims and studies by sample, design and practical relevance before changing a programme.

misconceptions.text: There is one optimal programme or technique that works identically for every lifter.
Autoregulation means training only when you feel like it and skipping hard work.
Findings from studies on untrained participants apply directly to advanced lifters.

concepts.name: Designing multi-year training plans
concepts.summary: Create long-range plans that sequence phases of building, specialisation and maintenance across years and changing life circumstances.

concepts.name: Fatigue management models
concepts.summary: Evaluate fatigue models and their limits to optimise the stimulus relative to recovery cost.

concepts.name: Coaching and technique correction
concepts.summary: Design cueing and progression strategies that diagnose and fix faults for lifters of differing abilities.

concepts.name: Custom programme design for populations
concepts.summary: Create safe, effective programmes for older adults, rehabilitating lifters, or those with limited equipment or time.

concepts.name: Critique of training systems
concepts.summary: Evaluate popular training systems against principles and evidence to find their strengths, weaknesses and appropriate users.

concepts.name: Integrating nutrition and recovery
concepts.summary: Synthesise training with energy balance phases, sleep and stress management to meet strength and physique targets.

concepts.name: Data-driven programme refinement
concepts.summary: Judge training data trends to decide when to change a plan, separating noise from true progress.

misconceptions.text: Advanced lifters should simply do the same methods as beginners with heavier weights.
A popular programme that worked for a champion will work for any client.
Every dip in performance means the programme has failed and must be changed.
